articles.title: De la multitarea a los emuladores: lo que no sabías que tu iPhone Duo puede hacer
articles.text:
El iPhone Duo ya es una realidad, y con su llegada Apple se suma de forma oficial a la categoría de los teléfonos con pantalla plegable. Más allá del panel flexible y de las funciones multitarea que acaparan los titulares, el terminal esconde una serie de herramientas poco conocidas que inciden directamente en la productividad, la privacidad y el entretenimiento del usuario.
De la posibilidad de abrir aplicaciones en pareja con un solo gesto hasta la opción de convertir el dispositivo en una consola portátil para emuladores, el recorrido por estas funciones demuestra que el plegable de Apple ofrece mucho más de lo que aparenta a simple vista.
Multitarea avanzada y gestión de aplicaciones en el iPhone Duo
La pantalla dividida es, sin duda, una de las bazas más comentadas del iPhone Duo. Sin embargo, existe una capa adicional que suele pasar desapercibida: el sistema permite crear parejas de aplicaciones para abrirlas juntas con un único gesto, en combinaciones como Safari y Notas o Mensajes y Fotos.
A esto se suma la posibilidad de reorganizar la posición de las ventanas de forma rápida mediante gestos, lo que agiliza el flujo de trabajo cuando se manejan varias tareas a la vez.
El terminal también ofrece soluciones para las aplicaciones que todavía no están optimizadas para pantallas plegables. Aunque cada vez más desarrolladores adaptan sus apps a este formato, algunas siguen mostrando franjas negras o distribuciones que no aprovechan el espacio disponible.
Para corregir esto, el iPhone Duo incluye ajustes de visualización que permiten que muchas aplicaciones saquen mejor partido a la pantalla, incluso sin que exista una optimización específica por parte de quienes las desarrollan.
La escritura en el dispositivo también se adapta al contexto de uso. El usuario puede elegir entre un teclado dividido, pensado para escribir con ambos pulgares, o uno a pantalla completa que recuerda a la experiencia de un portátil. La distribución dividida resulta más práctica para mensajes rápidos, mientras que la versión ampliada ofrece mayor superficie para correos electrónicos o textos largos.
Privacidad y accesibilidad: los ajustes menos visibles del plegable de Apple
En materia de privacidad, Apple ha incorporado un sistema que, con el terminal cerrado, limita de forma automática la visibilidad de la información que aparece en pantalla. Esta función resulta de utilidad en situaciones cotidianas como el uso del móvil en el transporte público, en cafeterías o en cualquier lugar donde otras personas puedan ver información sensible.
A esto se suma una opción pensada para facilitar el acceso con una sola mano. En lugar de deslizar desde la esquina superior derecha, el iPhone Duo permite abrir el Centro de Control pulsando directamente el grupo de iconos de batería, wifi y cobertura móvil situado en la barra de estado.
Esta alternativa simplifica el manejo del dispositivo, en especial cuando está plegado y la anchura dificulta alcanzar determinadas zonas de la pantalla.
Fotografía y videollamadas con el diseño plegable del iPhone Duo
El formato plegable del iPhone Duo también influye en el terreno fotográfico. El Modo de vista previa dual permite mostrar, de forma simultánea, la imagen captada por las cámaras delanteras y traseras, de manera que todas las personas que aparecen en la fotografía pueden comprobar el encuadre antes de disparar. El dispositivo, además, incluye animaciones pensadas para captar la atención de los niños durante este proceso.
El diseño con bisagra no se limita a ofrecer una pantalla de mayor tamaño. Cuando el terminal permanece parcialmente abierto, puede funcionar como reloj de mesilla, como soporte para videollamadas o como pantalla multimedia cuando se usa en modo manos libres.
Estas funciones aprovechan tanto la inclusión de la bisagra como la flexibilidad de uso que ofrece el dispositivo, y son, precisamente, las que diferencian al iPhone Duo del resto de la gama de iPhone.
Emuladores y videojuegos retro en el iPhone Duo
Para los aficionados a los videojuegos, el iPhone Duo ofrece una compatibilidad notable con emuladores. Su pantalla interna, de mayor tamaño, permite distribuir los controles virtuales en una mitad del panel y reservar la otra mitad para el juego, lo que se traduce en una experiencia cercana a la de las consolas portátiles clásicas.
Esta característica resulta especialmente atractiva para quienes disfrutan de títulos retro, ya que el plegable de Apple da un paso adicional frente a otros smartphones a la hora de emular consolas antiguas.

articles.title: TeamGroup warns the memory shortage has not reached its peak yet
articles.text:
Facepalm: Major memory manufacturers have repeatedly warned shareholders that the memory industry faces many more years of chaos and high prices. Now even smaller players such as TeamGroup are sounding the same alarm, saying conditions will soon turn brutal for both pricing and availability.
TeamGroup recently shared financial results for its latest quarter. Beyond the soaring figures and shifting market trends, the report highlights the worrisome direction the entire chip industry is heading toward. As it turns out, the worst of the memory shortage is still to come.
According to TeamGroup CEO Chen Ching-wen, prices will keep climbing for many months. The IT industry will endure its worst chip shortage from the final quarter of 2026 through the end of the second quarter next year. For now, customers can still buy chip-based products by paying a premium. Before long, Chen said, people won't be able to buy anything even if they have money to spare.
TeamGroup is a Taiwanese manufacturer operating several brands of computer memory, memory cards, solid state drives, mobile accessories, and other chip-based industrial products. The company relies on the major memory chipmakers for its supply, and those supplies are drying up fast.
Chen said TeamGroup has been trading and signing long-term supply agreements with chipmakers for around 30 years, but nothing about today's market is "traditional" anymore. A "ferocious" price rally is underway, the company confirmed. The contract price of DDR5 16Gb chips was $8.70 in October 2025 and climbed to $48 by September 2026. DDR4 8Gb chips have surged as well, and the spot market is even worse, with a 30% to 50% premium to pay.
"We have contracts but can't get enough volume, so we have to go to the spot market and pay a premium to grab supply," Chen said.
Prices aren't the only disruption TeamGroup highlighted. The company now does most of its business in the B2B market, supplying memory to enterprise customers and industrial control applications. B2B revenue climbed from roughly 24% in the first three quarters of 2025 to 64% in the first three quarters of 2026, while B2C end-consumer revenue fell from 75% to 35% over the same period.
Chen explained that TeamGroup isn't unilaterally changing its strategic positioning, but simply adjusting to massive shifts in demand and customer needs. Most of the industry's DRAM output has now been absorbed by AI data centers and other enterprise-grade applications.
Of course, this AI-driven market upheaval has a silver lining for TeamGroup and other memory makers. In Q3 2026, the Taiwanese company's revenue grew 33% from the previous quarter to NT$10.139 billion (around $311.5 million). Operating profit rose 46.8% to NT$4.511 billion, while net profit after tax went up nearly 50% to NT$3.618 billion.

articles.title: Anatel aprova roaming obrigatório para rodovias e pequenas localidades • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Anatel aprova roaming obrigatório para rodovias e pequenas localidades
Rodovias terão cobertura ampliada até para clientes de operadoras que não atendem os trechos. Medida abrange regiões do interior.
A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações aprovou hoje (04/11), por unanimidade, regras que tornarão obrigatório o roaming para clientes de outras empresas em rodovias estaduais e federais, além de pequenos municípios com menos de 30 mil habitantes e localidades não-sede, mesmo em cidades maiores.
O roaming permite que o celular se conecte à rede de outra operadora quando está fora da área de cobertura da sua prestadora original. Nos pequenos municípios e nas localidades não-sede, como vilas no interior, a obrigação valerá apenas para áreas incluídas em compromissos de cobertura (como os previstos em leilões de espectro), ou que tenham recebido financiamento federal para a instalação da infraestrutura.
Nas rodovias estaduais e federais, a exigência é universal, exceto nos trechos situados em áreas urbanas das sedes de municípios com mais de 30 mil habitantes.
As novas regras também preveem que o atendimento em roaming nestas localidades ocorra automaticamente e seguindo as condições do plano contratado pelo cliente, portanto, sem custo adicional.
As operadoras terão prazos entre 90 e 210 dias para implantação: as cidades de até 30 mil habitantes devem ser atendidas em 90 dias, as localidades não-sede terão 150 dias e as rodovias terão 210 dias. Some pelo menos mais 30 dias a esses prazos, já que a resolução ainda precisa ser publicada no Diário Oficial da União e sua vigência começa depois desse intervalo. As empresas também precisam assinar ou modificar seus acordos de roaming existentes para incluir as novidades.
As empresas podem pedir exceções em casos que seja inviável, mas a Anatel precisará aprovar tais casos. “Não são hipóteses de dispensa motivações de ordem puramente econômica, financeira, conveniência operacional ou dificuldades de negociação contratual entre prestadoras envolvidas”, afirmou a conselheira substituta Suzana Rodrigues, relatora da matéria, em declaração publicada pelo site especializado Telesíntese.
Liberar roaming para clientes de outras operadoras em localidades menores e rodovias é desejo antigo da agência reguladora: a Tomada de Subsídio nº 25, que tratou do assunto, aconteceu ainda em 2024 e diversos leilões de espectro feitos pela Anatel incluíram obrigações de cobertura do tipo desde 2007, quando o espectro para o 3G foi licitado.
A medida aprovada hoje deve finalmente encerrar a questão e garantir o uso da telefonia móvel em rodovias e localidades menores para clientes de prestadoras que não as cobrem, e deve aumentar a segurança em rodovias, já que permitirá contato de serviços de emergência e o uso de rastreadores de veículos e carga com menos empecilhos.

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake adds remarkable depth to the Hero of Time’s Hyrule in the subtlest of changes — and it’s a near-perfect retelling of Link and Zelda’s most beloved adventure
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Bathed in rays of golden sunlight and brimming with life, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time gorgeously reimagines the original game while retaining all that made it so beloved. There’s so much more to it than its beautiful audio-visual overhaul, though: from shrewdly redesigned locations and enemies to new features that add depth to the world of Hyrule. It’s a thoroughly well-thought-out retelling of one of the most loved video games of all time.
Reasons to buy
- + A feast for the eyes and ears with refreshed music and design
- + Thoughtfully redesigned puzzles, dungeons, and enemies
- + New features are light-touch, but well-calculated
- + Quality of life additions remove most, if not all, frustrations from the original
- + Cleaner translations, added cutscenes and dialogue take narrative to new heights
Reasons to avoid
- - Perhaps lacking a little ambition — and some difficulty
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Nintendo’s decision to remake The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 in celebration of the franchise's 40th anniversary was hotly anticipated, if not a little anxiety-inducing. Like legions of fans, I share fond memories of inventive puzzles that turned hardware limitations into creative opportunities, revolutionary mechanics that defined 3D action-adventure for years to come, and, of course, one of the most beautiful and well-written storylines in the video game hall of fame.
Platform reviewed: Nintendo Switch 2
Available on: Nintendo Switch 2 
Release date: November 5, 2026
28 years on from the release of the original Ocarina of Time, a lot has changed in the world of gaming. Hardware limitations, even on the Switch 2, are far fewer than ever before, and there’s a game for everyone.
So in a world that now includes everything from niche interests in PowerWash Simulator to AAA giants like GTA 6 to Fortnite’s bizarre multiverse of pop stars and anime icons, can a remake of a decades-old game that now feels relatively simplistic find its footing, or even be one of the best Nintendo Switch 2 games going?
Do you see that man with the evil eyes?
It’s natural that the phrase ‘don’t mess with perfection’ springs to mind when thinking about Metacritic’s best-ever-scoring video game, but a remake without meaningful changes is always going to feel like a nostalgia-baiting cash grab.
Flying in the face of that narrative, Ocarina of Time’s remake proves classic Zelda still has a place in current gaming, bringing meaningful additions and alterations across the board from level design to voice acting and even some juicy new lore while still staying faithful to the source material.
All areas of Hyrule have been revisited and retouched, with few drastic changes but plenty of improvements. A rich tapestry of flora and fauna, thick fog swirling at Link’s feet, organic terrain, and detailed furnishings bring every location to life.
The storybook visual direction of the remake comes together beautifully with this new detailed world, making its own mark on the Zelda franchise. Its vivid style might not be to everyone’s taste, but it’s certainly immersive, as is the rich, re-orchestrated soundtrack.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Walking into Zora’s Domain post-Water Temple and seeing it restored to its original glory felt like such a full-circle moment, but my favorite interaction I don’t remember from the original game was approaching King Zora from the side repeatedly and being granted special ‘standing close to the King’ privileges.
It runs beautifully too, with its buttery-smooth locked 60fps and no visible lag in my experience. While loading screens are still in place these barely create any friction, controls are snappy and it’s bug-free barring one occasion where I noticed a texture glitch in a waterfall.
The world is more alive in more ways than one. I do miss the mad panic of racing to Hyrule Castle gates before night falls in the original, but thanks to the constant day-night cycles within towns, you now see a lot more of the lives of non-player characters (NPCs).
While still fairly two-dimensional, the supporting cast are full of character, especially so thanks to a new feature of the Mask of Truth you earn through the Happy Mask Salesman quest line. Now, when wearing the mask, you can find the hidden truths behind folks around Hyrule; the Dancing Couple dropped a bombshell I won’t spoil for you, but it adds whole new dimensions to some of the people Link encounters on his quest.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
You’re encouraged to explore the world and its secrets with new mechanics like Fairy Messages (which replace some of Navi’s hints and reward you with Rupees, Mana, or Hearts, generally) as well as old favorites like Golden Skulltulas and Fairy Fountains, but most of all I found myself frequently looking for viewpoints from which to take in the world just for the sake of it. Quite a lot of the collectibles, grottos, and boulders are in the same or very similar places, but if you don’t have a photographic memory from the original, there’s plenty of fun to be had in rediscovering Hyrule.
As I expected from my preview, some of the vocal performances did win me over by the end of the game, and Matt Mercer reprising his role as Ganondorf absolutely nailed it (of course). Others, unfortunately, missed the mark; Navi’s original sound bites were so iconic and plucky, but it’s a fairly flat performance here, by comparison.
Even then, every cutscene was a delight. I loved some of the extended dialogue and how it adds depth and personality to the world, with more beautiful cinematography than ever. I laughed, I cried, I paused and googled if some small line was a reference to a deep lore video I watched the other weekend; the narrative is richer than ever, and it celebrates the original game in all the right ways.
Can Hyrule's destiny really depend on such a lazy boy?!
Especially if you’ve played the original any time recently, there’s an immediate sense of liberation when you load into Kokiri Forest for the first time; even having played the same area at a preview event several weeks before receiving my review code, I couldn’t resist the urge to jump, dash, and swing around the camera like a lunatic in celebration of unhindered freedom to move.
Combat also feels more fluid and fun. While there’s still a fair amount of waiting around for an opening, gone are Link’s sluggish movements, painstaking in-menu item swapping, and cumbersome crowd control. I love small details like how the camera focus shifts to blur the background when you target enemies, which also means other baddies politely waiting their turn to attack you don’t stick out as much.
Overall, it’s great; jumping and dodging around, quickly switching between weapons with the right trigger, and aiming projectiles with the gyroscope improve pacing massively.
That pacing improvement carries over to Temple design too, none more so than the dreaded Water Temple now that you can quick-equip Iron Boots with the D-pad. Some temples see more significant overhauls than others, but overall rooms and puzzles have been shrewdly redesigned, with a few new additions or expanded segments like in Hyrule Castle’s garden maze, which now also leads Link through the castle kitchens.
It’s often in the smallest adjustments that Ocarina of Time’s remake is at its best; for instance, changes to the environment around you in combat that make more narrative or gameplay sense. Some are subtle; I noticed one room in the Fire Temple especially with more dynamic platform design for Lizalfos to hop around, and in locations like the Forest Temple where new obstacles like acid pits replace empty pits in the floor.
I didn’t clock any fundamental changes to enemies, but the scale and range have been adapted for enemies like Iron Knuckles as well as some bosses like Volvagia. This, paired with tweaks to the attack strings, a few new moves, and some with higher stakes, ensures Link’s lighter feet are still challenged in combat.
When you fight the real me, it won't be so easy!
That being said, I wouldn’t say difficulty is the Ocarina of Time remake’s strength. I’ll caveat heavily with the reminder that this game is as much for kids as it is for us aging nostalgia-chasers, but given I only ran out of health a handful of times, mostly by making silly mistakes or getting distracted, it does feel like Ocarina of Time has moved one step closer to being nerfed.
It’s a similar story with items — I didn’t have to refill any supplies more than three, maybe four times in my entire save. A new item in the game, the Business Deku Seed, summons a shopkeeper with his stock of supplies, including potions. It’s one of the only new features I find to be a bit of a headscratcher, making the game easier still.
Add to that the golden webs that hint at the location of overworld Golden Skulltulas, more obvious traps and visual cues for important locations, doors, and boulders, and there were few times I was particularly mentally challenged, either.
Having rolled credits, I was therefore doubly disappointed to learn Master Quest isn’t offered to up the ante a little. I’m hoping this comes at a later date, and I’m really hoping it’s not DLC, because with a little more challenge, my only real complaint about the game would be quickly remedied.
It’s not enough to score the game down; it’s ticking all of the obligatory boxes for a good remake, and I loved every second of it. Still, I can’t help but feel just a tinge of disappointment that most changes to the game are limited to optimisations and err on the side of “safe”. The original Ocarina of Time was great, in part, for how it took the limitations of contemporary game design and created some of its best mechanics to work around them in a creative way; without that challenge, the remake at times feels just a little unremarkable.
Still, this one niggle didn’t impact my personal enjoyment of the game nor negate the many, many strengths it brings to the table, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake feels like exactly the game that the developers would have made in the late 90s were it possible on contemporary hardware.
From the first time I played the game at my dad’s knee, I fell in love with the world of Hyrule, and it was just as impactful for me in its third iteration as it was in its first. Whether you’re an adult or a child, when you boot up the remake, it’s not a game you’ll forget in a hurry.
Should you play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake?
Play it if...
You’re a big fan of the original
At its core, this is a faithful and loving remake of the original Ocarina of Time, and as such, a vast majority of Zelda fans will appreciate the efforts to reinvigorate the game for Zelda’s 40th Anniversary.
You’ve never played a classic Zelda game
A lot of newer fans to the series may have only played the more recent open-world titles or dabbled in ports of older games; this remake offers new fans the chance to experience a huge part of The Legend of Zelda’s history without sacrificing the comforts of modern gaming.
You love games with a story
One of Ocarina of Time’s strengths has always been in the beautiful story it weaves, and it’s never stronger than in the remake. With tighter translations, expanded dialogue and new cutscenes, it keeps the heart of what made the original great but adds plenty.
You love puzzle games
Ocarina of Time has some great head scratchers and inventive mechanics, and keeps adding new solutions into the mix right up until the endgame.
Don't play it if...
You want a challenge
Zelda games are never incredibly difficult beyond some of the puzzle mechanics, but Ocarina of Time’s remake feels fun-for-all-ages. That’s no bad thing; I first enjoyed the game as a pre-schooler, but you might want to manage expectations as an adult.
Accessibility features
Within the game’s settings, you can change the camera controls, speed, toggle motion-control aiming, and choose between one-click or press-and-hold targeting.
You can swap the jump controls, use one-handed ocarina-playing controls, toggle subtitles, and add speaker-name display. Accessibility is, as I’ve come to expect from Nintendo, a weak point, but there are a few more customization options here than I’ve seen in other titles.
How I reviewed The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake
I’ve completed the main storyline in my 25-hour save, as well as a vast majority of side quests and secret content. I played mostly docked to enjoy the sprawling scenery, but I did try handheld too, comparing my overall experience with the original as well as more modern action-adventure games, including Zelda titles like the original Ocarina of Time and modern entries like Tears of the Kingdom, as well as titles like Outer Wilds, Tunic, and more.
I played on the standard Nintendo Switch 2, listening to the gorgeously re-orchestrated soundtrack through my Corsair Void Max Wireless v2 headset and through the Switch 2’s speakers.
More generally, I’ve covered a huge array of games here at TechRadar, where I serve as Head of Video and previously as Managing Editor. I’ve reviewed a number of action-adventure and Switch 2 titles.
First reviewed November 2026
Josephine Watson is TechRadar's Head of Video, and an award-winning (PPA 30 under 30 2024), NCTJ-trained journalist. Having previously written on a variety of topics from pop culture to gaming and even the energy industry, she joined TechRadar to support general site management in 2021. Now, Josephine heads up TechRadar's social and video team and strategy. Generally, you'll find her fiddling with her smart home setup, watching Disney movies, playing on her Switch, or rewatching the extended edition of Lord of the Rings... again.

articles.title: HP Inc. Appoints Emma Walmsley as Chief Executive Officer
articles.text:
Wednesday, November 4th 2026
HP Inc. Appoints Emma Walmsley as Chief Executive Officer
HP Inc. (NYSE: HPQ) today announced that its Board of Directors has unanimously appointed Emma Walmsley as Chief Executive Officer, effective January 4, 2027. Ms. Walmsley most recently served as Chief Executive Officer of GSK and has been a member of Microsoft's Board of Directors for seven years. She will succeed Bruce Broussard, who has served as Interim Chief Executive Officer since February 2026. Broussard will become Chair of the Board effective January 4, 2027, succeeding Chip Bergh.
Bruce Broussard, Interim Chief Executive Officer"HP has tremendous potential at an important inflection point in technology, and we need a leader who can build on our innovation heritage and strengths to boldly shape the company's future. Emma is a proven CEO with a track record of leading organizations at scale and guiding them through significant change. She has the experience and skills to bring HP's businesses, capabilities and people together to capture the opportunities ahead as AI moves to the edge, transforming how we work and live in a more connected world. I look forward to supporting her as she leads HP into its next phase of growth".
"HP is an iconic company with a defining role in shaping the future of work on a global scale. I'm excited to join the team and, together, move forward with clarity and conviction. We will focus on harnessing the power of the AI era and putting HP's creativity and innovation to work to unlock new sources of growth and deliver lasting value for our customers, shareholders, partners and people," said Emma Walmsley.
Chip Bergh, Chair of the Board"Today's appointment follows a comprehensive global search focused on what HP needs to win in its next chapter. Throughout the process, Emma stood out for the strength of her leadership experience across multiple industries, the clarity of her strategic thinking and her ability to translate customer insights into new growth. She has a people-first leadership approach that aligns and inspires high-performing teams around clear priorities, strong execution and lasting value creation".
"I also want to thank Bruce for his strong leadership, which has enabled the Board to conduct an intentional and rigorous search leading to today's successful outcome. It's a privilege to hand the role of Chair to him, knowing he will provide important continuity and valuable guidance to Emma and the Board during the transition and in the years ahead," said Bergh.
Ms. Walmsley is the former Chief Executive Officer of GSK, where she served from April 2017 through December 2025. During her nearly nine years as CEO, she led a significant transformation of the global biopharmaceutical company and delivered a step-change in its operating performance. She sharpened the company's strategic focus on specialty medicines and vaccines, reinvigorated its R&D pipeline and strengthened the balance sheet following the successful separation of its consumer healthcare business, while enhancing GSK's leadership bench and succession pipeline. Ms. Walmsley joined GSK in 2010 and became CEO of GSK Consumer Healthcare in 2015 before being appointed Group CEO. Earlier, she spent 17 years at L'Oréal building and leading major global consumer businesses.
Bergh has served as Chair of HP's Board since 2017 and as a director since 2015 and will continue as Chair until Broussard assumes the role on January 4, 2027.
"Chip has provided strong leadership as Chair for the past nine years, helping guide HP through significant change while maintaining a sharp focus on governance, capital allocation and value creation," said Broussard. "I have appreciated his partnership while serving as Interim CEO."

articles.title: PHP vulnerability post-mortem reveals bug was known two years ago — Small team of maintainers knew of the issue before it was made public, as new PHP2Shell chained exploit ravages servers
articles.text:
PHP vulnerability post-mortem reveals bug was known two years ago — Small team of maintainers knew of the issue before it was made public, as new PHP2Shell chained exploit ravages servers
Long-standing technological debt is being charged with interest.
The phrase "when it rains, it pours" applies both to weather and computer security, as proven the week of October 19, 2026, when OpenAI's GPT 5.6-Sol discovered critical vulnerabilities in the open-source programming language PHP. As published in a post-mortem, a small team of maintainers knew of the issue two years ago. Security experts had warned for decades about mounting technical debt, as agentic AI exponentially sped up vulnerability scanning, to the point that the usual 90-day disclosure window for security exploits became pointless. PHP, one of the internet's ubiquitous software packages, was unlucky enough to in the crosshairs of bug-hunting AI agents.
PHP hosts around 70% of websites on the internet, and the vulnerability allows for remote code execution with enough attacker knowledge. That combination is enough to sound alarms, but the situation got worse once the collective internet realized that, at the time, 73% of PHP installations online were running end-of-life versions with no active support — eliciting face-palms from many techies, and an exasperated sigh from anyone familiar with the ecosystem, myself included. So ultimately the problem wasn't really the vulnerability, but the general complacency.
How the attack came to be
The root cause of the vulnerability was an ancient architectural decision in the PHP engine's error handling. When a PHP process runs out of memory, it'll call the longjmp() C function, which means "immediately jump the execution to another place, no questions asked." Using longjmp() without a very good reason is generally unadvisable, though that by itself wasn't the problem.
The real issue is that if that jump happens while building a data structure (like adding an array entry, or initializing an object), that half-baked data remains in the memory heap. When the PHP engine moves execution to its cleanup-end-exit mechanism, that code will execute expecting good, complete data, but instead acts on inconsistent leftover bytes.
With some clever injection of just the right content in a web request, this mechanism can be exploited to run any code with PHP's permissions, as shown by the ongoing PHP2Shell exploit.
Gaining a remote shell does require an attacker to know the exact version and build of PHP used, so it's not as trivial as just pressing the "Hack" button. Yet the wide blast radius, with tens of millions of vulnerable servers, many of them running the same exact version, is enough to give anyone pause. After the vulnerability was made public, many sysadmins disabled version number reporting on their PHP installation, so as not to aid prospective hackers.
The PHP Foundation's post-mortem indicates that the team had known about the issue for two years, but didn't immediately see it as a cause for concern, and went back and forth several times on the best way to fix the problem while maintaining compatibility with third-party extensions.
The team admitted it had made management mistakes, but it's a small outfit with one full-time employee and 14 part-time contractors, tasked with maintaining one of the most widespread pieces of software on the internet. This is a common pattern: open-source software that's of critical importance to modern computing, yet undermanned, underfunded, or both.
The exploit is only half of the problem
The standard patch process is reasonably trivial, needing only a point update and perhaps requiring a restart of some services. The currently maintained branches of PHP are 8.1 through the current 8.5. Sysadmins rarely install PHP directly, though, relying on their Linux distribution of choice or community repositories for updated packages.
Those 73% of sites still stuck with PHP 7 are now stuck between a rock and a hard place. When PHP moved from 7.4 to 8.0 in late 2020, there were a number of changes to the language, most of them minor, but still requiring revision work. Many folks likely expected their distro to keep backporting fixes, especially for LTS (Long-Term Support) variants still in their support period, with PHP 7.4 in tow. That excuse is arguably always a little thin, as even before the AI age there were already automated tools to upgrade existing PHP code with relatively little work.
Now, depending on their specific situation, those relying on ancient versions like 7.3 or older may be forced to bring their websites' code up to speed, given that not all distros are bound to have backported fixes. For reference, PHP 7.3 came out in 2018. Making matters worse, nearly 8% of PHP installations are of version 5.x, which came out in 2005. Plus, a number of network appliances, NAS boxes, and similar hardware carries PHP within, and that too will need updating. Palo Alto Networks issued an advisory for products powered by its PanOS system, for example.
It's not all doom and gloom, however. Since the PHP Foundation published source code patches for 7.4 up to 8.1, most anyone can devise a patch for the older versions. Many entities did so, and there are packages available for Debian/Ubuntu flavors from Ondřej Surý (Debian developer) covering PHP 5.6 to 8.1. CloudLinux and AlmaLinux have likewise produced backported fixes.
This is one occasion where paying for extended support comes in handy, as commercial vendors like Ubuntu Pro and Zend released packages for positively ancient PHP versions, down to 5.5. Old website code is likely to have vulnerabilities other than the PHP engine, so a wholesale update-and-upgrade is much preferable, but very few CTOs will ever listen to that song.
Other options
Given how broad the problem is, and how it'll be a while before every machine is protected, there are a number of other means to mitigate the issue — though the proper fix is to update to a patched PHP version. Web application firewalls (WAFs) like Immunify360 may block malicious requests from even getting to the server in the first place.
Content delivery networks (CDNs) like Cloudflare or Fastly universally offer options for adding a WAF to their setup. Both firms immediately issued their respective notices and added detection of PHP2Shell to their respective rulesets. Finally, server-level security suites like CrowdStrike can also detect and block malicious activity by the PHP binary itself, in case an attacker tries something funny. It's reasonable to guess that these protections have slowed exploitation efforts.
So where are we?
Right now, the PHP2Shell exploit is doing the rounds, with at least one high-profile case involving a campaign that chained the PHP vulnerability together with Fragnesia (aka Dirty Frag) to eventually get kernel-level access to 25 servers seemingly linked to the U.S. government. As of October 29, security firm BitSight had recorded copious attempts of PHP2Shell intrusion across its monitoring fleet, from many distinct origins.
BitSight's dark web forum sleuths indicate that there was no one-size-fits-all exploit package available at that date. This may indicate that hacking campaigns for now are likely to be specifically targeted, but a proverbial one-click red button is bound to appear at some point, likely with a deeper exploit in tow, as with the Fragnesia example above.
Meanwhile, several cybersecurity firms kept a close eye on patching progress since the October 19 reveal. Censys has a real-time view, updated hourly, and suffice it to say that things could be going a lot better. The initial count estimated the number of vulnerable PHP installs at around 45.7 million, out of 119 million total.
The number of unpatched services has mercifully dropped to around 29 million as of this writing, seemingly indicating a patch rate of around 1 million per day, depending on how you count. It's worth noting that fix backports may not change the version number, so those instances could still count as unpatched.
But remember how most everyone toggled off their server's PHP version number reporting. According to Censys, 62% of PHP servers it's consulting aren't reporting that datum at all, so there's no telling what the actual totals might be. If history is any indication, a significant percentage of those machines remain unpatched today.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Titan OS raises $46 million to expand its smart TV OS internationally | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Barcelona-based smart TV operating system maker Titan OS has raised $46 million in new funding, consisting of both equity and debt, the company announced on Wednesday.
The money comes from debt facilities provided by funds and accounts managed by BlackRock, along with existing investors like Highland Europe and Mangrove Capital Partners. The startup, which secured $58 million last year, has now raised $110 million in total. The company said that it could have chosen not to raise money and grow slowly, but it wants to be more ambitious to create more partnerships and expand into more geographies.
Titan OS’s promise to TV makers is that it offers better value from their unit sales by loading an operating system where they can generate money through partnerships with FAST channels (free ad-supported television) and ads on different screens.
The company now serves 30 million users, up from 18 million last year. This includes being a sales partner for TiVo in some regions, along with Tubi in the U.K.
Compared with last year, the startup has also added Sharp, AOC, Vestel, and Skyworth as partners. Its partnership with Philips has been a success, as the Dutch electronics maker has switched to Titan OS and ditched Google TV for its 2026 models.
The extended coverage means that it has a bigger advertiser footprint and better audience engagement metrics to offer to marketers.
“Our bread and butter is the monetization of our inventory on our own network. But the point is that we’re going beyond that. That’s why our reach has increased significantly, which then triggers the flywheel effect by also attracting more sales partners and more agencies that want to spend on our platform, whether it’s owned and operated or via our extensions,” Hyoung-Ung Kim, the company’s newly appointed CFO, told TechCrunch over a call.
In the last year, the company has increased its headcount to 250 people, and also opened an office in London to concentrate on advertising. It already has offices in Barcelona, Amsterdam, and Taipei.
With the new money coming in, the company wants to focus on a few areas. First is content discovery. It still takes everyone a long time to find something to watch. For that, it is using interface tweaks and AI to boost discovery, alongside partnering with more content providers like FAST channels.
“What differentiates us here from the walled gardens is that we do not have our own content offering. Like Google is trying to channel people to YouTube. We do not have that, and we are impartial in our role in content discovery. We are working and trying to reduce time spent searching,” Tobias Pfalzgraff, SVP of people and marketing at Titan OS, said.
Pfalzgraff also emphasized that the company is using AI to improve its ad recommendation and segmentation. While the company is dominant in Europe, it thinks that there are only a few manufacturers creating their own operating systems; more set makers would like to adopt its operating system, just like Philips did. The company also said that with increasing costs of hardware due to AI, manufacturers are thinking about long-term revenue generation opportunities as gadget sales slow down.
“The TV hardware industry is not a very profitable business. That’s why they are so reliant on partners like Titan OS that share revenue after the sale of the TV. But now, of course, the chip sets, the chip prices are increasing more and more. Right. With the AI boom, they have basically doubled down on our partnership,” Kim said.

articles.title: How Godzilla Minus Zero takes VFX and sound to the next level
articles.text:
Godzilla Minus One took the world by storm in 2023.
Quite masterfully, writer-director Takashi Yamazaki’s kaiju epic mixed incredible visual effects (VFX) with a powerful story of traumatized former kamikazee pilot Kōichi Shikishima trying to rebuild his life, creating a truly unforgettable blockbuster.
The fact that this was all achieved with a reported budget of less than US$15 million was all the more impressive — so much so, in fact, that it even took home the Oscar for Best Visual Effects, the first non-English-language movie to win in this category.
Now, Yamazaki and his team are back with Godzilla Minus Zero, a sequel that sees Kōichi, his family and their allies struggling to survive a war between Godzilla and King Ghidorah.
To learn more about this exciting follow-up, MobileSyrup sat down with members of the VFX and sound teams. Through translators, they gave some fascinating insight into just how much work goes into crafting the look and feel of a Godzilla film.
The VFX team
Godzilla Minus One is so beloved, in no small part, because of that incredible Oscar-winning VFX work from the team. Going into Minus Zero, how did you hope to expand upon what you had already achieved in that first film?
Takayuki Ueki (VFX supervisor): Godzilla Minus One was already quite tough in its own right, but going into Minus Zero, I think one of the biggest changes for the VFX team was the fact that there were two kaiju on screen. We’ve got Godzilla and King Ghidorah towards the end having a duel to the death, really, and we wanted to get that sense of scale to come across the screen, and that, of course, required a lot of man hours to properly execute. But the goal that we never lost sight of was creating an experience and something on screen that the fans are really going to enjoy. So in total, there were four animators who were working on that, three of whom were there from pre-vis to the end. And the scene I’m talking about is the Yahaza operation when they’re trying to trap Ghidorah and then pit him against Godzilla. So the team kind of saw the scene through from pre-vis all the way through final animation, and watching the scene kind of evolve, I think that’s really indicative of the tone we were trying to set for the entire Godzilla Minus Zero experience.
In Godzilla Minus One, the Warazumi operation was the climax of the film, where they’re out at sea trying to trap Godzilla, sink it, and bring it back to the surface, so that posed its own challenges to create all of that water and ocean and make it blend seamlessly with the effects. Something we wanted to attempt with Godzilla Minus Zero is really the human eye line, so putting kaiju and humans in the same space next to each other — not on a ship, on a battleship in the ocean. And we had to really sell this idea of this 300, 400 metres, over 1000 feet of space, because humans could be on the ground looking up and watching planes fly through, or looking up at the kaiju. So it required a lot more development and environment: the backgrounds — even down to the Ginza ruins. It required a lot more man-hours to render all of these backgrounds.
And that also extends to the dogfight, which there wasn’t much of in Godzilla Minus One. In the Narukami operation when they’re dropping the lightning rods, there was a huge sort of amount of screen time dedicated towards making sure the dogfights felt very authentic. So in order to do that and spin the camera around at all angles, we had to develop the entire city of Matsumoto in VFX, so that no matter where the camera was pointed, we would have some background. So the amount of VFX required between Minus One to Minus Zero, I would say, really exponentially increased when we read the screenplay. I think the whole team was thinking to themselves, “Oh my gosh, how are we going to achieve this?” So instead of creating backgrounds tailored to each individual shot, it’s almost as though the team created an entire city. So no matter where they wanted to place the camera, they would have some background coverage, and there was a lot of freedom to adjust that.
Tatsuji Nojima (visual effects artist and compositor): And there were, of course, challenges in the continuity. While there are two kaijus rampaging through a city, naturally from shot to shot, the city is not going to look the same. So we built this entire city, and then making sure, according to the shot, you’ve got fire and smoke in the right places, and all the different VFX that are happening. So, I would say the city probably took more computing power than some of the kaiju action in certain instances.
Minus Zero is the first Japanese production filmed for IMAX, which is really exciting. How did that larger ratio affect your approach to the VFX in Minus Zero?
Nojima: With IMAX and the increased screen aspect ratio, there are a lot of details that are on screen now that normally you wouldn’t see in a more traditional CinemaScope aspect ratio. So, of course, as the VFX team, we have to build out a lot more environments, especially on the ground, the debris, etc. So it, of course, increases the amount of work that we have to do. But everything from the ocean to the Narukami operation, I think it really gives it a different sense of scale because of the added room we have for shot compositions.
Ueki: And we spoke with the IMAX people, and they have sort of this general theory of how to create for IMAX, which is you take your traditional CinemaScope, aspect ratio, composition, and you expand above and beyond. So the top and bottom, you kind of expand whatever background or scenery or shot you want to do in IMAX. But with the kaiju film, if we had done that, if we see Godzilla in the middle of Ginza and we compose our shot and CinemaScope and expand at the top and bottom, it would make Godzilla feel very tiny relative to the screen itself. So in this case, we thought we had the chance to make these kaiju look absolutely amazing. We put aside IMAX theory and ignored that for a second, and instead focused on creating shock compositions for IMAX, and then afterwards, rearranging it for the CinemaScope aspect ratio.
And going back to the Ginza scene, if we mess up this, we would have so much sky or too much ground, and the balance would feel really off because of the IMAX screen ratio, so it was important that we were able to tilt the camera slightly differently for the IMAX version, so that we have just enough back sort of environment surroundings and debris in front, and just the right amount of sky above. But because of these sort of fine-tuning adjustments we had to make, it goes back to the previous question of why we had to build out this entire city so that we can place the camera differently according to our needs.
The sound team
One of the biggest reasons why Godzilla Minus One is so beloved is because of how well-made it is from a filmmaking perspective, especially as a blockbuster. Going into Minus Zero, how did you want to expand upon the sound design?
Hisafumi Takeuchi (production sound mixer and post-production sound mixer): Of course, you want to keep kaiju and Godzilla, the impact that these creatures have whenever they’re on screen, so that has been sustained between Godzilla Minus One and Godzilla Minus Zero. But what I paid extra attention to with Minus Zero is the human drama element of the story. So I really wanted to find and strike the right balance between how much impact we have versus how emotional, how much drama, we can get the audience to buy into.
And within that, we have dialogue, sound effects, and music — these three different levers to play with. And I really wanted the audience to feel the right distance to any scene, to anything that was happening on screen, so that it would feel as though what they’re seeing and hearing is happening in real life. So, how to sort of pull the audience into the screen was something I wanted to create with the sound design.
There have been so many kaiju movies over the years. As you were working on Minus Zero, how did you balance creating sounds for the likes of Godzilla and Ghidorah that feel authentic and pay tribute to that legacy of all those films, but also be distinct and have your own unique touch?
Natusko Inoue (sound designer and foley artist): With Godzilla, of course, but with King Ghidorah, especially, we could go in various directions, but we had to create sound from scratch, really. And what I felt was really important is to make sure we retain and inherit this soul that King Ghidorah has that has been sort of transpiring over several years. And I didn’t want to lose whatever that spirit of King Ghidorah is through the sound design. And the conclusion I arrived to, and sort of central theme that I have for King Ghidorah’s voice is this idea that King Ghidorah “sings fear,” so I wanted its cry to have an almost melodic tone to it and a harmony between three heads.
Springboarding off of that, I think a lot of us in the audience when we’re watching these movies probably take for granted what a kaiju film and blockbusters in general “should” sound like. But of course, a lot of work goes into it on your part to create those sounds. What would you say are some of the most challenging aspects of working on the sound design for a giant kaiju movie like Minus Zero?
Inoue: At first, I certainly felt a lot of that pressure, and I could see this sort of challenge that stood before us. And I think that there were moments where that worked, and moments where it kind of hindered the project having that added pressure. So what the sound team and I discussed was, “Let’s for a moment forget the fact that this is a sequel, forget the fact that it’s a mega-scale blockbuster type experience, and then just really look directly at the movie and just only focus on what the movie is supposed to do.” And I could feel there was a certain shift in the sound design team and process from that point onward. And I think it really improved the overall experience that we were able to kind of shed off the pressure of the sequel.
Takeuchi: After doing the first pass of sound design on the Narukami operation, where they’re trying to drop the lightning rods on Ghidorah, the sound felt very busy, very congested. It’s like we were in a traffic jam. So we were kind of at a loss of where to take this because it just didn’t feel quite right. So what we did next is we rewatched Godzilla Minus One, which was something that we also sound designed, as a reference point to kind of reset what our objective should be. And what I felt when watching Godzilla Minus One was that the sound was very authentic, very honest, very pure. It wasn’t sort of tainted or muddied by all this other pressure, extra added tension, I guess you could say.
And when working with the three levers I have to pull, dialogue, sound effects, and music, trying to push them all to the front equally, I think, was what got us in that trap and created that traffic jam. So the audience would be lost; they wouldn’t know what to listen to and what information to consume and process as part of this emotional experience. So, to find the right balance, at times I would pull back on the music and make the sound effects feel like they’re coming forward even more, or even subtract some volume in general and create more contrast between human drama scenes and the kaiju scenes.
So when you first see Godzilla roar, it’s supposed to have a ton of impact. And every moment Ghidorah is on screen, we wanted to make sure the audience felt its presence. And in doing so, we wanted to create a unique sonic experience, of course, while still paying a lot of respect to the history of Godzilla and the kaiju and what has brought this moment before us. But at the same time, I think it was important that we had our own interpretation of what “Godzilla-ness” means in this context and interpreting that into sound. And I really felt myself and the whole team, on behalf of them, that we succeeded in executing this. So there’s a huge emotional journey awaiting you.
Godzilla Minus Zero opens widely in theatres on November 6.
Image credit: Toho

articles.title: Apple veut fermer l'accès des mineurs aux applis de rencontre et aux compagnons IA
articles.text:
Apple veut verrouiller l’accès des mineurs aux applis de rencontre et aux compagnons IA romantiques. Elles seront désormais classées 18+ sur l’App Store. Une décision qui est tout sauf anodine.
Depuis plusieurs mois, la marque à la pomme renforce la protection des plus jeunes avec des outils de vérification d’âge plus poussés, qui bloquent déjà le téléchargement des applications 18+ dans plusieurs pays. En juin, elle a également présenté de nouvelles fonctions de contrôle parental. Elle va désormais plus loin, alors que la pression monte sur le secteur de l’intelligence artificielle (IA), sommé de mieux encadrer l’accès des mineurs à ses services.
Deux nouvelles questions destinées aux développeurs
En effet, dès le 16 novembre, les développeurs devront répondre à deux nouvelles questions dans App Store Connect, leur plateforme de gestion. Apple voudra d’abord savoir si l’application permet de partager sa position réelle avec d’autres personnes, puis si elle propose des rencontres ou des relations, y compris avec un compagnon virtuel capable d’échanges sexuels ou romantiques.
Concrètement, si une application répond à l’affirmative à cette deuxième question, elle recevra automatiquement un âge minimum de 18 ans. La plateforme disparaîtra alors de l’App Store des comptes d’enfants sous contrôle parental. Et si un mineur la repère malgré tout, il devra prouver sa majorité à la firme de Cupertino pour la télécharger.
À noter que les grandes applis de rencontre limitent déjà leur accès aux adultes, le vrai changement concerne surtout les compagnons IA, comme Replika ou Character AI.
Des jeunes déjà très exposés
Car c’est un fait, les compagnons IA occupent déjà une place importante dans la vie des jeunes. Aux États-Unis, 72 % des adolescents de 13 à 17 ans ont déjà utilisé un compagnon IA, et 52 % s’en servent au moins quelques fois par mois, d’après une étude de l’ONG Common Sense Media. 34 % d’entre eux ont déjà été mis mal à l’aise face à ses réponses.
Une tendance qui inquiète les professionnels. Dans un avis de santé publié en juin 2025, l’American Psychological Association explique que les adolescents peinent à distinguer l’empathie simulée d’un chatbot d’une véritable compréhension humaine. Ainsi, des psychologues observent des jeunes nouer des relations malsaines, voire dangereuses, avec des agents conversationnels.
Les conséquences peuvent être dramatiques : en 2024, un jeune de 14 ans a mis fin à ses jours après de longues conversations avec une IA de Character AI, son rôle étant directement impliqué dans l'affaire. Dans ce contexte, plusieurs enquêtes ont été ouvertes outre-Atlantique, et ciblent spécifiquement les éditeurs d’IA, particulièrement sur la manière dont ils mesurent l’impact de leurs technologies sur les jeunes utilisateurs.
De son côté, Apple n’a pas précisé ce que risquent les applications qui n’auront pas répondu à temps ; elles ont jusqu'au 12 janvier 2027 pour s’exécuter.

articles.title: BYD tente un record du monde de vitesse à 500 km/h, mais la voiture finit dans le mur
articles.text:
Rouler très vite est tout un art. À haute vitesse, les organes du véhicule sont mis à rude épreuve alors que le pilote doit faire preuve d’une concentration extrême pour filer droit. BYD le sait pertinemment après avoir décroché un record avec la Yangwang U9 Xtreme, qui avait atteint les 496 km/h en septembre 2025. Non contente de ce chiffre, la marque chinoise a décidé de remettre le couvert avec pour objectif de percer la barre des 500 km/h.
Et malgré une préparation que l’on suppose minutieuse, la dernière tentative de vitesse qui s’est tenue le 2 novembre dernier a débouché sur un accident pour le moins impressionnant. La supercar électrique de 3 018 ch a en effet dérapé avant de heurter une rambarde de sécurité sur un circuit en Chine. La collision a été particulièrement forte puisque l’auto s’est littéralement disloquée avant de partir en toupie.
Une supercar disloquée mais un miracle pour le pilote
Au premier contact avec la barrière, la voiture a immédiatement perdu ses parties avant et arrière. La zone centrale a néanmoins résisté avec brio, ce qui montre que la cellule de survie en fibre de carbone a parfaitement fait son travail malgré la violence du choc. Le pilote est ainsi sorti indemne de l’accident. Les dernières sources indiquent même qu’il a réussi à s’extraire lui-même de l’habitacle avant de se faire emmener aux urgences pour des examens.
Notons qu’aucun départ de feu n’a été signalé juste après l’accident. La batterie Blade 2.0 est donc restée parfaitement stable en évitant tout emballement thermique. On ignore cependant à ce jour ce qui a réellement causé le crash du véhicule. Le plus probable serait l’éclatement d’un pneu ayant entraîné la perte de contrôle de l’engin. Les investigations devraient activement se poursuivre.
En route vers Dubaï : BYD maintient-il son pari fou des 500 km/h ?
Il le faut, car Stella Li, la vice-présidente de BYD, a en effet confirmé que la Yangwang U9 Xtreme tentera de franchir les 500 km/h aux Émirats Arabes Unis en novembre. Hu Xiaoqing, directeur général des ventes chez Yangwang, a confirmé par la suite cette intention. Réitérer un accident similaire serait bien la pire chose qui soit pour la marque. À moins de vouloir créer à tout prix un bad buzz, ce qui marcherait du tonnerre…
Rappelons que la Yangwang U9 Xtreme possède quatre électromoteurs développant chacun 755 ch. Ce méchant quatuor est capable de tourner à un régime avoisinant les 30 000 tr/min, tandis que la plateforme 1 200 V permet des recharges ultra rapides. Ultra rapide est également le temps au tour du véhicule sur le Nürburgring, qui glisse sous les 7 minutes en s’établissant à 6:59.157.

articles.title: Stockal investors allege unauthorised sale of US stocks worth millions
articles.text:
Stockal investors allege unauthorised sale of US stocks worth millions
Nearly 30 Indian investors allege that their Stockal accounts were accessed without authorisation, leading to the sale of their US blue-chip holdings and purchases of a little-known stock that subsequently plunged nearly 60%.
Nearly 30 Indian investors who trade US shares through Stockal Securities have reported unauthorised access to their accounts, alleging that their blue-chip holdings, worth millions of dollars in total, were sold off without their consent and replaced with shares in a little-known company that subsequently lost almost 60% of its value.
According to the complaints, the proceeds from the forced sales were used to buy shares in Zhibao Technology Inc., which trades under the ticker ZBAO.
One affected investor, a senior official, saw stocks worth $335,768 sold and converted into 300,000 ZBAO shares at $1.05 apiece. The share price subsequently fell to $0.42, putting his losses at around Rs 4.26 crore.
The pattern has alarmed investors, who point out that coordinated buying across multiple accounts could inflate the price of a thinly traded stock, a tactic associated with so-called pump-and-dump schemes. However, the complaints do not establish who, if anyone, profited from the trades.
Stockal has said that the intruders used valid login credentials to access 26 accounts, attributing the breaches to phishing attacks that allegedly compromised customers' login details through deception. DriveWealth, the US brokerage partner that holds the accounts, has disputed this explanation and instead pointed to security weaknesses at Stockal.
The affected investors have lodged complaints with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and Bengaluru police. The disagreement between the two companies over the cause of the breaches has left investors uncertain about who is responsible for their losses.
The case also highlights risks for Indians investing in overseas markets through intermediary platforms. When a trade is made through an Indian app but settled by a US brokerage, questions can arise over the extent of investor protection, the division of responsibilities between the companies involved, and which regulator has jurisdiction to address grievances.

articles.title: Cyberattack disrupts blood storage refrigeration systems in France
articles.text:
France's national blood service has confirmed that a cyberattack targeting a refrigeration equipment provider raised temperature and defrost settings at three of its facilities, threatening stored blood products.
The French Blood Establishment (Établissement français du sang or EFS), which manages blood collection, processing, and distribution across France, said the incident occurred on November 2 and affected systems used to monitor and control cold-storage chambers.
According to a statement published on November 3, EFS was not directly targeted in the cyberattack, but was instead its refrigeration supplier.
While EFS has not named the affected supplier, European refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld Rentals confirmed in a statement that a cybersecurity incident involving remote monitoring software had affected a limited number of its refrigeration units.
Coolworld says the attackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party component, which was outside the company's direct control.
"The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control," the company said.
"Only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected, and Coolworld responded promptly and took appropriate measures."
The company said it is working with affected customers but will not comment on individual cases.
At EFS, the incident raised temperature and defrost thresholds in affected cold-storage chambers to extremely high levels.
These facilities store blood products before they are distributed to hospitals, as well as biological samples maintained by the EFS.
EFS says its monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the temperature change, allowing staff to fix impacted equipment or transfer products to other refrigeration facilities.
"No health impact has been identified, and no loss of blood products has been reported," EFS said in its statement [translated from French].
The organization confirmed that plasma bags intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines were either transferred or secured, preventing damage to the products.
Blood collection and distribution operations have continued without interruption.
EFS says its technical teams are working with France's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI) and the Ministry of Health, and it has strengthened monitoring of refrigeration equipment and temperatures.
The incident follows a wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems across Europe, where attackers remotely manipulate temperature settings or activate defrost functions that turn off cooling.
In October, cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration systems at an estimated 250 to 350 French supermarkets, including Intermarché, Carrefour Market, Monoprix, Leclerc, and Super U.
In those attacks, hackers reportedly compromised refrigeration controllers running older Danfoss software and remotely activated automatic defrosting functions, raising temperatures and forcing stores to discard fresh and frozen products.
These attacks targeted Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC and Copeland/Dixell XWEB refrigeration controllers, which are used to monitor and manage cooling equipment remotely.
A second wave of attacks occurred this month, affecting more than 115 stores across Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Estonia.
Some refrigeration systems were shut down entirely, while others had their temperature settings changed remotely.
At one Swedish supermarket, the system reportedly began generating heat, while another store reported that temperatures were changed to 50°C (122°F).
Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel previously said that attackers behind the November incidents exploited the same vulnerability used in October's attacks against French supermarkets.
In 2025, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) disclosed two vulnerabilities affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA controllers, tracked as CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2025-41451.
The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication and execute commands remotely on vulnerable systems, potentially giving them control over refrigeration equipment.
However, it has not been confirmed whether these vulnerabilities are being exploited in the attacks.

articles.title: L'IA de Google Photos va gérer votre galerie comme un vrai assistant personnel — Frandroid
articles.text:
Cela fait maintenant 2 ans que Google a dévoilé « Demander à Photos », une recherche dopée à l’IA Gemini directement dans l’application Google Photos. Pratique à l’usage, elle est cependant limitée à cette seule fonction : trouver les photos que vous cherchez à l’aide d’une requête que vous avez formulée en langage naturel.
Si vous voulez parler de retouches, de création d’albums ou d’organisation avec l’IA, ça se passe dans l’application Gemini après connexion avec Google Photos. Mais en fouillant dans la version 8.0 de Google Photos sur Android, nos confrères d’Android Authority ont découvert l’existence d’une mise à jour majeure voulant faire de « Demander à Photos » un véritable assistant en charge de votre galerie.
« Demander à Photos » bientôt capable d’accomplir des tâches complexes
En plus de chercher pour vous, l’option veut agir. Trois labels sont ainsi visibles dans le code de Google Photos v8.0 : « Demander », « Tâche » et « Automatisation ». Cela suggère la prise en charge de différents types de requêtes, en fonction de ce que l’IA devra mettre en œuvre pour les mener à bien.
Exemple de tâche : « Montre-moi deux photos de mon chien, améliore-les et ajoute-les à un nouvel album appelé « lucyyy » ». La requête combine donc recherche, retouche et classement. Voici le résultat en vidéo.
Comme vous avez pu le voir, Google Photos s’est chargé de tout en détaillant son travail et en demandant une validation de l’utilisateur à chaque étape. À la fin, l’IA prend l’initiative de proposer d’autres actions, ici partager l’album ou créer un collage. Tout se passe dans une seule fenêtre de conversation, comme avec Gemini.
    À lire aussi : 
L’onglet Collections de Google Photos se transforme (et devient enfin personnalisable)
« Demander à Photos » sera également capable d’afficher des actions contextuelles reprenant les fonctionnalités de Google Photos : créer un GIF, une photo cinématique, une animation, trouver des photos associées, etc. Ces boutons apparaissent quand vous téléversez une image ou une vidéo dans l’interface de l’IA. Cette dernière pourra aussi afficher des raccourcis vers les différentes sections de Google Photos (Collections, Favoris, Corbeille, Lieux…).
Toutes ces options pourraient prendre place dans une interface qui s’afficherait en bas de l’application Google Photos, dans le style de ce que fait Gemini sur Android. L’occasion d’utiliser des requêtes proposées par l’IA, qu’elles soient générales ou contextuelles.
Reste une inconnue, la fonction « Automatisation ». Android Authority n’a pas réussi à la faire fonctionner pour voir ce qu’elle cache. On suppose qu’il s’agit de définir des tâches récurrentes. Par exemple créer un album de vos meilleurs souvenirs du mois tous les premiers du mois. Google n’a pas communiqué sur ces nouveautés, et aucune date de déploiement global n’est connue à ce jour.

articles.title: Apple encuentra en los 2 nm una salida a sus problemas de fabricación
articles.text:
Los SoC más avanzados que podemos encontrar en el interior de algunos dispositivos de Apple, como los iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo o iMac 2026, han sido fabricados por TSMC en su nodo N2 (2 nm). Poco a poco esta tecnología de integración irá llegando a otros productos de la compañía de Cupertino, pero es probable que el despliegue de esta categoría de circuitos integrados sea más lento de lo que le gustaría a Apple.
De hecho, durante el último trimestre fiscal la capacidad de producción de los nodos más avanzados de TSMC ha limitado la disponibilidad de los SoC más sofisticados diseñados por la firma de la manzana. Este escenario representa un problema para Apple, y posiblemente también para otros clientes de este fabricante taiwanés de semiconductores, como Nvidia, AMD o Qualcomm. No obstante, afortunadamente para ellos, el panorama está empezando a mejorar.
TSMC no publica el rendimiento por oblea de sus nodos litográficos, pero esta información suele filtrarse. En marzo de 2025, según las filtraciones, el nodo N2 tenía un rendimiento por oblea de alrededor del 60%, por lo que solo 60 de cada 100 chips producidos funcionaban correctamente. Actualmente, de nuevo según las filtraciones, el rendimiento de este nodo está cerca del 90%. Esta es la evolución habitual de una tecnología litográfica, y para Apple y otros clientes de TSMC ese 90% es una gran noticia.
Los problemas de suministro no han desaparecido
La mejora del rendimiento de los nodos litográficos más avanzados no es el único desafío al que se enfrenta la industria de la fabricación de semiconductores. El apetito de los centros de datos para inteligencia artificial (IA) está acaparando algunos nodos de vanguardia porque para los fabricantes de chips suele ser más rentable producir los circuitos integrados que acabarán en los centros de datos que fabricar los semiconductores destinados al mercado de consumo.
Sea como sea, que los nodos más avanzados de TSMC en producción a gran escala ya hayan alcanzado un rendimiento por oblea cercano al valor óptimo parece estar aliviando la presión que ejerce el mercado sobre este fabricante de chips de vanguardia. Según DigiTimes, Apple ha reconocido que esta situación está mejorando, y también ha confirmado que ya está trasladando una mayor parte de su porfolio a esta tecnología de fabricación.
Apple se ha enfrentado a restricciones de suministro que han afectado a la producción de sus iPhone, Mac y iPad
Durante los últimos meses, esta compañía se ha enfrentado a restricciones de suministro que han afectado a la producción de sus iPhone, Mac y iPad, y prevé que durante el último trimestre de 2026 las limitaciones seguirán erosionando la producción de los Mac y los iPad. Ahora Apple atribuye el origen del problema a la disponibilidad de chips de memoria, y la presión que está soportando la cadena de suministro desde luego no ayuda.
Aunque esta compañía tenga acceso actualmente a más SoC de 2 nm que a principios de este año, no puede eludir la fragilidad de la cadena de suministro. Ni Apple, ni Google, ni Meta. Nadie puede hacerlo. Todas las compañías de tecnología que producen hardware están expuestas a los vaivenes del mercado de los minerales críticos y a las tensiones derivadas de la construcción de una gran cantidad de centros de datos para IA. Que los nodos de 2 nm de TSMC ya hayan alcanzado un rendimiento por oblea alto ayuda, pero el fin de la crisis de los componentes parece estar aún lejos.

articles.title: Los titulares de derechos de Elvis Presley demandan a Anthropic
articles.text:
Los propietarios de los derechos de 274 composiciones interpretadas por Elvis Presley han puesto en marcha una demanda contra la empresa Anthropic por supuestamente utilizar las letras de sus canciones para entrenar al asistente Claude sin su consentimiento y sin pagar por ello. Dicha demanda fue presentada en el Tribunal Federal del Distrito Norte de California el 23 de octubre de 2026.
Entre los demandantes está ABG EPE IP (que pertenece al grupo Authentic Brands Group). Entre las composiciones figuran “Can’t Help Falling in Love”, “All Shook Up” y “A Little Less Conversation”. Todo se centra en los contenidos de las letras de las composiciones y en los resultados que ofrece el asistente.
Qué reclaman los titulares de los derechos
Se expone que Claude ha utilizado contenido protegido desde sus primeros lanzamientos. Los demandantes afirman que las medidas de filtrado que ha implementado Anthropic para evitar este tipo de respuestas son insuficientes. Además, aseguran que la propia empresa sabía de estos problemas.
Por otro lado, en la demanda (firmada por el abogado Richard S. Busch) se acusa a Anthropic de montar su negocio sobre infracciones de derechos de autor sin precedentes. Según explican, a pesar de las salvaguardas implementadas, han seguido produciéndose.
Por cada obra supuestamente infringida, los titulares solicitan hasta 150.000 dólares. En total, para las 274 composiciones son 41,1 millones de dólares (unos 36,7 millones de euros al cambio de referencia del Banco Central Europeo). Es una solicitud de indemnización y no una condena.
Las reclamaciones de la industria musical y las medidas de Spotify
Se une al resto de reclamaciones que está llevando a cabo la industria musical contra el uso de sus obras por parte de empresas de IA. Universal, Sony y Warner han sido parte de algunos de estos litigios. Pero también los músicos han denunciado el uso indebido de sus obras y voces. Y además temen que puedan ser reemplazados por la IA. De hecho, en las plataformas de streaming ya se han colado canciones con voces de artistas reproducidas por medio de esta tecnología.
En el caso de Spotify, han desactivado de sus recomendaciones más de 50 millones de pistas que consideran de baja calidad o spam en 2026, según han anunciado. Relacionan estas medidas con el boom de contenido generado por IA. Estamos hablando de recomendaciones y no de eliminación de canciones del catálogo.
