articles.title: The long road towards 6G: Spectrum, investment and making 5G complete
articles.text:
The long road towards 6G: Spectrum, investment and making 5G complete
Why today’s spectrum and investment decisions will shape 6G
Mobile generations are not isolated events. More than five billion 6G connections are expected by 2040. Yet even then, 6G will only just have become the dominant mobile technology, with the crossover from 5G currently expected around 2035–2037. The 2030s will therefore be a decade of coexistence, with 5G and 6G networks operating alongside one another.
Luciana is Head of Spectrum and Ross is Senior Director of Spectrum Strategy at the GSMA.
The choices made today will help determine how much capacity mobile networks can deliver in the 2030s and how many people have access to them. Making sure 6G policies encourage investment and support widespread harmonization – delivering economies of scale – will help connect as many people as possible to robust, high-quality communications networks.
What is happening now?
Every generation of mobile technology is part of a long-term evolution that takes years of planning, investment, and coordination before reaching consumers and businesses at scale. Regulation, standards and spectrum all take years to develop in a harmonized fashion. That harmonization is critical to the success of every generation and will be for 6G. Harmonization does not have to mean all the world doing precisely the same thing, but means agreeing on a set of foundational parameters in spectrum, standards and policy.
These are already being developed. They include access to spectrum capable of supporting wide 200–400 MHz channels in relevant bands which not only provide the raw spectrum needed for higher data rates, but also enable more efficient radio technologies, improved network economics and help deliver future AI-native services. They also include finalizing 3GPP work on globally agreed standards that form the basis of the technology.
Finally, they include national digital policies that focus on network investment to ensure that the infrastructure is in place to maximize productivity and economic growth.
5G evolution
There are around 350 5G networks today, a number that still has a lot of space to grow. 5G launched in 2018 but we are only now starting its dominant period, with connections expected to overtake 4G later this decade.
The promise of 5G was a consistent user experience, and it has taken time and investment to deliver this. However, as 5G begins to mature, we are seeing network quality increase and, with that, traffic is growing. Investment needs to continue in many markets across two elements of technology – 5G standalone and subsequently 5G-Advanced.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Both can boost productivity and stimulate further traffic growth, but spectrum is required to realize their benefits. If spectrum is constrained to today’s levels, cities with over 50% of the world’s urban population will be capacity-constrained by 2030.
The success of 5G has not been about delivering a single killer application but rather – and indeed, rather quietly – ensuring that today’s networks keep up with data demand.
Capacity drivers
6G also needs to provide capacity. Network quality and data consumption are closely linked: as networks become faster and more responsive, users consume more data and new, more data-intensive applications become viable.
As AI, sensing and multi-device environments develop, the gap between connections and people will also become increasingly significant. Today there are around 8.8 billion mobile connections but only 5.8 billion unique subscribers. A future in which people, vehicles, machines, sensors and other devices interact continuously will see connections grow much faster than the number of people using them.
Spectrum policy during the 6G era is not simply about maximum speeds. It is about ensuring sufficient capacity where demand is greatest, often using mid-bands, while maintaining broad geographic coverage and a consistent quality of experience – parity between urban and rural areas requires low-band spectrum as well.
6G requirements
Two elements need to be considered when releasing spectrum for the 6G era in the 2030s. The first is ensuring investment in 6G networks is encouraged through forward-thinking government policies. This requires sufficient spectrum to be made available in a timely manner without artificial constraints or unnecessarily high reserve prices.
The history of mobile spectrum allocation offers a recurring lesson: the value of spectrum is not measured by the price paid for a license, but by the economic and social value created by the networks that use it.
The high prices generated by some 3G auctions highlighted the risks of prioritizing upfront revenues over investment. 4G then saw a greater focus on rollout and network economics, although the tension returned in some 5G awards as fragmented 3.5 GHz auctions occurred with no clear roadmap to further access. As operators sought contiguous 100 MHz channels for 5G, some 3.5 GHz awards resulted in high spectrum costs, highlighting the importance of a clear roadmap for future spectrum access.
The second element is understanding industry needs. 6G will require 200–400 MHz channels per operator alongside sufficient overall capacity, and analysis indicates that, on average, around 2–2.5 GHz of mid-band spectrum may be required per market by 2035–2040, rising to around 2.4–3.3 GHz in higher-demand markets.
This does not mean that all of this spectrum needs to be made available at once. A credible roadmap towards these figures will give operators visibility for long-term network planning, while widespread harmonization will deliver economies of scale and help keep devices affordable.
Creating a sustainable, equitable 6G environment can provide a platform for economic opportunity in the 2030s. The decisions taken on spectrum, standards, infrastructure and investment will determine not only how capable 6G networks become, but how widely their benefits are shared.

articles.title: Digital twins will create a new blueprint for data center design
articles.text:
Digital twins will create a new blueprint for data center design
Digital twins enable operators to run 'what if' scenarios
Digital twins are not simply tools for simulation. They’re assets that have the potential to reconfigure how data centers are designed, tested and optimized. Many operators have already been quick to catch on to the advantages these tools offer, de-risking critical decisions, accelerating innovation, and optimizing performance.
The majority of technology leaders in major corporations are already looking to implement digital twin initiatives. Despite this, only 42% of decision-makers in data centers are currently using digital twins, with many still perceiving them as internal tools.
In an industry where downtime is incredibly costly, and infrastructure decisions have long-term consequences, the ability to ‘test drive’ different scenarios in a risk-free environment isn’t just an advantage, it’s a gamechanger.
AVP Technology at GlobalLogic (a Hitachi Group company).
In fact, according to McKinsey, the implementation of digital twins can accelerate the creation and setup of new projects, including AI-enabled features, by up to 60% and cut costs by around 15%.
A 360-degree view of operations
The data center industry is facing a perfect storm of complexity. Rapid growth in AI workloads, stringent sustainability requirements, and unprecedented IT infrastructure investment are all converging. Traditional approaches to planning and testing – spreadsheets, static models, and gut instinct – simply can’t keep up. Enter digital twins: precise virtual replicas of physical data centers that enable operators to simulate scenarios, test configurations, and optimize performance before committing resources to real-world deployment.
Digital twins aren’t new. Manufacturing, aerospace, and energy sectors have been using them for years. But their application to data centers represents a significant leap forward in how the industry approaches design, operations, and resilience planning. By creating a comprehensive digital replica – from server racks to HVAC systems to power distribution – operators can run “what-if” scenarios that would be impossible or prohibitively expensive to test in production.
The value proposition is clear: reduce risk, accelerate time-to-market, and optimize resource allocation. But the devil is in the details. Building an effective digital twin requires more than just 3D modeling software. It demands deep integration across IT and OT systems, sophisticated data analytics, and the right talent to interpret results and translate them into actionable insights.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
AI initiatives face similar hurdles. Just 25% of AI implementations have achieved expected ROI, likely hindered by poor system integration and ineffective strategies for data management.
Eradicating IT/OT siloes
One of the most transformative capabilities of digital twins is their ability to expose hidden interdependencies between IT and OT systems. In traditional data center planning, these systems are often designed and managed in silos. IT teams focus on compute, storage, and networking. OT teams handle physical infrastructure – power, cooling, and building management. This separation creates blind spots that can lead to catastrophic failures under stress.
Let’s look at an example. Imagine that a data center provider simulates a regional power grid failure. Primary power is cut, backup generators take over seamlessly, and failover scripts reroute workloads to a secondary facility. HVAC and building management systems (BMS), which are not integrated with IT systems, continue running in standard operating mode.
The HVAC system, functioning separately to the simulated power outage and increased IT load, does not adjust cooling to match the spike in server activity. In a real-life scenario, this could result in server aisles nearing thermal shutdown. When systems are not “in dialogue” with one another, and the physical interdependencies between IT and OT systems are not well understood, operators end up with a false sense of readiness.
Another issue is that the industry currently lacks the talent to deploy digital twin technologies. 58% of operators in the UK currently struggle to fill critical roles, whilst 40% state that retaining their core team is particularly difficult. This revolving door of talent can make upskilling a challenge and, as things stand, there aren’t enough experts who understand how to direct simulations.
A test-drive – for the data center
Just as manufacturers test production line changes in their digital twin before implementing them on the factory floor, data center operators can simulate cooling adjustments, power reconfigurations, or workload migrations in their digital twin before touching production infrastructure. The ability to test failure scenarios such as power outages, cooling failures and equipment malfunctions enables operators to check if their disaster recovery procedures actually work and identify gaps before they become real-world crises.
Finally, digital twins are making a real difference in helping operators to draw up Service Level Agreements (SLAs) with customers, providing assurance that they can deliver on certain levels of uptime. As operators look to scale their infrastructure in line with the exponential growth of AI, digital twins have a critical role to play, ensuring performance isn’t comprised even as capacity expands.

Auto, Security and AI
                        WHITEPAPERS
		
How data center operators can protect critical data and communications without compromising the performance demanded by distributed AI and HPC workloads.
								November 4th, 2026 - 
								By: Rambus
								
							
AI and HPC workloads are transforming data center networking by creating distinct front-end and back-end network domains, each with different performance, scalability, and operational requirements. While front-end networks connect users, applications, storage, and management systems, back-end networks provide the high-speed connectivity required among GPUs, accelerators, and compute nodes. This white paper examines the architectural and security considerations associated with these specialized networks and explains how data center operators can protect critical data and communications without compromising the performance demanded by distributed AI and HPC workloads.

- How front-end and back-end networks serve different roles in modern AI and HPC infrastructure

articles.title: Intel Releases 0.9 PDK for 14A Node, Final Version in Q1 2027
articles.text:
Wednesday, November 4th 2026
Intel Releases 0.9 PDK for 14A Node, Final Version in Q1 2027
In late October, Intel released its process design kit (PDK) version 0.9 for the 14A node, marking a significant milestone for the Intel Foundry business. Intel's CEO, Lip-Bu Tan, referred to this version as the "holy grail" because it allows customers to evaluate Intel's node and start trial designs that can easily transition into production with PDK version 1.0. The company expects PDK version 1.0 for the 14A node to be available in the first quarter of 2027, which is just months away. This indicates that final specifications and requirements are already being established, and Intel is conducting final fine-tuning of the node to include in the design kit.
Intel plans to begin risk production of the 14A node in the second half of 2027, with high-volume production anticipated in 2028. The company has processed tens of thousands of 14A wafers in pilot production runs and is now focusing on yield improvements and minor node adjustments before starting risk production next year. The 14A node is designed to offer a 15-20% performance improvement at the same power level compared to Intel's 18A, or it can be optimized for a 25-35% power reduction at the same performance level. This will be accompanied by up to a 30% improvement in chip density compared to Intel's 18A, though it is unclear if this refers to logic or SRAM scaling, as the latter has been challenging for the industry.The company expects its 14A node to be within 5% of TSMC's A14 node, with both competing in the same sector. Determining exactly what this means is challenging, as there are many factors by which a node is characterized, including transistor switching frequency, power efficiency, and density. The "within 5%" figure could imply a 5% advantage, a 5% disadvantage, or a mix of both, so the technical specifics remain uncertain. Intel's recent nodes, like the 18A currently in production, are proving to be efficient and high-performing. However, TSMC's nodes are also strong, with both companies continuing development.

articles.title: Amazon ECS Gateway Arrives with Generated Hostnames and No Custom Domain Support
articles.text:
AWS recently released Amazon ECS Gateway, an account-level ingress resource that lets platform teams define networking once, and application teams attach services to it with a connector. Each service gets a generated hostname, and neither the announcement nor the documentation describes how to put a custom domain in front of it.
The gateway is described by principal developer advocate Channy Yun as:
a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.
It is available in all commercial regions where ECS runs, at no additional charge beyond the resources it provisions. The first question practitioners asked was how to put their own domain in front of it.
The split it introduces is organizational: platform teams create a gateway with its infrastructure IAM role, subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and optional WAF web ACLs, then associate it with clusters. Application teams add a gateway connector through CreateService or UpdateService, and for each service ECS provisions an ACM certificate, a hostname, a listener rule, a target group, and a security group that accepts traffic only from the load balancer.
Amazon ECS Gateway architecture. (Source: AWS News Blog post)
On Reddit, commenter zurnout went straight at the hostname:
I don’t get how this is useful at all since you get a random domain name for your ecs service. How am I going to direct traffic to that? It’s the same thing with ECS Express.
Asked whether a CNAME would solve it, he explained why it would not:
It creates host-based rules in the load balancer, so it wouldn’t know where to route if you used a CNAME.
Commenter ResponsibleWaltz1479 reached the same conclusion, calling the feature usable "for ephemeral /preview environments if the app is not hostname aware," but not for their existing setup.
The documentation supports the reading: each service "gets a generated hostname in the form https://<unique-id>.ecs.<region>.on.aws," and "Amazon ECS uses host-based routing to direct requests from a shared Application Load Balancer to the appropriate service." Custom domain names, Route 53, and CNAME records go unmentioned. Commenter Kralizek82 raised the one workaround nobody resolved, asking whether a gateway could serve as an internal CloudFront origin.
Opinion split on whether the service is substantial. Commenter bioJesusMain called it:
It’s just ALB and DNS with a wrapper
And commenter aneryx suggested:
It could even just be a CDK construct on top of ALB/NLB and Route 53
Commenter brokenlabrum answered that from experience:
Those higher level L3 constructs have often turned out to be a mistake because they need to expose every knob on the L2 constructs they wrap. And if they’re opinionated and don’t, ejecting from an L3 construct without it deleting your resources is hell.
Commenter Aggressive-Height167 put the case for it, noting that letting a cloud team define networking once while application teams deploy against it "seems like a pretty solid improvement." The test, they added, "is whether it actually removes complexity without taking away too much control."
The documentation adds a cost detail the announcement leaves out. A gateway adds load balancers as existing ones fill and removes them only when they empty, but it "does not consolidate load balancers" and "does not move services between load balancers, so several partly filled load balancers can remain after services leave." Each one is billed.
Commenter jregovic noted that more than 25 services means more than one load balancer. An AWS respondent answered that "multiple ALBs are handled by the gateway itself - so it’s not something that you need to worry about." The gateway does handle them, but it does not pack them, so the count still climbs with the number of services.
ECS also "does not repair changes made outside it," so modifying or deleting a managed resource means traffic "can stop," and later deployments, gateway updates, and cleanup operations may fail.
The limits are specific: twenty-five services share one load balancer, against a default maxAlbCount of 10 and a documented ceiling of 200 per gateway, and AWS warns that "if maxAlbCount is reached and no ALB has available capacity, the deployment fails." Listeners serve HTTPS on port 443 only, services must use awsvpc networking in the same VPC and account, and Express Mode services are excluded altogether.
The thread’s most upvoted comment dismissed the launch as "a promotion project," and several commenters asked why AWS Elastic Beanstalk did not already cover the ground, one pointing at its Cluster Mode release last month. On the other side, dmcnaughton1 said a current ECS migration was early enough to adopt it.

articles.title: iPhone Duo: nuevo plegable de Apple entre una novedad histórica y fallas técnicas
articles.text:
El iPhone Duo, el primer teléfono plegable de Apple, atraviesa un momento de contrastes: fue elegido como el mejor invento de 2026 por la revista Time, pero acumula denuncias de usuarios por grietas en su pantalla interna.
El dispositivo, anunciado en septiembre de 2026, representa el cambio de diseño más radical en la historia del iPhone y conforma la vigésima edición del equipo. Mientras la crítica especializada celebra su formato plegable, compradores en Reddit y en los foros de MacRumors documentan fallas que Apple ya reconoció de forma pública.
Por qué el iPhone Duo es considerado el mejor invento del año según Time
La revista Time publicó su selección anual de los mejores inventos de 2026 y ubicó al iPhone Duo en el primer puesto de la lista. El reconocimiento responde a que se trata del primer teléfono inteligente plegable desarrollado y comercializado por Apple, una apuesta que la compañía no había concretado hasta ahora pese a que otros fabricantes ya exploraban ese formato.
El equipo tiene un precio inicial de 1.999 dólares y combina una pantalla plegable de 7,6 pulgadas con una segunda pantalla en la cubierta exterior. Al cerrarse, queda reducido a un tamaño aproximado de 5,4 pulgadas, equivalente al de un pasaporte, lo que permite guardarlo en un bolsillo sin perder la posibilidad de desplegar una superficie similar a la de una tableta.
Esa pantalla ampliada habilita funciones como ver películas, navegar por dos sitios web en simultáneo, jugar o realizar videollamadas. Durante las llamadas por FaceTime, el Duo permite además utilizar dos cámaras para mostrar al mismo tiempo al usuario y aquello que observa.
Para sostener ese mecanismo, Apple desarrolló una bisagra con más de 100 componentes de precisión y una superficie fabricada con un polímero personalizado. Según la compañía, ese diseño reduce al mínimo la marca que suele quedar en el centro de las pantallas plegables, un problema habitual en otros modelos del mercado.
El dispositivo también incorpora un nuevo motor de pantalla que permite transiciones entre los paneles interno y externo, y trasladó las funciones principales de la interfaz hacia el lateral derecho para facilitar el acceso con el pulgar.
El defecto que afecta a los primeros compradores del iPhone Duo
Desde su salida al mercado el viernes 23 de octubre, numerosos compradores sometieron el mecanismo a aperturas y cierres constantes. En varios casos documentaron la aparición de una grieta en el pliegue acompañada de rayas visibles en la pantalla, con una línea de píxeles brillantes en uno de los laterales.
El problema se concentra en un punto específico: el pliegue central donde se ubica la bisagra. Según las fotos compartidas por los propietarios, casi todos los fallos aparecen en esa zona exacta del dispositivo.
Un propietario del iPhone Duo en Australia relató el caso con mayor detalle entre los reportes conocidos. Aseguró que su dispositivo se agrietó después de haber sido abierto menos de 20 veces, sin ningún daño visible previo.
“Tuve mi iPhone Duo durante unas seis horas y probablemente lo abrí menos de 20 veces. Se lo estaba enseñando a un amigo y, al abrirlo, sentí algo alrededor de la bisagra interna, debajo de la pantalla”, contó.
“Mientras seguía abriéndola, oí un crujido y la pantalla se rompió justo por la bisagra”, agregó el usuario, quien señaló que no había marcas ni daños previos en la superficie interior de la pantalla ni en la bisagra exterior que indicaran un enganche o un golpe. Tras el incidente, acudió a una Apple Store, donde la compañía reemplazó el equipo de manera inmediata.
A la par, circulan imágenes de pantallas rotas correspondientes a unidades de demostración en China, donde el iPhone Duo llegó horas antes que a Estados Unidos.
El origen de buena parte de ese material no está confirmado, y no se descarta que parte del daño responda al uso manual durante las exhibiciones. Analistas que probaron el equipo con anticipación lo sometieron a pruebas de plegado repetido sin registrar inconvenientes, aunque se trató de una muestra reducida.
Las fallas de bisagra derivadas de un uso normal quedan cubiertas por la garantía de un año, y quienes reciban el equipo en esta etapa conservan además dos semanas para devolverlo.
La respuesta de Apple ante la ola de reclamos en redes sociales
Frente a la multiplicación de publicaciones en redes sociales, Apple admitió la existencia de un “problema” con la pantalla interna del Duo y recomendó a los afectados gestionar un reemplazo a través de su servicio técnico. La compañía atribuyó el inconveniente a una proporción acotada de unidades.
La respuesta oficial llegó de la mano de Alex Kirschner, vocero de la empresa, en declaraciones que compartió con el medio The Verge. “La respuesta de los primeros usuarios al iPhone Duo ha sido increíblemente positiva, y estamos viendo avances prometedores por parte de los desarrolladores, quienes están actualizando rápidamente sus aplicaciones para aprovechar su formato único”, señaló Apple.
“Somos conscientes de un problema que afecta la pantalla interna en un pequeño número de unidades del iPhone Duo. Si experimenta problemas con la pantalla de su iPhone Duo, debe comunicarse con AppleCare para obtener un reemplazo”, añadió la compañía.
Medios especializados advirtieron, sin embargo, que no todos los reclamos virales son genuinos: algunas de las fotografías que circularon en Reddit y X mostraban daños generados mediante inteligencia artificial, lo que complica distinguir entre fallas reales y contenido manipulado.
Con el alto volumen de ventas de estos primeros días, cierto nivel de fallos resulta previsible, aunque no está claro todavía cuál es la magnitud real del problema ni si las quejas seguirán en aumento.

articles.title: Egypt’s MoneyHash helps Luno recover one in four lost deposits - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Egyptian payment orchestration startup MoneyHash is powering the payments infrastructure of crypto and investment platform Luno, helping it launch local payment options faster and recover deposits that would otherwise have failed.
Founded in 2021 by Nader Abdelrazik and Mustafa Eid, MoneyHash has developed a proprietary payment orchestration platform and end-to-end payment operating system. After a successful beta launch in 2022, attracting key players in the region such as Foodics, Rain, and Tamatem, the startup launched its enterprise suite last October, targeting large enterprises.
The startup, which secured US$5.2 million in pre-Series A funding early last year, has been expanding its international operations recently, with key partnerships agreed in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq, Bahrain, Oman and South Africa.
Founded in Africa in 2013, Luno has grown into a global platform serving millions of customers across multiple markets. That growth came with a headache – more than 25 payment providers and local bank connections, each of which its engineering team had to build, maintain and monitor.
By routing those providers through MoneyHash, Luno now manages payments centrally and can direct transactions based on provider performance, trying alternative routes when one fails. This has helped it recover one in four deposits that might otherwise have been lost, while cutting the engineering time spent on integrations and speeding up the rollout of local payment options in new markets.
“Having MoneyHash handle our payment integrations meant our internal teams didn’t have to spend capacity managing payment rails,” said Cornel Smit, head of payments at Luno. “We can focus our engineering energy where it belongs: on revenue generation and building products for our users.”
“Our role is to take the complexity out of managing multiple payment providers, so Luno’s teams can move faster, improve payment performance and keep their focus on building for their customers,” said Abdelrazik.

articles.title: Microsoft's AI PC roadmap shows where Ryzen AI 500 and Intel Nova Lake fit into Windows
articles.text:
Forward-looking: Neither AMD nor Intel has formally announced its next wave of laptop chips. Microsoft, however, already seems to have a spot picked out for them. A slide that appears to come from the company sorts Windows PCs into four AI tiers by memory. Ryzen AI 500 and Core Ultra Series 4 both land in its mainstream Copilot+ class.
Known leaker HXL posted the slide on X on Tuesday. Titled "Windows is the home for hybrid intelligence," it lines PCs up along a memory scale that runs from 8GB to beyond 128GB. Chip names only appear underneath, almost like footnotes.
Those footnotes still carry the biggest news, though. Microsoft splits its Copilot+ tier into three bands, from quick local questions at 16GB to delegated tasks at 32GB and long-running jobs at 64GB. Core Ultra Series 3 and 4 sit in the first two, right next to Ryzen AI 400 and 500.
As for timing, a small "CY26-27" label beside the chip list offers a rough window. That lines up with leaks pegging Core Ultra Series 4 as Intel's Nova Lake and Ryzen AI 500 as AMD's Zen 6-based Medusa Point, both reportedly due in 2027.
Spend more on memory, and the chip list changes completely. At 64GB, the mainstream parts disappear in favor of Ryzen AI Max+ 400, Nvidia's RTX Spark and an unnamed "Core Ultra Next" from Intel. The same trio carries over into the 128GB Builder PC tier, which is meant for building and serving models locally.
Past that sits a Supercomputer tier for desk-side machines running frontier models – a sign of how far Microsoft wants Windows to stretch.
An 8GB laptop, meanwhile, gets stuck in a plain "Windows PC" tier limited to local context and basic actions, whatever chip it runs. That includes Microsoft's own 8GB Surface models from June.
Microsoft and Qualcomm said in September that they'd stopped calling new devices Copilot+ PCs. On this slide, though, the label still anchors the biggest tier.
None of this is confirmed yet. The slide's wording does match the hybrid intelligence push Microsoft kicked off last month with the RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra. On Copilot+ PCs, that push means Copilot will eventually read local files, take actions and tap on-device models.
If anything, the slide is a reminder to check the RAM before the chip. A fast NPU alone won't unlock Copilot+ features without at least 16GB of memory backing it up. And that extra memory has only gotten pricier this year as AI data centers soak up supply.

articles.title: Siri AI va pouvoir agir dans toutes vos applications… mais Apple laisse encore la France de côté
articles.text:
Avec la bêta d’iOS 27.3, Apple permet à n’importe quel développeur de brancher son application sur Siri AI. L’assistant pourra agir dans les apps tierces, sans que l’utilisateur ait à les nommer. En Europe, en revanche, il reste indisponible.
Cette ouverture change la nature de Siri AI : l’assistant ne se contente plus des applications d’Apple, il peut désormais orchestrer des tâches à travers tout l’écosystème iOS. Encore faut-il que vous y ayez accès, et que les apps suivent.
Siri AI sort du cercle des apps Apple, mais seulement en bêta
Comme l’indique The Verge, Apple annonce que les développeurs peuvent intégrer les nouvelles fonctions de Siri AI dans « toutes les apps » : compréhension du contexte personnel, requêtes en langage naturel et conscience de l’écran. Selon la documentation d’Apple, aucun nouveau programme développeur distinct n’est nécessaire.
Cela dit le périmètre reste étroit, le Developer Preview n’est utilisable que via des builds signés avec un profil de développement et des testeurs internes TestFlight. Ni les testeurs externes ni les versions publiées sur l’App Store n’y ont accès. Apple évoque une première livraison aux clients « dans quelques mois », avec l’ouverture des soumissions à l'App Store au printemps, sans date précise.
Autre garde-fou : l’app doit exposer elle-même ses actions. Siri n’obtient pas un accès automatique à tout son contenu.
Les « app skills » apprennent à Siri à enchaîner plusieurs actions
Pour les demandes complexes, les développeurs peuvent créer des « app skills », qui guident Siri à travers plusieurs actions regroupées en une seule. Apple donne l’exemple de sneakers favorites : Siri les retrouve dans une app, identifie votre partenaire dans Contacts, puis envoie l’information via la messagerie désignée.
Dans plusieurs cas, il ne sera plus nécessaire de citer l’application : quand elle est au premier plan, qu’une « Live Activity » est active ou au fil d’une conversation qui la mentionne. Dire « change l’adresse de ma course » suffira si une activité de VTC est en cours. Un confort réel, qui dépendra toutefois de la qualité des intégrations. Apple promet d’ailleurs de préciser prochainement les conditions d’usage des expériences passant par Siri AI.
Côté Apple, l’assistant gagne aussi des actions dans Calendrier, Fichiers, Mail, Messages, Photos, Safari ou Météo, entre autres.
En Europe, Siri AI reste bloqué sans calendrier
Voici le point qui fâche pour nous autres Français : la note d’Apple est explicite, Siri AI est « actuellement indisponible dans l’UE » sur iOS, iPadOS et watchOS. La firme dit travailler « de manière constructive » avec l'UE pour trouver une issue, sans échéance ni détail sur le blocage.
Paradoxe : le français figure bien parmi les langues prises en charge, avec l’anglais, le japonais, le coréen, le portugais et l’espagnol. La langue n’est donc pas le problème, la région si. Le service exige aussi un appareil compatible Apple Intelligence réglé sur une langue gérée, et certaines fonctions peuvent varier selon les pays.
Concrètement, un développeur européen peut travailler sur ces intégrations, mais ses utilisateurs de l’Union ne pourront pas en profiter tant que le dossier n’avance pas. Les premières apps compatibles arriveront de toute façon après le printemps.
Siri AI s’ouvre donc au monde entier, sauf à celui qui parle français depuis Paris, Bruxelles ou Lyon. Reste à voir qui, d’Apple ou de Bruxelles, fera le premier pas.

articles.title: Marvel ya habría elegido al próximo actor de Lobezno (Wolverine): es bajito y ha ganado 2 premios Emmy
articles.text:
Con la nueva película de X-Men en marcha, los fans de Marvel llevan meses preguntándose quién será el nuevo actor de Lobezno (Wolverine). Hace unas semanas, la compañía anunció a los primeros miembros del reparto del filme. Pero aunque se revelaron nombres muy importantes para el equipo mutante, no había ni rastro de Logan. Algunos incluso bromearon con que Disney mantendría de nuevo a Hugh Jackman en el papel para hacer realidad el chiste de Deadpool de que el australiano seguirá en el papel hasta que tenga 90 años.
Sin embargo, esto evidentemente no será así. Por mucho que duela, la nueva saga de X-Men necesitará a su propio Lobezno (Wolverine) como miembro indispensable del equipo. Y por lo que parece, el estudio ya tendría un candidato muy firme. Se trata, de hecho, de uno de los actores más de moda de todo Hollywood.
Y es que, según ha informado el insider Jeff Sneider, Marvel quiere a Jeremy Allen White como Lobezno (Wolverine) en sus nuevos X-Men. El actor, de 35 años, es de sobra conocido por su papel protagonista en la serie The Bear, que le ha valido dos premios Emmy. También cuenta con otros roles muy destacados como la serie Shameless o las películas El clan del hierro, Deliver Me From Nowhere e incluso las recientes The Mandalorian & Grogu y El precio de la red.
Jeremy Allen White sería Lobezno (Wolverine) en X-Men
Precisamente estos últimos filmes no han funcionado como se esperaba en taquilla. Por eso, no sería de extrañar que Jeremy Allen White acepte el papel de Lobezno (Wolverine) en X-Men para reencontrarse con el éxito del gran público. Lo cierto es que a nivel físico, cumple de sobra. El personaje en los cómics es un hombre muy fuerte y bajito (aproximadamente 1,60 m - 1,65 m). White ya ha demostrado estar muy en forman y además mide 1,70m. Mucho más cerca de la altura correcta del personaje que Hugh Jackman, por ejemplo, que alcanza el 1,90m de estatura.
Si se confirma el fichaje de Jeremy Allen White como Lobezno (Wolverine), Marvel habrá conseguido otro nombre de éxito para sus nuevos X-Men. Porque recordemos que el reparto incluye a varias grandes estrellas de la industria, como Sadie Sink (Jean Grey), Adam Driver (Mr. Siniestro), Inde Navarrette(Pícara), Kit Connor (Cíclope) o Samara Weaving (Emma Frost), entre otros.
X-Men se estrena en cines el 5 de mayo de 2028.

articles.title: Une banque française vient d'être piratée : 100 millions d'euros volés suite à des « opérations frauduleuses »
articles.text:
Mise à jour du 4 novembre à 12H02
Selon le journaliste crypto Gregory Raymond, « l’équivalent de 133 millions de dollars auraient été sortis de la banque par des hackers, puis acheminés vers de multiples comptes ouverts sur des plateformes d’échange crypto, dont Crypto.com ». Il assure qu’un réseau criminel est à l’origine de l’attaque, qui a spécifiquement visé Fortuneo, la banque en ligne du groupe Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.
Les fraudeurs auraient pu émettre des virements depuis Fortuneo en choisissant eux-mêmes le nom du bénéficiaire. L’argent aurait été envoyé vers des comptes ouverts sur des plateformes crypto (Kraken, OKX, Crypto.com) avec de fausses identités, assez solides pour passer les contrôles.
 🔴 Grosse info : Crédit Mutuel Arkéa (@cmarkea) victime d’une fraude d’au moins 133 millions de dollars, blanchis en cryptos
L’information a été révélée dans la nuit par l’enquêteur onchain @ZachXBT
👉 Je travaille sur cette affaire depuis hier, voici ce que j’ai réuni :
L’équivalent de 133 millions de dollars auraient été sortis de la banque par des hackers, puis acheminés vers de multiples comptes ouverts sur des plateformes d’échange crypto, dont @Cryptocom
“Ce n’est pas de la crypto qui a été volée directement à la banque. C’est du fiat (monnaie traditionnelle, ndlr) qui aurait été sorti, puis changé en cryptos pour permettre le blanchiment”, m’a expliqué une source proche du dossier.
Un tel procédé serait tout à fait inédit.
Ma source décrit un réseau organisé, reposant sur de nombreux comptes de “mules”.
Contactée hier soir autour de 18h (heure de Paris) par mes soins, la banque n’a pas souhaité faire de commentaire.
“À ce stade, nous ne sommes pas en mesure de confirmer ces informations”, m’a-t-elle répondu.
Étant donné que rien n’était encore vérifié et que le nom de la banque n’était pas connu publiquement, j’ai préféré ne rien publier.
Selon ma source anonyme, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa aurait compris tardivement qu’elle était concernée et aurait été “complètement dépassée”.
Un délai qui serait lourd de conséquences : en l’absence de confirmation officielle par la banque, les plateformes et les émetteurs de stablecoins n’auraient pas pu bloquer les fonds à temps.
Dimanche, ZachXBT avait déjà signalé des retraits de plus de 106 millions de dollars en USDC et en USDT au détriment d’une “entité européenne non identifiée”, avant de relever son estimation à 133 millions ce mardi.
Une partie des retraits est intervenue après sa première alerte.
D’après son analyse, l’auteur convertit les stablecoins en ETH, passe par des services d’échange instantané (WellWallet, Kyrrex) puis échange les fonds contre du Monero (XMR), conçu pour rendre les transactions intraçables.
ZachXBT écarte “avec un haut degré de confiance” la piste du groupe nord-coréen Lazarus.
Il estime enfin que plus de 30 millions de dollars auraient pu être gelés si l’incident avait été déclaré rapidement.
— Grégory Raymond (@gregory_raymond) November 4, 2026
Le Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, dont le siège se trouve dans le Finistère, a été victime d’une cyberattaque d’envergure. Ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026, le groupe bancaire breton a reconnu avoir été victime d’une attaque informatique ayant permis « la réalisation d’opérations frauduleuses ». La banque assure que l’incident est « aujourd’hui maîtrisé ».
Selon Le Télégramme, qui a révélé l’affaire avant le communiqué d’Arkéa, les pirates ont détourné 133 millions de dollars, soit environ 118 millions d’euros. La banque n’a pas confirmé le montant dérobé par les attaquants pour le moment. D’autres sources parlent également d’un piratage de plus de 100 millions d’euros.
À lire aussi : Piratage de Binance : plus de 6 milliards de dollars de cryptos ont été volés, que s’est-il passé ?
Un butin converti en cryptos
L’argent détourné a été promptement converti en cryptomonnaies. C’est d’ailleurs un spécialiste des cryptos qui a donné l’alerte au début de la semaine. ZachXBT, célèbre enquêteur de la blockchain, a identifié la banque comme la victime présumée d’un vol de cryptomonnaies de grande échelle. L’expert a fait part de ses investigations en temps réel sur son compte Telegram, bien avant que la banque bretonne ne prenne la parole. À ce stade, Arkéa n’a donné aucun détail sur la façon dont les pirates se sont introduits dans ses systèmes informatique. L’attaque n’a pas encore été revendiquée.
La banque cherche à rassurer ses clients. Selon l’établissement, l’attaque « n’a aucune conséquence financière » pour eux, et « leurs intérêts sont pleinement protégés ». De prime abord, il semble d’ailleurs que les comptes en banque des particuliers ne sont pas concernés. Les clients n’échappent pas à quelques désagréments. « Par mesure de précaution », certaines transactions ont été temporairement suspendues. Depuis quelques heures, l’application de la banque bretonne affiche par ailleurs un message d’erreur. Il est aussi impossible d’effectuer des virements.
« La reprise de ces opérations interviendra rapidement, dans des conditions de sécurité optimales, dès lors que les dernières vérifications et mesures de sécurisation auront été réalisées », a précisé la banque à l’AFP.
À lire aussi : « Des fonds en attente » : cette nouvelle arnaque vise les Français, la Caisse des Dépôts lance l’alerte
Gare aux faux conseillers bancaires
Comme toujours après une cyberattaque médiatisée, les escrocs risquent de profiter de la situation pour piéger les Français. Les clients d’Arkéa doivent se méfier des appels, SMS ou de mails provenant de prétendus conseillers bancaires qui évoquent le piratage. Rappelez-vous qu’une banque ne vous demandera jamais d’informations sensibles, comme vos codes bancaires.

Source : Le Télégramme

articles.title: Un ciberataque golpea a supermercados franceses y pone sus sistemas de refrigeración a 50 grados
articles.text:
Durante la madrugada del 11 al 12 de octubre de 2026, varias cadenas de supermercados de Francia sufrieron un ciberataque contra sus neveras y congeladores. Los atacantes trastocaron los sistemas de refrigeración para que dieran calor en lugar de frío, con algunos equipos programados a 50 grados, y muchas tiendas tuvieron que tirar su mercancía.
Cientos de tiendas afectadas. El ataque alcanzó a cientos de establecimientos, entre ellos de Intermarché, Netto, E.Leclerc y Coopérative U, según confirmaron las cadenas a AFP. Esas tiendas utilizaban equipos de frío de un fabricante danés, que una fuente cercana al caso identificó como Danfoss, y el director general de Coopérative U, Dominique Schelcher, calificó el ataque de inédito y de una gravedad extrema.
Equipos sin actualizar. ¿Y cómo entraron? Pues Danfoss explicó a la misma agencia que la mayoría de los equipos afectados eran modelos antiguos que ya no reciben actualizaciones de seguridad, y alguno funcionaba con un firmware desactualizado. Eso sí, no detalló la vía exacta que utilizaron los atacantes.
Descubierto al abrir. Como todo ocurrió de madrugada, nadie se dio cuenta hasta la hora de apertura, cuando algunas cámaras y congeladores ya estaban a temperaturas más propias del trópico. Un supermercado de Alsacia calculó sus pérdidas en 220.000 euros, y la NOS daba por hecho que la factura nacional sería de muchos millones. Las empresas no daban cifras, aunque el consejero delegado de Intermarché, Thierry Cotillard, habló en BFM TV de decenas de millones de euros, según la agencia Reuters.
Reunión de urgencia. La mañana del 12 de octubre Danfoss reunió a los supermercados y a empresas frigoristas, según el mismo medio francés. Y la agencia francesa de ciberseguridad (ANSSI) contactó con el fabricante y empezó a buscar otras empresas afectadas, según la AFP.
El ataque coincidió además con un incidente de ciberseguridad en Albert Heijn, Etos y Gall & Gall en Países Bajos. Allí fallaron las etiquetas electrónicas de precios y el reparto de pedidos online, como explicaba la NOS sobre Albert Heijn, y el incidente también afectó a las tiendas belgas de Delhaize. Pero Ahold Delhaize, su matriz, aseguró a Reuters que no había motivos para relacionar ambos incidentes.
Foto | Brittani Burns

articles.title: Farouk Ibrahim is learning to build what people actually need
articles.text:
Farouk Ibrahim, a product engineer, once went from hostel to hostel at the University of Ibadan, in Oyo State, southwestern Nigeria, trying to sell his software.
This software, Peernet, let lecturers share learning materials with students over a private network. Ibrahim charged ₦100 ($0.074) after 20 free tries, but nobody paid; rather, students called him to unlock the app.
He couldn’t understand it.
“Why won’t you just give me ₦100?” he remembers thinking. The experience stayed with him. “Building a product is less than half the work. Getting people to care about what you’ve built is arguably the bigger challenge,” he says.
That lesson has shaped his work with startups, including OpenInsured, an AI company building a real estate data platform. In 2026, he says his work contributed to its $8 million raise, despite writing fewer than 100 lines of code that year.
“I used to hate selling. I used to hate asking people for money,” he says. “Now, selling is something I see as very important. It is the ability to make people care about what you build.”
Paper toys
Before software, Ibrahim says he made toys. Growing up in Ibadan, he repaired broken toys or made paper replacements, sometimes selling them to schoolmates for ₦5 ($0.0037). His paper laptop was his most popular invention, featuring a stick-fighting game controlled by pulling threads attached to broomsticks.
“It became very popular then, and it made me famous, actually,” he says.
He also enjoyed drawing and imagined becoming an architect, so much that his father bought cardboards for him to recreate buildings they spotted during road trips. But that ambition changed when his mother bought a Dell desktop for a remote course.
At the time, Ibrahim was about 10 years old and initially forbidden from touching the computer. But when his mother finished the course, he finally had access to it.
“It was the best gift I ever had, although it wasn’t directly gifted to me,” he says. “Or rather, it was the best thing I ever stole, if I should put it that way. And that was when I stopped drawing.”
He first used the computer to play games, but Wolfenstein, a modifiable first-person shooter, caught his attention after a friend shared game DVDs.
“I tried to learn how to modify the game,” he says. “That was actually when I started getting interested in coding and making things happen on the computer.”
His parents considered him too young for the Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME), a national exam for students seeking university admission, so he took Cambridge A-levels, where he met other students interested in computers.
“I wasn’t the only one who knew about computers,” he recalls.
He learnt about 12 programming languages, including C++, Java and C#, and built an operating system and kernel to understand how they worked.
After missing university admission on his first attempt, he spent another year at home studying computer science materials. He eventually gained admission to the University of Ibadan through direct entry, skipping his first year.
From selling software to learning the value of his skills
By his final year, Ibrahim had several software products online, including Peernet, which he modified and listed on platforms such as CodeCanyon and Envato.
“I made my first dollar online,” he says. “When people were buying the products, I thought that maybe it was just numbers going up. And then when the money dropped into my account, that’s when I knew that, oh God, I’m the next billionaire.”
Another product was RapidBazz, a Postgres-based platform with functionality similar to Firebase. Ibrahim says it attracted about 10 purchases. One buyer, a UK-based man named John, wanted to turn it into a startup.
“I took it off the platform and worked with him to develop it properly,” Ibrahim says. But they could not continue after he lost contact with John, whom he believes had suffered a major loss.
After graduating from the university in 2019, Ibrahim wanted to build products rather than take a conventional job.
“I wasn’t looking for a job; I just wanted one of my software products to blow up really,” he says.
Unfortunately, none took off as he hoped, and the COVID-19 pandemic made his finances more difficult.
“When the coronavirus came in, it dawned on me that I need to be sustainable for myself,” he says.
As he prepared for the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) in 2021, his father contacted a family friend who co-owned ICMA Professional Services, an audit and consulting firm with government clients, including Delta State. Posted to the state, Ibrahim secured a placement at its office in Asaba, the state’s capital.
ICMA used Excel to reconcile government revenue payments and identify the departments they belonged to. Ibrahim then built an application that used text processing and patterns in previous transaction descriptions to classify new payments, leaving accountants to verify the results rather than sort transactions manually.
By the end of his service year, the company wanted to retain him. Its offer included an apartment and a monthly salary of ₦200,000 ($148.7) up from the ₦30,000 ($22.31) he had initially received. Ibrahim, then 23, declined.
“I got an offer letter from them, but I wanted to do real tech stuff, not what they wanted me to do,” he says. “That experience made me realise the value of my skills and the importance of solving problems wherever I find myself. When you can connect what you know how to do to a problem that needs solving, people begin to see the value you bring as a professional.”
Learning to build with a team
After declining the offer, Ibrahim returned to Ibadan in 2022 as a full-time employee at Crop2Cash, an agritech company where he had completed his industrial training in 2018.
Crop2Cash was building a financial platform to help smallholder farmers document their activities and use the records to access grants and loans. Ibrahim built backend analytics to process the data and a targeting engine that ranked farmers by yield.
At Crop2Cash, he joined a larger team of project managers and DevOps engineers, after years of working largely alone.
“I learned collaboration because I had already been working alone all this while,” he says. “Before, everything was always done by me, because I liked the solo journey. But then collaboration changed everything. The things that come out of collaboration are usually very massive.”
He also began to appreciate the relationships that came with teamwork. “That’s actually when I knew that there was the human side to this technical thing we do,” he says, describing it as his first career family. He was there for less than a year.
When OpenAI’s ChatGPT launched in 2022, Ibrahim said he followed its development closely and began building projects that incorporated AI. The technology soon took much of his attention.
Finding his way into AI
Ibrahim had read about machine learning, but ChatGPT’s 2022 release changed how he thought about building software.
He began publishing AI prototypes on his website, fibdev.com. In 2023, one caught the attention of a UK cybersecurity company seeking a system to train financial institutions’ staff to recognise social engineering attempts.
It wanted to move beyond chatbots and simulate phone calls with bank employees. Ibrahim therefore built a demonstration connecting a conversational AI agent to a phone line, prompting the company to approach him.
“It was really exciting for me because this was my first global recognition since I met John,” he says. “This was 2023, and I am getting to speak with someone abroad again who wants me to come work with him.”
The company initially offered him $500 a month. Ibrahim asked for double, though he worried the request might cost him the opportunity. It eventually offered between $600 and $800, with the possibility of a raise if his work went well. He accepted and joined Bilic UK as an AI engineer in October 2023.
At Bilic, he worked on the social engineering simulation platform, which was piloted with financial institutions. He later became interim Chief Technology Officer while the company’s chief technology officer (CTO) was away, an experience that taught him to think beyond engineering and consider product decisions.
Convinced he could build a company of his own, Ibrahim left Bilic in March 2024 to found Mock0.com, a platform that helped e-commerce businesses build product recommendation systems and AI-powered search without developing their own models.
He applied to Y Combinator but was unsuccessful. Without the funding needed to sustain the business, Mock0 eventually ran out of money.
“I absolutely loved the idea. I was so convinced we would get into YC because, at the time, I hadn’t seen anyone else doing quite what we were doing,” he says.
After Mock0 folded, Ibrahim continued publishing AI prototypes. Founders began approaching him for help, and he started consulting for $50 to $200 an hour. The work brought him into contact with more founders.
Building for AI and real estate
One consulting connection led Ibrahim to Jide Ogunjobi, former Chief Technology Officer of the mobility startup, Moove, who was building a company in the United States called Context Data and looking for an AI engineer.
Ibrahim says Jide contacted him after someone shared his profile in a group. He initially joined as a consulting AI engineer. After three months, Jide asked him to come on full-tim, and Ibrahim joined Context Data in September 2024.
Context Data was building infrastructure that made company data available to generative AI systems and agents. Ibrahim worked across data and agents, developing techniques to help models understand that information.
“My job was to make the model understand the data, so I did some context engineering, then invented some new techniques that people really loved.”
He left Context Data in October 2025.
By January 2026, a recommendation from Julia Kingsley, a former colleague and mentor, had led him to another role. Zach Schofel, OpenInsured’s founder, was building an AI platform to analyse real estate data and brought Ibrahim on to develop its minimum viable product (MVP) for potential investors.
Ibrahim negotiated equity and salary increases tied to milestones. Schofel made an exception by hiring him remotely, he says, although the company wanted its entire team in New York.
“I needed to prove him and Julia right,” he says.
It became his hardest project. With only two engineers on the team, Ibrahim worked 13 to 15 hours a day to organise and interpret difficult real estate data.
“I would say it is my hardest project so far because the real estate data is so rough and so messed up and you have to get an AI system to understand it,” he says.
Four months after Ibrahim joined, he says OpenInsured raised a $5 million seed round. About six weeks later, it raised another $3 million.
For Ibrahim, the significance went beyond the funding. “It was not about the money. It was the fact that I worked on something that birthed that kind of money that really made the whole thing really cool,” he says.
After the funding, Ibrahim was expected to relocate to New York, but attempts to secure a US visa were unsuccessful because of the visa ban on Nigerians. Given his role and the sensitivity of the work, he says continuing remotely was not feasible. His contract ended in August 2026.
“We parted on good terms. I sold my equity and the company also showered me with gifts,” he says. “I encountered some of the most humbling problems in my entire career that made me question my ability. But I am grateful to have worked with people who challenged me and pushed my standards higher.”
Building beyond code
Building AI products was challenging, but working across time zones meant 12- 13-hour days. His offer letter described a “6-day work week grind culture”, which he initially considered his strong suit.
“I actually suffered some headaches that even paralysed some parts of me whenever I had them. The headaches were really terrible, and I would say it was quite scary,” he says.
Still, the difficult problems kept him engaged. “I love the challenge. AI has some of the most exciting problems we have ever seen. I enjoy working on these problems and how much better they make me as a builder,” he says.
He is now more conscious of the need to protect his health and no longer wants the long engineering hours.
He now helps startups and organisations build with AI while developing a platform to identify and upskill “10x plus one engineers”: people who can do more than prompt AI tools and turn founders’ ideas into products customers care about.
“Coding is no longer the reason why a company will hire you because anyone can use Claude and ChatGPT to code,” he says. “They are looking for someone they can give their idea to and tell what to build, and he would build something that customers would care about.”
Ibrahim ultimately wants to become a founder himself, although he has yet to settle on an idea. For now, he is focused on helping other founders build while figuring out what he wants to create next.

articles.title: Después de los supermercados, el último objetivo de los ciberataques en Francia son los bancos de sangre
articles.text:
Hace unos días hablábamos de que, supuestamente con ayuda de la IA, alguien había atacado los congeladores y cámaras frigoríficas de varios supermercados. Aparte del daño económico y material, ele comentario pivotaba sobre la idea de que la inteligencia artificial iba a permitir atacar dispositivos que, hasta ahora, no estaban en el punto de mira, pero no dejaban de ser frigoríficos. El problema llega cuando se atacan otros frigoríficos: esas cámaras de los bancos de sangre con muestras destinadas a transfusiones.
Y esto deja una terrible lectura: nada está a salvo y, sobre todo, no se va a respetar absolutamente nada.
Qué ha pasado. Como vemos en El País, el Gobierno francés ha comunicado que el Servicio Nacional de Sangre de Francia (EFS) ha sido atacado. Los perpetradores no han realizado el ciberataque directamente contra el EFS, sino contra los equipos de refrigeración de Coolworld, la empresa que suministra los congeladores al organismo francés.
La forma de proceder fue la misma que con los frigoríficos de los supermercados: elevar el umbral de temperatura haciendo que las cámaras pasaran de -30 grados Celsius a 110 grados. Pero claro, en lugar de polos, aquí se conservan muestras de plasma para transfusiones.
Tirita a tiempo. El Gobierno asegura que no han perdido nada porque han atajado la herida a tiempo, comentando también que no han visto consecuencias y que tanto la extracción como la distribución de sangre continúa con normalidad. Tanto la agencia nacional de ciberseguridad francesa como el Ministerio de Sanidad han puesto manos a la obra para investigar el ataque.
Cruzando la línea. Antes hablábamos de los frigoríficos en los supermercados y tengo la incómoda sensación de que puede que no se tomara esto con la seriedad que amerita. Durante esa semana se podía leer el "buah, ¿te has enterado de que han hackeado los frigoríficos del super para derretir la comida?" y es posible que no se cayera en la lectura más allá de que si se puede hackear eso, se puede hackear cualquier otra cosa que consideramos segura.
En otros ciberataques, el objetivo suele ser hacer daño robando datos para filtrarlos o venderlos en paquetes a empresas de spam. También hacerse con datos sensibles como pueden ser de identidad o de formas de pago. En este caso, parece que es un ataque que responde al objetivo único de hacer daño a algo tan delicado como unas reservas de sangre que se destinan a personas que realmente lo necesitan.
La IA otra vez en el punto de mira. A la espera de más detalles sobre el incidente, debemos volver a mencionar la inteligencia artificial. Como con el episodio de los supermercados, no está claro si hubo IA implicada o no, pero es fácil pensar que sí porque, hasta ahora, había ciertas infraestructuras que no se atacaban no porque fueran muy seguras, sino por la "pereza" que daba hacerlo.
Sistemas obsoletos con medidas y protocolos anticuados que no salía "rentable" atacar porque ese tiempo se podía invertir no en apagar un congelador, sino en entrar en un archivo en el que realmente hubiera información que se pudiera robar y vender, por ejemplo. Con las herramientas de IA, todo lo relacionado con el software se ha acelerado, desde el spam al correo hasta la creación de aplicaciones y, cómo no, buscar los puntos flacos en la seguridad.
Llevamos al menos 15 años, además, construyendo un ecosistema tanto casero como empresarial basado en el IoT porque es más fácil de gestionar en remoto, pero hemos construido todo eso sin saber que este día llegaría y, cuando ha llegado, resulta que atacar estos dispositivos se ha vuelto pan comido.
Qué toca ahora. De nuevo, a la espera de la investigación y como ha ocurrido con los supermercados de varios países europeos, no se sabe aún si la IA ha tenido algo que ver, pero es evidente que los equipos de seguridad van a tener que ampliarse para proteger absolutamente todo lo que esté conectado a Internet.
El propio Centro Nacional de Ciberseguridad de Reino Unido estima que los ataques malintencionados usando la IA se multiplicarán de cara a 2028 con el objetivo puesto en la infraestructura crítica del país. Y si alguien no pensó en los bancos de sangre, el ejemplo francés demuestra que nada está a salvo.

articles.title: Sysdig Adds Runtime Security and Governance for AI Agents
articles.text:
Without adequate governance, agentic AI threatens to autonomously, invisibly and rapidly morph from a business boon into a business disaster.
Sysdig has turned its runtime visibility skills into providing governance to agentic AI. The need is clear: “AI is moving from answering to acting. It used to be chat machines. Now agentic AI does stuff for us,” explains Loris Degioanni, Sysdig founder and CTO.
The problem is it can do more than we tell it, faster than we can control it, and has no sense of morality.
Sysdig has stepped into this space with the announcement of Sysdig AI Defense offering runtime security and governance for AI agents.
“AI has moved from answering to acting, and agents now ship code, change infrastructure, and reach into production systems at a speed no team can review by hand,” warns Sysdig. Unattended, the problem of AI agents going rogue is likely to increase over time: agents are designed with increasing autonomy, complexity and ‘reasoning’ to maximize their undoubted economic benefit. Increasing complexity increases the potential to drift into error.
Sysdig AI Defense sees and monitors every action an agent takes, from its origin to its completion. This is no simple task. Agents can assume new powers very rapidly as they seek to complete their assumed tasks. Every action an agent takes may be logged; but underlying the action, there may be five or more processes visible only to the operating system kernel. These processes could be invisibly adapting the function of the agent.
“The agent deployed in the morning isn’t always the one running in the afternoon,” warns Sysdig; and “only the kernel shows what actually ran.” If safety requires an agent action to be blocked, it must be immediate. “There is a need for solutions that operate at runtime, can operate extremely quickly, and can include response,” explains Degioanni. “For example, any blocking response must happen in real time, in line, as the action happens and before the action completes.” This is the purpose and function of Sysdig AI Defense.
“An agent can misreport a tool call, but it can’t rewrite its interactions with the system or the external world,” said Degioanni. “An agent’s own account of what it did is useful context, but it’s not evidence. When what an agent reports and what its actions show disagree, you have a detection. Watching software in real time and stopping it when it steps out of line is the core of Sysdig’s runtime foundation, and Sysdig AI Defense brings that same truth to the moment an agent acts.”
The firm claims several distinct benefits from its AI Defense product. It provides a live inventory of agents, harnesses, models, MCP servers, skills, and plugins, built from runtime telemetry. Every agent can be traced to an accountable human.
Risky agentic actions can be detected, held for human review or blocked before they can complete. Policy templates can be predefined with rules mapped to frameworks such as the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Each policy starts in alert mode and is moved into enforcement mode when the organization is ready.
Actions taken by an agent and AI Defense are recorded as they happen. A live action graph shows each step in order, pairing what an agent said it was doing with what it actually did, what it could reach, and whose authority it acted under.
The result is audit quality immutable records showing which policies were applied, when, and who signed off.
Earlier this year, the IBM Institute for Business Value reported on the current state of agentic governance. “As AI agents move from pilots to production, systems make autonomous decisions at volumes no human governance can realistically supervise,” it notes. It also warns that this problem is rapidly worsening. “By 2027, enterprises expect to deploy an average of 1,661 AI agents – a 38% increase from today. At that rate, tech leaders are tasked with managing hundreds of thousands of autonomous decisions daily. And manual governance can’t keep up with that math.”
Sysdig AI Defense is purpose-built to provide automated runtime security and governance for AI agents.

articles.title: Intel Readies "Moon Lake" and "Wildcat Lake Refresh" Built on 18A Node
articles.text:
Wednesday, November 4th 2026
Intel Readies "Moon Lake" and "Wildcat Lake Refresh" Built on 18A Node
Intel is reportedly preparing two new processor SKUs focused on extremely low-power computing. The first, called "Moon Lake," is designed as a pure low-power efficiency (LPE) core SoC. The "Moon Lake" generation features no P-Cores and up to 4 "Darkmont" LPE-Cores on the Intel 18A die. Unlike "Wildcat Lake," which includes at least 2 P-Cores, "Moon Lake" is intended to be a much smaller design for embedded devices like NAS. The base power of "Moon Lake" is reportedly rated at 6 W, similar to an SoC typically used in smartphones. The number of Xe3 cores in this SKU is unknown, but since "Wildcat Lake" has up to 2 Xe3 cores, we expect "Moon Lake" to have half of that to maintain its 6 W TDP. Intel has manufactured "Moon Lake" on its 18A node and placed it on the BGA1516 package, the same platform used by "Wildcat Lake." The official moniker for "Moon Lake" is MNL, and it could be a successor to the N-Series, like the previous "Alder Lake-N" series of low-power processors.
Additionally, Intel is preparing an overhaul of "Wildcat Lake" with the new "Wildcat Lake Refresh." When Intel launched the Core 300 Series "Wildcat Lake" earlier this year, these processors came with up to 2 P-Cores, 4 E-Cores, and up to 2 Xe3 GPU cores, with a package reaching up to 35 W. However, the new "Wildcat Lake Refresh" is expected to increase the number of P-Cores to 4 while keeping the same base microarchitecture of "Cougar Cove" and maintaining 4 "Darkmont" LPE-Cores. The integrated graphics remain similar, with up to 2 Xe3 cores. Importantly, this refresh adds support for Intel's vPro technology, meaning that enterprise customers are in for a surprise with a new low-cost option for their PCs.All three platforms—"Wildcat Lake," "Wildcat Lake Refresh," and "Moon Lake"—are reportedly well-received in the low-power computing space, as Intel is actively pushing their development. All three are based on the 18A node for manufacturing, with Intel Foundry handling the work, and they share the BGA1516 package.
Update November 4: Famous Intel leaker Jaykihn notes that "Wildcat Lake Refresh" will use 18A-P node, which is an enhanced version of the vanilla 18A, while the "Moon Lake" design remains on the regular 18A. Launch date for "Wildcat Lake Refresh" is scheduled for Q2 2027, while "Moon Lake" is arriving a bit later in Q4 2027.
Source:
				Jaykihn on X

articles.title: Apple Music vai permitir gravar vídeos de karaokê no iPhone • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Apple Music vai permitir gravar vídeos de karaokê no iPhone
Selfie Sing filma o usuário enquanto exibe letras sincronizadas e permite aplicar efeitos à voz.
A Apple está expandindo a função de karaokê do Apple Music. O novo recurso, chamado Selfie Sing, apareceu na versão beta do iOS 27.3 e permite usar a câmera frontal e as letras sincronizadas das músicas para fazer gravações.
Durante o vídeo, o usuário pode acompanhar a letra na tela enquanto canta e, depois, ajustar o volume da própria voz e aplicar efeitos de áudio. O vídeo pode ser salvo no Fotos ou compartilhado com outras pessoas, segundo o desenvolvedor Aaron Perris, do MacRumors, que compartilhou um vídeo demonstrando a função.
As novidades em preparação para a próxima versão do iOS já começam a aparecer apenas cerca de uma semana após mudanças trazidas com o iOS 27.2, com uma nova identidade visual que atingiu, inclusive, a interface do app, agora mais “sóbrio”. A assinatura do serviço vai de R$ 23,90 no plano individual para R$ 40,90 no plano familiar.
O Selfie Sing funciona como uma extensão do Apple Music Sing, recurso de karaokê lançado no iOS 16.2, em 2022, que permite reduzir o volume dos vocais originais de músicas compatíveis para cantar junto.
Com o novo modo, um botão de câmera aparece junto aos controles do Sing. Ao acioná-lo, o Apple Music abre uma interface de gravação com a câmera frontal e mantém as letras sincronizadas visíveis. Após a gravação, é possível equilibrar o volume da voz captada pelo microfone com o da música.
O Apple Music também oferece quatro efeitos para modificar a voz:
No iPhone Duo, o modo aproveita o formato dobrável de maneira diferente. Com o aparelho fechado, o usuário pode usar a câmera traseira principal para se filmar, enquanto acompanha as letras pela tela externa.
Por enquanto, aliás, o Selfie Sing aparece apenas nos iPhones. Segundo o Apple Insider, o recurso não foi encontrado em um iPad Pro com a mesma versão beta, apesar de o tablet também oferecer acesso ao Apple Music.
Mesmo nesta fase de testes, a Apple também disponibilizou uma playslit dedicada ao Selfie Sing, segundo o MacRumors. A seleção inclui músicas como “Girls Just Want to Have Fun”, de Cyndi Lauper; “Like a Virgin”,, de Madonna”; e “Baby One More Time”, de Britney Spears.
A playlist pode já aparecer para usuários do iOS 27.2, lançado oficialmente pela empresa na semana passada, mas não significa que o modo de gravação esteja liberado na versão atual. A Apple ainda não liberou o Selfie Sing na versão estável do sistema.

articles.title: Pour tester son futur missile nucléaire M51.4, la France mise sur une fusée bien plus petite
articles.text:
Les félicitations sont venues de Catherine Vautrin, ministre des Armées et des Anciens combattants, mais aussi de Patrick Pailloux, délégué général pour l’armement et patron de la direction générale de l’armement (DGA). « Une nouvelle avancée pour notre dissuasion », s’est exclamée la première, tandis que le second a salué « la réussite du nouveau tir exo-atmosphérique de la fusée-sonde française SyLEx. »
Tandis que tout le monde avait les yeux tournés vers les États-Unis, où se jouaient les élections de mi-mandat, la DGA a discrètement supervisé le tir de SyLEx dans la nuit du mardi 3 au mercredi 4 novembre 2026. Cela s’est passé dans son centre d’essais de Biscarrosse, dans les Landes. C’est le deuxième tir de SyLEx, et son premier vol opérationnel, après un vol de démonstration réussi le 28 novembre 2025.
SyLEx, qui signifie Système de Lancement d’Expériences, emportait cette fois, selon ArianeGroup, une « charge utile expérimentale majeure » au profit de la DGA et du ministère des Armées, dont la nature n’a pas été précisée. Plus généralement, ni la DGA ni ArianeGroup (qui a conçu l’engin) ni l’armée n’ont communiqué sur les caractéristiques du vol.
On sait seulement que la fusée-sonde a franchi la frontière atmosphère / espace durant son ascension (établie par convention à 100 km d’altitude), et qu’elle est restée suborbitale pour mener les expériences attendues. Autrement dit, sa vitesse ne suffisait pas pour se placer en orbite, comme le fait un satellite.
SyLEx a volé dans sa version à un seul étage. Une version à deux étages est actuellement en préparation, avec un premier vol prévu d’ici à 2027, selon ArianeGroup. Sur le papier, ArianeGroup annonce une altitude de 140 à 400 km selon la version, soit aussi haut que la Station spatiale internationale (ISS), à environ 400 km, mais sans la vitesse qui permet de rester en orbite.
SyLEx intéresse particulièrement l’armée, puisque les tests accumulés avec ce système vont aider au développement des prochaines évolutions de la dissuasion nucléaire. Catherine Vautrin a d’ailleurs salué ce tir moins d’un mois après celui d’un missile M51.3, en service depuis octobre 2025, depuis le sous-marin Le Vigilant.
Un banc d’essai volant pour la tête du M51.4
Les apports de SyLEx concernent d’abord la charge utile du M51.4, futur missile nucléaire en cours de conception depuis 2025. Confié à ArianeGroup en septembre 2025, le M51.4 doit gagner en portée, en précision et en capacité à percer les défenses adverses. La DGA a mobilisé ses radars et moyens de mesure de Biscarrosse et d’Hourtin pour suivre le tir, ainsi que ceux du bâtiment d’essais et de mesures Monge.
SyLEx ne sert pas qu’aux missiles : ArianeGroup la destine aussi à des clients civils, en particulier européens, pour des expériences en microgravité (4 à 5 minutes avec un étage, plus de 6 avec deux) ou des essais de rentrée atmosphérique.
ArianeGroup, qui l’a développée en moins de trois ans, la présente comme la seule capacité française de lancement suborbital : jusqu’à 600 kg d’expériences dans sa version à deux étages, 300 avec un seul. La France était privée de ce type d’essais depuis plusieurs décennies, au point de dépendre d’une fusée américaine pour le premier vol, en juin 2023, de son planeur hypersonique V-MaX, un engin qui vole à plus de 5 fois la vitesse du son.
« Ce lanceur national permet de tester en vol de nouvelles technologies au profit de la dissuasion française, du développement de démonstrateurs hypervéloces et d’applications civiles. Plus encore, il redote la France d’une capacité souveraine de vols suborbitaux et d’essais en haute atmosphère, dont elle était privée depuis plusieurs décennies », a réagi Catherine Vautrin.
Le tir du M51.3 depuis Le Vigilant, un sous-marin nucléaire lanceur d’engins (SNLE), le 6 octobre, servait à valider le retour du sous-marin après sa grande révision. Celui de SyLEx a permis, selon la ministre, de « conduire de nouvelles expériences essentielles au développement du missile M51.4 », dont la mise en service est attendue dans le courant de la prochaine décennie.
