articles.title: ShareChat parent Mohalla Tech records 40% rise in revenue for FY26
articles.text:
ShareChat parent Mohalla Tech records 40% rise in revenue for FY26
The company attributed the growth to its micro-drama business, which contributed Rs 293 crore in subscription revenue in its first full year. Mohalla Tech also reported narrowing EBITDA losses by 58% in FY26 and expects to turn EBITDA-positive for the full year in FY27.
Mohalla Tech, the homegrown social media company that operates ShareChat, Moj and QuickTV, reported a 40% increase in revenue in FY26 to Rs 1,016 crore, compared with Rs 723 crore in FY25.
The company said the growth was driven by its diversification into micro-dramas, which are monetised through both advertising and subscriptions. This added a third major revenue stream alongside its existing advertising and live-streaming businesses. Subscription revenue, driven by its micro-drama app QuickTV and Moj+, contributed Rs 293 crore in its first full year.
Mohalla Tech said its annual recurring revenue (ARR) had already reached Rs 1,500 crore in the first half of FY27. It also expects to close FY27 with its first-ever full-year profit at the EBITDA level, with EBITDA of nearly Rs 25 crore.
The company said its EBITDA losses narrowed by 58% to Rs 91 crore in FY26, compared with Rs 219 crore in FY25. It added that it had recorded positive cash flows for four consecutive quarters and positive EBITDA for two consecutive quarters by the end of the first half of FY27.
“After a few years of strategic discipline, we have turned the corner in our path to profitability. A year ago, we had achieved the mission of building a sustainable core business and were shifting gears to accelerate growth. Now, we are EBITDA positive, generating cash, and funding the next phase of growth entirely from our own cash flows,” said Ankush Sachdeva, Co-founder and CEO, Mohalla Tech.
While subscription revenue drove growth in FY26, the company said its advertising business was also regaining momentum. Ad revenue grew 40% year-on-year in Q2 FY27 and is expected to accelerate further during the festive season.
According to the company, daily consumption of micro-dramas grew 6.5-fold over 12 months, crossing 1 billion [units] a day.
“Our ads business in particular gained strong momentum during the last couple of quarters, and we expect it to pick up further in the upcoming festive months. Most importantly, we’re continuously improving profit margins while maintaining a strong revenue growth trajectory,” said Manohar Charan, Co-founder and CFO, Mohalla Tech.
The company said free-to-watch and ad-supported micro drama has also widened its advertiser base, across ShareChat and Moj.

articles.title: Google Calendar phishing campaign hijacks sessions, bypasses MFA
articles.text:
Since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been harvesting live Google sessions from corporate users. Every signal defenders usually rely on to judge a link returned a reassuring answer, and the operator built the chain that way on purpose.
Material Security’s Threat Research team identified the campaign and has taken down hundreds of domains used by attackers in what they have dubbed Operation CloudFire. Here’s what they learned along the way.
The lure: Google Calendar invites
The messages arrive as Google Calendar invites, sometimes delivered by BCC and often sent from an organization the recipient has already corresponded with. The pretexts are mundane: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices.
Most links point to Google itself. The typical pattern is Google’s own /url redirector with the real destination in a query parameter, though other waves used share.google and Drive file links for the same purpose. One variant used Intuit transaction notification links.
In every case, when the message is scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation displayed are legitimate and trusted.
The capture: Reverse proxy in front of a Google sign-in page
The attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the genuine Google sign-in page. The victim enters a password, receives a real prompt, and approves it, all while the operator watches the session in real time.
The server relays SMS codes, authenticator codes, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, and phone-based account recovery to Google as each one arrives, so none of the second-factor controls stop the session from being captured.
The framework behind this, Nyasher, has been documented publicly since February, after a hardcoded key was found in its JavaScript.
Why the controls don’t fire
Reputation systems answer a question about ownership: who registered the domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was assembled so that those answers were consistently benign, and it has three layers.
The first layer is Google’s redirector. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, which in some builds is the genuine widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third layer is the password-capture page itself, which has no static website to scan.
The Javascript constructs it in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. To Material’s knowledge, no one had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented.
The infrastructure is disposable by design. The initially observed campaign used many lure domains across multiple registrars, most registered only days before use. Receiving endpoints were staged one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served.
One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was registered. Blocking any single component costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon of work.
Automated Email Security for Google Workspace & Microsoft 365
Material detects and remediates phishing, BEC, and targeted attacks automatically, even after delivery.
No complex rulesets, no user quarantines, no endless manual triage.
Get a Demo
What defending it has looked like
Material has tracked the campaign since its start, following each variant as lures, gates, and receiving endpoints rotated. Since August, once the campaign was identified and detections built, Material has caught over 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%.
This has been a continuous effort as the attacker shifted their TTP’s, themes and lure text to evade static, ML and agentic detections.
The approach works because no single signal decides the outcome. Reputation alone would not have caught this, and neither would link analysis by itself, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser constructs it.
Material scores technical indicators, the apparent intent of the message, where links actually resolve, and the sending relationship behind the message. Any one of those can be enough to act on.
A detection built around one signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has spent considerable effort mapping them.
Where the analysis runs also matters. A calendar invite is a poor fit for a gateway designed to inspect mail in transit, yet much of this campaign arrives as an invite.
Material treats calendar invites as a threat surface in their own right and uses the account’s full history as context alongside the technical signals.
Where the damage lands
When the outcome is a hijacked session rather than a stolen password, the evidence appears in Workspace audit logs. A live Google session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius extends well past the inbox.
Defenders should ask two questions: who is reviewing those logs, and how quickly can they be acted on? Equally important is whether the team can revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour.
Many programs cannot, and an attacker with a live session can do a great deal in that time.
Operation CloudFire: Targeting the infrastructure
By late September, Material concluded that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents would not solve the problem alone. Detection protects customers but does nothing about the operator who is preparing the next wave.
Material’s Threat Research team therefore launched Operation CloudFire to target the infrastructure itself.
The team analyzed the gateway and backend URLs as the messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team validated the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then applied its own phishing interstitial to those destinations.
This had two effects. The attacker’s infrastructure was burned: each reported gateway and receiving endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. The broader internet also benefited.
Anyone who clicked a reported link, whether or not they were a Material customer, saw a warning rather than a credential form.
The numbers over one month
These figures come only from customers who agreed to share data with Material, so the true totals are higher. Over a month of Operation CloudFire, Material recorded:
- 68,676 campaign messages blocked
- 2,112 unique malicious URLs analyzed
- 897 unique domains taken down
- 8,570 unique compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains
- Send cadence that followed US business hours
The sender count shows how the campaign achieved its credibility. Each compromised address belonged to an account the attacker controlled before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the victim’s saved contacts, among other addresses.
Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a plausible time. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it, so every layer that scores ownership and history returned a reassuring result.
Where things stand
The phishing themes have shifted, from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Material has not seen a matching rise in other lures or TTPs, and activity from this group appears to have dispersed. The campaign looks finished.
That is a status update, not a verdict. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, the framework has been public since February, and the operator shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code.
The branch includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the brand requires dropping in a file rather than changing any code.
The operator has built the follow-on and has not activated it. Material reads the theme rotation as iteration, not retirement, and expects the next pivot to look much like this one with a different brand.
The full technical breakdown, including indicators and a timeline, is available in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there.

articles.title: Gemini for Home now plugs into AT&T’s smart security system
articles.text:
AT&T’s smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home. The company says its Connected Life system is the “first” home security product to integrate with Google Home Premium, enabling a bunch of Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events, search your video history, and more.
Gemini for Home now plugs into AT&T’s smart security system
AT&T’s Connected Life system now supports Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events and more.
With the update, Gemini for Home can provide detailed descriptions about events captured by your security cameras, such as who delivered a package and how many items they dropped off. You can also search recorded video footage using natural language questions, like “What dug up the yard last night?” or “Who let the dogs out?”, as well as review daily summaries of activity in and outside your home.
These features are only available with AT&T’s professional $29.99 / month Connected Life monitoring plan. AT&T is also adding the ability to automatically arm or disarm your home based on your proximity to your home.
AT&T launched its Connected Life system last December in partnership with Google and Abode. It’s now taking advantage of Google’s Gemini-powered Home APIs, which allow smart home brands and developers to build AI-powered features into their devices. ADT has also hinted at bringing Gemini for Home features into its security systems.

articles.title: Disgruntled software developers start ambitious open-source revolt, using AI to clone common services — OccupySaaS AI-powered project wants to kick Auth0, Salesforce, and other pricy service-as-software to the curb
articles.text:
Disgruntled software developers start ambitious open-source revolt, using AI to clone common services — OccupySaaS AI-powered project wants to kick Auth0, Salesforce, and other pricy service-as-software to the curb
Subscription exhaustion is a real thing.
AI-powered software cloning is quite the hot topic. Software companies are likely unhappy with the notion of vibe coders ganging up to try and copy their software. Simultaneously, users tired of subscription models, price hikes, and drops in software quality are more than happy to rebel, as proven by the buzz around the Adobe-replacement ArtCraft. Now, OccupySaaS is the latest user-led revolt against the software system, aiming to create clean-room, open-source reimplementations of common services using AI tools.
The initiatives already underway in the project look to replace Auth0 and Salesforce with minty fresh alternatives called ZeroAuthy and SalesCompel, respectively. Given that these services all run on their companies' servers, there are no binaries to examine and decompile — the reimplementations are done referencing available documentation, APIs, development kit behaviors, and any applicable open standards. Judging from the project website, it seemingly wants new software to acts as a API-compatible drop-in replacement where applicable.
The project puts a sharp pin on its development ethics and requirements: all work must be a fully clean-room reimplementation, with no decompiled code, no confidential information (including source code) taken from any previous employers, and no copying of UI assets or any other trademarks.
Creating software in this manner is both easier and harder than usual. On the one hand, the only thing that matters is that whichever user inputs are processed and produce the same outputs as the original software, and those behaviors are largely defined by the aforementioned specifications.
At the same time, hosted software is effectively a black box with internal behaviors and "gotchas" that aren't immediately obvious. Just as with console emulators, any drop-in replacement needs to reproduce extant API bugs to be fully compatible — looking at you, Jira.
Besides the aforementioned services, OccupySaaS intends to find replacements for services offering document-and-wiki management, issue tracking, software feature flagging, software/server observability, and customer support. Our guesses for the targeted replacements in each of those categories are Confluence, Jira, LaunchDarkly, Datadog, and Zendesk.
The language of choice is Go, picked over Rust simply because it allows for easily compiling and linking all its dependencies into the one binary that doesn't need an installer and can just be copied to a target system and executed. According to OccupySaaS, that characteristic makes it ideal for packaging into a Docker container or other forms of self-hosting.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Some people may quickly point out that the entire point of renting a SaaS to begin with is that any snafu with the code or the infrastructure is always Someone Else's Problem, and that running your own instance is backwards. However, since OccupySaaS's software is Apache 2.0-licensed, there's nothing stopping anyone from providing a service for it. Examples include Red Hat Enterprise Linux, GitLab, and of course, Wordpress.
The project appears to be the brainchild of Thomas Meadows, a software engineer with two decades of experience. In his personal homepage, he claims is strong suit is project management, which is a good skill to have in this day and age of directing AI agents towards a goal. The website reads like a manifesto, pointing out that per-seat licensing taxes growth, and that the same people who created the software are now being fired — "the software built by the 99% belongs to the 99%."
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Moroccan startup PhiDoc launches “PhD operating system” for African researchers - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Moroccan ed-tech startup PhiDoc has launched an integrated research platform designed to give African PhD candidates and early-career researchers coordinated access to funding information, mentorship and peer networks.
Founded earlier this year by Oussama Elasri and two co-founders, PhiDoc went live in September, mapping thesis progress, surfacing funding calls and conference opportunities filtered by discipline and career stage, and offering a researcher directory for networking and collaboration.
It also includes a research assistant for methodology support and connects emerging researchers with mentors across the continent.
“Across Africa, doctoral researchers face identical obstacles: limited funding visibility, isolation from peer networks, and absence of accessible mentorship,” Elasri told Disrupt Africa. “Information moves through WhatsApp groups and email forwarding, reaching some researchers months after deadlines close, or not at all.”
Elasri, a PhD researcher in management sciences at Cadi Ayyad University in Marrakech, came up with the idea after discovering an Erasmus+ opportunity in 2025, a day after it had closed. He began tracking funding calls and conferences in a spreadsheet, which colleagues shared, and within weeks dozens of researchers were using it.
“There are multiple disparate platforms globally that support researchers, but nothing specifically designed to be the all-in-one solution that gathers all researcher needs. That’s our DNA,” he said.
PhiDoc now has a community of around 1,500 researchers, and the platform is available in English, French and Arabic. It is built to work in low-bandwidth environments, functions offline, and is accessible via basic mobile phones. The startup has also opened institutional access, allowing universities and doctoral centres to give their researchers full access to the platform, and is piloting its mentorship programme with diaspora researchers.
PhiDoc makes money through institutional subscriptions for universities, doctoral schools and research labs, premium features for individual researchers, and a diaspora programme through which mentors and institutional partners can sponsor researcher access.
“Our initial pricing is designed to be accessible to researchers while being sustainable as we scale,” said Elasri. “We’re targeting unit economics that work in lower-income African markets while remaining viable.”
The startup has so far been bootstrapped by its founding team, but is in early conversations with impact investors and development finance institutions. It is working on partnerships with academic institutions and plans to expand into francophone Africa and the wider MENA region, with East and Southern Africa to follow.
“The infrastructure gap we’re solving isn’t Moroccan, it’s African and regional,” Elasri said.

articles.title: Des frigos à plus de 100°C : après les supermarchés, des pirates s’attaquent aux congélateurs du don du sang
articles.text:
Dans la nuit du dimanche 1er au lundi 2 novembre, des pirates ont pris le contrôle des systèmes de réfrigération de l’Établissement français du sang (EFS), révèlent nos confrères du Canard enchaîné. Ces chambres froides sont maintenues en permanence à -30 °C pour préserver l’intégrité des échantillons de donneurs. À distance, les pirates les ont programmées pour atteindre 110 °C. Pour y parvenir, ils ont piraté Coolworld, un prestataire qui assure la maintenance de conteneurs de stockage de l’EFS, notamment en Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, indique l’hebdomadaire.
À lire aussi : « La partie émergée d’un iceberg » : après les frigos, quels appareils risquent aussi de se faire pirater ?
Une catastrophe évitée in extremis
Bonne nouvelle, le pire a été évité. En effet, « un technicien de permanence a constaté dans la nuit de dimanche à lundi une remontée en température dans les chambres froides », explique l’Établissement français du sang au Canard enchaîné. Le technicien a alors pu agir avant que les échantillons ne soient compromis par la chaleur. Le ministère de la Santé indique qu’« il y a zéro conséquence opératoire, car la situation a été repérée » à temps.
Il n’y a eu aucune conséquence ni sur les transfusions, ni pour les patients. « Du plasma congelé destiné à la transfusion » était stocké dans les frigos qui ont été piratés. Si l’incident n’avait pas été décelé à temps, les conséquences auraient pu être dramatiques pour les poches destinées à des malades. « À cette température-là, ça devient du boudin ! », souligne un chirurgien interrogé.
« Une telle chaleur détruit les anticorps, on ne peut plus transfuser le sang », explique une salariée de l’Établissement français du sang.
Le même scénario que dans les supermarchés
Ce mode opératoire rappelle évidemment la cyberattaque qui a frappé la France à la mi-octobre. Le mois dernier, des pirates ont en effet pris le contrôle des frigos de centaines de supermarchés à travers toute la France. Les températures étaient montées jusqu’à 50 °C, ruinant des montagnes de nourriture. Selon l’ANSSI, les pirates ont exploité des « défauts de sécurisation élémentaires ».
Par ailleurs, la cyberattaque contre l’Établissement français du sang est survenue la même nuit qu’une nouvelle vague de piratage à l’encontre des frigos de supermarchés en Europe. Des centaines de frigos, répartis dans plusieurs pays européens, dont la Belgique, le Luxembourg et la Suède, se sont transformés en fournaise au beau milieu de la nuit. Pour le moment, rien n’indique que les attaques sont liées entre elles, mais la coïncidence est plus que troublante.
Pour les spécialistes de la cybersécurité, l’attaque contre le don du sang n’a rien d’une surprise. Dès la cyberattaque nationale contre la France, plusieurs d’entre eux ont redouté que le monde de la santé ne soit touché à son tour. Interrogé par 01net, Samuel Hassine, PDG de Filigran, soulignait que les mêmes boîtiers qui pilotent les frigos dans les supermarchés se trouvent aussi dans « des pharmacies hospitalières, des laboratoires et des entrepôts logistiques ». Même son de cloche du côté de Pierre-Henry Poiret, ingénieur en cybersécurité chez HarfangLab, qui souligne que les « risques dépassent la grande distribution ».

articles.title: La fusée-sonde française SyLEx a quitté l’atmosphère avec succès pour préparer le futur missile nucléaire M51.4
articles.text:
La fusée-sonde SyLEx d'ArianeGroup a réussi un tir exo-atmosphérique dans la nuit du 3 au 4 novembre, depuis Biscarrosse. Pour la DGA, ce deuxième vol marque une étape majeure vers le futur missile M51.4.
La Direction générale de l'armement (DGA) a mené avec succès, cette nuit, un tir exo-atmosphérique de la fusée-sonde SyLEx, développée par ArianeGroup, depuis son centre d’essais de Biscarrosse. Moins d'un an après le vol de démonstration, l'engin réalisait cette fois sa première mission opérationnelle, avec une charge expérimentale pour le ministère des Armées et des Anciens combattants. Selon la DGA, ce tir a permis des expériences essentielles pour le futur missile M51.4 et confirme le retour d'une capacité souveraine longtemps perdue, sur fond de dissuasion nucléaire de demain.
ArianeGroup envoie sa fusée-sonde SyLEx hors de l’atmosphère au service de la dissuasion nucléaire
C'est depuis Biscarrosse, sur le site Landes du centre DGA Essais de missiles, que SyLEx (pour Système de Lancement d'Expériences) a pris son envol. Dans sa version mono-étage, elle a réalisé un tir dit exo-atmosphérique, c'est-à-dire qu'elle a quitté l'atmosphère terrestre. Contrairement à un lanceur qui place des satellites en orbite, une fusée-sonde se contente d'un aller-retour en altitude, le temps pour ses expériences de faire leur travail en plein vol. Pour la DGA, ce tir confirme sa fiabilité comme ses performances hors de l'atmosphère.
Le tir a permis de conduire des expériences « essentielles au développement du missile M51.4 », et le ministère des Armées évoque « un nouveau jalon majeur ». Ce futur missile balistique, qui équipera les sous-marins nucléaires lanceurs d'engins (SNLE), est l'une des pièces maîtresses de la dissuasion française. Ce vol prépare plus précisément le développement de sa charge utile, c'est-à-dire la partie située au sommet du missile, celle qui emporte les têtes nucléaires. L'objectif est de la rendre la plus performante possible face aux systèmes adverses, autrement dit face aux défenses antimissiles qu'elle pourrait rencontrer.
Chez ArianeGroup, tout le monde a bien conscience de l'enjeu. « Ce vol était particulièrement important puisqu'il emportait une charge utile expérimentale majeure », insiste Vincent Péry, son directeur des programmes Défense. Concernant le calendrier, la séquence est rythmée, puisque ce tir survient moins d'un mois après le tir d'acceptation numéro 6, effectué depuis le SNLE Le Vigilant. Un automne plus qu'animé donc, et réussi, pour la dissuasion française.
Une fusée-sonde souveraine qui prépare déjà la suite
Outre la défense, SyLEx touche à la question de la souveraineté, on y revient. Selon la DGA, cet essai rend à la France une capacité de vols suborbitaux et d'essais en haute atmosphère dont elle était privée depuis plusieurs décennies. ArianeGroup va plus loin et présente SyLEx comme la seule capacité souveraine de lancement suborbital du pays. L'industriel est maître d'œuvre et rappelle avoir développé le système en moins de trois ans. La DGA en est le maître d'ouvrage. Le vol de démonstration avait eu lieu le 28 novembre 2025.
Côté fiche technique, on a ici un système qui comprend deux modèles de fusée, mono-étage et bi-étage, cette dernière n'ayant pas encore volé, ainsi qu'une base de lancement dédiée. SyLEx peut emporter jusqu'à 600 kg de charge utile et atteindre une altitude comprise entre 200 et 400 km. Selon la mission, elle peut emporter plusieurs expériences à la fois, de l'étude de la rentrée atmosphérique à celle de la microgravité (la quasi-apesanteur), en passant par les démonstrateurs hypervéloces, ces engins conçus pour voler à très grande vitesse. De quoi intéresser des clients civils mais aussi militaires sur le marché européen. Notons que l'essai a mobilisé les radars, moyens optiques et de télémesure de la DGA, répartis entre Biscarrosse, Hourtin et le bâtiment d'essais Monge.
Vincent Péry estime que ce succès « confirme la capacité d'ArianeGroup à mettre à disposition de ses clients une plateforme souveraine d'essai suborbital indispensable aux grands développements ». Et le groupe franco-européen ne compte pas s'arrêter là. « Nous continuons en parallèle à travailler avec la DGA à la prochaine étape de notre feuille de route incrémentale », poursuit-il, en visant désormais la version bi-étage.

articles.title: En visant les marques chinoises, l'Europe s'apprête à pénaliser une marque qui n'avait rien demandé
articles.text:
L’Europe veut fermer la porte aux voitures chinoises, et c’est Toyota qui risque de se coincer les doigts dedans. Ce mardi 3 novembre, Automotive News Europe a interrogé des analystes sur l’Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). Avec ce texte, Bruxelles veut réserver les aides à l’achat aux voitures électriques fabriquées en grande partie dans l’Union européenne. D’après ces analystes, la règle frapperait surtout les constructeurs dont les pièces viennent du monde entier, et gênerait à peine les marques chinoises.
Les voitures 100 % électriques, les hybrides rechargeables et les voitures à hydrogène sont concernées. Pour toucher une aide à l’achat ou une aide d’État, ou pour être achetées par une administration, elles devraient être assemblées dans l’Union européenne, et 70 % de la valeur de leurs composants (batterie exclue) devrait en provenir. Dès février, les constructeurs européens se divisaient sur la définition même du « made in Europe ». Même l’ACEA, l’association qui représente les constructeurs automobiles en Europe, émet des réserves. Elle trouve légitime de protéger les usines européennes, mais elle craint que le texte bouscule des chaînes d’approvisionnement installées depuis longtemps.
BYD et Chery sont déjà dans la place
Pedro Pacheco, vice-président de la recherche au cabinet Gartner, rappelle que les constructeurs chinois construisent déjà leurs usines en Europe. BYD prévoit de lancer la production en série de son usine de Szeged, en Hongrie, d’ici la fin de l’année, et Chery assemble des voitures en Espagne, dans une ancienne usine Nissan. Leurs modèles fabriqués sur place pourraient donc atteindre les 70 % sans trop d’efforts. Philipp Seidel, associé au bureau munichois du cabinet Arthur D. Little, estime que la loi peut faire grimper la production en Europe, mais rien ne garantit qu’elle profite d’abord aux constructeurs non chinois.
Toyota, lui, coche toutes les mauvaises cases. Le bZ4X et le C-HR+ arrivent du Japon, tandis que la variante électrique du petit Urban Cruiser vient d’Inde. Seuls ses utilitaires électriques Proace sont fabriqués en Europe, car ce sont des clones de modèles de Stellantis. En 2025, Toyota a importé, tous modèles confondus, pour 6,9 milliards d’euros de véhicules depuis le Japon.
Les opposants au texte, Toyota et Jaguar Land Rover en tête, disent qu’il va faire grimper le prix des voitures électriques. Pedro Pacheco ne croit pas à cet argument. Pour lui, certains constructeurs européens ne savent pas produire seuls une électrique abordable et doivent de toute façon réorganiser leurs chaînes d’approvisionnement. Il cite Tesla, qui fabrique le Model Y en Allemagne. En septembre, le Model Y a été la voiture la plus vendue en Europe, toutes motorisations confondues, avec 40 971 immatriculations, 55 % de plus qu’un an plus tôt, selon les chiffres provisoires du cabinet Dataforce. L’exemple montre aussi que la production locale peut profiter d’abord à une marque non européenne, ici américaine.
Philipp Seidel voit un risque plus grave. Les usines pourraient rester en Europe pendant que la recherche, le développement et l’ingénierie partent en Chine. « L’IAA néglige la façon dont fonctionnent aujourd’hui les chaînes de valeur automobiles », juge-t-il, en demandant d’autres outils pour garder les ingénieurs et les designers sur le continent. Le texte compte la valeur des pièces, sans tenir compte du pays où les voitures sont conçues.
Proposé par la Commission européenne en mars, l’Industrial Accelerator Act n’est encore qu’un projet, discuté par le Parlement européen et les États membres. Le seuil de 70 % et la façon de le calculer peuvent donc encore changer. En l’état, les voitures de l’usine hongroise de BYD pourront prétendre aux aides si elles contiennent assez de pièces européennes, alors que les électriques importées par Toyota en resteront exclues.

articles.title: Freshworks posts $18.3M net profit in Q3 of 2026
articles.text:
Freshworks posts $18.3M net profit in Q3 of 2026
Nasdaq-listed Freshworks reported a 14% year-on-year growth in Q3 2026 revenue to $245.4 million. The SaaS company also crossed $1 billion in ARR ahead of its year-end target.
Nasdaq-listed software-as-a-service (SaaS) company Freshworks reported a net profit of $18.3 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared with a loss of $4.7 million in the same period last year.
Revenue for the quarter stood at $245.4 million, marking a 14% year-on-year growth. Freshworks also said it had crossed $1 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) at the end of the third quarter, achieving the milestone ahead of its projection of reaching it by the end of 2026.
“Our momentum upmarket accelerated, with new multi-product EX (employee experience) deals increasing over 35% and partners participating in more than half of our new business. Customers want a unified platform and single data model for service operations, and they are increasingly choosing Freshworks,” said Dennis Woodside, CEO of Freshworks.
According to Freshworks, the number of customers contributing more than $100,000 in ARR stood at 1,821, an increase of 25% year-on-year. The number of customers contributing more than $50,000 in ARR rose 18% to 4,257, while those contributing more than $5,000 in ARR increased 5% to 25,498.
The company said that mid-market and enterprise customers accounted for over 60% of its total ARR.
Freshworks reported a net dollar retention (NDR) rate of 104%, unchanged from the second quarter of 2026, but down from 105% in the third quarter of 2025.
For the fourth quarter of 2026, Freshworks has projected revenue in the range of $253.5 million to $254.5 million, translating into year-on-year growth of around 14%.
For the full year 2026, the company expects revenue to be between $965 million and $966 million, representing growth of around 15%.

articles.title: Tired of Roku and the like? Spain's Titan OS just raised €40 million to provide you with an alternative. | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Titan OS, a Barcelona-based technology, entertainment and advertising company, today announced a €40 million ($46 million) financing round to further develop their smart TV Operating System.
The round saw participation from existing investors Highland Europe and Mangrove Capital Partners as well as a credit facility from funds and accounts managed by BlackRock. This follows their €50 million Series A, as reported by EU-Startups in December 2025, bringing total funding to date to €97 million ($110 million).
Hyoung-Ung Kim, CFO of Titan OS, says: “Three years after launch, Titan OS is already in millions of homes and continues to deliver strong year-on-year growth as Europe’s leading independent operating system for connected TVs.
“Investments from BlackRock alongside Highland Europe and Mangrove gives us the capital to build on that foundation, expand into new markets, and do it from a position of financial strength. Our goal is clear: to become a true global player, built from Barcelona, in a market currently dominated by US and Asian companies.”
In 2026, EU-Startups has reported further investment in adjacent marketing technologies, including Sweden’s Funnel (€67.1 million), UK-based Searchable (€11.9 million) and Dragonfly AI (€5.7 million), Portugal’s DOJO AI (€5.1 million), Sweden’s Fluencify (€3.7 million), the Netherlands’ Aizy (€2 million) and Spain’s Modelia (€1.03 million).
Together, these 2026 rounds amount to approximately €96.5 million, or €136.5 million including Titan OS’s new financing.
Laurence Garrett, General Partner at Highland Europe, adds: “Since our first investment, we’ve watched the Titan team build a rare flywheel. TV makers earn a share of the revenue their screens generate for years after the sale. Advertisers reach millions of homes across many TV brands. And unlike the walled gardens, Titan is a partner, not a competitor. That attracts more TV brands, which brings more viewers and more advertisers. We’re excited to double down.”
Founded in 2023 by entrepreneur Jacinto Roca, previously founder of Wuaki.tv (acquired by Rakuten), and his co-founders Timothy Edwards, Miquel Barba and Tobias Pfalzgraff, Titan OS offers an independent, Linux-based smart TV OS that replaces platforms like Android TV or Roku on television screens.
For TV manufacturers (like Philips and JVC), it provides customisable software and a revenue-sharing advertising model, allowing brands to earn continuous money from on-screen ads and pre-installed Free Ad-supported Streaming TV (FAST) channels. For everyday viewers, it delivers a smooth, localized user interface that bundles major global apps, live television, and free streaming content into a single smart TV home screen.
Titan OS has reportedly scaled revenues by 15 times and licensed its technology to major global TV brands including Philips, AOC, JVC, Vestel, Skyworth and Sharp.
With this new round of funding, Titan OS will strengthen its position as an independent TV OS from Europe, expand its global OEM partnerships, and invest further in product innovation and advertising technology that enhance both user experience and monetisation opportunities for its ecosystem partners.

articles.title: SonicWall warns of unpatched flaws in end-of-life GMS software
articles.text:
SonicWall warned customers of two security flaws affecting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems that will not be patched.
Global Management System (GMS) helps IT admins deploy and manage thousands of SonicWall security appliances from a single interface, but SonicWall has officially replaced it with the Network Security Manager (NSM) management platform.
The two vulnerabilities were found and reported by Pentest-Tools security researchers and affect systems running SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier.
The first GMS flaw disclosed this week is tracked as CVE-2026-109593, and it enables unauthenticated attackers with network access to vulnerable instances (running GMS 9.5.2 and earlier versions) to steal sensitive information by reading internal files.
SonicWall also flagged a second security issue (CVE-2026-109594) that can let threat actors with high privileges access or modify information stored in the GMS database through low-complexity SQL Injection attacks.
On Tuesday, SonicWall also urged customers to upgrade to NMS, as it will not release security patches because the vulnerable systems have now reached end of life.
"The affected product has reached End-of-Life (EOL). As a result, no remediation or security update will be released for these vulnerabilities," SonicWall warned on Tuesday.
"Organizations using the product should be aware of the associated security risks and are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the SonicWall Network Security Manager (NSM)."
Attackers often target SonicWall vulnerabilities in the wild and have exploited multiple ones in zero-day attacks since the start of the year.
In February, SonicWall asked customers to patch two SMA1000 zero-days (CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410) and two more (CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410) in July. It also patched three other SMA1000 flaws exploited as zero-days in September (CVE-2026-83548 and CVE-2026-83549) and October (CVE-2026-102255).
Over the last four years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added 19 SonicWall vulnerabilities to its list of actively exploited flaws, 13 of them also abused by ransomware gangs.
SonicWall serves more than 500,000 customers (including small and medium-sized businesses, large enterprises, and government agencies) in more than 215 countries and territories through a network of over 17,000 partners.

articles.title: Helium Health secures $2.5 million Google grant to tackle maternal deaths with AI
articles.text:
Helium Health, a Nigerian healthtech startup, has secured a ₦3.4 billion ($2.5 million) grant from Google.org, tech giant Google’s philanthropic arm, to deploy artificial intelligence (AI) tools that help identify pregnancy risks and improve maternal healthcare delivery in Nigeria.
The funding will support the rollout of HeliumMum, the company’s maternal health initiative that aims to reach 1.9 million pregnant women over three years. The programme will begin in Lagos, the initiative’s operational base, before expanding to Delta, Kano, and Oyo states.
Nigeria contributes nearly 10% of global maternal deaths, and Helium Health hopes its AI-powered intervention will help address this burden by identifying pregnancy complications earlier and connecting women to appropriate care, and contribute to a 30% reduction in maternal mortality.
“For the past decade, Helium Health has been building the technology and partnerships needed to improve healthcare delivery across Africa,” Dimeji Sofowora, Helium Health’s chief executive officer, said in a statement. “Through our maternal health initiatives, we’ve already reached over 3.5 million women, and Google.org’s support gives us an opportunity to build on that foundation, scale what works, and reach even more women with quality maternal healthcare.”
The grant comes three months after Adegoke Olubusi, Helium Health’s co-founder and CEO, stepped down after nearly a decade, handing leadership to Sofowora, another co-founder who assumed the role in August. The leadership change followed the departure of another co-founder, Tito Ovia, in 2022, leaving Sofowora as the last founding team member actively involved in leading the business.
Helium Health was the only Nigerian organisation selected among 15 recipients of Google.org’s $30 million Impact Challenge: AI for Government Innovation, announced in September 2026. The challenge supports organisations working with governments to use AI to improve public services, including healthcare.
The funding will finance the deployment of AI-powered clinical decision-support tools within primary maternal healthcare services. Through HeliumMum, the company wants to help community health workers identify potential pregnancy complications earlier and connect expectant mothers to appropriate healthcare providers. The system will combine AI-driven risk detection with electronic medical records and clinical decision-support tools used by healthcare providers.
Helium Health says it has already reached more than 3.5 million women through its maternal health initiatives. With the Google.org funding, it wants to reach another 1.9 million. The company will also receive technical support from Google engineers and AI product experts through a dedicated Google.org Accelerator.
“AI holds incredible potential to transform public services, but there is often a gap between promise and practice,” said Maggie Johnson, Global Head of Google.org. “By equipping the 15 selected organisations with funding and pro bono support from Google’s own AI experts, we are empowering the people closest to the problem to show what is truly possible. Together, we can ensure that AI makes a profound, positive difference in the everyday lives of communities worldwide.”
Founded in 2014 by Olubusi, Sofowora, and Ovia, Helium Health started by building electronic medical records and hospital management software to help healthcare providers digitise patient records. Over time, the company expanded and began offering tools for medical records, billing, practice management, and healthcare financing. In June 2023, Helium Health raised $30 million in a Series B funding round led by AXA IM Alts, bringing its disclosed funding at the time to about $40 million.
The grant also comes as Nigerian healthtech companies face a more challenging fundraising environment. According to TechCabal Insights’ State of Healthtech in Nigeria 2026 report, funding into the sector peaked at nearly $55 million in 2023 before falling to approximately $18 million in 2024 and $3 million in 2025. The decline is due to the high costs of building healthcare infrastructure and slow adoption of digital tools.
Google.org’s grant will help Helium Health expand beyond digitising healthcare facilities into delivering AI-powered public health services. It could also bring the company’s technology closer to primary healthcare centres and community health workers who may not have the clinical support needed to identify high-risk pregnancies early and ensure women receive timely care.
“Ultimately, we want to ensure that no woman loses her life simply because she didn’t know she was at risk or couldn’t access the care she needed,” Dr Shona Oluwatola, Head of Public Health at Helium Health, added.

articles.title: Cómo tener el mismo número de mi celular si viajo de vacaciones fuera de mi país
articles.text:
Mantener la conectividad telefónica durante viajes internacionales tradicionalmente implicaba dos opciones restrictivas: asumir las altas tarifas del roaming (itinerancia) de los operadores locales o adquirir un chip físico (SIM) en el país de destino, lo que obligaba al usuario a perder temporalmente su número telefónico original.
En 2026, la consolidación de la tecnología eSIM y las funciones de doble línea en los sistemas operativos móviles permiten conservar el número principal para llamadas y mensajes, utilizando simultáneamente un plan de datos local a bajo costo.
Qué es y cómo funciona la tecnología eSIM
La eSIM (embedded SIM) es un microchip de identidad de abonado integrado directamente en la placa base del teléfono móvil durante su fabricación. A diferencia de las tarjetas plásticas extraíbles, la eSIM no requiere manipulación física.
La activación del servicio se realiza mediante la descarga de un perfil digital, un proceso que requiere únicamente el escaneo de un código QR proporcionado por el proveedor o la introducción de un código alfanumérico en el menú de configuración de redes del dispositivo.
Esta arquitectura permite almacenar múltiples perfiles de operadores en un solo teléfono y alternar entre ellos de forma digital. La eliminación de la bandeja física para tarjetas SIM es un estándar en dispositivos de gama alta actuales, lo que convierte a la eSIM en el método principal de conectividad internacional.
Configuración de doble línea para mantener el número
Para conservar el número telefónico original sin incurrir en cobros adicionales, el usuario debe configurar el dispositivo para separar el tráfico de voz del tráfico de datos. El protocolo técnico es el siguiente:
- Mantener la línea principal activa: el perfil o tarjeta SIM del país de origen debe permanecer encendido en la configuración del teléfono, pero se debe desactivar obligatoriamente la opción de “Itinerancia de datos” (Data Roaming). Esto permite seguir recibiendo mensajes de texto (SMS), como códigos de verificación bancaria, sin generar cobros por uso de internet en el extranjero.
- Asignar la eSIM para datos: tras descargar el perfil de la eSIM de viaje, esta línea debe configurarse como la red principal y exclusiva para “Datos Celulares”.
- Llamadas por Wi-Fi (VoWiFi): si el operador de origen lo soporta, el usuario puede habilitar la función de “Llamadas por Wi-Fi”. En los dispositivos modernos, esta tecnología permite enrutar las llamadas de la línea principal utilizando la conexión a internet proporcionada por la eSIM de datos secundaria, permitiendo hacer y recibir llamadas internacionales con el número habitual sin pagar tarifas de roaming.
Proveedores de eSIM para viajeros
El ecosistema de telecomunicaciones actual cuenta con empresas tecnológicas especializadas en conectividad global diseñadas específicamente para el turismo y los viajes de negocios. Proveedores como Airalo, Holafly o Nomad comercializan paquetes de datos prepagos específicos por país o con cobertura multipaís para toda la región de América Latina y el resto del mundo.
Estos servicios operan bajo un modelo completamente digital: se contratan exclusivamente por internet o mediante aplicaciones móviles antes de iniciar el vuelo, no exigen firma de contratos físicos y eliminan la necesidad de visitar tiendas de telefonía locales. Una vez instalado el perfil, el plan de datos se activa de manera automática al momento de que el dispositivo detecta la red celular tras aterrizar en el país de destino.
Requisitos de compatibilidad
Antes de adquirir un plan de datos digital, es imprescindible realizar una auditoría de compatibilidad del equipo. El dispositivo debe cumplir dos requerimientos técnicos: integrar el hardware necesario para soportar perfiles eSIM y encontrarse liberado de fábrica, es decir, sin restricciones de red o bloqueos impuestos por el operador original.

articles.title: La psicología dice que las personas que hablan alto y a veces gritan no son agresivas; en realidad, sienten las emociones con más fuerza que el resto
articles.text:
Los gritos pueden ir asociados a emociones de todo tipo. Podemos estar entusiasmados, tener miedo o estar enfadados. Por ello, los gritos están relacionados con la expresión emocional. Sin embargo, no podemos saber qué sentimientos tiene la persona que está gritando solo por el volumen. También hay investigaciones relacionadas con esto.
Por ejemplo, en un artículo de 1996 en el Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Rainer Banse y Klaus R. Scherer) los autores analizaron 224 interpretaciones de 14 emociones por parte de actores profesionales.
El procedimiento es importante porque lo que tienen son grabaciones diseñadas para mostrar estados emocionales. De este modo pueden analizar aspectos de expresión y reconocimiento. Para poder decir que las personas que hablan alto sienten más que otras, deberíamos comparar su experiencia emocional habitual. En este caso no se hizo un análisis comparativo entre grupos de personas según su nivel habitual de volumen.
Cómo influye la forma de hablar en las emociones
Además de estos trabajos en los que se analiza el volumen de voz, también se han hecho otros en los que se manipula el estilo de habla. En un estudio de 1993, Aron W. Siegman y Stephen Boyle pidieron a los participantes que recordasen eventos personales y los relatasen utilizando diferentes estilos de habla. Cuando contaban situaciones de miedo y ansiedad utilizando un estilo de habla más rápido y alto, presentaban los mayores niveles de activación emocional (tanto subjetiva como cardiovascular). Se encontró una interacción entre expresión y experiencia.
Algo similar habían encontrado en 1990 Siegman y sus colaboradores con la ira. En este caso, los participantes contaban episodios que les provocaban enfado. Cuando utilizaban un estilo de habla rápido y fuerte, mostraban mayores niveles de ira declarada y una mayor reactividad de la presión arterial y la frecuencia cardiaca que cuando utilizaban su estilo normal. Pero estos son resultados obtenidos en tareas específicas de laboratorio.
También podría ser que se utilice el volumen como una estrategia de intimidación. En un trabajo de 2024, los autores analizaron más de 3000 vocalizaciones humanas y llevaron a cabo cuatro experimentos de percepción. Encontraron que el habla fuerte es una estrategia efectiva de comunicación de fuerza y agresividad.
Para comprender el proceso de una conversación, es importante diferenciar entre emoción y conducta. Según la Asociación Americana de Psicología, la agresión es un comportamiento dirigido a causar daño. La ira no es necesaria ni suficiente para que aparezca. Es posible que una persona tenga enfado sin agredir.
En el mismo trabajo se encontraron diferencias según la emoción. En el caso de los eventos tristes y depresivos, los mayores niveles de activación (tanto subjetiva como cardiovascular) se producían cuando los participantes hablaban lento y bajo. No es que cuanto más alto, mejor.
El ruido también cambia el volumen de la voz
También hay que tener en cuenta el contexto acústico. Existe un fenómeno llamado efecto Lombard. Consiste en que, cuando hay ruido, aumentamos involuntariamente el esfuerzo vocal para que nos oigan. Antes de pensar que alguien está mostrando una emoción porque habla fuerte, tenemos que pensar si es que está tratando de hacerse oír en un contexto ruidoso.
En un experimento (publicado en abril de 2026), los participantes (21) generaron sílabas en dos momentos de silencio y uno de ruido (80 dB). Tras el momento de ruido, pasaron 5 minutos de descanso. En el momento de ruido aumentaron la intensidad de voz en promedio en 5,2 dB. Tras el descanso, volvieron a niveles cercanos a los iniciales.

articles.title: The App Is Just the Tip: What It Takes to Build Mobile Infrastructure at Scale
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Moving response aggregation, feature-flag evaluation, and error handling off the mobile client into a server-side gateway cut product-detail render time roughly in half and reduced per-screen network calls from five-to-seven down to one.
- A backend-driven UI lets teams change what users see by editing gateway configuration instead of shipping an app release, dropping time from code-complete to majority rollout from one-to-two weeks to under four hours.
- Server-driven UI (SDUI) is not a single decision: full SDUI, hybrid, and data-only each trade adoption cost against product velocity, with a hybrid model fitting an established app with bespoke components.
- Classifying every downstream call per screen as required, preferred, or optional in a dependency-criticality matrix co-owned by engineering and product decides degradation behavior before an incident rather than during one.
- A live, high-traffic system can be migrated without a faithful staging environment by running shadow mode, comparing responses, then graduating traffic through canary stages with automated rollback tied to error-rate thresholds.
I spent six years at a large e-commerce platform, the kind with tens of millions of monthly active users, hundreds of backend services, and an Android and iOS app that had to hold it all together. For the first few years, I was an Android developer, building features that users could see and touch. Then I crossed over to the other side. I stopped writing mobile code and started building the backend infrastructure that every mobile developer on the team depended on: a gateway layer that sat between the mobile apps and everything else.
That transition changed how I think about mobile development entirely. Most conversations about mobile apps focus on the UI, the framework, and the design system. But the thing that determines whether your app feels fast, ships often, and stays stable at scale is not the app itself. It is what sits behind it.
This article is about that layer: what it does, why it exists, what it takes to design it correctly, and what happens when you try to migrate a live, high-traffic product onto it without a safety net.
The problem with smart apps
Mobile apps run on the user's device. That sounds obvious, but the implications are easy to underestimate when you're designing a system. The device has a limited battery, limited memory, and a network connection that is often unstable, slow, or both. Every piece of logic you push into the app competes for those resources.
When your app is small, this is manageable. When your app serves millions of users and interacts with hundreds of backend services, each owned by a different team, the weight of client-side logic can start to compound. The app gets slower. Crash rates climb. Battery drain increases. And every fix requires a new release, which means going through app store review, waiting for rollout, and hoping users bother to update.
To make this concrete, here is what our architecture looked like before we built the gateway:
Figure 1. Direct client-to-service communication before introducing the mobile gateway. [Source: Diagram created by the author with ChatGPT assistance.]
The mobile app knew about every downstream service. It made multiple network calls per screen, merged responses client-side, evaluated feature flags locally, and handled each service's error modes individually. A single product detail screen required calls to five or six services, and the app contained the logic to stitch those responses together into a renderable view.
The costs were measurable. On mid-range Android devices — which represented roughly 60% of our user base — the product detail screen took 2.8 seconds to render. Of that, approximately 1.1 seconds was network time (multiple sequential and parallel calls), and 0.9 seconds was client-side data transformation. The app's cold start time had crept past 4 seconds. APK size grew by roughly 2 MB per quarter, driven partly by the accumulation of client-side service integration code.
When a mobile app is primarily a client to remote services, it should own as little backend orchestration as possible. The more of that logic lives on the client, the more fragile the app becomes.
The gateway pattern: one interface, hundreds of services
We built a proxy layer that sat between all mobile clients and the rest of the platform's backend. The system had two primary responsibilities.
First, it prepared data for mobile developers so they could consume it without having to understand the complexity beneath it. A large marketplace has a sprawling backend: inventory systems, pricing engines, delivery logistics, recommendation services, payment processing, and many more. A separate team owns each, sometimes structured as a separate business unit with its own codebase and deployment pipeline.
A mobile developer building a product card screen should not need to know how to call five different services, merge their responses, handle partial failures, and transform the result into something the UI can render. The gateway did that for them.
Second, the gateway absorbed logic that would otherwise have lived in the app. Data transformations, feature flag evaluation, response aggregation, and error handling for downstream failures — all of this moved to the server.
Figure 2. Gateway-mediated architecture, with aggregation and orchestration moved to the server. [Source: Diagram created by the author with ChatGPT assistance.]
The app now makes a single request per screen. The gateway resolved which backend services to call, called them in the optimal order (parallelizing where possible), composed the response, applied feature flags and experiment variants, and returned a pre-shaped payload that the app could render with minimal processing.
Measured impact after full migration:
| Metric | Before | After | Change | 
| Product detail screen render time (p50, mid-range Android) | 2.8s | 1.4s | −50% | 
| Network calls per screen load (product detail) | 5–7 | 1 | −80% | 
| Client-side payload processing time | 900ms | <120ms | −87% | 
| App cold start time | 4.1s | 2.9s | −29% | 
| APK size growth rate | ~2 MB/quarter | ~0.8 MB/quarter | −60% | 
| Crash rate (monthly) | 0.41% | 0.26% | −37% | 
Trade-offs of the gateway pattern
This architecture is not free. Introducing a gateway creates a new critical dependency, adds a network hop (typically 5–15ms within the same data center), and requires a team to own and operate it.
Latency. The gateway adds a hop, but it removes multiple sequential client-to-service calls and replaces them with a single client-to-gateway call followed by parallel server-to-server calls. Server-to-server calls run over low-latency datacenter links rather than mobile networks, so the net latency is almost always lower. In our case, the additional gateway hop was far outweighed by the elimination of 4–6 mobile network round-trip.
Operational complexity. You now have a service that must handle all mobile traffic. This demands investment in redundancy, autoscaling, and circuit breakers from day one. We ran the gateway across multiple availability zones with a target of 99.99% uptime — stricter than any individual downstream service — because a gateway outage means a total app outage.
Coupling risk. A gateway can become a monolith if you are not careful. We avoided this by making the gateway configurable rather than code-heavy. Screen definitions were declared in configuration files, not in application code. Adding a new screen or modifying an existing one did not require deploying new gateway code; it required updating a configuration that specified which services to call, how to compose their responses, and what fallback behavior to use.
Team boundaries. The gateway team becomes a dependency for every mobile feature. We mitigated this by building a self-service model: mobile teams could define their own screen configurations, and the gateway would execute them. The gateway team owned the runtime and the framework; product teams owned their screen definitions.
My path into this work was not typical. I started as an Android developer and spent years building features in the app. Then I moved into Android infrastructure, improving the internal tooling used by other mobile developers. That gave me visibility into the pain points: where developers were struggling, where the app was doing too much, and where the boundary between client and server was drawn poorly. When I eventually crossed into backend work to design the gateway, I carried all of that mobile context with me. It is hard to build a good mobile backend abstraction without first having lived on the mobile side.
Backend-driven UI: decoupling velocity from the app store
Once we moved the bulk of the logic into the gateway, something important happened: we stopped depending on mobile app releases for most product changes.
The release cycle is one of the most underappreciated bottlenecks in mobile product development. Shipping a new version of an app means going through the Google Play or App Store review process. It means a gradual rollout over days or weeks. It means that even after rollout completes, a significant percentage of your user base will still be running older versions, because people do not reliably update their apps. Research consistently shows that users dislike frequent updates; each one costs bandwidth and time, and too many of them erode trust.
For the business, this creates a painful tension. Product teams want to iterate quickly: run experiments, tweak layouts, adjust flows based on data. But every change that lives in app code requires a release, and releases are slow. A feature that takes two days to build can take two weeks to reach most users.
Our gateway architecture resolved this by making the app a rendering layer rather than a decision-making layer. The server described what the app should display — which components to render, in what order, with what data — and the app displayed it. We could change what users saw by updating the gateway configuration without touching app code, bypassing the store, and without the user noticing anything.
If we want to change product behavior without releasing a new app, the business logic that controls that behavior needs to live on the server, not in the client.
Release velocity, before and after:
| Metric | Before gateway | After gateway | 
| Time from code-complete to 50% user rollout | 10–14 days | <4 hours | 
| Product experiments launched per month | 3–5 | 15–25 | 
| Rollback time for a broken experiment | 2–5 days (new release) | <10 minutes (config change) | 
| Percentage of changes requiring app release | ~80% | ~15% | 
| App versions active in production (trailing 30 days) | 8–12 | 3–4 | 
Once you move logic to the backend, the app becomes a canvas. You control what gets painted on it.
Backend-driven UI: pattern selection
There are several approaches to backend-driven UI, and the right choice depends on your constraints:
Full server-driven rendering (SDUI). The server sends a complete component tree: which components to render, their properties, and their ordering. The app is a generic renderer. This gives maximum server-side control but requires a mature component library on the client and careful versioning — old app versions need to handle component types gracefully that they do not recognize.
Hybrid approach. The server controls data and layout configuration (which sections appear, in what order, with what data), but the app retains ownership of how individual components render. This is easier to adopt incrementally and works well when you have an established app with complex, bespoke UI components.
Data-only gateway. The server aggregates and shapes data, but the app retains all layout and rendering decisions. This captures the performance benefits (fewer network calls, thinner payloads) without the product velocity benefits of server-controlled layout.
We chose the hybrid approach. Full SDUI offered the most flexibility but would have required a generic rendering system, strict schema versioning, and robust compatibility handling across app versions. A data-only gateway was simpler, but it would not have solved the release-cycle bottleneck for layout and experiment changes. The hybrid model gave us a middle ground: the gateway controlled screen structure — sections, ordering, visibility rules, and experiment variants — while the app retained ownership of rendering. The cost was an additional server-client contract that had to be versioned, validated, and kept backward-compatible with older app versions. Adding a new section type still required an app release; only existing sections could be reordered, hidden, or reconfigured entirely from the server.
Migrating a live system with no dry run
We designed the gateway from scratch. But the hard part was not the design. It was the migration.
The platform was a live, high-traffic application serving tens of millions of users. The existing architecture had the mobile apps talking directly to various backend services, with significant logic residing on the client. We needed to redirect all of that traffic through the new gateway, re-implement the data preparation logic server-side, and do it without users noticing a difference. No staging environment faithfully replicates production traffic at that scale. You cannot simulate millions of real users, real devices, and real networks. You test what you can, you build in observability, and then you do it live.
The migration was incremental. We moved screens and flows one at a time, following this process:
- Shadow mode. The gateway ran alongside the existing direct calls. Both paths executed, but the app only used the response from the old path. We compared the two responses on the server, logging discrepancies.
- Canary rollout. Once discrepancy rates fell below 0.1%, we routed 1% of traffic to the new path. We monitored screen load time, error rate, and downstream service call patterns for at least 48 hours.
- Graduated rollout. We increased to 5%, 25%, 50%, and 100% over one to two weeks per screen, with automated rollback triggers. If the error rate for a screen exceeded the baseline by more than 0.5 percentage points, traffic automatically reverted to the old path.
- Old path removal. After four weeks at 100% with stable metrics, we deleted the old client-side integration code.
The trickiest part was handling the long tail of edge cases that only surface at scale. A service that returns slightly different data under load. A timeout that is acceptable at the 95th percentile but catastrophic at the 99.9th. A downstream team that deploys a change without telling you, and suddenly, your gateway is sending malformed data to a fraction of your users. These are the problems that no amount of unit testing prepares you for. You learn to solve them through instrumentation, gradual rollout, and a healthy dose of paranoia.
We migrated the entire app to the new architecture while it was running. Since production conditions could not be fully replicated in advance, we relied on a carefully staged migration strategy.
Making the system reliable at scale
After the migration, my focus shifted to resilience. A gateway that sits between your entire mobile user base and every backend service is, by definition, a single point of failure. If it goes down, the app goes dark.
Making it reliable enough to earn that position required sustained, deliberate work.
The basics are well-known: redundancy, circuit breakers, timeouts, retries with backoff, and graceful degradation when downstream services fail. What I found more interesting were the less obvious challenges.
Defining "degraded" at the product level. If a recommendation service is down, should the product page show a blank recommendations section, a cached version, or no recommendations section at all? The technically correct answer depends on the product context. A missing section might appear to be a bug. A stale section might show irrelevant items. Removing the section entirely might be the cleanest option, but the product team might object because it reduces engagement. These decisions cannot be made solely by the infrastructure team. They require tight collaboration among engineering, product, and design, and need to be codified in a configuration that the gateway can act on automatically.
We built a dependency criticality matrix that classified each downstream service call per screen as required, preferred, or optional:
- Required: The screen cannot render without this data. If the call fails, the gateway returns an error to the app (e.g., product price and availability on the product detail screen).
- Preferred: The screen degrades without this data, but a fallback exists. The gateway serves cached data or a simplified response. (Example: personalized recommendations fall back to popularity-based recommendations.)
- Optional: The screen is complete without this data. If the call fails, the section is omitted. (Example: "customers also bought a carousel.)
This matrix was co-owned by engineering and product. Every new screen definition required filling it in. It eliminated ambiguity during incidents and allowed on-call engineers to focus on restoring service rather than making product judgment calls at 3 a.m.
Understanding actual capacity. Load testing helps, but production traffic patterns are not replicated by synthetic load. Real users cluster around promotions, flash sales, and time-of-day peaks in ways that create hotspots you did not anticipate. We learned to instrument aggressively and to treat capacity planning as a continuous activity. We tracked p50, p95, and p99 latencies per screen, per downstream service, and per availability zone, and reviewed them weekly.
The goal is a system that is boring in production. If you are thinking about it while it is running, something has gone wrong.
What this work requires
Building and maintaining mobile infrastructure at this level selects for a specific set of skills for a gateway engineer. You need to understand mobile constraints deeply enough to make good trade-offs for mobile developers who will never see your code. You need to understand backend systems deeply enough to anticipate failures, manage dependencies, and reason about latency budgets across dozens of services. You need enough product sense to know which degradation modes are acceptable. And you need communication skills to work across organizational boundaries, because the services your gateway depends on are owned by teams with their own priorities, release schedules, and definitions of "working correctly."
Practical takeaways
If you are building or operating a mobile application that has outgrown its original architecture, here is what I would recommend based on this experience:
- Audit where your logic lives. Map which decisions are being made in the app versus on the server. If the app is doing data aggregation, feature flag evaluation, or complex conditional rendering, those are candidates for extraction to a gateway layer.
- Start with the highest-churn screens. The screens that change most frequently in response to product experiments are the ones where backend-driven UI will pay off fastest. Migrate those first.
- Invest in observability before you migrate anything. You need per-screen, per-flow metrics for latency, error rates, and payload sizes. Without them, you are flying blind during migration.
- Define degradation behavior explicitly and collaboratively. Build a dependency-criticality matrix for product and design. Classify each downstream call as required, preferred, or optional. Do not leave this to the judgment of whoever is on call at 3 a.m.
- Choose your SDUI depth deliberately. Full server-driven rendering, hybrid, or data-only — each has different adoption costs and different payoffs. Match the approach to your team's maturity and your product's iteration cadence.
- Treat the gateway as a product, not a utility. It has users (your mobile developers), requirements (reliability, performance, developer experience), and needs investment over time. If you starve it, the costs show up in app quality.
- Staff it with people who understand both sides. The best gateway engineers are the ones who have worked on mobile and backend, because they can reason about constraints on both sides of the boundary. If you cannot find people with that dual background, invest in cross-training.
Conclusion
The mobile app is what users see. But the infrastructure behind it has an effect on how fast it loads, how often it crashes, how quickly the product team can iterate, and how gracefully it handles failure. That layer is invisible to users and often invisible to the broader engineering organization. Building it well is among the most technically demanding and business-critical work in mobile product development.
It is also, in my experience, some of the most satisfying. You are building something that every other engineer on the team depends on. When it works, everyone moves faster. When it does not, everyone feels it. That kind of accountability is a privilege, and it keeps you honest.
