articles.title: I’ve never played World of Warcraft, but a few weeks with its Dungeons & Dragons’ expansion has me convinced it’s the perfect first Universes Beyond tie-in for the popular TTRPG
articles.text:
Dungeons & Dragons’ World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion isn’t just perfect for WoW fans, every D&D player and DM should pick it up
For the Horde!
Universes Beyond has finally leapt from Magic: The Gathering and into Wizards of the Coast’s other hugely popular game, Dungeons & Dragons, with the release of its World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion — a 256-page book detailing precisely how the planet of Azeroth should be adapted into the most popular tabletop RPG.
I’ve spent the last couple of weeks devouring this new book, and while I’ll admit to already being a fan of Universes Beyond — I think it has done an amazing job of introducing my favorite trading card game to complete newcomers, and I have hopes it’ll do the same for D&D — whether you’re in my camp, or you’re someone who would rather keep your game worlds isolated, I think you’ll struggle to find complaints with this module.
Of course the book heavily focuses on the WoW-ness of the additions it makes to the TTRPG, yet so many of the new races, subclasses, monsters, and other rules could easily slot into any campaign setting. And if you need a little extra nudge, this book includes the long-awaited refresh of some fan-favorite subclasses which had yet to receive their post-2024 update (like the Swashbuckler Rogue and Way of the Drunken Master Monk, renamed to Warrior of Mystic Brews).
Though perhaps best of all, none of this excellent new content will destroy your bank balance. The Gameplay Expansion costs $59.99 / £49.99 / AU$84.99, which, while at the higher end of what D&D books sell for, feels like a reasonable price considering the amount here for players and Dungeon Masters. Plus, third-party retailers are sure to sell you this expansion for less than MSRP, especially during sales periods when D&D books are known to get a price cut.
My only disappointment is that I feel it’s not the most newcomer-friendly if you’re looking to be the Dungeon Master — the person who has to run the games. Just a quick one-shot adventure would do the trick to get the ball rolling, but as is, I’d suggest the DM is someone with D&D experience. Which is a shame considering Universes Beyond’s new-player appeal.
That said, I think this expansion is excellent no matter your affinity for WoW, but if you’re still unsure whether you should grab the World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion for Dungeons & Dragons, let me explain a little more why I love it.
A feast of flavour, and heroes
Let’s begin where this book does: Chapter 1: Character Classes. Every class in Dungeons & Dragons features in this World of Warcraft expansion to give players a guide for how the TTRPG can be adapted to fit the champions Azeroth locals will be familiar with. Admittedly, some get more attention than others, but what I loved to read was that every class gets at least something new — rather than some being ignored entirely like with other recent expansions.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
For those on the shorter end of the stick — Druids, Wizards, Fighters, Warlocks, and Rangers (though they’re a special case I’ll get back to later) — this means just some new spells, Battle Master maneuvers, or Eldritch Invocations. Though I’m not complaining after reading through their new tools.
Conjuration-focused Warlocks will love the Expendable Minions invocation, which turns downed minions into healing for you or an ally, while the new version of Mass Polymorph feels like a hilariously perfect way for a more chaotic Wizard to dispatch a surrounding army — transforming any number of terrifying foes into harmless goats.
You’ll also notice these classes, and all others, have simple guides to follow for what spells and feature choices to make so that the D&D class feels most like the World of Warcraft specializations. Some class names have changed too. Wizard is Mage, Fighter is Warrior, and Rangers are Hunters (I’ll highlight other class name variations as we go).
One step above are Monks, Paladins, Clerics (Priests), Rogues, and Barbarians (Shamans), who all get a new subclass or two, or at least a revised version of a subclass, yet to be updated since the 2024 rules update.
In that latter camp are the Swashbuckler Rogue and Drunken Master Monk, which has been renamed Warrior of Mystic Brews. As with other post-2024 rules update refreshes, these subclasses feel very familiar, though there are some mechanical tweaks here and there to better balance the player option against the other choices you could make — or, in the case of Warrior of Mystic Brews, make the subclass feel like a more distinct option in your repertoire.
The brand-new subclasses steal the show to some extent because of their freshness, and I’m desperate to play an Oath of the Holy Paladin in my next campaign. This version of the knight is far more focused on healing than fighting — fulfilling a more supportive tank role; however, I still wouldn’t want to get struck by its Divine Smite.
Finally, circling back on the Ranger’s ‘special case,’ you’ll find three so-called Hero Classes — the Death Knight, Demon Hunter, and Evoker. This never-before-seen flavor of character option is a sort of subclass, but rather than building on the existing class’s base, they tear down and rebuild some core aspects (something subclasses don’t tend to do).
For example, the Oath of the Ebon Blade Death Knight takes away the Paladin’s healing Lay on Hands and turns it into a damaging Death Coil, and transforms the heavenly Divine Smite into a demonic Runic Smite.
Calling them ‘Hero Classes’ does perhaps suggest a level of superiority; however, I haven’t necessarily felt that from the options present. These don’t feel like the new best way to play a class, merely an alternative way. The Hero Class designation just denotes that there’s a layer of complexity because the core class is altered — though I found the World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion’s guide very easy to follow, and I expect newcomers won’t struggle to build one of these three options if they follow it.
Azeroth professionals
Characters are more than their class, however.
Unfortunately, the World of Warcraft expansion doesn’t provide us with any new Backgrounds — pre-adventure origins which determine the starting skills of the player’s character — but there is a wide selection of fantastical races to select from, and various WoW factions for their party members to develop an affiliation with.
Much like classes, if there is an existing Dungeons & Dragons native — such as Dwarves or Elves — you’re asked to lift the rules from the Player’s Handbook, but races or variants of races that exist only in WoW are given bespoke traits. The monastic Pandaren can use their Inner Peace to recover more health when resting, and leave foes quaking after an attack, while Dracthyr can use their wings to glide — taking no falling damage if the drop is under 100ft, and being able to travel horizontally as they plummet.
Of course, there are also a few pages spared for mounts and creature companions — iconic World of Warcraft pets that you can ride into battle, or which offer some small buff if your friendship with them is high enough.
Factions are lifted wholesale. The Alliance and the Horde (and their respective subfactions) take center stage, but there are other groups a party may prefer to build a relationship with. There are some mechanical advantages to building renown with various factions, but they’re generally a narrative device — Dungeon Masters have a reliable quest giver in the form of friendly faction leaders; they could lock greater quest progression behind first gaining the trust of a new faction, or force players into a strained truce with rival factions to work together to achieve some greater goal (requiring careful role-playing scenarios to ensure the two sides don’t resume their hostilities).
I’ll get back to the toys and tools this Gameplay Expansion affords DMs, but finishing things off on the players' side, we need to talk about Professions.
Professions expand the basic crafting rules from the 2024 Player’s Handbook and Dungeon Master’s Guide by providing players specific guidance on how to develop their character’s foraging and item-making skills — and how to take advantage of these abilities.
For parties who spend a lot of time among civilisation, these skills aren’t going to change their games very much, I expect, but if you’re planning a campaign which ventures deep into the wilderness (which I now am after being inspired by these rules), they’ll provide a vital way for the group to replenish and upgrade their gear.
The basic idea is that crafted items and foraged resources are given specific values based on their rarity and where they were found. Collect enough resources, and you can create an item that’s worth as much as the combined value of the resources you’re using — provided they’re of the appropriate type, i.e., foraged plants and animal viscera are perfect for potions, while mined ores and animal skins are used for weapons and armour.
The rulebook stays away from generating specific recipes outside one or two examples, but it encourages DMs to bring the crafting system to life within their game world. This could involve requiring specific quantities of specific resources rather than merely generic value — i.e., a potion of waterbreathing needing five pieces of common stranglekelp, and two vials of oil extracted from the rare blackmouth fish rather than merely 100GP of parts — or turning getting a specific rare resource into a side quest — such as a Staff of Fire requiring a ruby plundered from an adult dragon’s horde, or tracking down an expert blacksmith if crafting a magic sword for the first time.
Though the rulebook encourages DMs and players to not turn their D&D adventure into a grinding slog. Repetitive actions are boring, and constantly diverting attention away from the main quest might derail the campaign into one about crafting gear with no real purpose behind the item making. Even if collecting enough of a resource might take a character a week to do in-game, this could be handled with just a couple of die rolls and only take a few minutes of real-world time — with that week either using up the character’s downtime allotment or impacting the ongoing quest if there are time-sensitive elements.
The world of Warcraft
The second half of the book is dedicated to describing the world of Azeroth. It takes you through the planet’s mythology, a brief history, and its geography — providing a quick description of key locations — before delving into a selection of iconic dungeons you could explore on your adventures, and a bestiary of foes you could face off against.
It’s very much a section dedicated to the Dungeon Master, the ‘player’ who runs the whole game for the party. Providing them with many of the tools they’ll need to manage an engaging campaign, or one-shot for the group.
Much like the rest of the book, it strikes a balance between in-depth information and leaving room for the DM’s creativity. And while it’s not the most relevant to players, I think it’s a smart idea that it’s included in this singular expansion rather than being a standalone product — making this WoW 5e release feel very approachable because you don’t need to decipher which selection of books you need; it’s just this one and the three core rulebooks (Player’s Handbook, Dungeon Master’s Guide, Monster Manual).
As a more experienced DM, I love the more light-touch approach — it provides more freedom for me to adapt the Azeroth elements for my own campaigns on or off its world — however, I do think newer Dungeon Masters will struggle with the resources here.
I understand that Dungeons & Dragons modules tend to lay things out alphabetically, but I think it would have been smarter to order the pre-made dungeons in challenge rating order so that it’s easier to find the noob-friendly expeditions. I also wish there was a more fleshed-out starter adventure that takes pre-made characters from level one to levels three or four, with guidance on how to manage running puzzles, combat encounters, and social interactions.
Coming from Magic: The Gathering, I’ve seen how Universes Beyond excels as an onboarding tool for newer players, and for the most part this World of Warcraft expansion hits the mark. However, on the actual adventure-running side, without a proper, even just a quick one-shot to guide newer Dungeon Masters through the motions of running a game, I can see it being a struggle for complete newcomers to jump into their first TTRPG game.
This one-shot would also simplify the resources you need out of the gate, because the premade character sheets and adventure could include any relevant details you’d find in the core rulebooks, like race traits and stat blocks. This reduces the barrier to entry to just this one World of Warcraft book to get into your first adventure, without removing the need to pick up the core rulebooks if you’re keen to play a full-on campaign.
As it stands, I think the World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion for Dungeons & Dragons is mostly excellent. As someone with little affinity for this Universes Beyond IP, I’ve been pleasantly surprised by how much I have been inspired by its contents, and how excited I am to use its new player options and rules in future games.
For D&D newcomers, this expansion is superb for players — the guides under each class for how to best build its WoW counterpart are a superb detail that should help remove the initial decision paralysis that can afflict newer players who aren’t 100% sure what they should choose — but I wish it offered more support to new DMs. Folks with some experience will adore the light-touch approach, but budding Dungeon Masters (especially any drawn to the game because of this Universes Beyond tie-in) would have been well served by a dedicated one-shot guide that eases them into running a game before setting them loose.
If you’re looking for an excellent gift for the D&D fan in your life as we head into the holiday season, you’ll be hard-pressed to find a better expansion pick than this. This holds true for the World of Warcraft enjoyer in your life, but consider also offering to run their first game in Azeroth for them.

articles.title: Exclusive: Top 10 largest investments by EIC in 2026 - so far | EU-Startups
articles.text:
EU-Startups has received exclusive investment data directly from our partners at the European Innovation Council (EIC), revealing the ten companies that secured the largest EIC Fund commitments during the first three quarters of the year.
From quantum computing and nuclear fusion to biotechnology and space technology, the total 85 investments made by the EIC in 2026 offer a closer look at where European public investment is flowing – with the top 10 representing the forefront of European innovation.
We’ve ranked the companies by their total EIC Fund commitments signed between January and September 2026, combining multiple investments in the same company and outlining EIC contributions from larger funding rounds involving other investors. Here are the ten biggest recipients so far!
The European Champions
€34.5 million
EnduroSat (Bulgaria): Founded in 2015 by Raycho Raychev, EnduroSat is a Bulgarian SpaceTech company making satellite technology accessible and affordable. The startup designs, manufactures and operates satellites, offering a satellite-as-a-service model that allows clients to deploy space missions without developing their own spacecraft.
Its €34.5 million EIC commitment was signed on 17 August 2026. The company subsequently announced a €182 million ($205 million) funding round in September, with the EIC among its backers.
€33.3 million
Reverion (Germany): Founded in 2022 as a spin-off from the Technical University of Munich, Reverion is developing reversible power plants that can generate electricity from gases such as biogas and hydrogen, while also converting surplus electricity into storable fuels. The company is working to make renewable energy available when solar and wind production cannot meet demand. Its EIC commitments total €33.3 million across two investments signed in June and August 2026.
EU-Startups covered Reverion’s €154.2 million Series B round in September 2026, which included participation from the EIC Fund alongside Kembara, Allianz, KfW Capital and other investors.
€30 million
Pasqal (France): Founded in 2019, Paris-based Pasqal develops quantum computers powered by neutral atoms manipulated using lasers. Its technology aims to tackle complex calculations in areas such as materials science, optimisation and pharmaceutical research. The company was co-founded by a team including Alain Aspect, the 2022 Nobel Prize winner in Physics.
Pasqal secured an EIC Fund investment of almost €30 million on 30 January 2026, when it was still a privately held quantum computing scaleup. The company subsequently went public on Nasdaq in August 2026, marking a significant milestone in its growth.
Focused Energy (Germany): Founded in 2021, Darmstadt-based Focused Energy is working to turn nuclear fusion into a commercially viable electricity source. The company uses powerful lasers to compress and heat fuel, pursuing a fusion process that could eventually generate electricity without the carbon emissions associated with fossil fuels.
The German-American startup secured an EIC commitment of almost €30 million in May 2026. That same month, it announced a €213 million ($240 million) Series A, with investors including RWE, SPRIND, Prime Movers Lab and the EIC Fund. The company aims to develop a laser-fusion power plant in Biblis, Germany, during the 2030s.
€25 million
SMART Photonics (The Netherlands): Founded in 2012 and headquartered in Eindhoven, SMART Photonics manufactures photonic integrated circuits, chips that use light to transmit and process information rather than relying exclusively on electrical signals.
Its indium phosphide technology has applications in telecommunications, data centres, artificial intelligence infrastructure and sensing. The company operates as an independent manufacturer, allowing customers to develop their own chip designs without building fabrication facilities.
SMART Photonics secured €25 million from the EIC Fund in May 2026. The investment comes as the company participates in efforts to expand European photonic chip manufacturing, including a new six-inch wafer pilot line in Eindhoven.
€20 million
Leyden Labs (The Netherlands): Founded in Amsterdam in 2020, Leyden Labs is developing nasal sprays designed to protect people against respiratory viruses, including influenza and coronaviruses.
Rather than relying entirely on traditional vaccination approaches, the company’s technology delivers broadly protective antibodies directly to the respiratory tract, where many airborne infections begin. Its research aims to develop protection against multiple viral strains, including emerging variants.
Leyden Labs received an EIC commitment of almost €20 million in April 2026. EU-Startups covered its €40 million funding round in June, which brought together the EIC Fund, Invest-NL, the Gates Foundation Strategic Investment Fund, ClavystBio and other investors.
€14 million
Quandela (France): Founded in 2017 near Paris, Quandela is building quantum computers that use photons, or particles of light, to process information. The company develops both the hardware behind these machines and the software infrastructure needed to make quantum computing accessible to researchers and businesses.
Its technology combines photonic processors, single-photon sources and cloud-based computing services. In April 2026, the company reached another milestone with the inauguration of Lucy, a photonic quantum computer installed at France’s CEA computing centre.
Quandela secured an EIC Fund commitment of almost €14 million in July 2026.
€12.5 million
AURA AERO (France): Founded in 2018, Toulouse-based AURA AERO is developing lower-emission aircraft, including electric training planes and hybrid-electric regional passenger aircraft.
Its product portfolio includes the INTEGRAL family of aircraft and ERA, a proposed hybrid-electric regional airliner. The company is also developing unmanned aerial systems as it works towards expanding production in Europe and the United States.
AURA AERO received an EIC commitment of almost €12.5 million in March 2026. In April, it announced a €50 million Series B round, backed by the EIC Fund, Bpifrance’s French Tech Souveraineté fund, Safran Corporate Ventures, Innovacom and other investors.
Quobly (France): Founded in 2022 in Grenoble, Quobly is developing silicon-based quantum computers using semiconductor manufacturing techniques. A spin-off from CEA-Leti and CNRS, the startup aims to make quantum processors easier to manufacture and integrate into existing computing infrastructure.
Its approach uses silicon qubits built with industrial semiconductor processes, potentially helping quantum computing move beyond specialised research environments.
Quobly secured an EIC Fund commitment of almost €12.5 million in May 2026. EU-Startups covered its €115 million Series A round in June, led by Bpifrance, SEALSQ and STMicroelectronics, with participation from the EIC and other investors.
Proxima Fusion (Germany): Founded in 2023 as a spin-off from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, Munich-based Proxima Fusion is developing nuclear fusion power plants using stellarators, magnetic confinement devices designed to hold extremely hot plasma in place.
The company is working towards its Alpha demonstrator, a major step in testing the technologies needed for commercial fusion energy. Its longer-term ambition is to develop power plants capable of delivering electricity at scale.
Proxima Fusion secured an EIC commitment of approximately €12.48 million in July 2026. EU-Startups covered its €411 million financing round that same month, with participation from the EIC Fund alongside investors including XTX Ventures, East X Ventures, RWE and Google.
More Information
Together, these ten companies account for approximately €224.1 million in EIC Fund investment commitments signed during the first nine months of 2026.
Interested in learning more about the EIC? Watch our interview with Momchil Sabev, Director of the European Innovation Council and SMEs Executive Agency (EISMEA).
Editor’s Note: Exclusive EIC Fund investment data shared with EU-Startups, covering Q1, Q2 and Q3 2026. Amounts have been rounded for readability, with rankings determined using the original commitment figures. These figures represent EIC Fund commitments rather than total funding rounds or confirmed cash disbursements.

articles.title: AI-Linked Breaches Mount as WorkOS, Northflank, Trigger.dev Disclose Hacks
articles.text:
AI-related cyberattacks are surging, with hackers stealing AI access keys to monetize them and using AI tools to speed up their intrusions.
Over the past month, at least a dozen AI developer platforms were hit, with the most recent incidents involving CommandCode, Northflank, Trigger.dev, Chainstack, and WorkOS.
Across all incidents, the hackers appear to have been hunting for AI access tokens they could monetize, relying on AI agents to speed up and streamline their attacks.
While part of the same industry-wide trend, the attacks do not appear to be related, and initial access varies from compromised credentials to third-party dependencies and vulnerability exploitation.
The attackers hit Andromeda, Brev (NVIDIA), CommandCode, Fireworks AI, Lightning AI, Northflank, OpenCode, Railway, Trigger.dev, Warp, and Zeabur, mainly looking for stored customer secrets.
“Intruders are reaching AI provider credentials through the intermediary layer of hosting platforms, evaluation services, and developer consoles, and recent gateway compromises show the same interest in these secrets. Because that layer holds credentials on behalf of many downstream customers, a single intrusion can expose keys for many inference accounts at once,” Cloud Security Alliance pointed out.
Per Wiz’s analysis of the incidents, the surge is caused by the rise of LLM-jacking and LLM broker infrastructure, which make the stolen AI access tokens easily monetizable and will likely attract more threat actors to credential theft.
The cybersecurity outfit notes that this demand is also driven by distillation (training a cheaper model on the outputs of a more advanced one), “notably alleged against Chinese AI labs”.
Wiz says it has observed hackers abusing enterprise credentials compromised in these attacks, including two cases that “shared an identical first unauthorized activity, which happened within 30 minutes of the reported credential access within the vendor breach.”
The company observed multiple threat actors using the same compromised keys, which “suggests a robust market for this type of credential”.
Artex used to automate attacks
This week, blockchain infrastructure and Web3 services provider Chainstack and API platform for building enterprise applications WorkOS disclosed cyberattacks that relied on the open source AI penetration testing framework Artex for automation.
Multiple companies have linked attacks attributed to the Chinese APT Storm-0940 to the use of Artex, including a recent campaign targeting ConnectWise customers.
Chainstack was hit on October 26, and the attackers accessed a development environment and parts of the company’s production environment through a third-party component.
“The attacker accessed a database containing customer account information. Information that may have been exposed includes organization names, account holder names, the email addresses of your organization’s members on Chainstack, and password hashes,” the company said this week.
Node credentials might have been exposed as well, as the attackers had access to systems storing them, and Chainstack prompted customers to rotate those credentials.
On October 30, WorkOS says, the hackers compromised an internal application used by its sales team and accessed business contact details and summaries of customer communications.
The information includes names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, company affiliations, customer account histories, sales details, customer-relationship information, customer communications, and information about customers’ use of WorkOS products.

Related: Mythos 5 Ignored Real-World Harm in July Attack
Related: ‘Context Bombs’ Cut AI Attack Success by Misleading Agents With Fake Targets

articles.title: Ada to merge with Dialpad in deal reportedly valuing firm at $600 million | BetaKit
articles.text:
Toronto-based customer service technology company Ada has confirmed that it is merging with Dialpad, a US firm that also sells AI-powered software to businesses.
The news: Ada officially announced the deal on Wednesday in an X post and blog post. The company indicated that it is combining with California-based Dialpad “to create a new leader in agentic customer communications.” According to The Globe and Mail, which first reported the deal on Tuesday, the all-share transaction is set to value Ada at approximately $600 million CAD, a fraction of the $1.2 billion USD ($1.7 million CAD) Ada was worth when it closed its Series C financing in 2021 during the peak of the pandemic tech bubble.
From the source: Allen Lau, co-founder and former CEO of Wattpad, which was one of Ada’s first customers and investors through his venture capital firm Two Small Fish Ventures, congratulated Ada’s team on the deal. “Building a startup is never a straight line,” Lau wrote in a post on X. “Mike, David, and the team navigated many challenges and built something of tremendous value.” BetaKit has reached out to both Ada and Dialpad for comment on the deal and its terms.
The context: Ada, which was founded in 2016 by co-founder and CEO Mike Murchison and former chief product architect David Hariri, got its start helping other companies set up their own customer service chatbots. Since then, the firm has reoriented to leverage large language models (LLMs) and AI agents while laying off staff. Dialpad, which has been around since 2011 and has also transformed to take advantage of recent AI advances, provides communications, contact centre, and sales engagement software to businesses. Murchison said joining forces with Dialpad will accelerate their joint product roadmap.
Final thought: Ada is competing in the AI customer service space against better-funded players like Decagon and Sierra. While the quality of AI customer service has come a long way in recent years, surveys suggest many consumers would still prefer to speak to humans over bots. Many other Canadian tech firms that previously raised money at sky-high valuations are also now struggling to grow into them amid a rapidly shifting AI landscape.
Feature image courtesy Ada.

articles.title: AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history — $17B guidance would exceed Intel's projections
articles.text:
AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history — $17B guidance would exceed Intel's projections
AI boom drives record quarterly revenue, but client and gaming business faces double-digit declines going into 2027
AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds.
As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history.
AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year.
Data center business now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue
AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%.
The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems.
AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025.
"We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth."
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Client revenue up, gaming revenue drops
AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter.
Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago.
Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%.
"In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint."
AMD projects its Client and Gaming business to contract by more than 20% sequentially in Q4 2026 as higher memory prices weaken PC demand. The company is also preparing for a double-digit decline in PC shipments in 2027, although it expects to outperform the market by concentrating on enterprise, premium consumer, and desktop processors. Unfortunately, AMD did not provide a specific revenue forecast for its Client and Gaming segment for 2027.
Embedded business strong, set to accelerate
As for AMD's Embedded business, it also demonstrated strong growth as its revenue increased by 29% year-over-year to $1.11 billion and operating income rose by 60% to $453 million. The company attributed the improvement to stronger demand from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers.
AMD expects its Embedded business to grow by double digits sequentially in Q4 2026, then experience double-digit annual revenue growth over the next several years.
"Data center build-outs are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SoCs in control plane and optical networking applications," said the head of AMD. "We remain on track to close more than eighteen billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year."
Beating Intel
For those of our readers who have been following the CPU market in general as well as AMD and Intel in particular for decades, arguably the most earth-shattering part of AMD's earnings report is its outlook for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies a 66% year-over-year increase and 27% sequential growth at the midpoint.
In contrast, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion amid weakening PC demand and manufacturing capacity constraints.
If AMD meets its guidance, its quarterly sales will surpass those of its considerably bigger rival Intel for the first time in history. In fact, AMD will not only leave Intel formally behond, but its projected advantage will be approximately $1.5 billion at the midpoint of both companies' forecasts, which is a tangible lead.
The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Smart Reports: Was Vorgesetzte jetzt über die Claude-Nutzung von Mitarbeitenden erfahren können
articles.text:
Smart Reports: Was Vorgesetzte jetzt über die Claude-Nutzung von Mitarbeitenden erfahren können
Mit „Smart Reports“ hat Anthropic eine neue Funktion angekündigt, mit der Führungskräfte theoretisch die Claude-Nutzung ihrer Mitarbeiter:innen überwachen können. Soweit zumindest die Theorie. In einem Beitrag auf der Hilfeseite weist das Unternehmen nämlich selbst darauf hin, dass die Funktion nicht dafür konzipiert wurde, individuelle Leistungen zu bewerten oder Beschäftigungsentscheidungen zu treffen. Aber wozu dienen die „Smart Reports“ dann?
Unternehmen sind von hohen Kosten überrascht
Laut einer AWS-Studie setzen nur 15 Prozent der deutschen Unternehmen KI so umfassend ein, dass daraus neue Produkte oder Prozesse entstehen. Der Trend ist sogar rückläufig, denn im Vorjahr waren es noch 21 Prozent. Ein Grund ist finanzieller Natur: So gab im Rahmen einer Umfrage des Digitalverbandes Bitkom ein Drittel der Firmen in Deutschland an, dass sie von den hohen ihres KI-Einsatzes überrascht wurden. Auch Torsten Slok, Chefökonom bei dem US-amerikanischen Vermögensverwalter und Finanzinvestor Apollo Global Management, hat in einer Analyse erklärt, dass Unternehmen außerhalb der Tech-Branche bisher nicht messbar von der Technologie profitieren. Stattdessen würde der Einsatz immer öfter als Kostenfaktor betrachtet, der die Margen belastet.
Um die Kosten im Blick zu behalten, setzen einige jetzt auf das sogenannte Modelmaxxing. Anders als beim Tokenmaxxing-Trend, bei dem es darum geht, den eigenen Verbrauch möglichst in die Höhe zu treiben, zielt das Modelmaxxing auf das genaue Gegenteil ab. Anstatt pauschal die teuersten und leistungsfähigsten Spitzenmodelle zu verwenden, nutzen Unternehmen je nach Aufgabe gezielt unterschiedliche KI-Modelle. Aus diesem Trend sind sogar schon erste „Model Routing“-Startups entstanden. Sie bieten Plattformen, die Aufgaben je nach Komplexität dem Modell zuweisen, das möglichst kosteneffizient arbeitet. Andere haben begonnen, ihren Tokenverbrauch zu tracken. Auch die neue Analysefunktion von Anthropic setzt genau hier an.
„Smart Reports“ soll besseren Überblick bieten
Laut Unternehmensangaben können die neuen, smarten Berichte Einblick in unterschiedliche Bereiche geben. Sie zeigen zum Beispiel, wie ein Team Claude konkret nutzt und welche Aufgaben erledigt werden. Dabei wird auch ersichtlich, welche Kosten zum Listenpreis anfallen, wo es zu Reibungsverlusten kommt und welche wiederkehrenden Muster sich effizienter bündeln lassen. Die Funktion steht Enterprise-Kund:innen kostenlos zur Verfügung, ist aber standardmäßig deaktiviert. Jedes Unternehmen kann monatlich bis zu zehn Berichte erstellen.
Nur autorisierte Führungskräfte haben Zugriff auf die Funktion. Sie legen fest, was analysiert wird – etwa ein bestimmter Zeitraum oder die Arbeit eines Teams. „Claude liest dann eine Stichprobe der Transkripte in diesem Umfang, gruppiert sie nach Arbeitsabläufen und Ausgabetypen, ordnet jeder Gruppe die entsprechenden Kosten zu und fasst die Ergebnisse zusammen“, heißt es in dem Anthropic-Beitrag. Sitzungen, die Claude als vertraulich einstuft, sollen nur in die aggregierte Analyse einfließen und keine persönlichen Details enthalten. Anthropic weist darauf hin, dass dieser Einblick nicht der individuellen Beurteilung einzelner Mitarbeiter:innen oder Teams dienen soll. Trotzdem lassen die „Smart Reports“ Rückschlüsse auf ihre Effizienz zu.
Welche Rolle spielt der geplante Börsengang?
Laut Futurism könnte die neue Funktion ein Versuch von Anthropic sein, neue Unternehmenskund:innen zu gewinnen, die bisher Probleme mit der Kostenkontrolle ihres KI-Einsatzes hatten. Medienberichten zufolge sollen diese rund 80 Prozent des Umsatzes des Claude-Anbieters ausmachen. Neue Funktionen, die gezielt die Bedürfnisse dieser Zielgruppe ansprechen, könnten daher im Vorfeld des Börsengangs eine wichtige Rolle spielen.

articles.title: Nothing teases a screen-free AI device ahead of launch next month
articles.text:
Nothing CEO Carl Pei said in a post on X that the company’s launching its first AI device in December. That’s just a little over a year after Pei announced plans for “AI-native” devices and an AI operating system. He didn’t give away much about what exactly the new device is, only that one feature it won’t have is a screen:
Nothing teases a screen-free AI device ahead of launch next month
CEO Carl Pei says Nothing’s first ‘AI-native’ device ‘couldn’t have been an app.’
“Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”
Pei shared an image with the post that says “NOTHING(R)” in the top left corner, above an ambiguous black rounded corner. Last month, a rumor claimed Nothing is planning to launch two pairs of AI smart glasses, including one without cameras, and an earlier rumor said it’s “repositioning itself as an AI-first company” with a shift to AI accessories.
Nothing’s AI device wouldn’t be the first screen-free AI gadget, following the likes of the Humane AI pin, the Friend, and even AI stuffed animals. OpenAI is also reportedly working on an AI smart speaker with Jony Ive. Pei alluded to earlier AI devices, saying, “the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life.” He added, “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end.”

articles.title: Telescópio da NASA cai na Terra após 22 anos no espaço
articles.text:
O telescópio espacial Swift, da NASA, encerrou sua trajetória de mais de duas décadas no espaço nesta quarta-feira (4). O observatório reentrou na atmosfera terrestre de maneira descontrolada, três meses depois de uma tentativa de resgate realizada por uma empresa privada fracassar.
Batizado oficialmente de Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, o equipamento foi lançado em novembro de 2004 para estudar explosões de raios gama, alguns dos fenômenos mais energéticos do Universo.
Segundo informações citadas pelo Space.com, o telescópio reentrou na atmosfera às 9h39 (horário de Brasília) sobre o norte de Sumatra (Indonésia). O equipamento pesava aproximadamente 1.450 kg e tinha dimensões semelhantes às de um micro-ônibus.
A maior parte da estrutura deveria se desintegrar durante a passagem pela atmosfera. Antes da reentrada, a NASA estimou em apenas uma chance em 2,1 mil a possibilidade de algum fragmento sobrevivente atingir uma pessoa na superfície terrestre.
Telescópio deveria funcionar por apenas dois anos
- O Swift foi desenvolvido inicialmente para uma missão de dois anos, com o objetivo de identificar explosões de raios gama, determinar suas posições e direcionar rapidamente seus instrumentos para observar os locais dos eventos;
- A agilidade era fundamental: o observatório conseguia realizar esse processo em aproximadamente um minuto, permitindo registrar fenômenos cujos sinais posteriores desapareciam rapidamente;
- O desempenho superou as expectativas. O equipamento continuou realizando observações científicas por cerca de 22 anos, aproximadamente dez vezes mais do que o período inicialmente previsto;
- Ao longo de sua trajetória, o telescópio identificou mais de duas mil explosões de raios gama e 1,4 mil supernovas. Também estudou buracos negros, asteroides, cometas e outros fenômenos astronômicos;
- Sua última observação científica ocorreu em 20 de outubro de 2026.
Leia mais:
Tentativa de resgate fracassou em setembro
O retorno à Terra poderia ter sido adiado. Em setembro de 2025, a NASA concedeu contrato de US$ 30 milhões (aproximadamente R$ 165 milhões) à empresa americana Katalyst Space para desenvolver uma missão robótica capaz de elevar a órbita do Swift.
O observatório estava perdendo altitude gradualmente por causa do arrasto atmosférico e não possuía propulsores próprios para compensar esse efeito.
Para realizar o resgate, a empresa desenvolveu a LINK, espaçonave robótica com três braços e dimensões semelhantes às de uma geladeira. O equipamento foi lançado em 3 de julho de 2026, com o objetivo de alcançar o Swift em agosto.
A operação, entretanto, não aconteceu como planejado. A LINK apresentou problemas no sistema de propulsão e nas rodas de reação responsáveis por manter sua orientação no espaço, impedindo o encontro com o telescópio. A própria espaçonave de resgate acabou retornando à Terra em 25 de setembro.
Apesar do resultado, a NASA considerou que a iniciativa trouxe aprendizados importantes para futuras operações de manutenção e extensão da vida útil de satélites.
Queda de satélites deve se tornar mais frequente
A reentrada do Swift não é um acontecimento isolado. Segundo um relatório de 2025 citado pelo Space.com, pelo menos três objetos de grande porte — satélites desativados ou partes de foguetes — retornam à atmosfera terrestre diariamente, em média.
A tendência é que esse número aumente nos próximos anos, à medida que a humanidade amplia a quantidade de satélites em órbita, especialmente por meio de megaconstelações.
O fim da missão Swift, portanto, também evidencia um desafio crescente para a atividade espacial: administrar a quantidade cada vez maior de equipamentos que permanecem ao redor do planeta e planejar o destino dessas estruturas quando deixam de funcionar.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
articles.text:
What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
Don’t expect huge reversals right away, but we could see more support for renewables.
I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.
While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.
Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans.Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before.
What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second
Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto.
So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election.
There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process.
The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump.
With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations.
Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action. Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout.
Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4.
And AI critics fared well in their races, too. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly.
We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election. But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change. We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.

articles.title: AMD posts record $13.4 billion revenue as AI boom fuels growth, but gaming sales are down 40%
articles.text:
Bottom line: AMD's Instinct accelerators and Epyc server processors pushed the company's third-quarter 2026 revenue to a record $13.4 billion, up 97% from a year earlier. The quarter showed how quickly AMD is becoming an AI infrastructure company, while the demand behind that shift is hurting the consumer hardware side of its business.
The data center segment, which includes both product lines, produced $8.5 billion of the total, or about 63% of net revenue. AMD expects to set another record next quarter with about $17 billion in revenue.
AMD's gaming revenue fell 40% from a year ago to $773 million, as AI data centers buy up memory and other components and push up prices on the PCs and consoles that use AMD chips.
CEO Lisa Su called the quarter "the largest and most profitable in our history" on Tuesday's earnings call. She said AMD expects revenue to "grow more than 80% in 2027," and added that "data center will be the largest contributor."
CFO Jean Hu went further when asked about the company's revenue mix. "Looking ahead of 2027, we actually think our data center business will be more than 80% of total company revenue," she said.
The numbers already point that way. AMD's total revenue rose $1.9 billion from the second quarter, and $1.8 billion of that came from its data center business. For the past couple of years, the company's overall growth has closely followed its server and accelerator sales.
AMD's combined Client and Gaming segment brought in $3.7 billion, down 8% from a year earlier. The Client business, which sells Ryzen processors, grew 7% to $2.9 billion. AMD said that growth came mainly from strong sales of Ryzen mobile processors for laptops and mini PCs. Its desktop processors and graphics cards, which have been hit by higher memory and component costs, did not drive the gain.
The gaming decline came from lower semi-custom and graphics revenue. Semi-custom covers the chips AMD designs for Sony's PlayStation 5 and Microsoft's Xbox Series X|S. It also includes the mobile systems-on-chip in handheld PCs such as Valve's Steam Deck, the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X and the Lenovo Legion Go 2. The graphics side includes desktop Radeon RX 9000 series GPUs. Prices for all of these products have risen sharply over the past year.
Credit: App Economy Insights
Su said the increases have slowed sales. "Our view is, this is one of those times – when, you know, component prices go up, it affects overall system pricing. One would expect the consumer markets to be more sensitive to that, and so we have seen a bit of a slowdown in the sell-through," she said.
AMD is not expecting conditions to improve soon. The company is planning for the 2027 PC market to "decline by a double-digit percentage." Su said, "We are planning with the current environment for a down year for 2027."
Other chipmakers expect the shortage to last as well. Intel has said it does not expect the memory shortage to improve next year. SK Hynix expects it to last until 2030.
AMD still expects to beat the shrinking market. It is counting on its Ryzen roadmap, which appears to include consumer Zen 6 processors due next year, and a larger presence among commercial PC buyers.
One part of the graphics business is growing. The Radeon AI PRO Series, aimed at workstations and AI work, is growing strongly, and AMD expects that to continue. The cards are outperforming the rest of the GPU lineup.
If Hu's forecast holds, AMD's results will soon depend mostly on server and accelerator sales.

articles.title: Women TechEU Allies: supporting women-led DeepTech startups across Europe | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Women TechEU is a European Union initiative that supports the growth of women-led DeepTech startups across Europe. Between 2026 and 2028, the programme aims to support 160 startups through grants of €75,000 each, alongside mentoring, training, expert guidance, networking, and opportunities to connect with investors and other European funding programmes.
To extend this support beyond the programme itself, Women TechEU has created the Allies network, bringing together organisations that want to help women-led DeepTech startups grow. The network includes investors, technology companies, innovation organisations, media partners, EU projects, and public institutions.
Who are the Women TechEU Allies?
The Women TechEU Allies network brings together organisations from across Europe that can offer startups valuable connections, expertise, resources, and visibility.
Its members include investors such as Alma Angels, Antler, and Playfair Capital, which help connect startups with investment opportunities and funding networks.
Technology companies and ecosystem organisations such as Microsoft, FundingBox, Women in Tech, the Western Balkan Startup Alliance, allWomen, Impulse4Women, and WomenTechIceland contribute through mentoring, knowledge sharing, and access to entrepreneurial communities.
Media and event partners, including TechBBQ, Web Summit, and Wolves Summit, help increase the visibility of women-led DeepTech startups. European initiatives such as EIT Deep Tech Talent, PQreact, and Ready2Scale also participate, supporting collaboration and access to additional opportunities.
Together, these organisations help create a stronger network of support for women entrepreneurs across Europe.
What does being an ally involve?
Becoming a Women TechEU ally means joining this network and contributing to the growth of women-led DeepTech startups.
Allies can support startups in different ways, including offering mentoring, sharing business and funding opportunities, making introductions to investors or corporate partners, and promoting women-led innovations through their networks.
In return, Allies gain access to the Women TechEU Partner-Hub, an online platform where startups, investors, companies, and other ecosystem organisations can connect and collaborate.
Through the Partner-Hub and the wider network, Allies can:
- Connect with women-led DeepTech startups and other European innovation stakeholders.
- Participate in investment events, corporate challenges, meetups, and networking activities.
- Receive a dedicated ally badge on their Partner-Hub profile.
- Gain visibility through Women TechEU’s website and social media channels.
- Receive a communications pack to help promote Women TechEU within their own networks.
How to become a Women TechEU ally
Joining the Allies network is a straightforward process.
First, interested organisations register on the Women TechEU Partner-Hub, the programme’s online networking platform. During registration, they simply select the option indicating that they would like to become an ally.
Within one week, the Women TechEU Helpdesk team contacts them with further information and a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). This is a document that sets out the collaboration between Women TechEU and the organisation.
Once both parties sign the MoU, the organisation officially becomes a Women TechEU ally and can take part in the network’s activities.
The Partner-Hub therefore serves two purposes: it is where organisations express their interest in becoming Allies, and it is also the online space they use to connect with startups and other members of the Women TechEU community.
By joining the Allies network, organisations can contribute their expertise, connections, and resources to help more women-led DeepTech startups access opportunities and grow across Europe.
Interested in becoming an ally? Visit the Women TechEU website to learn more and access the Partner-Hub.
Funded by the European Union. Views and opinions expressed are however those of the author(s) only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union or the European Innovation Council and SMEs Executive Agency (EISMEA). Neither the European Union nor the granting authority can be held responsible for them.
The Women TechEU scheme is an EU-funded project supporting women leading deep tech startup companies from Europe. As part of the consortium team implementing the programme, our mission is to foster inclusive innovation by supporting women-led startups, including under-represented deep tech sectors and European regions. We believe that diversity drives innovation, and we are here to provide women in deep tech with more opportunities, resources, and support in order to build market-shaping companies at global level.
Between 2026-2028, the current project consortium will run a continuous open call with 4 cut-off dates. Following a rigorous evaluation process, 160 total beneficiaries will be selected. Each beneficiary will receive €75k grants (non-dilutive finance), as well as a tailored package of mentorship, training, expert guidance, matchmaking and networking opportunities, and support in bridging the gap to other EIC funding and support schemes.

articles.title: Certified Android TV manufacturer put unauthorized backdoor in 1.3 million set-top boxes, Google reveals — OEM sold access to criminal affiliates, used massive network as botnet for ad fraud, residential proxy
articles.text:
Certified Android TV manufacturer put unauthorized backdoor in 1.3 million set-top boxes, Google reveals — OEM sold access to criminal affiliates, used massive network as botnet for ad fraud, residential proxy
The company has been getting away with it for years, too.
Google just shut down a massive botnet operation involving an OEM and ODM manufacturer. According to the company blog, Videostrong Technology Co., which was a certified Android TV partner, purposefully installed a backdoor into 1.3 million set-top boxes and then sold access to criminal affiliates. This allowed for the installation of hidden software that the bad actors could use to conduct ad fraud, build residential proxy networks, and even remotely install malware on the device itself to target the end-user.
“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the company said in the Google Cloud blog post. It also added, “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”
While Google did not mention when Videostrong started loading malware into its products, the company said that the pre-installed malware evolved into a complex, three-stage design in 2024. This meant that the manufacturer has been exploiting millions of devices for years now, with the latest developments designed to make the malware more resilient and allow for multiple bad actors to take advantage of the system. Even though the company has already terminated its business relationship with Videostrong, the open-source nature of Android means that it could continue using the operating system on its products.
There have been supply chain attacks in the past, wherein a third-party compromises a trusted product to steal data, like some Ledger hardware wallets that have been sold by a reseller in Southeast Asia and Europe. Although Google did not characterize this as a supply chain attack, as it was perpetrated by the manufacturer itself and not a third-party operator, it still compromised a supposedly trusted operating system, leading to millions of victims. This incident also shows how even the simplest of devices can be used to execute complicated attacks, like how a Chinese couple hid a PC behind a fridge in a Japanese hotel and targeted 2.4 million victims.

articles.title: Beyond The Chip: How AI Is Reshaping Semiconductor Design And Manufacturing
articles.text:
Power delivery, connectivity, advanced packaging, and supply chain resilience are emerging as the primary constraints on AI scaling.
While AI is transforming nearly every industry, one of its most significant impacts is happening behind the scenes, inside the semiconductor factories responsible for building the chips that power today’s AI revolution.
During a recent presentation at the Global Semiconductor Alliance (GSA) European Executive Forum, I discussed how the conversation around AI scale is evolving. For years, the semiconductor industry focused primarily on transistor scaling. Today, however, the biggest challenges facing AI designers extend far beyond the transistor. Power delivery, connectivity, advanced packaging, and supply chain resilience are emerging as the primary constraints on AI scaling.
At Intel Foundry, we’re addressing these challenges on two fronts. First, we’re developing advanced process and packaging technologies that help customers build increasingly capable AI systems. Second, we’re using AI and machine learning (ML) throughout our technology development and manufacturing operations to improve quality, accelerate yield learning, and help customers bring products to market faster.
Three major AI trends are shaping what modern silicon must deliver:
Agentic AI introduces multistep reasoning workloads that are far less predictable than traditional computing. Autonomous agents place new demands on power delivery and high-performance connectivity, making efficient scaling increasingly important.
Physical AI brings intelligence to edge devices and real-world systems. Scalable AI-enabled automation and modeling are essential for cost-effective, high-yield manufacturing. The foundry industry increasingly views both agentic AI and physical AI as significant long-term growth drivers.
Sovereign AI initiatives are increasing demand for secure, resilient, and geographically diverse manufacturing and supply chains to support both business continuity and national security needs. By maintaining Intel Foundry’s production capabilities across North America, Europe, and Asia, customers gain flexibility in determining where their products are manufactured while improving supply chain resilience and security.
A decade ago, the semiconductor industry largely focused on the system-on-chip (SoC) model, where a single chip integrated as much functionality as possible. Today, innovation has shifted toward a system of chips, using chiplet architectures that combine multiple specialized dies, memory stacks, and accelerators into a single solution. This approach provides greater modularity, scalability, and faster innovation cycles while enabling the performance required for advanced AI workloads.
At the same time, scaling is no longer simply a matter of shrinking transistors. The industry is increasingly focused on optimizing performance across the entire system, from compute and memory to packaging and interconnects. Advanced process technologies such as gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, including Intel 18A with RibbonFET GAA technology, provide improved electrostatic control and support scaling beyond traditional FinFET architectures.
Power delivery also has been reimagined. Intel 18A uses PowerVia, our backside power delivery technology that routes power through the back of the wafer rather than sharing frontside interconnect layers with signal routing. By separating power and signal paths, PowerVia reduces resistance, voltage drop, and power delivery noise. Combined with high-density metal-insulator-metal (MIM) capacitors, the architecture improves power integrity. PowerVia delivers up to a 10% increase in cell utilization¹ and a 4% improvement in ISO-power performance.² Connection to the transistor layer is enabled through innovative nano through-silicon vias (TSVs) that are approximately 500 times smaller than conventional TSVs.
While backside power adds manufacturing complexity, Intel Foundry optimized the overall cost structure by maintaining 32 nm lower-metal pitches on the frontside, enabling direct-print patterning rather than more expensive multi-patterning approaches. This balanced architecture allows Intel 18A and Intel 18A-P to deliver improved performance-per-watt and more efficient power delivery for AI-era workloads while remaining cost competitive. Intel 18A with PowerVia can provide approximately 18% performance-per-watt improvement versus Intel 3.³ Now in risk production, Intel 18A-P is expected to deliver an additional 9% performance-per-watt improvement over Intel 18A⁴ (see the Intel 18A family technical brief for details).
As systems become increasingly modular, chips must communicate efficiently with one another. This is where Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) plays a critical role. UCIe provides a standardized interconnect for high-bandwidth, low-latency communication between chiplets, simplifying integration and enabling more scalable heterogeneous systems.
Advanced packaging serves as the glue that connects all these technologies together. A complete AI package may combine I/O dies, advanced logic silicon, HBM, 2.5D integration, and 3D integration. Intel Foundry supports these designs through technologies including Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge-T (EMIB-T), Foveros, and Foveros Direct.
EMIB-T incorporates power-transfer capabilities directly into the bridge structure, helping improve power delivery efficiency and reduce inductive power droop in multi-die AI systems. It can also reduce package material requirements by eliminating the need for a full silicon interposer in many applications.
Foveros Direct uses hybrid bonding to enable 3D integration, allowing designers to stack leading-edge compute dies on optimized base dies. This approach helps customers balance performance, power efficiency, and total cost of ownership (TCO) by placing each function on the process technology best suited to its requirements.
While AI is creating new challenges for chip designers, it is also helping solve many of the challenges associated with manufacturing advanced semiconductors.
At Intel Foundry, AI and ML are already deeply integrated into our manufacturing workflows, actively supporting how we develop and manufacture leading-edge process technologies (see Figure 1). One area where AI is delivering value is design technology co-optimization (DTCO). Advanced process nodes involve enormous design spaces with countless tradeoffs between power, performance, and area (PPA). AI helps engineers explore these possibilities more efficiently and identify optimal solutions.
Fig. 1: Intel Foundry’s deployment of AI and ML efforts across the manufacturing flow.
AI’s role extends beyond product design and into every stage of the manufacturing lifecycle, transforming how we identify and correct manufacturing issues. Our factories collect nearly a billion images each week, generating petabytes of manufacturing data. ML systems analyze these images to detect defects, classify failure patterns, identify yield risks, and improve design rules. This enables designers targeting Intel 18A to identify and address potential layout issues earlier in the design process, reducing risk before designs reach production.
Beyond defect detection, we use ML techniques including neural networks and ensemble decision trees to isolate root causes and accelerate defect resolution. The result is faster learning cycles and more predictable yield progression as new technologies ramp into production.
We also use digital twin technologies and predictive maintenance systems to monitor manufacturing equipment continuously. By identifying potential tool issues before they disrupt production, these systems help maintain the high levels of uptime required in semiconductor manufacturing operations that run around the clock.
In AI system design, success depends on optimizing the entire platform rather than simply choosing the most advanced transistor technology. By using AI throughout the manufacturing lifecycle, Intel Foundry is helping customers bring the next generation of AI systems to market faster and more efficiently.
