articles.title: Fortra says AI could save file transfer admins up to 160 hours a year
articles.text:
Fortra says AI could save file transfer admins up to 160 hours a year
Fortra makes software that moves files between companies on a schedule and says AI could give admins back up to 160 hours a year. That’s 3.1 hours a week admins would otherwise spend figuring out why a transfer failed.
Managed file transfer (MFT) sits behind payroll exports, bank settlements, and purchase orders. Fortra ships two MFT platforms, GoAnywhere MFT and Globalscape EFT. The new AI feature behind the estimate here is Guided Diagnostics, which works inside GoAnywhere.
Heath Kath, Team Lead, Solutions Engineering at Fortra, is joining me for a demonstration on Thursday, November 19, at noon (9 a.m. Pacific). Kath will run Guided Diagnostics against a simulated failure and take questions on how the estimate was built.
You have successfully registered for the webinar.
One failed transfer took 50 minutes to figure out
Kath tells The New Stack that most failed transfers he sees come down to a connection or login problem with an outside trading partner. The log usually shows one of four error types: authentication, network, permissions, or a missing file. He mostly works in GoAnywhere and said the pattern holds on Globalscape and other MFT platforms.
He points to an example of a financial services company that sends a daily settlement file to a trading partner over SFTP, a secure way to move files between servers. And one day, the partner reports the file never arrived.
So the admin searches logs to find the right one, which shows an authentication failure. The admin then checks the SFTP connection settings and tests the password. When that doesn’t work, the admin asks the partner to inspect its own server logs.
And that’s where the answers are found. The partner had rotated its SSH keys without notifying others, so GoAnywhere was signing in with a key the partner no longer accepted. The team deployed the right key, tested the connection, and reran the job. The file went out as expected.
Kath’s tally:
Forty minutes of the 50 were spent investigating the problem. The fix took only 5 to 10 minutes.
“The opportunity isn’t simply making file transfers faster,” Kath says. “It’s reducing the administrative friction around managing them.”
Guided Diagnostics points to the likely cause and leaves the fix to the admin
Guided Diagnostic lives in GoAnywhere’s admin console. So when a job fails, it reads the failure and lays out a ranked list of things to check. The admin can skip the set that matches logs, settings, and help articles.
On the settlement-file failure, it would flag “Authentication failure detected,” list the likely causes, and suggest next steps. It doesn’t change any setting, Kath says. “It would reduce the effort required to identify the likely cause and determine the next appropriate action.”
The admin can still make the change, and that’s the right call for software that handles a bank’s settlement files.
This online event will also cover three related features: Anomaly detection, log insights, and AI-generated documentation of how to build each workflow.
160 hours of troubleshooting
The 160 hours is one part of a bigger number. Fortra MFT asked dozens of customers how long routine MFT tasks take by hand, then compared that with the same tasks using the AI features. Across each task it asked about, the estimate reached 571 hours a year per user. Troubleshooting spent up to 160 of the 571 hours.
Here’s how Kath splits the troubleshooting estimates.
In Kath’s own example, the root cause was on the partner’s own server. The time spent waiting for the partner to respond was not part of the estimate.
Repeat errors get the most help
Kath expects Guided Diagnostics to help with the common failures that leave an error message behind. It helps less with intermittent network drops, problems found on the partner’s side, complex workflow failures, performance bottlenecks, or custom integrations.
A good admin should still take over when the cause sits outside GoAnywhere, when several things break simultaneously, when a fix carries security or operational risk, or when no one on the team has experienced the specific error.
Kath will take questions on all of this during the live Q&A on November 19. Register here to join the discussion. The research behind the number will also appear in The Next Era of MFT: How AI Transforms Managed File Transfer, an upcoming ebook from Fortra. Sign up to get an advance copy here.

articles.title: HUMAIN acquires Saudi tech firm CNTXT to expand enterprise AI services
articles.text:
HUMAIN acquires Saudi tech firm CNTXT to expand enterprise AI services
- Saudi Arabia's HUMAIN, a Public Investment Fund (PIF) portfolio company, has brought Riyadh-based AI and cloud technology company CNTXT into its operations. The financial terms and ownership structure of the transaction were not disclosed.
- Founded in 2022 and headquartered in Riyadh, CNTXT provides cloud transformation, data analytics, AI, cybersecurity, enterprise integration and managed technology services to public- and private-sector organisations.
- The transaction will integrate CNTXT's proprietary technology solutions, workforce, enterprise expertise and existing customer relationships into HUMAIN's platform, expanding its capabilities across AI infrastructure, cloud computing, advanced models and enterprise applications.
- The integration is intended to strengthen HUMAIN's ability to help organisations deploy and manage AI solutions, from initial strategy and implementation to cybersecurity, ongoing operations and technical support.
Press release:
HUMAIN, a PIF portfolio company delivering full-stack artificial intelligence capabilities globally, today announced that CNTXT has joined HUMAIN, strengthening the company’s ability to deliver enterprise AI, cloud, data and technology services at scale.
CNTXT brings deep experience in helping organisations access, adopt and deploy advanced cloud, data and artificial intelligence technologies. Its capabilities span cloud transformation and managed cloud services, data and analytics, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, enterprise integration, professional services, implementation and ongoing technology support.
CNTXT also brings a portfolio of proprietary technology solutions developed around the practical needs of organisations adopting cloud, data and AI, together with established relationships across the private and public sectors.
As part of HUMAIN, these capabilities, solutions and customer relationships expand HUMAIN’s ability to support customers across the full lifecycle of AI adoption, from strategy and infrastructure through implementation, integration, cybersecurity, operations and continuous improvement.
CNTXT’s proprietary solutions, enterprise expertise and established customer base will further strengthen HUMAIN’s ability to serve private- and public-sector customers with greater flexibility across their cloud and AI environments. Customers will benefit from a more integrated path to advanced cloud, data and AI technologies, supported by CNTXT’s solutions and services alongside HUMAIN’s infrastructure, compute, models, applications, cybersecurity and enterprise capabilities.
Looking ahead, HUMAIN will build on CNTXT’s enterprise delivery capabilities, proprietary solutions and customer relationships to support organisations adopting AI at scale. CNTXT’s expertise extends HUMAIN’s reach from the technologies it develops into the enterprise environments in which those technologies are deployed, enabling customers to move from initial planning through implementation, production deployment and ongoing managed services.
CNTXT’s product capabilities also add an important application layer to HUMAIN’s broader proposition, helping translate cloud, data and AI technologies into purpose-built solutions for enterprise and public-sector requirements.
“CNTXT joining HUMAIN significantly expands our ability to deliver AI where it matters most: inside the enterprise,” said Tareq Amin, CEO of HUMAIN. “We are building a uniquely integrated AI ecosystem, and CNTXT brings the technology, talent, customer relationships and implementation depth to turn that ecosystem into real operational impact. Together, we will accelerate how customers deploy AI by delivering measurable value at scale.”
Tareq Amin, CEO of HUMAIN
The addition of CNTXT creates new opportunities for HUMAIN to combine its portfolio of AI infrastructure, compute, data, models and applications with CNTXT’s proprietary solutions, enterprise delivery capabilities, services portfolio and customer relationships. For customers, this provides a more complete path to accessing advanced technologies and deploying, integrating, securing and operating them within their organisations.
“Joining HUMAIN represents an exciting new chapter for CNTXT and an opportunity to contribute to a much larger AI platform. We have built deep expertise in helping organisations turn advanced cloud, data and AI technologies into enterprise capabilities, supported by our proprietary solutions and the trust of our customers. As part of HUMAIN, we can accelerate the deployment of AI and help customers realise its value at a greater scale.”
Abdullah Jarwan, CEO of CNTXT
CNTXT’s people, expertise, products, proprietary solutions and client relationships now become part of HUMAIN’s growing platform, strengthening HUMAIN’s ability to deliver a broader range of AI, cloud, data and enterprise services, support customers across sectors, accelerate adoption and turn advanced technology into lasting real-world impact at scale.

articles.title: ABLIC’s Strategy For High-Value Analog Semiconductors - EE Times
articles.text:
ABLIC is a comprehensive analog semiconductor manufacturer focused on five key sectors: lithium-ion battery protection, automotive applications, medical and high-voltage applications, magnetic and temperature sensors, and battery-less water leak sensors. By building on low-power-consumption technology developed over more than half a century, a legacy rooted in developing semiconductors for watches, ABLIC continues to create high-value-added products prized by customers for their performance and accuracy. We spoke with Satoshi Hanazawa, ABLIC’s Director, Senior Vice President, and CPO (Chief Product Officer), about market conditions, product strategy, and the company’s development system.
● Achieving continuous growth in analog semiconductors even under stagnant market conditions
– What can you tell us about the current state of business?
Satoshi Hanazawa: Business has been strong. In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, the whole industry was left with excess inventory, followed by a period of adjustment. As a result, the analog semiconductor market remained flat from 2023 to 2025, yet ABLIC continued to grow, achieving over 10% year-over-year sales growth in FY 2025. We believe this growth was the result of consistently providing high-value-added products that make ABLIC our customers’ first choice.
Looking at the market overall, the AI sector is definitely where all the attention is focused. Since competition is already fierce, we want to respond quickly to market demand. In the future, we have high hopes for humanoid robots, commercial drones, and autonomous driving.
● Expansion into new markets with medical and high-voltage applications and battery-less water leak sensors
– Tell us about the current products or technologies receiving attention.
Hanazawa: Our focus is on five key sectors: lithium-ion battery protection, power management ICs for automotive applications, medical and high-voltage applications, Hall effect ICs (magnetic sensor ICs), and battery-less water leak sensors powered by CLEAN-BoostTM technology. These are fields where we have a proven track record and where we expect further growth. Among these, the medical and high-voltage sectors and battery-less water leak sensors are where we expect the highest growth.
In the medical and high-voltage sectors, transmitter ICs for ultrasound diagnostic systems have always been one of our strengths. In December 2024, the company acquired Socionext’s medical business, thereby gaining access to receiver LSIs that are low-power, compact, and lightweight while delivering high diagnostic image quality. This acquisition allowed us to offer comprehensive transmitter-receiver solutions for ultrasound diagnostic systems.
Thanks to synergies between transmission and reception technologies, the ABLIC viewphii series of ultrasound solutions for handheld devices continues to evolve steadily. We are currently developing a third-generation model, which is scheduled for mass production in 2027. The new model will improve diagnostic image quality for deep-tissue imaging by increasing transmission voltage to ±100V. We plan to showcase our rapidly expanding viewphii series for handheld devices at RSNA 2026 in Chicago, Illinois, this November. We’ll also share our product lineup and development roadmap for transmitter ICs and high-voltage switch ICs, which deliver even higher performance, functionality, and reliability for conventional cart-based systems.
ABLIC has a long history of collaborating with medical device manufacturers to quickly bring products that meet their needs to market. This approach allows medical device manufacturers to begin evaluating ICs as early as the development stage, enabling a swift transition to mass production once the ICs are completed. This has been one of the factors driving the rapid growth of our medical-related business, and we expect that growth to continue in the future.
Our battery-less water leak sensor is powered by CLEAN-BoostTM technology, a power storage and boost circuit technology. This wireless water leak sensor draws its power from the tiny electrical charge generated when it contacts water, giving it the sensitivity to detect even a few drops and the accuracy to minimize false alarms (an explanatory video is available at the end of the article).
While these sensors have traditionally been installed in factories and buildings, the increasing number of water-cooled AI servers has led to growing demand from data centers. Other companies also manufacture water leak detection sensors, but most rely on changes in resistance between electrodes. In contrast, battery-less water leak sensors from ABLIC identify leaks based on the chemical reaction between water and metal. This mechanism allows the sensor to detect leaks even in pure water, which has low electrical conductivity. Furthermore, these sensors can be easily retrofitted to existing infrastructure in large data centers and smart city developments in Europe because they require no power wiring or battery replacement.
Our battery-less water leak sensors are already widely adopted in Japan, building a strong track record, with trial tests now underway at several infrastructure facilities. In the US and EU markets, we obtained FCC certification, a communication and safety standard, and began sales last year. In June 2026, we showcased our battery-less water leak sensor overseas for the first time at BOMA 2026, an international trade show in Los Angeles, California, which generated a great deal of interest.
We intend to propose lithium-ion battery protection solutions for industrial equipment, including energy storage systems (ESS) and battery backup units (BBUs) that guard against momentary power interruptions in AI servers.
We will also expand the product lineup to include 48 V-compatible products, ensuring that our in-vehicle power supplies can be used in a broad range of electric vehicles (EVs) and related applications.
In addition to the five key sectors, including the medical and high-voltage sectors and CLEAN-BoostTM, we plan to develop new fields that will constitute the sixth and seventh pillars of our business.
● Also underway: efforts to improve development efficiency through AI
– Are there any other initiatives by the company related to product and technology development?
Hanazawa: We aim to increase the proportion of new products in the company’s total sales, and that effort is progressing as planned.
ABLIC will continue to focus its investments on technology and talent. M&As are an additional means of creating high-value-added products. The company is also working to improve development efficiency with AI. We intend to train AI to acquire design expertise so that it can eventually handle all stages of the process. At the same time, we believe it is important for humans to make all final decisions. Given the security concerns involved, we are consulting with EDA vendors on how to proceed.
● Delivering high-value analog semiconductors based on the concept of “Small Smart Simple”
– Given the increasingly fierce global competition in the semiconductor industry, could you tell us again how ABLIC plans to make the best of its strengths?
Hanazawa: ABLIC is committed to a vision of inspiring customers with our ”Small, Smart, Simple” analog semiconductor solutions. The company started out by developing semiconductors for watches, and ABLIC has always placed a high priority on low power consumption. This philosophy continues to shape the current business. In the future, ABLIC will continue to explore ways to leverage these strengths for the benefit of customers and consider what combinations of technologies will help to make contributions in new fields. The company is committed to creating products with even higher added value than ever before.

articles.title: Les data centers étaient aussi soumis au vote aux États-Unis : les premiers résultats sont sans appel
articles.text:
Choisir ses élus, puis décider si un data center peut s’installer près de chez soi : aux États-Unis, les deux peuvent se faire sur le même bulletin. Le 3 novembre 2026, les Américains ne votaient pas seulement pour renouveler la Chambre des représentants et une partie du Sénat. Selon leur lieu de résidence, ils pouvaient aussi élire un gouverneur, des responsables locaux ou se prononcer directement sur des décisions publiques.
Ces questions, appelées ballot measures, permettent d’approuver ou de rejeter une proposition à l’échelle d’un État ou d’une collectivité. Certaines sont soumises par les autorités, d’autres par des habitants ayant recueilli suffisamment de signatures. Les sujets varient donc d’un bulletin à l’autre : fiscalité, règles locales… et, cette année, construction de data centers.
Dans plusieurs dizaines de collectivités, les électeurs devaient ainsi décider s’il fallait autoriser un projet, interdire certaines installations ou renforcer l’encadrement des data centers. Et les premiers résultats sont très défavorables à leur développement.
Les restrictions dominent les premiers résultats
Selon les données de Data Centers on the Ballot, compilées par Redbud Consulting et mises à jour le 4 novembre à 12h16 (heure de Paris), le camp des restrictions était en tête dans 39 des 40 consultations disposant de résultats. Le site recensait 45 mesures pour le scrutin du 3 novembre. Ce bilan comprend des dépouillements encore en cours et les résultats ne sont pas encore certifiés.
À Trenton, dans l’Ohio, près de 80 % des votants ont approuvé une modification de la charte municipale interdisant la construction de data centers dépassant 25 mégawatts de puissance électrique. La proposition avait été portée par un groupe de riverains, qui avait recueilli des signatures pour obtenir son inscription au scrutin.
À Wilmington, toujours dans l’Ohio, les habitants ont voté contre un projet de data center en refusant que quatre terrains puissent accueillir des activités industrielles. Chacun de ces changements nécessitait un vote distinct : les quatre propositions ont été rejetées à environ 80 %, selon les résultats publiés par le comté de Clinton.
Ces votes montrent une forte opposition dans les communes concernées. Ils ne permettent toutefois pas de conclure que l’ensemble des Américains partage cet avis : seuls les habitants de certains territoires étaient consultés.
Des votes qui n’interdisent pas tous les data centers
Si les résultats vont largement dans le même sens, les habitants ne répondaient pas partout à la même question. Certaines communes proposaient d’interdire les nouveaux data centers, d’autres de limiter leur taille ou de soumettre leur construction à des conditions supplémentaires.
Il arrivait aussi que le vote serve uniquement à recueillir l’avis de la population. À Monroeville, dans l’Ohio, près de 88 % des votants se sont ainsi prononcés contre l’accueil de data centers. Mais la consultation n’étant pas contraignante, ce résultat ne suffit donc pas à en interdire la construction.
À Trenton, en revanche, le vote impose une limite de 25 mégawatts aux nouvelles installations. Le campus Amazon de 1 000 mégawatts, que la ville envisageait d’accueillir en agrandissant son territoire, dépasse largement ce seuil : sa construction est donc compromise, rapporte la radio locale WVXU. Le sort du data center de 250 mégawatts que Prologis construit déjà dans la commune reste, lui, incertain.
La municipalité mettait pourtant en avant des financements pour les écoles et des avantages fiscaux pour les habitants. Ces arguments n’ont pas empêché près de quatre électeurs sur cinq de voter pour l’interdiction des grandes installations.
Car derrière les services comme ChatGPT, il faut des serveurs, de l’électricité pour les faire tourner et des systèmes pour les refroidir. La course à l’IA multiplie ces besoins, avec des conséquences très locales : des terrains à mobiliser, une demande supplémentaire sur le réseau électrique, une consommation d’eau qui dépend du refroidissement choisi et le bruit des équipements.

articles.title: OPINION: Ireland is losing Irish companies because they can’t scale here | EU-Startups
articles.text:
When Ireland’s Government recently announced Budget 2027, it focused on addressing a problem that has beset Ireland’s startup community for decades.
A €1 billion Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) scaling programme would seek to provide startups with greater access to growth capital. The need was made particularly stark after, in 2025, the Department of Enterprise grimly projected a €1.1 billion equity-financing gap for Irish enterprises by 2030.
The Budget recognised a problem that startups here have known about for years: Ireland is excellent at getting businesses started, but too many founders struggle to raise the money they need to scale and expand.
Ireland’s scale-up funding gap
This is particularly the case for those seeking Series B investment and beyond. In fact, a 2026 survey from Scale Ireland shows that three-quarters of Irish startup founders find it difficult or very difficult to attract private capital.
Their response tends to be one of two options: sell to a foreign acquirer or move to bigger markets like the UK or US where there is a much larger pool of investors. And why wouldn’t they? It makes sense for the survival and growth of their company.
It does, however, raise a bigger question for Ireland: how do we help more companies grow internationally while keeping their roots here?
Turning investment promises into action
The new ISIF programme is aimed at addressing the right issue, but its impact will depend on how it works in practice. What companies can access it, how will the money be deployed and on what terms, and how much process will founders have to navigate? These are the important questions that need to be answered with tangible solutions.
The proposed €1 billion is exciting, but only if the timing and application are right. In 2025, the European Commission revealed that Ireland performed below the EU average for innovation-friendly regulation, highlighting the need for better and clearer support infrastructures. Therefore, it is crucial to know if capital will be available at the point when a company needs it.
Budget 2027 also extends existing startup and small business investment schemes. Again, this is most welcome but also sort of a non-announcement. Of course we want these schemes to continue, but the extension does not address the underlying problems. In reality, processes remain complex, funds are slow to be administered and it is unclear who qualifies.
The Capital Gains Tax reduction from 33% to 31% is another positive signal. But a two-point reduction on its own is unlikely to close the scale-up funding gap. The wider goal should be to encourage more investment in Irish companies and give founders the confidence to reinvest in growth.
Growth requires more than capital
Founders need practical improvements: less time spent navigating national requirements, clearer processes and a more straightforward path to customers and investors in other member states. Europe has the scale to be a powerful growth market; it needs to work more like one.
Capital is vital, but it is not the only ingredient required for a growing company. Founders also need customers, experienced people, local knowledge and trusted connections. Starting a business can be lonely. A supportive community can help founders find advice, collaborators and opportunities through the conversations that happen when people spend time together.
Ireland has built a strong base of entrepreneurs and international connections. According to the European Commission, Ireland sits 7th of 27 EU member states on the European Startup and Scaleup Scoreboard, highlighting the potential in our competitive startup environment.
Helping Irish startups scale from home
The next task is to build the conditions that help more of those businesses raise later-stage capital and reach international markets from here. The Budget’s announcements are a start. Their success will be measured by whether companies can use the supports in time, whether private investment follows and whether more Irish businesses can scale without having to leave to do so.

articles.title: Amazon-Kunden entdecken ein verstecktes Profil: Was es über sie verrät
articles.text:
Was weiß Amazon über Kunden? Ein verstecktes Profil verrät es
In Deutschland ist Amazon aus dem Online-Handel nicht mehr wegzudenken. Einer Studie zufolge kaufen 97 Prozent der Menschen, die im Internet shoppen, wenigstens gelegentlich bei Amazon. Das facht nicht nur den Umsatz an, der Konzern bekommt auch Zugriff auf jede Menge persönliche Daten. Und aus denen lassen sich Vorlieben ableiten, wie eine Threads-Nutzerin mit dem Kontonamen „fangirlinmegan“ festgestellt hat. Sie stieß in der App des Versandhändlers auf ein mehr oder weniger gut verstecktes Menü in den Einkaufseinstellungen. Dort hat Amazon abgebildet, was das Unternehmen aus den Einkaufsgewohnheiten der Kundin ableitet.
Flaches Gesäß und Kindle-Bücher unter der Dusche
„Besitzt einen Kindle Paperwhite“ ist dabei noch eine der harmloseren Angaben, die die Kundin in dem Menü vorfand. Das Lesegerät dürfte sie direkt beim Hersteller, also Amazon, erstanden haben. Die App listet außerdem auf, dass sie gerne Mottopartys veranstaltet, ständig eine Haarball-Behandlung für Katzen einkauft, eine Geburtstagsfeier mit dem Motto des Comic-Hundes Bluey vorbereitet habe, „wahrscheinlich“ einen Shark-Saugroboter besitze und „ein flaches Gesäß“ habe. Vor allem der letzte Punkt veranlasste die Kundin zu einem Posting auf der Meta-Plattform Threads.
„Ich meine, das ist nicht falsch, aber verdammt, warum musst du das so zur Schau stellen“, fügt fangirlinmegan in einem zweiten Posting hinzu. Gefolgt von einer Anleitung, wie man selbst herausfindet, welche Daten Amazon über einen gesammelt hat. Was die Kundin zu dem Zeitpunkt offenbar nicht ahnte: Der Beitrag gewann schnell an Traktion. Andere Amazon-Kunden sprangen auf und teilten Screenshots aus ihren eigenen Apps.
„Beides zutreffend und direkt von einer Bewertung“, schreibt eine weitere Kundin, der Amazon zuschreibt, sie würde „alles von Allison Saft“ lesen und die Netflix-Serie Das Damengambit zu ihren Lieblingsserien zählen. „Liest ausgiebig romantische Fantasy-Geschichten“, erfährt ein Nutzer über sich. „Will keine Weihnachtsmusik auf der Playlist“, schreibt Amazon dem nächsten Kunden zu, obwohl dieser von sich aus sagt, das treffe nur auf zehn Monate im Jahr zu.
Bei anderen erkennt Amazon, dass sie „wilde Vögel“ regelmäßig füttern, die Pflanzensammlung regelmäßig erweitern, ihr Smartphone unter der Dusche nutzen, um Kindle-Bücher zu lesen, oder glauben, dass es nicht seltsam sei, sich mit einem Eichhörnchen anzufreunden. Den vielleicht besten Beitrag zeigt der Account „rosewrecker„. „Ist zu klein, um in einen 40 Zoll (101,6 Zentimeter) tiefen Karton zu greifen“, „Ist kein großer Spongebob-Fan“ und „Kann echte Pflanzen nicht am Leben erhalten“, steht dort.
Weiß Amazon zu viel?
Und so geht es viele Beiträge lang weiter. Die meisten Nutzer nehmen die Fundstücke in der Amazon-App mit Humor. Sie zeigen aber gleichzeitig auch, dass das Unternehmen seine Kund:innen sehr gut kennenlernt. Nicht wenige der über 7.000 Antwortenden schreiben schließlich dazu, dass die gefundenen Angaben grundsätzlich korrekt sind.
Die Daten sammelt das Unternehmen nach eigenen Angaben aus der Einkaufs-Historie, Unterhaltungen mit der Shopping-Funktion von Alexa, Bewertungen, erstellten Listen und Suchanfragen. „Um Ihnen hochwertige und relevante Empfehlungen anbieten zu können, ist es unerlässlich, Ihre Vorlieben zu kennen“, schreibt das Unternehmen dazu. Immerhin kann man diese Vorlieben nicht nur einsehen, sondern auch anpassen.
In Deutschland gibt es diese Über-dich-Seite übrigens nicht. Um sie zu finden, müsste man in der App den eigenen Account aufrufen, die Einkaufseinstellungen öffnen und hier auf die „Über dich“-Seite tippen. Hierzulande lassen sich Vorlieben lediglich händisch eintippen. Das verringert den Cringe-Faktor. Die Daten dürfte Amazon aber trotzdem sammeln.

articles.title: The Download: blended meat, restored sight, and the agentic web
articles.text:
The Download: blended meat, restored sight, and the agentic web
Plus: Democrats have dealt tech billionaires a major midterm setback.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu. Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat.
Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef.
Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat.
Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef.
—Meghan McCarron
This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off. Until now, no treatment could restore their vision. A system called PRIMA changes that.
It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones.
—Linda Marsa
MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here
In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.
At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.
This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Democrats have dealt tech billionaires a major midterm setback
The results could bring tougher scrutiny of AI and data centres. (CNBC)
+ Musk poured millions into Texas, but both his candidates lost. (Wired $)
+ Several winners promised to restrict data centre construction. (FT $)
+ Stock futures slid as Democrats won big. (NBC News)
+ The tech left said it’s ready to “wipe the floor.”  (Vanity Fair $)
2 Google is shutting off Search for schools that reject AI
The company said AI and Search can no longer be untwined. (CNN)
+ Critics accused Google of pressuring schools to adopt AI. (NBC News)
+ AI is the end of search as we know it. (MIT Technology Review)
3 The Binance hackers used fake job interviews in their record heist
They targeted an engineer through LinkedIn. (NBC News)
+ Researchers had repeatedly warned about the tactics. (TechCrunch)
+ The breach could boost demand for specialist crypto custodians. (CNBC)
4 Materials maker 3M will pay $7.35 billion to settle “forever chemicals” lawsuits
The suits involve PFAS in firefighting foam. (WSJ $)
+ New tech could help rid water of PFAS. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Finland is opening a nuclear waste vault built to last 100,000 years
It will bury spent fuel 400 metres underground. (New Scientist $)
+ It's time to make new plans for nuclear waste. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Russia wants underground data centers after Ukrainian strikes
Drone attacks have disrupted services used by millions. (Ars Technica)
7 Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
FlashProve uses cryptography to verify a model’s outputs. (TechCrunch)
+ “Personhood credentials” could prove you’re human. (MIT Technology Review)
8 Old jet engines are being scavenged to power data centers
But environmentalists warn they will produce more pollution. (NYT $)
9 Dinosaur blood has been found in fossils for the first time
The discovery advances research into ancient biomolecules. (Guardian)
10 Chernobyl’s dogs appear to be evolving
Scientists found differences linked to DNA repair and immunity. (Wired $)
Quote of the day
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time 🤷♂️"
—Elon Musk tries to laugh off a costly loss on X after the Republican candidates he spent record sums supporting got drubbed in the US midterm elections.
One more thing
Want to understand the current state of AI? Check out these charts.
If you’re following AI news, you’re probably getting whiplash. AI is a gold rush. AI is a bubble. AI is taking your job. AI can’t even read a clock. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index—the field's annual report card—cuts through the noise.
The data reveals a technology evolving faster than we can manage. From the China-US rivalry and model breakthroughs to public sentiment and the impact on jobs, here are the index’s key findings on the state of AI today.
—Michelle Kim
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ A 99-year-old woman has become the world's oldest wing walker.
+ Strap in for a rider's-eye view of the fastest urban downhill mountain bike run in history.
+ From a bodybuilding Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 images changed how we see men (for good and bad).
+ 50 years after the Ramones’ first LP dropped, members of Green Day, blink-182, and Rancid played a concert honoring the legendary band.

Plus: 22 nations have called for a new global body to oversee AI.

articles.title: 4 heures pour piller Binance : la plateforme crypto révèle ce qu'il s'est vraiment passé lors de la cyberattaque
articles.text:
Binance est revenu en détail sur la cyberattaque éclair qui l’a délesté de plus de 6 milliards de dollars de cryptomonnaies. Le géant de l’industrie commence par présenter ses excuses à ses utilisateurs « pour l’inquiétude, les perturbations et l’incertitude » découlant du vol, et rappelle que près de 2,85 milliards de dollars de cryptos dérobés ont été gelés ou interceptés. Binance assure à nouveau qu’il absorbera toutes les pertes, et que 98 % des actifs touchés ont déjà été reconstitués au 31 octobre.
 https://t.co/sU9dUqLQDH
— Binance (@binance) November 3, 2026
Un faux entretien d’embauche à l’origine de la cyberattaque
D’après les investigations menées par Binance, le casse a été préparé pendant des mois. Les premières traces de l’opération remontent au mois de juin. Au début de l’été, un ingénieur de l’équipe chargée des portefeuilles chez Binance se met à la recherche d’un outil de codage par IA sur un moteur de recherche. Sans s’en rendre compte, il finit par télécharger une version piégée de Homebrew, un outil très utilisé par les développeurs. L’équipe de sécurité de Binance repère rapidement l’anomalie et remplace l’ordinateur professionnel de l’ingénieur. Malheureusement, le virus, logé dans le code du faux Homebrew, est parvenu à mettre la main sur des informations relatives au travail de l’ingénieur. Les pirates savent désormais quel est le travail exact de celui-ci, et de plusieurs de ses collègues.
En septembre, un deuxième ingénieur est visé par les pirates. Celui a été contacté sur une plateforme de recherche d’emploi par un faux « directeur de projet ». Sans se douter de la supercherie, il passe un premier entretien vidéo avec un prétendu recruteur. Ce faux recruteur lui montre même ses photos et ses vidéos personnelles sur les réseaux sociaux pour gagner sa confiance. Lors d’un second entretien en ligne, le développeur rencontre le PDG d’une entreprise fictive. Il est alors invité à télécharger un « exercice » sur son ordinateur de travail. Le fichier contient un logiciel malveillant inconnu, qui parvient à contourner les outils de sécurité de la machine. Dès l’installation, le virus remplace discrètement pyenv, un outil très courant chez les développeurs Python, par une version piégée. Cette version malveillante reçoit des ordres en temps réel d’un serveur sous le contrôle des cybercriminels.
Le 20 octobre, neuf jours avant le casse, les pirates passent à l’attaque avec un outil d’IA interne. Les hackers se servent de l’intelligence artificielle comme tremplin pour passer de l’ordinateur piraté à la machine de deux autres ingénieurs. Binance reste assez évasif sur la méthode employée par les pirates. Fort logiquement, la plateforme d’échange prévient que « certains détails techniques resteront confidentiels » pour ne pas aider d’autres pirates à mener des attaques. Sur l’un des ordinateurs piratés, les truands mettent la main sur un jeton d’accès qui permet de déployer des logiciels sur l’infrastructure de Binance.
Quatre heures de pillage
Avec ce jeton d’accès, les pirates passent à l’action dans la soirée du jeudi 29 octobre. Tout d’abord, ils prennent le contrôle du service interne qui signe les transactions des portefeuilles de Binance. Trois heures plus tard, le vol commence. En quatre minutes, 233 millions de XRP sont transférés depuis les portefeuilles de la plateforme. D’autres cryptomonnaies sont ensuite siphonnées, suivies par 18 270 bitcoins. Binance suspend aussitôt les retraits… mais le pillage continue. Les pirates ont eu l’idée d’exploiter EIP-7702, un mécanisme de la blockchain Ethereum qui permet de donner le contrôle partiel d’un portefeuille à un contrat intelligent (smart contract). Ce contrat peut agir à la place de l’utilisateur, ce qui a permis aux attaquants de vider un portefeuille sans passer par le système de retrait de Binance.
« La suspension des retraits ne pouvait pas, à elle seule, stopper tous les mouvements d’actifs non autorisés », explique la plateforme dans son rapport.
Pour stopper le vol, Binance devait impérativement barrer la route au contrat intelligent. Dans les détails, la plateforme devait trouver le moyen d’annuler l’autorisation que les pirates ont donnée sur le portefeuille. En clair, il fallait signer une nouvelle transaction avec la clé du portefeuille. Par mesure de sécurité, Binance avait préalablement découpé la clé privée en plusieurs fragments, répartis sur différents serveurs. Cette précaution doit éviter que des cybercriminels ne mettent la main sur la clé privée, mais elle a retardé la réaction de Binance et de ses équipes. Le dernier transfert frauduleux a donc été validé peu avant minuit, près de quatre heures après le début du casse.
À lire aussi : Le Bitcoin est dans le rouge – le hack de Binance plombe tout le marché crypto, 1,5 milliard de dollars envolés
57 cyberattaques nord-coréennes depuis le début de l’année
Sans surprise, Binance assure avoir colmaté tous les points d’entrée utilisés par les pirates, reconstruit les systèmes touchés et remplacé tous les appareils compromis. La plateforme promet que des experts indépendants vont auditer ses systèmes pour en déceler d’éventuelles failles. Citant les conclusions du FBI, Binance attribue l’attaque à TraderTraitor, un groupe de pirates nord-coréens qui fait partie de la constellation Lazarus. Ce groupuscule criminel est connu pour piéger les développeurs avec de faux recruteurs. Ces dernières années, plusieurs campagnes d’envergure, similaires à celles contre Binance, ont été recensées.
En amont du vol du 29 octobre, la plateforme précise avoir déjoué 57 tentatives d’attaques liées à des hackers nord-coréens depuis le début de l’année. De son côté, la Corée du Nord dément fermement être à l’origine de la cyberattaque. Pour Kim Yo-jong, la sœur du dirigeant Kim Jong-un, il s’agit « d’une provocation éculée » de la part des États-Unis.

articles.title: Pasos para limpiar la papelera de WhatsApp y conseguir que el teléfono funcione más rápido
articles.text:
WhatsApp acumula archivos de forma constante y, con el tiempo, puede convertirse en una de las aplicaciones que más memoria consume en un celular. Para liberar espacio y mejorar el rendimiento del dispositivo, la aplicación ofrece una función de limpieza de almacenamiento, también conocida como ‘papelera’, a la que se accede desde los ajustes del propio programa.
Cómo vaciar la papelera y liberar memoria en el celular
El procedimiento consiste en ingresar a Ajustes, luego a Almacenamiento y datos y, dentro de ese menú, a Administración de almacenamiento. Allí, hay que bajar hasta el apartado Revisa y elimina elementos. Para borrar un archivo, basta con pulsar Seleccionar, elegir los elementos deseados y tocar el ícono de la papelera.
Vaciar esta sección puede traducirse en una mejora notable en la velocidad del teléfono. Cuando el almacenamiento interno se acerca a su límite, es habitual que ciertas funciones se vuelvan más lentas o que el sistema muestre avisos de falta de espacio.
El rol de la papelera en la gestión del almacenamiento
La papelera de WhatsApp funciona como un paso intermedio entre el contenido que el usuario decide descartar y su eliminación definitiva del teléfono. En la práctica, opera como un depósito temporal de fotos, videos, audios y documentos que ya no se visualizan en los chats o que fueron descartados, pero que de todos modos ocupan espacio en la memoria del dispositivo.
Su función principal es facilitar la gestión del almacenamiento. Dado que la aplicación recibe y envía archivos de manera permanente, esos elementos se acumulan con rapidez. La sección de limpieza, dentro de Administración de almacenamiento, permite identificar qué contenido ocupa más espacio y eliminarlo de forma selectiva: videos pesados, archivos reenviados en múltiples ocasiones o material duplicado, entre otros casos.
Esta herramienta permite liberar memoria sin necesidad de desinstalar la aplicación ni de borrar conversaciones completas. Además, concentra el proceso de descarte en un único apartado, lo que evita que el usuario deba revisar chat por chat para encontrar archivos pesados.
En los celulares con poca capacidad de almacenamiento, esta función puede resultar determinante. Cuando el sistema está casi lleno, el rendimiento general suele deteriorarse, pueden fallar las actualizaciones del software y la cámara puede tener dificultades para guardar nuevas fotos o videos.
Por qué la aplicación ocupa tanto espacio
El consumo elevado de memoria por parte de WhatsApp responde a su propia naturaleza: es una aplicación basada en el intercambio constante de archivos. Cada día circulan fotos, videos, audios, documentos y stickers en los chats, y una parte de ese material permanece almacenada en el teléfono, incluso cuando el usuario ya no lo recuerda.
Uno de los principales factores es la descarga automática de multimedia. Si esta opción está activada, cada imagen o video recibido queda guardado de manera automática en la memoria del dispositivo. A esto se suman los grupos, donde el volumen de mensajes y archivos compartidos suele ser considerablemente mayor, lo que multiplica con rapidez el material acumulado.
Los reenvíos también inciden en este fenómeno: un mismo video o imagen puede aparecer repetido en distintas conversaciones, lo que incrementa el peso total de los archivos guardados. A su vez, las conversaciones no se limitan al texto. Los mensajes de voz pueden sumar un volumen considerable cuando se acumulan, mientras que los videos en alta calidad figuran entre los archivos más pesados.
A estos elementos se agrega que la aplicación genera y conserva archivos de respaldo y datos temporales necesarios para su funcionamiento habitual, lo que también contribuye al uso del almacenamiento. Por este conjunto de factores, con el paso del tiempo la aplicación puede llegar a ocupar un porcentaje considerable de la memoria disponible en un celular.

articles.title: En España ya hay tanatorios que permiten a las mascotas despedirse de sus dueños muertos
articles.text:
Compartimos con ellas nuestro día a día, las alegrías y penas, incluso (cada vez más) nuestras vacaciones y grandes celebraciones, exactamente igual que si se tratara de un miembro más de la familia, así que… ¿Por qué no hacer partícipes a las mascotas también de nuestra última despedida? ¿Por qué no abrirles las puertas de los velatorios, permitiéndoles despedirse de sus dueños y, de paso, hacer el trance más llevadero al resto de la familia?
Hay quien ya ha pasado de las preguntas a la práctica.
“Protocolo Haru”. Hace algo menos de un año y medio el Ayuntamiento de Puerto Real (Cádiz) anunció en su web un nuevo servicio a disposición de sus 42.500 vecinos, uno que, presumía el Consistorio, lo convertía en un “pionero” en España. El servicio en cuestión se bautizó como ‘Protocolo Haru’ y básicamente facilita que las mascotas puedan acceder al tanatorio y cementerio para despedirse de sus dueños.
De hecho, ‘Haru’ es el nombre de un gato rescatado por la edil de Bienestar Animal de Puerto Real, Virginia Mera. La fidelidad y comportamiento del minino llevó a la concejala a preguntarse cómo reaccionaría si ella falleciera. De ahí que se sentase con la empresa de servicios funerarios gaditana Cemabasa para buscar la forma de que los animales de compañía pudiesen despedirse de sus dueños difuntos.
¿Y cómo lo plantean? “El ‘Protocolo Haru’ establece las condiciones y medidas necesarias para que los animales puedan acceder de forma segura y respetuosa a las instalaciones del tanatorio y cementerio, acompañados siempre por un responsable y bajo la supervisión del personal”, comentan desde el Consistorio. “La ceremonia de despedida se realiza en un espacio privado y con un tiempo limitado, garantizando el respeto y solemnidad para todos las personas presentes”.
Puerto Real insiste en el “vínculo afectivo que une a las personas con sus animales” y asegura que hay estudios que constatan que tras el fallecimiento de su dueño las mascotas “pueden experimentar ansiedad e incluso una profunda sensación de abandono”. “Permitirles despedirse ayuda a mitigar estos sentimientos y facilita la asimilación de la pérdida”.
Hace poco ABC confirmó que el protocolo ya está en vigor y en mayo se celebraron las primeras despedidas con mascotas. El servicio también se ha implantado en el Cementerio Mancomunado de Chiclana.
Más allá de Cádiz. Puerto Real no es el único municipio que ha decidido replantearse la relación entre las mascotas y los velatorios. En Bilbao hay un tanatorio dog friendly que permite que las familias puedan despedirse de sus seres queridos acompañadas de sus peludos y El País publicó hace poco una crónica en la que cita otros dos casos interesantes: el de PFB Serveis Funeraris, al frente de varios centros en Cataluña, y Grupo Albia. Hay otros municipios (caso de Mataró) en los que hay usuarios reclamando cambios.
¿Todos los casos son iguales? No. El enfoque no es el mismo en todos los casos. El protocolo pactado entre Puerto Real y Cemabasa permite a los animales despedirse de sus dueños. “Se les abre el ataúd y se permite que el animal tome conciencia de que la persona ha fallecido”, explica a El País José Luis Ferrer, gerente de Cemabasa. “No es solo acompañar a la persona fallecida”. En otros casos no se va tan lejos y lo que hacen los tanatorios es convertirse en espacios dog friendly abiertos a mascotas, que de esa forma participan del velatorio y apoyan al resto de familiares.
Grupo Albia señala por ejemplo que “todos sus centros en el país permiten el acceso de animales de compañía para que puedan acompañar a las familias en el momento de la despedida de un ser querido”. Solo exige que se cumplan ciertos “requisitos de seguridad, higiene y bienestar”. No se habla del acceso de la mascota al féretro. Por su lado, PFB ofrece “un espacio íntimo en los tanatorios para que las mascotas puedan despedirse de sus seres más queridos”. Lo hace en “un horario especial” y con el animal siempre acompañado.
Más allá de los velatorios. Iniciativas como la de Puerto Real pueden resultar chocantes, pero en realidad suponen solo un paso más en una tendencia que se remonta años atrás. En España cada vez es más fácil encontrarse con tanatorios, crematorios e incluso cementerios para mascotas, igual que aumenta la oferta de otros servicios orientados a su cuidado. No es nada sorprendente si tenemos en cuenta que en nuestro país ya es más fácil ver animales de compañía que niños.
Con ese telón de fondo hay una pregunta que suena cada vez con más fuerza: ¿Cómo viven los animales de compañía la muerte de sus humanos? ¿Pasan un duelo como tal? ¿Afecta a su salud? Y si es así, ¿cómo hacerles el trance más llevadero? En Cádiz esperan al menos “mitigar” su sensación de abandono y facilitarles “la asimilación de la pérdida”.

articles.title: Noruega se plantea prohibir gafas inteligentes con cámara en parques y colegios
articles.text:
El Gobierno de Noruega ha anunciado que quiere prohibir el uso de gafas inteligentes en algunos lugares públicos (como parques o colegios) de forma provisional. El motivo es que con ellas pueden hacerse fotografías o grabaciones de vídeo sin que las personas que están frente a la lente sean conscientes de ello. Asimismo, pueden grabarse conversaciones sin que las personas que participan en ellas sean conscientes de ello.
El ministro de Digitalización y Administración Pública, Torgeir Micaelsen ha explicado que esto da tiempo para analizar la tecnología y discutir sobre cómo debe ser la regulación en el largo plazo. El Ejecutivo va a presentar cuanto antes un proyecto de ley en el Parlamento noruego. Es una iniciativa legislativa.
Los lugares que podrían quedar afectados
Entre los lugares que podrían quedar afectados están playas, museos, centros comerciales y eventos públicos (además de parques). Por otro lado, están los lugares con menores de edad (escuelas, guarderías, zonas de juego y clubes juveniles).
Otra de las preocupaciones son las instalaciones sanitarias y deportivas. Esto puede afectar a consultas médicas o piscinas y gimnasios (con vestuarios y duchas). También se plantea su estudio en universidades y otros centros de educación superior.
Los dispositivos y las excepciones previstos
Por otro lado, está pendiente de decidir qué tipo de dispositivos van a estar sujetos a esta norma. El Ejecutivo va a analizar si deben estar sujetos a esta norma las gafas inteligentes que tienen cámara y grabación de sonido; las que tienen cámara e inteligencia artificial; u otros dispositivos que se lleven en el cuerpo y tengan estas características.
En este plan hay espacio para el uso privado y en aquellos lugares donde no haya riesgo de hacer fotografías o vídeos sin el consentimiento de las personas. Hay excepciones para grupos vulnerables y usos de interés social en determinadas situaciones. Asimismo, el Gobierno ha anunciado un grupo de expertos que va a asesorar sobre la regulación nacional en el largo plazo.

articles.title: Adieu Google à l’école : les établissements qui refusent l’IA perdront le moteur de recherche
articles.text:
Google va couper son moteur de recherche aux écoles qui refusent son IA, provoquant un scandale aux États-Unis
Google ou l’IA, il faudra choisir. Mardi 3 novembre, le géant a prévenu les écoles américaines : refuser ses outils d’IA en bloc coûtera aussi la recherche Google. Les élèves verront un message d’indisponibilité à la place des résultats, et la règle fait déjà réagir jusqu’à la mairie de New York.
Aux États-Unis, des dizaines de millions d'élèves travaillent sur des Chromebooks, parfois dès la maternelle. Après le déploiement de Gemini dans les établissements scolaires, Google annonce, dans un billet de blog publié le 3 novembre 2026, une révision des contrôles de Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom et Google Search.
Pour les comptes d'élèves, de la maternelle à la terminale, tout sera désactivé par défaut. Les administrateurs pourront rallumer chaque produit séparément, dans les prochains mois.
Un interrupteur sans position intermédiaire
Le piège tient au regroupement. Search figure dans le même lot que les trois outils d'IA, et la recherche classique sans les réponses générées par l'IA dans Google Search disparaît du menu. Chris Phillips, vice-président de Google chargé de l'éducation, l'a expliqué au New York Times.
	
La recherche et l'IA sont profondément intégrées. Les élèves n'auront pas accès à la recherche, et ils verront un message de leur école indiquant qu'elle n'est pas disponible.
Le compromis rêvé par Los Angeles s'évapore : le district espérait garder Google tout en coupant les AI Overviews, selon Forbes. Avec New York, les deux districts pèsent environ 1,4 million d'élèves.
Un recul après la colère de l'été
En août, Google avait activé par défaut des fonctions d'IA dans Classroom, au grand dam d'enseignants et de parents qui réclamaient la décision pour les directions d'établissement. Le sujet nourrit depuis un moment les inquiétudes des enseignants et des parents face à l'arrivée de l'IA dans les classes. Le nouveau cadre corrige ce faux pas.
En septembre, New York a décrété un moratoire d'un an sur l'IA générative en classe jusqu'à la huitième année, soit environ 14 ans, et Los Angeles a restreint ces outils à son tour. Une prudence qui rejoint les alertes sur les risques d'une utilisation excessive de l'IA dans les apprentissages. La gouverneure Kathy Hochul a, la semaine précédente, signé une loi interdisant à certains chatbots de s'adresser aux mineurs, rapporte Engadget.
Le maire de New York, Zohran Mamdani, accuse Google de vouloir “forcer” l'IA dans les écoles, d'après CNN. Morgan Polikoff, professeur d'éducation à l'Université de Californie du Sud, voit dans l'affaire une illustration de l'insistance de la tech.
	
Voilà un exemple particulièrement clair de l'industrie tech qui met tout en œuvre pour nous imposer l'IA à tous.
Guided Learning s'installe dans les classes
Google met en avant Guided Learning, disponible dans Classroom dans le monde entier dès le 3 novembre. Ce mode du chatbot Gemini pose des questions et propose des quiz au lieu de livrer la réponse. Les enseignants pourront relire les échanges des élèves, alors que certains utilisent déjà l'IA générative en classe. Google prévoit de l'étendre à Search pour les comptes scolaires, avec un test dès ce mois-ci dans certaines écoles américaines.
Rien n'indique pour l'instant que la mesure concernera la France, où l'Éducation nationale avance de son côté avec sa propre stratégie d'intelligence artificielle pour l'éducation.

articles.title: Microsoft says Windows is now 20% more responsive and 40% faster at multitasking on 8GB PCs
articles.text:
What just happened? Microsoft has been promising Windows 11 performance improvement for 8GB PCs for several months. Now, the Redmond giant has dived into the specifics of what that means. It claims the OS is up to 20% more responsive and multitasking is up to 40% faster, but those figures will be best-case scenarios.
Microsoft has spent much of 2026 vowing to improve Windows 11. With the AI-driven memory crisis continuing to make RAM prices akin to that of gold, part of the upgrades has been to make the OS run better on 8GB machines.
Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's executive vice president of Windows and Devices, writes that the company is taking a 3-pronged approach to this task: making better use of the memory in Windows 11 PCs, protecting the interactions that need to feel instant even under load, and ensuring key apps and Windows require less memory.
Microsoft does acknowledge that Windows 11 PCs with 16GB or 32GB are still going to be better, performance-wise, but it adds that "we're making sure you can do more, even with 8GB."
Those 20% more responsive and 40% faster figures come from Microsoft's own lab tests, so don't expect to see an exact replica of these results.
It was reported last month that Windows can retain up to 2GB more active data in RAM instead of shunting it to slower storage. Tweaked compression should mean fewer reloads when returning to an app or browser tab.
Windows also eases off background tasks such as search indexing to prioritize what you're actually doing. The responsiveness claims cover actions such as opening Start, Settings, and File Explorer, compared with January's update.
The multitasking test involved opening 20 Edge tabs, a 4K video, large Office files, Outlook, and File Explorer, keeping everything running.
Microsoft also claims its Windows, Edge, and Microsoft 365 changes reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900MB in multitasking tests, leaving more room for apps.
There are smaller savings, too. Widgets only load when opened on PCs with 8GB or less, reducing memory commitment by roughly 200 MB while closed, while Edge now puts inactive tabs to sleep after 15 minutes rather than two hours.
To get the improvements, Microsoft says to install Windows 11 26H2 build 26300.9818 or later, and keep Edge, Microsoft 365, and Teams updated.
The improvements can't come soon enough for Microsoft's own hardware. A July review of its 8GB Surface Laptop found it freezing during Teams calls with around 10 Chrome tabs, Slack, and Signal open, plus random hangs in Google Docs.

articles.title: Canadian Extradited to US Over Cryptomining Hacks on University Supercomputers
articles.text:
Two Canadian men face federal prosecution in New York after allegedly orchestrating a multi-year cyber incursion campaign that hijacked computing resources across American universities to secretly mine cryptocurrency.
A federal grand jury indicted Ryan James Roach, 35, of Saskatchewan, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, of Ontario, on charges of conspiracy to obtain information and cause damage to protected computers, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional computer damage.
Roach was extradited from Canada on October 28, while extradition proceedings against Stubbings remain underway before Canadian courts.
According to the indictment, the intrusions spanned from June 2016 through December 2019, compromising systems at academic institutions in New York, Massachusetts, North Carolina, and Tennessee.
The two allegedly set up multi-country virtual private server infrastructure using fraudulent identities to manage the campaign. “These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials,” the DOJ explained.
The threat actors specifically singled out campuses maintaining supercomputers, using previously compromised machines as pivot points to conceal their origins.
Canadian court filings revealed that the hijacked university hardware was repurposed to mine a cryptocurrency called Electroneum.
“Once inside a network, Roach and Stubbings used sophisticated techniques and tools to conduct reconnaissance and expand their access within the network,” prosecutors stated.
If convicted, the offenses carry a maximum statutory penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine on each count.

articles.title: Choosing The Right Power Transistor: Why Application Fit Matters More Than Technology
articles.text:
Silicon MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC MOSFETs, and GaN HEMTs each offer meaningful advantages, but those advantages do not carry the same value across every converter, motor drive, or power stage.
Selecting a power transistor has become less about identifying a universally superior technology and more about matching device behavior to the demands of the application. Silicon MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC MOSFETs, and GaN HEMTs each offer meaningful advantages, but those advantages do not carry the same value across every converter, motor drive, or power stage. The decisive factors are the electrical and thermal realities of the design: bus voltage, current profile, switching frequency, allowable temperature rise, control strategy, commutation behavior, PCB parasitics, and system cost targets.
The discussion begins with the switching and conduction mechanisms that shape the behavior of every power transistor, including crossover loss, inductive switching, parasitic capacitance, reverse conduction and charge-recovery behavior, and the practical distinction between hard-switched and soft-switched operation. These operating modes create different selection priorities: hard-switched stages are often strongly influenced by turn-on loss and commutation behavior, while soft-switched stages depend on the charge to be commutated, the available current, and the ability to maintain soft switching across the operating range. On that basis, it compares silicon MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC MOSFETs, and GaN HEMTs in terms that matter to designers working on real hardware: voltage range, current capability, switching performance, gate-drive implications, thermal behavior, and implementation sensitivity.
The discussion then moves into application context, including PFC, resonant conversion, synchronous rectification, and motor-drive design decisions, where lower device loss alone does not guarantee the best overall result. Thermal margins, board design, control choices, and total system cost all influence whether a given device technology improves the converter in a meaningful way. The application examples also show when direct transistor substitution can address the dominant limitation and when a topology change or hybrid implementation offers a more effective path. The role of simulation is also considered, showing where modeling is useful for relative comparison and where hardware validation remains essential before a design decision is finalized.
The result is a practical framework for choosing among silicon, IGBT, SiC, and GaN technologies based on application fit rather than technology fashion, enabling power-electronics designers to select the device, and where appropriate the topology, that best aligns with the converter’s actual operating conditions and design priorities.

articles.title: Quantum Roadmaps Are Finally Meeting Reality - EE Times
articles.text:
Quantum computing passed $1 billion in worldwide revenue in 2025. In the same year, three companies from the first wave of quantum-sector SPACs reported about $138 million against roughly $1.2 billion they had once forecast for 2025.
Those numbers do not cancel each other out. They tell us something more useful. Quantum has reached the point where technical progress, commercial adoption, and market expectations can finally be judged separately.
Five years ago, that was much harder. Companies could show laboratory results and publish ambitious roadmaps, but there was little commercial history against which to test them. Now some of those forecasts have reached their due dates.
Old forecasts can finally be tested
Roughly 12 cents delivered for every forecast dollar is an uncomfortable result. I do not think it proves that quantum computing has failed. It shows that early commercial expectations ran well ahead of what the market delivered.
A missed forecast can come from very different places. Customer adoption may be slower than expected. A hardware milestone may slip. The cost of scaling may rise. An application that looked close to commercial use may turn out to need another generation of systems.
Engineers already think this way. A design target is useful, but the built system is what tells you whether the assumptions held. Quantum companies are increasingly reaching the stage where investors and customers can make the same comparison.
Revenue needs a closer read
The first billion-dollar revenue year is meaningful. It shows that customers are willing to spend on quantum hardware, cloud access, software, and services before broadly useful fault-tolerant machines exist.
Much of that revenue is still exploratory, with customers paying to learn, to pilot, and to understand the technology.
That is real commercial activity, but it is not yet the same thing as showing that a quantum computer beats the best classical alternative on an economically important workload. Revenue from clear quantum advantage is still ahead in many applications.
For me, the next useful signal is not simply whether revenue grows. It is what customers are paying for, whether that spending repeats, and whether it is moving from exploration toward applications with a measurable advantage.
Read the roadmap from both ends
Technical roadmaps deserve the same discipline. For years, physical qubit count was an easy number to put on a slide because it gave the industry a simple way to show scale. The discussion is now moving toward logical qubits and fault-tolerant systems.
That is a better direction, but logical-qubit numbers are not automatically comparable. An error-detected result is different from an error-corrected one. Some demonstrations rely on post-selection. Architectures have different error models, and experiments run under different conditions.
So I do not start with the largest number on the roadmap. I start with what has already been demonstrated, under what conditions, and what has to happen technically to reach the next milestone.
Recent research suggests that error-correction overhead could fall substantially in some architectures. That is encouraging, but the results are still architecture-specific. The gap between demonstrated performance and promised performance remains one of the most useful measures of credibility in the sector.
Cash is part of the technical plan
For quantum hardware companies, financing is not separate from engineering. Scaling a system can require specialist teams, fabrication, packaging, control electronics, cryogenic or optical infrastructure, testing, and repeated hardware iterations.
That is why I pay attention to cash raised, not only valuation. In a SPAC transaction, for example, shareholders can redeem before the merger closes. The headline transaction value can therefore look large while the company receives much less cash than an outside observer might assume.
If several hardware generations still need to be built, that difference matters. A roadmap may be technically plausible and still be difficult to finance. At that point, financial due diligence becomes part of technical due diligence.
Utility is still the harder question
I still do not know exactly when quantum computing becomes broadly useful, and I do not think the field has a reliable date. Larger logical systems are expected later this decade, but the threshold for useful quantum advantage will depend heavily on the application.
Chemistry, materials, optimization, and other workloads may reach that point at different system sizes. At the same time, the classical benchmark is moving. GPUs keep improving, and other specialized computing approaches are advancing too.
We simply have more evidence now. There are technical demonstrations to compare with roadmaps, customer spending to examine, financing histories that show whether development plans are funded, and old forecasts that can finally be checked against reality.
That is enough to change how the sector should be judged. The useful question is no longer whether a company can publish an ambitious roadmap. It is what has already been demonstrated, what customers are actually paying for, and what engineering steps still separate the two.

articles.title: Oman's mamun secures $3 million to expand Gulf–Asia trade financing
articles.text:
Oman's mamun secures $3 million to expand Gulf–Asia trade financing
- Oman-based fintech startup mamun has raised $3 million in seed funding, led by Phaze Ventures through its Oman Fund, with participation from UAE-based Jasoor Ventures.
- Founded in 2019 by Saleh Al Tamami, Mohammed Al Tamami and Ahmed Al-Issaei, mamun operates a Shariah-compliant trade finance platform connecting businesses with investors to finance imports, exports and working capital. The company is based in Muscat, Oman, with entities in Abu Dhabi and Hong Kong.
- Licensed and regulated by Oman's Financial Services Authority under its crowdfunding framework, the platform uses AI-powered underwriting to assess businesses, buyers, contracts, shipping documents and trading histories. Around 40% of its trade finance settlements are processed through Hong Kong-based institutions and businesses.
- The funding will support the expansion of mamun's AI-powered trade origination and underwriting capabilities, increasing its capacity to finance cross-border transactions along the Greater Bay Area–Oman–UAE trade corridor.
Press release:
mamun, the Sharia-compliant platform building capital infrastructure for trade finance, has raised a US$3 million seed round led by Phaze Ventures through its Oman Fund, with participation from Jasoor Ventures.
An exporter in Muscat ships today and gets paid in 60 to 90 days. Banks rarely bridge that gap, as they usually rely on a long financial track record that many small exporters find hard to provide. The Asian Development Bank puts the global trade finance gap at US$2.5 trillion, and 41% of SME trade finance applications are turned down.
mamun's AI-native underwriting assesses the company behind the trade, alongside the shipment itself: the contract, the buyer, the trade documents and the trading history between them. Its origination engine finds and screens that trade as it forms. Then investors on the platform finance the gap.
The hard part is the border. A cross-border transaction spans two regulators, two banking systems and two legal regimes, with settlement that has to land in another jurisdiction on time, and the collateral is in motion, travelling with the goods along the route.
That complexity is why most of the region's financing platforms have stayed domestic, and it is mamun's moat. The platform was built across the corridor: an FSA-regulated home and origination base in Muscat; Abu Dhabi for Gulf capital and UAE flows; and Hong Kong SAR, the financing gateway of the Belt and Road Initiative, for the Greater Bay Area and the Gulf–Asia trade routes.
Roughly 40% of the platform's trade finance settlements already clear through Hong Kong-based financial institutions and businesses.
mamun's licence sits within the FSA's crowdfunding framework, which allows the platform to bring in investors from inside and outside the Sultanate, and to finance companies inside and outside the Sultanate, subject to the platform's eligibility criteria and the laws applicable in each investor's country.
The corridor is growing. Oman's non-oil exports ran about 10% higher year-on-year through the first seven months of 2026 and re-exports 13.6% higher, with the UAE its largest non-oil trading partner. New corridors bring new counterparties: businesses trading together for the first time, with no shared history for a lender to underwrite against.
The round brings together capital from Oman and the UAE: Phaze Ventures invests through its Oman Fund, dedicated to homegrown, AI-enabled Omani businesses, and Jasoor Ventures is an early-stage venture capital firm backing technology founders across the Middle East, North Africa, and Turkey.
The US$3 million will scale that AI-native origination and underwriting, growing the volume of trade the platform can originate, assess and finance along the Greater Bay Area – Oman – UAE corridor. It is where the industry is heading: 84% of banks in the Asian Development Bank's January 2026 survey already apply AI to trade finance risk. mamun was built that way from origination onward.
"The businesses moving goods between the Gulf and Asia are growing faster than the financing behind them. We built mamun in Muscat, under Omani regulation, to serve trade along the corridor between the Gulf and Asia. This round scales that engine — and the corridor it serves."
— Saleh Al Tamami · Co-Founder & CEO, mamun
"Our thesis is backing the homegrown companies that turn Oman's diversification agenda into regional infrastructure. mamun is exactly that — structured across the corridor, and built by a team that has executed quietly and precisely. It is a natural commitment from the Oman Fund."
— Abdullah Al Shaksy · Co-Founder & CEO, Phaze Ventures
mamun was founded by Saleh Al Tamami, Co-Founder & CEO, Mohammed Al Tamami, Co-Founder & Chief Commercial Officer, and Ahmed Al-Issaei, Co-Founder & CTO, and was named a Rising Star on the Deloitte Technology Fast 50 Middle East 2025, ranking 26th.

articles.title: Quand Starlink se prend pour Hadopi : cet abonné a reçu un avertissement pour avoir téléchargé une série sur un site pirate
articles.text:
Et si Starlink commençait à se prendre pour une sorte de Hadopi ? C’est ce qu’on pourrait croire en lisant l’histoire d’un abonné aux Pays-Bas, qui a reçu un avertissement de la part de l’opérateur de réseau satellite.
Starlink envoie une « lettre » à son abonné, comme le ferait Hadopi
C’est l’histoire d’un certain Sam Guichelaar, instructeur de vol néerlandais, qui a téléchargé il y a quelques jours un épisode de Dexter : Ressurection en torrent. Illégalement donc. Deux jours plus tard, il a reçu un mail de la part de Starlink, son fournisseur d’accès à Internet.
 To all the tech bro’s who are seeing this and talking about VPN’s, ‘opsec’ and ‘wow you just admitted it, you’re insane’.
It’s a fucking torrent for a single episode. I’ve been torrenting for 24 years and never once had any notice. VPN’s aren’t a great solution for torrenting.
— Sam Guichelaar (@SamGuichelaar) November 1, 2026
On peut y lire ceci : « votre service Internet Starlink a été utilisé pour télécharger des contenus protégés par le droit d’auteur sans en avoir le droit. » En effet, Starlink explique dans ce même message avoir reçu une alerte de la part de Paramount, société qui possède les droits de cette série et qui naturellement tente de bloquer la circulation des épisodes. Starlink poursuit en écrivant que « le téléchargement de contenus protégés par le droit d’auteur sans licence ni autre droit d’utilisation constitue une violation de la Politique d’utilisation acceptable (AUP) de Starlink ».
Si ce Sam Guichelaar continue de télécharger des films et des séries illégalement via sa connexion Starlink, l’opérateur se réserve le droit de suspendre ou résilier son abonnement en plus d’exposer le client « à des poursuites judiciaires de la part du détenteur des droits. »
Starlink semble ne pas faire comme les autres opérateurs Internet en Europe et « balance » ses clients
Interrogé, ce client explique ne pas avoir utilisé de VPN pour télécharger en torrent, considérant que ce n’était pas nécessaire dans l’Union européenne (et que ce n’était pas commode pour télécharger en torrent). Il ajoute que les fournisseurs d’accès à Internet néerlandais refusent habituellement les demandes de studios comme Paramount. C’est pourquoi il n’a jamais reçu une telle alerte.
Mais l’américain Starlink semble ne pas faire comme les autres et applique une politique de propriété intellectuelle qui interdit l’utilisation de son service pour porter atteinte aux droits d’auteur. Dans sa « Politique d’Utilisation Acceptable », la société s’appuie sur l’article 512 du Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), la loi américaine qui encadre les avis de retrait et les fournisseurs de services en ligne. Et même pour un FAI américain, Starlink semble parmi les plus favorables aux ayants droits.
Le RGPD « protège » les internautes qui piratent des films et des séries
Avec cette loi, un titulaire de droits peut signaler une adresse IP, un port, un protocole et un horodatage associés à un partage non autorisé. Les fournisseurs d’accès transmettent ensuite l’avertissement au titulaire de l’abonnement concerné, sans avoir besoin d’inspecter eux-mêmes le contenu des communications de son client. Le cas de cet internaute néerlandais met en lumière les pratiques des FAI européens. Par exemple aux Pays-Bas, l’organisme anti-piratage BREIN avait demandé à Ziggo, alors premier FAI du pays, de transmettre des avertissements à des abonnés identifiés via des adresses IP, comme l’a raconté PCMag.
Le tribunal d’Utrecht avait jugé il y a quelques années que Ziggo ne pouvait le faire sans une autorisation distincte de traitement des données, car relier une adresse IP à un nom et une adresse relève du RGPD. Ziggo doit donc avoir une autorisation pour lier une adresse IP aux coordonnées d’un abonné pour transmettre les avertissements. Ce qui a créé un frein juridique (et pratique) à ce transfert systématique des alertes anti-piratage par les FAI. Une jurisprudence que connaît très bien ce fameux Sam Guichelaar : « Je suis habitué au fait que nos fournisseurs d’accès à Internet néerlandais refusent tout simplement ces menaces des entreprises. Ils refusent tous de les aider. Les tribunaux ont toujours confirmé ce droit. »
