articles.title: Peppermint Robotics bags Rs 100 Cr in pre-Series B funding round
articles.text:
Peppermint Robotics bags Rs 100 Cr in pre-Series B funding round
The startup, which makes autonomous cleaning robots, is backed by pi Ventures and Crane Venture Partners.
Peppermint Robotics, which makes autonomous cleaning robots, has raised Rs 100 crore (about $10.5 million) in a pre-Series B round led by pi Ventures and Crane Venture Partners. Asiana Fund also participated in the round.
The round involved fresh capital and secondary share transactions.
The money arrives on the back of rapid growth by Peppermint.
The Pune- and Austin-based startup said it doubled its revenue last year and grew nearly sixfold between FY24 and FY26. It last raised Rs 34 crore ($4 million) in a Series A round in April 2025. Peppermint has a presence in nine countries, with the US being its biggest market.
Founded in 2019 at the Society for Innovation and Entrepreneurship at IIT Bombay, the company's autonomous cleaning robots are deployed across a range of commercial and industrial environments, including factories, hospitals, airports, malls, warehouses, hotels and universities. Its machines scrub floors and move materials in factories, hospitals, airports, malls, warehouses, hotels and universities. They are designed to fit into existing routines rather than disrupt workflows.
The company primarily serves facility management companies that oversee cleaning operations, including the selection of equipment, chemicals and cleaning processes.
One of its more challenging deployments is at a global pharmaceutical company, where its cleanroom robots have passed qualification testing in an EU GMP Grade cleanroom, among the most tightly regulated settings a cleaning robot can enter, Peppermint said, in a statement.
Cleanroom robots are specialised manipulators engineered to operate in controlled, contamination-free environments.
The startup builds its hardware, software and perception systems in-house and assembles its robots in Pune. They run on proprietary Peppermint OS, using computer vision and LiDAR to map spaces, plan routes, and avoid obstacles. Operators can monitor them in real time through a cloud dashboard. For security-sensitive sites, the company offers fully offline 'stealth' robots that meet stringent information securtiy requirements.
Runal Dahiwade, Founder and CEO of Peppermint Robotics, said, "Cleaning teams keep hospitals, factories and airports running. Our robots work alongside them and take on the most repetitive, physically demanding jobs, like floor scrubbing and material transportation. Our customers judge us on one thing: a clean floor, every shift.
"So we build our robots heavy-duty, to last multiple years, and we stay with every machine for its whole lifecycle. This round lets us build more of them, closer to our customers worldwide."
The newly raised capital will go towards next-generation robotics and expanding manufacturing capacity. An assembly line in North America is also being planned over the coming months.
Peppermint also intends to step up business development in the United States and Asia, grow its presence in Europe, and hire senior leaders and engineers.
On the product side, it plans to widen its range of floor-cleaning and material-handling robots and develop its cleanroom line.
Investors are optimistic about Peppermint's potential and promise.
Shubham Sandeep, Partner at pi Ventures, pointed to the company's "clear ROI" in demanding settings such as healthcare and hospitality. Anandamoy Roychowdhary of Crane Venture Partners said Peppermint has built a production-grade cleanroom robot for mission-critical businesses. articles.title: “Signing in to your company’s plugins one by one is annoying”: Anthropic’s fix puts Claude in the identity business
articles.text:
“Signing in to your company’s plugins one by one is annoying”: Anthropic’s fix puts Claude in the identity business
Anthropic is now letting businesses automatically connect employees to approved Claude plugins, saving staff from having to sign in to and authorize each service individually. The feature also allows Claude to verify users’ organizational membership directly, making it easier for companies to manage access to workplace applications.
The feature builds on the Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) extension to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which debuted back in June. As The New Stack reported at the time, this ushered in a way for companies to manage MCP connections centrally through their existing identity providers, with Okta becoming the first to support it.
Anthropic also announced support for the extension in Claude, Claude Code and Cowork on the same day, and published implementation guidance for developers building compatible MCP servers.
In its original guise, the approach relied on the company’s identity provider being compatible with EMA. Okta was the first to support the extension, and adoption among other providers remains limited, meaning many organizations have still had to authorize connections individually.
“Claude itself can issue the signed identity assertions that participating MCP services use to recognize employees.”
On the ClaudeDevs X account on Tuesday, Anthropic introduced another option: Claude itself can issue the signed identity assertions that participating MCP services use to recognize employees. This effectively means businesses can enable automatic connections without requiring their identity provider to support the extension.
“If you’re building plugins for Claude, add support so users get started faster and stay connected without re-authorizing,” the company writes.
The new Claude authorization feature is available in beta now, for Team and Enterprise customers.
Claude takes over the identity check
Taking to X on Tuesday, Boris Cherny, head of applications at Anthropic, points to the frustration of employees having to repeatedly authenticate workplace applications.
“Signing in to your company’s plugins one by one is annoying.”
“Signing in to your company’s plugins one by one is annoying, so we let Claude auto-connect to them now,” Cherny writes.
Administrators can choose which supported services to enable, and which employee roles should receive access. For example, a company might be comfortable giving all employees access to a general-purpose productivity tool, while restricting access to more sensitive systems, such as company databases, to specific roles because of the risks associated with exposing confidential information or making unauthorized changes.
When an eligible user opens a plugin, Claude sends a signed assertion identifying them as a member of the organization. The receiving service checks that assertion before providing an access token.
The process also handles subsequent connections automatically, so users don’t have to repeatedly authorize the same service when tokens expire.
The initial rollout spans a broad array of more than a dozen services, including Amplitude, Apollo.io, Atlassian, Datadog, Dropbox, Figma, Granola, HubSpot, Linear, Mixpanel, Notion, PagerDuty, Semrush, and Supabase.
In a November 3 blog post, Supabase explained that customers can now use Claude to authenticate employees accessing its MCP server, even if their identity provider lacks EMA support.
Indeed, the company points specifically to the limited adoption of the extension among enterprise identity providers as a key obstacle that the new feature addresses.
“Okta was the only identity provider that supported the extension at launch and most still don’t,” Supabase writes. “Organizations on those providers no longer have to wait because Claude can now be the issuer instead.”
To configure the connection, a Supabase administrator first approves Claude for the organization. An administrator then selects Claude-issued authorization in Claude’s connector settings, registers the unique issuer URL in Supabase, tests the connection and enables access for the relevant employee roles.
It’s worth noting that employees must already have a matching Supabase SSO account, and their existing permissions determine what they can access. The company also cautions that removing someone from the company’s identity provider alone will not revoke Claude-issued access, and administrators must remove departing employees from both Claude and Supabase.
Claude as an identity provider?
The upshot of all this is that Claude is now taking on a role traditionally handled by enterprise identity providers, vouching for users when they access third-party services. While it’s still early days, and the feature is currently limited to those in the business realm, the announcement has already prompted some positive reactions.
“Tired of reauthorizing in every other session.”
“This is soo good, tired of reauthorizing in every other session,” one user writes on X.
Others are keen to see more companies support the feature, with one eager for payments giant Stripe to join the party. “I spend more time reconnecting Stripe than every other plugin combined,” the user writes.
The implications for enterprise authentication also caught people’s attention. “Claude becoming an identity provider,” one user remarked, raising a broader question about Anthropic’s growing role in verifying user identities.
Technically, Claude is acting as a trusted issuer for participating MCP services, verifying that users belong to a particular Claude organization. It doesn’t provide the full range of functions associated with a traditional identity provider, and connected services remain responsible for enforcing their own access permissions.
So for now, Claude’s identity ambitions extend only as far as the services willing to take its word for who you are.

articles.title: Hackers use n-day exploits in zero-click attacks on iOS, Android devices
articles.text:
A large-scale watering hole attack associated with Russian hackers has been targeting iOS and Android users visiting compromised sites or fake ones impersonating legitimate portals.
The campaign used multiple high-profile websites in the U.S., Ukraine, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria that delivered the same payload for profiling visitors and their devices.
This initial stage allows the attacker to determine the browser version to deploy "platform-specific n-day exploit chains without user interaction."
Researchers at cybersecurity company Sekoia attribute the operation with moderate-to-high confidence to APT29 (aka Midnight Blizzard), a Russian threat group that was recently linked to hotel WiFi attacks.
Based on their findings, compromised legitimate sites belong to a Ukrainian gas producer, a U.S. chemical industry trade association, and a Bulgarian military-related site.
Lookalike domains impersonated the official America250 site and Raffles London at The OWO hotel, relaying content from the real sites in an adversary-in-the-middle attack model.
The researchers also discovered that the threat actor had compromised Ukrainian web analytics service Plerdy and modified its SEO tracker, which was loaded by thousands of websites, mostly in Ukraine, between August 27 and September 3.
In all cases, the initial payload was JavaScript code that profiled website visitors to determine their devices and browser versions. The command-and-control (C2) server then pushed the correct exploit chain.
According to Sekoia, the threat actors exploited the following vulnerabilities to extract cookies, messaging app databases, and credentials:
- CVE-2025-43529 and CVE-2024-27834 (in iOS 16.7). The payload targets cookies stored in Safari.
- CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, and CVE-2025-43520 (in iOS 18.5). The payload harvests WhatsApp and Telegram databases, Keychain credentials, location data, and photos.
- CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038 (in Chrome for Android 139 to 145, excluding 143). Uses AndroSnitch to collect Chrome cookies, login data, browsing history, and saved WiFi credentials.
The researchers identified four other vulnerabilities in unreachable code or alternate exploit paths, but they were not used in the analyzed chains.
CVE-2025-43529 is linked to the “DarkSword” exploit kit, first documented in March, and leveraged in attacks since at least November 2025 by multiple threat groups.
Sekoia says that none of the payloads APT29 used in these attacks established persistence, allowing a device reboot to stop the malicious activity until visiting a compromised site again.
Regarding its attribution to APT29, Sekoia notes similarities to past watering-hole operations by the same threat group, infrastructure overlaps, and a compromised site that a partner linked to a 2025 APT29 campaign.
Apple and Google have patched all flaws targeted in this campaign, with fixes even reaching older iOS releases, so users are recommended to apply the latest available security updates for their devices.

articles.title: Black Friday : Cdiscount efface la hausse de prix du MacBook Neo 512 Go
articles.text:
Depuis la hausse des prix des Mac décidée par Apple en juin, le MacBook Neo 512 Go est affiché 899 € sur l’Apple Store, contre 799 € à son lancement. Cdiscount le ramène à 799 € pour le Black Friday, en Indigo avec Touch ID : un Mac noté 7/10 par notre rédaction, pensé pour les usages légers.
Lancé en mars, le MacBook Neo est le Mac portable le plus accessible d’Apple : un 13 pouces de 1,23 kg animé par la puce A18 Pro de l’iPhone 16 Pro, avec un cœur graphique en moins. Cette version double le stockage, à 512 Go, et ajoute le lecteur d’empreintes Touch ID, absent du modèle de base. Cdiscount la propose à 799 € au lieu de 899 € en coloris Indigo, soit 100 € de moins que sur l’Apple Store aujourd’hui.
Ce n’est pas le prix le plus bas vu cette année : cet été, nous avions relayé la même configuration à 719 € chez Amazon, dans un autre coloris. L’offre vise surtout les étudiants et ceux qui veulent macOS pour la bureautique, le web et le streaming.
Le MacBook Neo 13 pouces 512 Go avec Touch ID, coloris Indigo, passe à 799 € au lieu de 899 € chez Cdiscount pour le Black Friday.
Pourquoi choisir le MacBook Neo 512 Go ?
- Un silence total : Sans ventilateur, le MacBook Neo ne fait aucun bruit, et nous n’avons relevé qu’un point chaud de 41 °C en pleine charge processeur.
- Un écran bien réglé d’usine : La dalle Liquid Retina de 13 pouces affiche 2 408 × 1 506 pixels et dépasse un peu les 500 cd/m². Nous l’avons mesurée avec un DeltaE inférieur à 2, gage de couleurs fidèles pour les photos comme pour les séries.
- Touch ID et 512 Go : Ce sont les deux ajouts de cette version sur le modèle à 256 Go, et l’absence de Touch ID faisait partie des regrets de notre test. Le stockage doublé compte d’autant plus que rien ne s’agrandit après l’achat.
Cours, séries et traitement de texte : son vrai terrain de jeu
La puce A18 Pro est à l’aise dans tout ce qui fait le quotidien d’un étudiant : traitement de texte, navigation avec de nombreux onglets, visioconférence et streaming. En mono-cœur, elle devance même des PC Windows de milieu de gamme. Le clavier, proche de celui du MacBook Air, se prête aux longues prises de notes, mais il n’est pas rétroéclairé. Côté endurance, comptez environ 10 heures en usage polyvalent et près de 11 heures en lecture vidéo.
Dans notre test du MacBook Neo, nous le recommandons d’abord aux étudiants, aux nouveaux venus dans l’écosystème Apple et à ceux qui cherchent un portable d’appoint à côté d’un ordinateur fixe. Il convient moins dès que le travail devient lourd : montage vidéo exigeant, retouche RAW avancée ou modélisation 3D dépassent ses capacités, et 8 Go de mémoire vive laissent peu de marge pour les années à venir. Enfin, le chargeur n’est pas fourni et une recharge complète prend un peu moins de trois heures.
MacBook Neo ou MacBook Air : où passe la différence
Le MacBook Air M5 13 pouces, affiché à 1 699 € dans notre comparatif des meilleurs PC portables, reste la référence pour qui a besoin de puissance et de 16 Go de mémoire vive. Le MacBook Neo coûte moins de la moitié et en garde l’essentiel pour un usage courant : macOS complet, châssis en aluminium, haut-parleurs que nous avons jugés proches de ceux d’un iPad Air. Il cède en revanche sur des points concrets : trackpad mécanique et non haptique, second port USB-C limité au débit de l’USB 2.0, SSD parmi les plus lents que nous ayons mesurés.
✅ Les points forts
- Fonctionnement totalement silencieux, sans ventilateur
- Écran 13 pouces lumineux et bien calibré
- Touch ID et 512 Go de stockage sur cette version
- Clavier confortable, proche de celui du MacBook Air
- Châssis en aluminium et clavier remplaçable, pour une meilleure réparabilité
❌ Les limites
- 8 Go de mémoire vive, sans évolution possible
- Trackpad mécanique bruyant, non haptique
- SSD lent et second port USB-C en USB 2.0
- Chargeur non fourni, recharge en près de trois heures
Avant de valider votre panier, vérifiez sur la fiche Cdiscount qu’il s’agit bien du modèle Indigo 512 Go avec Touch ID, affiché à 799 €.
À 799 €, le MacBook Neo 512 Go retrouve chez Cdiscount le prix auquel Apple l’avait lancé en mars, avant la hausse de juin. Vous obtenez la version la plus cohérente de la gamme : Touch ID et assez de stockage pour ne pas jongler avec un disque externe. La remise de 100 € est réelle face à l’Apple Store, sans être exceptionnelle, puisque la même configuration est déjà descendue à 719 € cet été.
Pour un étudiant, un premier Mac ou un ordinateur d’appoint dédié aux cours, au web et aux séries, l’offre tient la route. Si vous montez des vidéos, retouchez beaucoup de photos ou comptez garder votre machine de longues années, les 8 Go de mémoire vive vous feront hésiter à juste titre.

articles.title: Tráfico global de las redes de telecomunicaciones crecerá entre 3 y 7 veces
articles.text:
El tráfico global de las redes de telecomunicaciones podría multiplicarse para el año 2034, según un nuevo estudio de Nokia presentado en América Latina. El informe plantea dos escenarios: uno conservador, en el que el tráfico se triplicaría, y uno agresivo, con un incremento de hasta siete veces respecto a los niveles actuales.
En cifras concretas, esto representaría entre 2.277 y 4.878 exabytes (EB) mensuales, con una tasa de crecimiento anual compuesto de entre el 13% y el 22%, de acuerdo con los distintos escenarios proyectados.
El estudio tiene como objetivo asistir a los operadores de telecomunicaciones (telcos) en sus procesos de toma de decisiones y planificación de infraestructura. Abarca el período comprendido entre 2024 y 2034 y se enfoca en el tráfico de red de área extensa (WAN) de operadores y empresas.
Este análisis incluye el Internet público, los servicios WAN privados y gestionados, además del flujo de datos entre centros de datos. Queda fuera del alcance del informe el tráfico privado que permanece dentro de una red local en una sola ubicación o edificio.
Tres segmentos de tráfico y el peso del video
El documento clasifica el tráfico en tres categorías: consumidor, empresarial/industrial y el generado por la inteligencia artificial. Dentro del segmento de consumo, que incluye accesos fijos, móviles e inalámbricos (FWA), el video continuará como el caso de uso predominante, con más del 70% del tráfico total generado por los usuarios. Le siguen en relevancia las redes sociales, el gaming y la navegación por Internet.
Para 2034, el estudio anticipa un mayor peso del tráfico vinculado al almacenamiento de contenidos personales en la nube y al uso de inteligencia artificial conversacional, lo que modificará gradualmente la composición actual del consumo de datos.
En paralelo, el tráfico empresarial e industrial mostrará un ritmo de crecimiento igual o superior al del segmento de consumo. Este comportamiento estará impulsado por nuevos casos de uso, entre ellos agentes y copilotos de inteligencia artificial, robótica, realidad mixta (XR) e Internet de las cosas (IoT).
El impacto de la inteligencia artificial en las redes
El crecimiento acelerado de la inteligencia artificial, al que el informe denomina el superciclo de la IA, genera múltiples efectos sobre el tráfico de redes. En primer lugar, surge un tipo de tráfico inédito derivado de estos usos: tanto las solicitudes iniciadas por humanos (prompts) como la actividad autónoma de máquina a máquina (M2M) ejecutada por agentes de inteligencia artificial.
Este tráfico también repercute sobre las redes de transporte, ópticas e IP, ya que genera una demanda constante de conectividad en redes de alta capacidad. Dicha demanda se dirige tanto hacia el centro de datos consultado como hacia otros centros de datos, y afecta el flujo desde el borde metropolitano (metro edge) hasta el núcleo metropolitano y regional.
El tráfico generado por la inteligencia artificial presenta un comportamiento distinto al tradicional: es más simétrico, requiere latencia ultrabaja e interconexión masiva, según precisa el estudio.
“El superciclo de la IA impactará el tráfico global, por lo que las redes de telecomunicaciones tendrán que adaptarse gradualmente”, afirmpó Santiago Escalona, director de Estrategia de Negocios para América Latina en Nokia.
Avances tecnológicos para la próxima generación de redes 6G
Investigadores de la Universidad de Glasgow desarrollaron un sistema que permite a las superficies inteligentes reconfigurables (RIS) filtrar interferencias electromagnéticas sin debilitar la señal útil, un avance con impacto potencial sobre la fiabilidad, la seguridad y el consumo energético de las futuras redes 6G.
A diferencia de enfoques anteriores que intentaban cancelar el ruido, el método analiza su patrón estadístico y lo combina con un barrido de direcciones de la señal para concentrar la energía únicamente en los usuarios autorizados. En pruebas de laboratorio, la tecnología logró identificar y bloquear a interceptores externos mientras mejoraba las tasas de datos y la precisión de localización para los usuarios legítimos, con aplicaciones proyectadas en ciudades inteligentes, atención sanitaria conectada y sistemas autónomos.

articles.title: The Greatest (Prime Video) : on a vu la série sur Mohamed Ali, voici notre avis
articles.text:
The Greatest (Prime Video) : on a vu la série sur Mohamed Ali, voici notre avis
Prime Video propose à ses abonnés la première série de fiction autorisée sur la vie du célèbre boxeur Mohamed Ali. Voici ce qu'on a pensé de The Greatest.
Ce mois-ci, Prime Video dévoile une nouvelle série biopic à ses abonnés. The Greatest se penche sur la vie de Mohamed Ali et nous livre la première série de fiction autorisée sur le fameux boxeur qui proclamait être le meilleur de tous. Imaginée par Ben Watkins (Cross) et produite entre autres par Lonnie Ali, veuve du sportif, la série arrive le 4 novembre sur le service de streaming d'Amazon.
En amont de leur sortie, Les Numériques a pu voir les huit épisodes de The Greatest et voici notre avis, garanti sans spoiler.
L'histoire de la série
Les moments marquants de la vie et de la carrière de Mohamed Ali, sur et hors du ring, hors des projecteurs. Le monde se souvient d'une icône, mais The Greatest parle d'un homme, d'un mari, d'un père, d'un frère et d'un fils.
Les débuts d'un champion
The Greatest aurait pu s'ouvrir sur la première fois que le jeune Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. a mis des gants de boxe, ou sa première victoire sur le ring. La vie et la carrière du boxeur qui deviendra plus tard Mohamed Ali est cependant pleine d'exploits et la série choisit de prendre son départ en 1960, alors que Cassius Jr. vient de remporter une médaille d'or.
C'est l'événement qui a changé la donne pour lui, ouvrant la porte à ce boxeur amateur vers le monde professionnel et son premier but : devenir le plus jeune champion du monde poids-lourds de l'histoire. La série chronique alors la montée en puissance de Clay, creusant tour à tour ses ambitions, ses frustrations, ses exploits, ses peurs, et son évolution.
Au fur et à mesure des victoires, d'un épanouissement personnel et religieux, Cassius devient Ali. Il ne change pas tout de suite de nom, ni de religion, mais il devient l'homme qui a marqué l'histoire, l'athlète qui affirmait non pas être l'un des plus grands mais "le plus grand" (d'où le titre de la série).
L'acteur Jaalen Best est bluffant sous les traits de Cassius, incarnant avec brio l'assurance et le sens du spectacle de cet icône de la boxe sans jamais tomber dans le piège de l'imitation. Face à lui, la série dispose d'une distribution tout aussi convaincante, en particulier Omari Hardwick dans le rôle de son père Cassius “Cash” Clay Sr. et Dana Gourrier dans celui de sa mère, Odessa “Bird” Clay.
Mais là où les performances de la série et sa manière d'aborder l'histoire de la vie d'Ali sont sans accroc, on peut reprocher à The Greatest une mise en scène un peu trop lisse et conventionnelle, pas à la hauteur de son sujet.
Dans la forme, le show se contente de donner vie à un biopic classique et passe à côté de l'opportunité d'insuffler un souffle ou une proposition visuelle originale à ce type d'histoire, surtout dans les scènes montrant Ali sur le ring. Quand on voit ce qu'on fait Michael B. Jordan et Ryan Coogler avec Creed, on regrette que les scènes de combat de Ali ne soient ainsi pas filmées avec plus de créativité.
Dans son ensemble, The Greatest propose ainsi une plongée fascinante dans les premières années de la carrière du célèbre boxeur, et explore avec soin et intelligence l'incroyable ambition d'un athlète qui, par son attitude sur et en dehors du ring, ne réalisait pas encore tout à fait à quel point il allait changer le monde.
Les huit épisodes de The Greatest sont à voir dès le 4 novembre 2026 sur Prime Video.

Happy mid-week. ☀️️
Anthropic is preparing for a massive initial public offering (IPO), potentially on November 16, but it has an expensive problem: keeping up with demand for its AI tools.
The Claude maker earned $17 billion in revenue in Q3 2026, yet spent about $10 billion on the computing power needed to run its models. Anthropic now has to convince investors that its fast-growing business can eventually make money without spending so much to keep the lights on.
Let’s get into today’s dispatch.

Fintech
Grey secures CBN licence to process international transfers into Nigeria
Grey, a Y Combinator-backed cross-border payments company, has received approval from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) to operate as an International Money Transfer Operator (IMTO). The regulatory nod allows Grey to facilitate inbound transfers from people and businesses abroad to recipients in Nigeria.
What does this unlock? Under the CBN’s 2024 IMTO guidelines, the licence will let Grey process inbound transfers, allowing recipients to be paid in naira. The approval covers person-to-person, business-to-person, and business-to-business (B2B) transfers, Grey said. That means it can serve Nigerians receiving money from relatives overseas, professionals being paid by foreign employers, or local businesses receiving payments from international customers.
Grey is not the first fintech to get into this business. Nigeria’s IMTO market now counts over 100 CBN-approved operators, including Western Union, MoneyGram, Remitly, Sendwave, and WorldRemit. Nigerian remittance fintechs such as LemFi, Flutterwave, Paga Remit, and Raenest are also targeting the same market.
Why this matters: Nigeria received about $22.8 billion in personal remittances in 2025, according to the World Bank, showing that the opportunity is viable despite the competition. The market remains challenging, with Moniepoint’s decision to discontinue MonieWorld in August showing how difficult it can be to make remittances profitable.
An IMTO licence gives Grey a regulated way to participate more directly in the remittance market and build international payment corridors. It also follows Grey’s launch of Paycheck, a new product that lets professionals earning in foreign currencies set aside income in salary accounts, at Moonshot by TechCabal on October 28.

Egypt’s Banque du Caire has gone public. But investors aren’t celebrating.
Imagine throwing a party, having 27 times more people than you invited show up, and still struggling to get anyone excited once the music starts. That’s visually how Egypt’s biggest initial public offering (IPO) in at least a decade went.
What happened? On November 2, Banque du Caire, one of Egypt’s largest state-owned banks, listed on the Egyptian Exchange (EGX) after its parent company, Banque Misr, sold a 45% stake for $658 million.
Investors came in droves. Institutional investors placed orders worth nearly six times the available shares, while retail investors requested 27 times their allocation. But shares of Banque du Caire, Egypt’s sixth-largest commercial bank, ended their first trading day just 0.19% above the offer price. Not quite the grand entrance.
Explain like I’m new here: An IPO is when a company sells shares to public investors for the first time. When demand exceeds the number of shares available, it’s called oversubscription. But high demand doesn’t guarantee that a company’s shares will rise once trading begins.
Why the slow start? Banque du Caire’s shares were priced at their estimated fair value, leaving little room for quick gains. And with Egyptian treasury bills offering yields above 20%, investors had other places to park their money.
Zoom out: Egypt isn’t selling its banks just for the applause. The government plans to use up to half the IPO proceeds, about $329 million, to reduce public debt as it pushes ahead with a state privatisation programme tied to its International Monetary Fund (IMF) commitments.
Egypt hopes to raise between $3 billion and $4 billion from state asset sales before year-end. Banque du Caire has shown that investors will come to the party. Making them stay may require better bargains.
M&A
Kenya’s NCBA transfers shares to acquirer, South Africa’s Nedbank
South Africa’s Nedbank has finally collected the keys to one of Kenya’s biggest banks. And the deal has sent Nairobi’s stock market into overdrive.
What’s buzzing? On Tuesday, Nedbank completed the final step in its acquisition of a 66% stake in NCBA Group after 1.087 billion shares were transferred on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE). The transaction pushed the exchange’s daily trading value to KES 107.7 billion ($830 million).
Explain like I’m new here. In January, Nedbank announced plans to buy a controlling stake in NCBA, Kenya’s fifth-largest bank by assets, as it sought to expand its business in East Africa. After months of regulatory approvals and shareholder negotiations, the acquisition is now finalised. NCBA will keep its name, management, and stock market listing, but Nedbank now has the biggest say in its strategic direction.
What’s the deal? Nedbank is paying 80% of the purchase price in its own shares and the remaining 20% in cash. Participating NCBA shareholders are exchanging part of their ownership in the Kenyan bank for a stake in its new South African lender.
Zoom out: When one publicly listed bank buys another, the challenge isn’t always finding the money. It’s convincing shareholders that the deal is worth their shares. Just ask Spain’s BBVA, whose €16.3 billion ($18.2 billion) bid to acquire fellow-listed Banco Sabadell collapsed in October 2025 after shareholders representing only 25.47% of voting rights accepted its offer.
Nedbank has had better luck, securing its targeted 66% stake in NCBA, with some shareholders offering more shares than it needed. But with 80% of the purchase price paid in Nedbank shares, participating NCBA investors are now betting on the South African lender’s future, too. The acquisition is settled, but whether it pays off is another story.
Banking
Egypt’s Raya Holding plans digital bank through fintech subsidiary
Raya Holding, an Egyptian investment company, has confirmed plans to launch a digital bank through Aman Holding, its financial services subsidiary, in partnership with international investors.
The company disclosed the plan to the Egyptian Exchange on Monday. It is still preparing the feasibility studies and documents required to apply to the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE). It has not named its prospective partners or disclosed the bank’s proposed capital, launch date, or operating model.
Explain like I’m new here: Raya has been listed on the Egyptian Exchange (EGX) since 2005; it operates across technology, retail, manufacturing, logistics, hospitality, and financial services. Aman, its financial services arm established in 2016, offers digital payments, consumer financing, microfinance, agent banking, and SME financing. It has more than 150,000 point-of-sale (PoS) terminals and more than 250 branches. In H1 2026, Aman generated EGP 5.4 billion ($97.6 million) in revenue, up 38% year-on-year.
Egypt’s digital banking race is taking shape: Egypt has been laying the groundwork since 2023, when the CBE introduced rules for digital banks. Applicants need at least EGP 2 billion ($36 million) in paid-up capital to conduct general banking activities, rising to EGP 4 billion ($72.3 million) if they want to finance large companies. The regulator also requires a financial institution to hold at least 30% of the bank’s capital.
In March, Onebank, backed by state-owned Banque Misr, secured an operating licence. Qatar National Bank (QNB), one of the Middle East and Africa’s largest banking groups, also received CBE approval in October 2025 for its digital-first bank, ezbank
Egypt’s financial inclusion rate reached 77.6% by the end of 2025. The opportunity lies in getting customers to do more with their digital accounts, including accessing credit or savings products.

articles.title: The Art and History of the Video Game Parry
articles.text:
If you've ever played literally any game with combat in the last few years, chances are you already know what a parry is. It's that little window where instead of running or blocking like a total coward, you hit the exact right button at the exact right time and suddenly the fight flips in your favor. It feels amazing when you land it, and... absolutely brutal when you don't.
But this hasn't always been the case. I recently realized something very obvious: parrying wasn't always everywhere in gaming. Somewhere along the way, developers looked at combat and decided, "What if instead of just blocking, you could punish someone for attacking you?" That idea has taken all sorts of forms, from old-school fighting games to some of the biggest RPGs around.
Finding the first person to put it in a game is trickier. Does a well-timed sword block count? Does it need to stagger the attacker? What about batting away a projectile?
Depending on where you draw those lines, you get a different family tree. The interesting part is how those branches grew.
So Where Does the Word Parry Even Come From?
The word "parry" wasn't always a gaming word. It's borrowed from fencing, with roots in the French parer, meaning "to ward off." This makes sense once you think about it. Fencing is literally two people trying to land a hit on each other while also trying not to get hit themselves, and that's, well, a pretty good pitch for a video game.
One early example is a straight-up fencing sports game. Epyx's Summer Games II (1985) had a foil event in which you positioned your blade and swept aside an incoming attack. A successful block briefly immobilized the opponent's foil, giving you an opening to strike. Its manual explicitly discusses parrying, too. The terminology and the idea were already there, even if the controls and rhythm weren't what a Sekiro player would expect.
Then there's The Mysterious Murasame Castle, released for Japan's Famicom Disk System in 1986. Takamaru could use his katana to deflect incoming projectiles. That's another branch of the idea: timing an attack to protect yourself, without necessarily putting the enemy into a special stagger state.
Prince of Persia followed in 1989 with sword fights built around advancing, retreating, striking, and parrying. You had to read an opponent's swing and time your defense, then choose when to strike back. It wasn't waiting for a later game to make it a "real" parry. It was an earlier, less elaborate version of a familiar exchange.
By the mid-1990s, fighting games were making weapon defense part of a more elaborate mind game. Samurai Shodown II (1994), for example, included a command for catching an opponent's sword while disarmed. It's an important stop on this tour, but that isn't the same thing as the universal tap-forward parry Street Fighter III would later popularize. Calling one game the undisputed inventor means ignoring older examples – or defining them out of contention.
Weaponlord (1995) deserves more than a passing mention here. Developed by Visual Concepts and published by Namco, it had "thrust blocks" that turned defense into an opening. Namco's Soul Edge, the mid-1990s predecessor to Soulcalibur, also made timed defense central through Guard Impact. This wasn't simply two unrelated teams arriving at the same idea.
In a retrospective interview, Weaponlord co-designer James Goddard said his team showed Namco its weapon and parry systems and that the publisher adapted ideas from their work. That's a developer's account of influence, rather than proof that every detail of Guard Impact came straight from Weaponlord. But it makes the historical connection much more interesting than a coincidence.
When Fighting Games Made the Parry Famous
Killer Instinct 2 (1996) brought its own version, complete with serious stakes. Parry a standing normal attack and you could follow with a special move that dizzied the opponent, opening the door for a huge combo. The parry set up that punishment; it didn't automatically deliver the dizzy all by itself.
But if you ask gamers which series made parrying famous, plenty will say Street Fighter. The series introduced it in Street Fighter III: New Generation in 1997. Players tapped toward the opponent for a high parry or down for a low one, just as an attack connected. Unlike blocking, a successful parry prevented chip damage and let you turn the exchange around without spending a defensive meter.
Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike (1999) added another wrinkle: Guard Parry, commonly called a Red Parry. This let you switch from blocking into parrying during an attack sequence, with especially demanding timing. It's a specific variation, rather than the name for every Street Fighter III parry.
Then came Evo Moment #37 in 2004, aka one of the greatest comeback moments in competitive gaming. Playing Ken against Justin Wong's Chun-Li, Daigo Umehara had so little health left that simply blocking her super would have finished him. Instead, he parried all 15 hits and countered to win the round. You don't need a spreadsheet of frame data to understand why the room lost its mind.
Tekken was developing its own variations alongside all this. Tekken 3 (1997) gave select characters, including Ling Xiaoyu, low-parry options. Tekken Tag Tournament's 1999 arcade release made the low parry universal: every character could time a down-forward input to redirect susceptible low attacks.
The combo mechanics need a little untangling. Tekken 6 introduced Bound, a bounce that extended combos. Its Bloodline Rebellion update made successful low parries put opponents into that state, using up the normal Bound extension. Tekken 7 replaced Bound as the main combo extender with Screw, also called Tailspin. Low parries still used the old bounce, so a Screw extension remained available afterward. Tekken 8 then introduced Tornado, and its low parry immediately uses that state, leaving you without another ordinary Tornado extension in the follow-up combo.
The names sound like weather reports, but the point is simple: the reward for reading a low attack changes with the surrounding combat system. Character-specific moves add more variety. "Sabaki," for example, describes an attack with a built-in parry window during its startup. These different kinds of parry don't all catch the same attacks or lead to the same punishment.
Parrying Goes RPG with Dark Souls
Tekken and Street Fighter can duke it out over who refined the mechanic best, but parrying didn't stay confined to fighting games. In action RPGs, the series most people will point to is Dark Souls, though this part of FromSoftware's history goes back one game further, to Demon's Souls (2009). Its high-risk, high-reward parry-and-riposte system helped establish a familiar ritual: invite a hit, knock it aside, then make the attacker regret it.
Dark Souls (2011) carried that idea forward and made it feel even more deliberate. With suitable equipment in your left hand, you used the parry action as a parryable attack reached you. Nail it, and the enemy was vulnerable to a critical riposte at close range. It sounds simple written out like that. It feels rather less simple when something twice your size is trying to rearrange your face.
Dark Souls II (2014) changed the timing and handling again. Different tools have different startup, active, and recovery periods, so learning one parry doesn't mean you've learned them all. Your choice of equipment could make that familiar gamble feel very different.
Next came Bloodborne in 2015, and FromSoftware changed the flavor completely. In place of the familiar shield-first approach, you had a firearm in your off hand. A well-timed shot could interrupt a susceptible enemy mid-attack and open it up for a close-range visceral attack. You're still reading an incoming blow and gambling on the timing. You're just doing it with a gun.
That fits a game which also lets you regain recently lost health by immediately striking back. Bloodborne wants you engaged, aggressive, and very aware of how close you are to dying. It doesn't make every enemy attack parryable, and firing from a safe distance won't magically put you in position for the follow-up.
Dark Souls III followed in 2016, returning to shields and other parrying tools within its faster-paced Souls combat. Small shields, fist weapons, and parrying daggers offered different timing and practical trade-offs.
And Then Sekiro Put Deflection at the Center
Hidetaka Miyazaki directed Demon's Souls, Dark Souls, and Bloodborne, so by the time Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice came out in 2019, it was pretty clear the guy loved high-stakes, high-drama counterplay. In Dark Souls, parrying was already one of the flashiest things you could learn. Sekiro made that exchange the rhythm of the whole fight.
You play as a shinobi trying to rescue your kidnapped lord in a fictional, supernatural version of Sengoku-era Japan. There are still other tools: stealth, dodging, combat arts, and a prosthetic arm full of extremely unfriendly gadgets. But you can't build your way into a completely different weapon class or summon another player to do the hard part. Learning to stand your ground matters much more.
The system works through something called Posture. Attacks and successful deflections build up the enemy's Posture gauge until their stance breaks, exposing them to a Deathblow. Health still matters, too: wounded enemies recover their Posture more slowly, so wearing them down can make the decisive break easier.
Press guard just before a blow lands and you deflect it. Press early and keep holding, and an ordinary block may save you – at a higher Posture cost. Press too late and you still get hit. Add perilous attacks that demand a different response, and suddenly that apparently forgiving safety net feels a lot smaller.
What makes it work so well is how the animations, enemy attack patterns, and metallic back-and-forth all reinforce the same rhythm. When it clicks, you stop feeling like you're waiting for permission to attack. You're participating in the entire exchange. When it doesn't click... well, the title did warn you about dying.
Sekiro won Game of the Year at The Game Awards in 2019, and years later it's still a touchstone for deflection-focused combat.
At This Point, You Can Parry Anything
Other action RPGs have kept running with the idea. Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order (2019) and Jedi: Survivor (2023) let you do it with a lightsaber. Nioh 2 (2020) has weapon-specific counter skills, alongside its separate Burst Counter system. Elden Ring (2022) offers traditional parrying tools and skills such as Carian Retaliation, with timing that varies by the tool you choose. Wo Long: Fallen Dynasty (2023) goes further toward making deflection a constant part of combat.
Then there's Lies of P (2023), which wraps its Perfect Guard system in a moody Belle Époque aesthetic. Nail the timing and you prevent damage while helping push an enemy toward a stagger opportunity. You can still dodge or use an ordinary guard, but there's a reason people keep bringing Sekiro into the conversation.
Resident Evil 4's remake (2023) even lets Leon parry enemy attacks with his knife, including the spectacularly ridiculous ability to stop a chainsaw. Apparently, a sufficiently well-timed kitchen utensil can solve almost anything.
Nine Sols followed in 2024, bringing deflection-focused combat into a 2D exploration-and-platforming adventure. Its developers explicitly cite Sekiro, but this isn't just the same Posture bar squeezed sideways. Successful deflections build Qi, which you can spend on talisman attacks. Defense becomes fuel for offense in a different way.
And then there's Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 (2025), which puts demanding dodges and parries inside turn-based battles. Your party still takes turns selecting attacks and abilities, but an enemy's turn doesn't mean it's time to put the controller down.
That broader concept has plenty of history. Super Mario RPG (1996) already used timed defensive commands, and Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door (2004) went further with Superguard. Its tighter timing could negate damage from compatible attacks and even hurt the attacker. A conventional timed guard that reduces damage and a tougher defensive command that completely turns the hit around were already sharing the same battle system.
What Clair Obscur does particularly well is make that choice dramatic, readable, and central to almost every encounter. Dodging gives you more timing leeway. Parrying asks for more precision, and parrying an entire enemy combo rewards you with a powerful counterattack. Long, differently paced attack strings make the enemy's animation something you have to learn, rather than a flourish you watch between menu selections.
I can see why that pulls some action-game players into a genre they'd normally skip, and why others would rather their turn-based RPG asked less of their reflexes. Either way, the achievement isn't inventing timed defense. It's making a familiar idea feel like the star of a very different kind of game.
And it's not just the headline-grabbing releases. Blasphemous (2019) folds parrying into its brutal, gothic combat. Thymesia (2022) makes deflection and dodging major defensive choices. Smaller indie and game-jam projects have built their entire premise around getting that one satisfying exchange right.
With that many games leaning on it, parrying has naturally spawned its own corner of the internet. Look for high-level gameplay and you'll find players turning supposedly terrifying bosses into demonstrations of rhythm and timing. Watching someone like ONGBAL can make you feel that you understand a fight perfectly. Recreating it yourself is, unfortunately, a separate purchase.
So, What's Next for the Parry?
Some of what used to be "next" is already here. Capcom's Onimusha: Way of the Sword launched on early September, bringing the series back with sword clashes and timed defense at the center of its appeal.
Phantom Blade Zero arrived in late October, bringing fast wuxia-style combat and plenty of opportunities to turn an attack back on its owner. Nexon's Vindictus: Defying Fate, meanwhile, is targeting 2027. Its characters have distinct defensive tools, so it would be misleading to describe every one of them as another Sekiro protagonist.
Further out, the Stellar Blade sequel now has a name, Stellar Blade: Blood Rain. It's still in development without an announced release date, and its final combat balance is something we'll have to judge when we can play it.
Batara: Fate Unbound likewise has no announced release date, but its developers are explicitly pitching parry-focused combat. That's a pretty good indication of how much weight this one mechanic now carries.
If you zoom out for a second, you realize how wild this all is. "Has a good parry system" can be more than a footnote in a review. It's become its own marketing pitch, the same way "open world" or "roguelike" has turned into shorthand for entire design philosophies. So yes, it's safe to say the parry isn't going anywhere anytime soon. And frankly, I don't think we want it to.

articles.title: US Army successfully flies a hybrid electric drone with 3D-printed heavy-fuel rotary engine — 400v motor-generator uses advanced engineering to ditch a bulky liquid cooling system
articles.text:
US Army successfully flies a hybrid electric drone with 3D-printed heavy-fuel rotary engine — 400v motor-generator uses advanced engineering to ditch a bulky liquid cooling system
The engine drives a 400v motor-generator that electrically drives the propellers.
Researchers at U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Army Research Laboratory (ARL) recently successfully flew the VICTOR hybrid electric drone with a heavy-fuel rotary engine, rapidly developed thanks to metal 3D printing — allowing the drone to extract more performance out of the denser but less volatile military fuel source.
The heavy fuel (JP8) used in the drone is a denser kerosene-based fuel source compared to regular jet fuel, making it desirable to reduce total fuel load or increase mileage. The JP8 fuel is part of the military’s initiative to power as much of its gas equipment on a single fuel source. However, JP8 is less volatile and harder to atomize, making it a challenge to achieve peak efficiency. Furthermore, the fuel’s flash point is 140℉, compared to gasoline’s -40℉, requiring the engine to have a much higher compression to ignite it, making pressure leaks a common issue.
JP-8 fuel on aircraft and drones is not uncommon; however, the ARL researchers wanted to further optimize the heavy-fuel rotary engine to extract more performance and improve its design. The researchers used computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and a clean-sheet design (designing from scratch, essentially), allowing the engineers to come up with more innovative solutions to get more out of the engine with less.
"The use of advanced manufacturing, including 3D metal printing, allowed us to rapidly redesign engine components based on lessons learned through experimentation,” Dr. Kweon, one of the ARL researchers, said to Army.mil. Dr. Kweon further explained that 3D printing allowed them to design an air-cooled engine and ditch a bulky liquid cooling system, reducing the size of the propulsion system. The rapid iteration eventually allowed the researchers to improve fuel atomization and decrease compression leaks.
The heavy-fuel rotary engine doesn’t actually drive the drone’s propellers directly; it uses the engine to spin a 400-volt motor-generator to generate electricity to drive the propeller motors, allowing the engine to spin independently at its most optimal RPM — similar to some hybrid EVs on the road today, except that the engine doesn’t have a mechanical link to the propellers. This system may include a battery for the drone to fly without the engine running; however, the US military has not disclosed much about the VICTOR drone’s battery configuration.
The VICTOR drone is a vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) unmanned aircraft, able to fly without a runway. The US Army has shared a video of its first flight, and the drone is able to land and take off in terrain that would otherwise be impossible for other non-VTOL two-winged aircraft. With a battery system, the drone could cover large distances on a single fuel-up, and air-cooling gives it another layer of robustness, avoiding maintenance on a liquid cooling system.

articles.title: Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
Some of the questions you ask when evaluating an agent are narrow and repeatable. Did this response stay on policy? Is this tool call safe to approve? Does this answer match the retrieved context? Decision models answer exactly that kind of question. They take a structured state and a fixed set of allowed answers and return a calibrated probability over them, rather than free-form text whose confidence drifts from run to run. That makes them a strong fit for the scoring step in an agent evaluation, where you want a label and a number you can threshold and trust.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scores an agent through its entire lifecycle, on demand during development, in batch jobs against stored sessions, and online against production traffic. Alongside 15 built-in evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations supports custom evaluators that you define as either an LLM-as-a-judge or a code-based evaluator. Custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators apply your instructions and rating scale with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Code-based evaluators run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, and that logic can call your choice of external system, model, or API, including a decision model.
Decision models suit questions with a fixed set of answers that an informed person could decide at a glance, such as whether the agent refused a request or whether a response stayed on topic. After you validate a question on your own traffic, a decision model can be sufficient for that decision or score, and you can extend the same approach to specific harmfulness or stereotyping categories in your policy. Because both backends can answer several questions about the same state in a single request, you can use them as a screening layer rather than a replacement, running a pass or fail signal across your metrics to select the turns that warrant deeper assessment by the built-in evaluators, whose explanations help you investigate what went wrong.
This post shows how to connect two decision model backends to AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators. The first is Jev, a hosted decision model from TypeSafe. The second is Strands Decider 2B, an open-source decision model you run yourself. By the end of this post, you will know how to convert the AgentCore evaluator input into a decision model request, and the model’s probabilities back into an AgentCore evaluation result. First, though, when should you reach for a custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluator, and when does a decision model fit better? The next section breaks down what a decision model is and the trade-offs involved.
Decision models
A decision model is a small, specialized model trained to select from a fixed set of options and return calibrated confidence scores rather than generating free-form text. A general-purpose large language model (LLM) evaluator produces a score with a rationale. A decision model instead produces a probability distribution over predefined answers. That gives you a direct confidence measure you can threshold, aggregate, and act on programmatically. This makes decision models well-suited for evaluation tasks where the judgment can be stated as a choice among a fixed set of options: “Is this response grounded?” or “Did the agent complete the user’s goal?”
Decision models are most useful when you want a well-calibrated confidence score alongside the label, not just a binary judgment. They are also appropriate when you want to enforce a specific rubric consistently without relying on a general-purpose LLM to interpret it.
Jev, the hosted decision model from TypeSafe, and Strands Decider, an open-source, 2-billion-parameter decision model from the Strands Agents team, both support three types of questions. A noul question poses a yes/no question and returns a probability between 0 (no) and 1 (yes). A choice question asks which of up to 255 options applies, returning the most probable option along with the full distribution and a confidence. A score question asks which of 2 to 10 ordered levels applies, returning a probability-weighted score, the distribution over levels, and a confidence. Many evaluation rubrics fit one of these types. “Is every fact in this response supported by the tool results?” is a yes/no question, and “How helpful was this response, on a four-level rubric?” is a score.
Decision models versus LLM-as-a-judge
The built-in evaluators in AgentCore today use a general-purpose LLM to assess the agent response against a rubric and explain its judgment. This is valuable when the evaluation requires connecting evidence, identifying missing information, or working through a response in depth in tasks where the explanation is as useful as the score. Decision models are not a replacement for LLM evaluators. They’re an addition that the code-based evaluator framework makes possible. Use them for narrow, well-defined checks alongside the built-in evaluators’ broader assessment.
Solution overview
To show how these evaluator types work together, this post builds an end-to-end example of an HR Assistant agent evaluated by deterministic code-based checks, built-in LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, and decision-model evaluators backed by Jev or Strands Decider 2B.
The agent is built with Strands Agents and deployed to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It answers employee questions using five tools that return fixed mock data such as paid time off (PTO) balances, PTO requests, HR policies, benefits, and pay stubs. We use fixed data in this code sample to make it straightforward to verify evaluator behavior from LLM-as-a-judge and decision models. When you additionally have ground truth, you can confirm whether each evaluator catches the right failures. This code sample helps you set up the framework for testing decision models compared to LLM-as-a-judge for your own use cases.
Prerequisites
To deploy the sample, you need the following:
- An AWS account in a Region where AgentCore Evaluations is available. The sample defaults to US West (Oregon).
- Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled in the account.
- Access to a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock.
- Python 3.12 or later, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), and Docker.
- Jev requires a TypeSafe API key. Visit typesafe.ai for access details.
- Strands Decider requires a host running the Strands Decider server. You can run it locally for testing, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) inside your virtual private cloud (VPC) so the Lambda function can reach it.
Seeing it in action
You can find the full code sample in the AgentCore samples GitHub repository. Two Python scripts handle everything:
- ../utils/deploy.py deploys the HR Assistant to AgentCore runtime.
- evaluate.py deploys evaluators, invokes the agent, and runs the evaluation modes.
Running evaluate.py without flags executes five steps:
- Creates the Lambda execution role (AgentCoreLambdaEvaluatorRole).
- Packages and deploys two deterministic Lambda evaluators: hr-response-length (a trace-level evaluator that checks whether the agent’s response stays within length bounds) and hr-fact-checker (a session-level evaluator that regex-validates HR facts against the known mock data).
- Registers both as AgentCore code-based evaluators through the control plane.
- Runs on-demand evaluation with EvaluationClient and OnDemandEvaluationDatasetRunner across five labeled scenarios, combining the code-based evaluators with Builtin.Correctness, Builtin.Helpfulness, and Builtin.ResponseRelevance.
- Creates an online evaluation configuration that continuously scores live sessions at 100 percent sampling.
At this point you have a working evaluation pipeline with deterministic checks and LLM-as-a-judge scoring. Decision-model evaluators are opt-in. You can add them with a flag, and they run alongside the base evaluators with no changes to the existing flow. Using the flags --with-jev --jev-secret-arn <ARN> deploys jev-evaluator and registers three evaluators: JevGroundedness, JevHelpfulness, and JevGoalCompletion. Using the flag --with-decider deploys strands-decider-evaluator and registers the same three evaluators backed by Strands Decider 2B. Add --decider-ec2 to auto-provision the Amazon EC2 instance, security groups, IAM role, and Lambda VPC configuration without manual console steps.
Each decision-model backend contributes three evaluators:
| Evaluator | Level | Question type | Label | Value | 
| JevGroundedness / DeciderGroundedness | TRACE | noul | Grounded or Ungrounded | P(grounded) | 
| JevHelpfulness / DeciderHelpfulness | TRACE | score (4-level) | Most probable level | Expected level, scaled 0–1 | 
| JevGoalCompletion / DeciderGoalCompletion | SESSION | choice (3-way) | Most probable option | Probability-weighted value | 
Build the evaluator with decision models
Using the flags --with-jev and --with-decider creates a custom code-based evaluator, where you have complete control of the code you want to run as your evaluator. We create AWS Lambda functions where the decision model is invoked inside an AWS Lambda function and returns a label or a numeric value. This Lambda function is registered as the code-based evaluator in AgentCore Evaluations.
The Lambda that is registered as the evaluator receives OpenTelemetry spans of the agent. The spans.py module normalizes the shapes OpenTelemetry content can arrive in and then formats it appropriately to make the call to the decision model. For trace-level evaluation, only the targeted turn and brief prior history are sent, whereas the full conversation is included for session-level.
The adapter converts the model’s probability distribution into a result that AgentCore evaluation expects. For a noul question, the probability of true becomes the value and the most probable answer becomes the label. For a score question, the value is the probability-weighted expected level scaled to [0, 1]. For a choice question, it is the weighted average of predefined option values.
Validate a decision-model evaluator on your own traffic
When you rewrite a rubric as a decision model question, you’ve created a new measurement rather than a copy of the old one. A reframed rubric often lands stricter or looser than the original intended, and you won’t see that drift until you check it against real sessions. Before you gate a release on a decision-model evaluator, validate it the same way you’d validate any new measurement, against a labeled sample of your own traffic. The goal of this section is to walk you through that validation end to end, so you finish with an evaluator you can threshold with confidence.
The procedure has five steps.
Step 1. Build a labeled sample. Pull a set of stored sessions from your agent’s traffic, with enough coverage of the failures and edge cases you care about. A sample that covers only the happy path tells you nothing about where the evaluator breaks.
Step 2. Get human reference labels. Have three independent labelers score each turn for the property your question measures and take the majority vote as the reference label. Keep track of which turns were unanimous and which were split. Although unanimous turns are the clear-cut cases, the split-vote turns are the valuable ones, because they reveal ambiguity in the rubric itself before the model ever sees it.
Step 3. Run both evaluators on the same inputs. Run the decision-model evaluator and the matching built-in evaluator over those same sessions in a single batch evaluation. Scoring identical inputs is what makes the comparison apples to apples.
Step 4. Read the results through three lenses. With the majority-vote labels and the easy and hard split in hand, you can now answer the three questions that tell you whether the evaluator is ready.
- Agreement rate: does it match your humans? Measure how often each evaluator agrees with the majority-vote labels, and do it per question, since one question’s accuracy says nothing about another’s. Then break the numbers out by easy (unanimous) and hard (split-vote) cases. An evaluator that stumbles only on the hard cases is behaving a lot like your human labelers did, which is exactly what you want.
- Calibration: do the confidence scores mean something? Group turns by the evaluator’s reported probability and compare each group’s agreement with the labels. Higher confidence should track higher accuracy. Then check whether easy cases consistently draw higher confidence than hard ones. If they do, the model’s uncertainty is tracking genuine ambiguity, and you can use those groups to pick a decision threshold per evaluator instead of defaulting to 0.5.
- Disagreement analysis: where and why do they differ? Find the turns where the two evaluators disagree with each other, and check whether those are the same turns your humans found ambiguous. Read them. Most disagreements trace back to the wording of the question, and a revised question clears them up. When the errors cluster in the hard cases, the rubric is the problem rather than the model.
Step 5. Re-run the check when anything changes. Treat this as a repeatable check rather than a one-time gate. Any time you reword a question or move to a new model version, run it again. Each result’s explanation records the model version that produced it, so you know which version a given score came from.
Choosing the best set of evaluators for your agent
The built-in evaluators remain the foundation of broad evaluation strategy in AgentCore Evaluations. They assess the response against a rubric and its supporting context, and explain the judgment so developers can investigate what went wrong. For the HR Assistant, a faithfulness evaluation can identify a claim that contradicts a tool result, whereas a helpfulness evaluation can point out that the agent answered a balance question but left a requested action incomplete.
Faithfulness, helpfulness, and correctness can require connecting evidence, identifying missing information, or working through a solution. The preprint JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure describes a related distinction as “reading versus deriving.” A narrow decision-model check can flag a turn for attention, whereas the built-in evaluator provides the broader assessment and reasoning needed to review it. Decision models shine brightest when you treat them as a gate rather than a replacement. The cascade pattern works like this. First, run a fast, calibrated decision model on every turn of every session to get a cheap pass/fail signal. Then invoke a full LLM evaluator only on sessions where the signal falls below your threshold.
| Criterion | LLM as Judge | Decision Models as Judge | 
| Output | Score + explanation | Calibrated probability | 
| Latency | 2–10 s | ~hundreds of ms (network) | 
| Customizable | Limited (fixed prompt templates) | Question definitions | 
| Best for | Qualitative nuance, explanation | Calibrated judgment | 
We recommend the following setup:
- Configure online evaluation with the built-in evaluators you rely on, as the standard measure of quality across your agents.
- Add decision-model evaluators for domain-specific yes/no and choice questions to the same configuration, along with deterministic code-based evaluators for anything you can compute exactly.
- Each week, or on whatever schedule suits your release cycle, query the online results for sessions where a decision-model check failed or scored near its threshold, and run batch evaluations on those sessions with the built-in evaluators to get explanations.
- Gate releases on the built-in evaluators and on the decision-model evaluators you have validated against labeled data, and track how often the two agree.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, run the cleanup.py that deletes the agent hosted on AgentCore runtime, the evaluators and evaluation config, the AWS Lambda functions that are registered as the evaluators, the EC2 instance that hosts the Strands Decider model, AWS Secrets Manager key and the associated log group on CloudWatch.
Conclusion
In this post, you connected two decision models, Jev and Strands Decider, to AgentCore Evaluations using code-based evaluators, and the accompanying code sample gives you a framework for testing those models and seeing where they add value as evaluators. The built-in evaluators remain your baseline. Decision models add narrow, validated checks that come with a measure of certainty you can threshold and act on. The practical path forward is to add decision-model checks alongside the built-in evaluators you already run, measure how often they agree with your reference labels on your own traffic, and expand coverage only once you trust them.
To get started, review the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations documentation, integrate custom evaluators using code-based evaluators and take a deeper look into Strands Decider model. Get started with code samples by deploying the sample evaluators from the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore sample repository.

articles.title: Copenhagen’s Biograil raises €20 million for oral drug delivery device designed as an alternative to injections | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Biograil, a Copenhagen-based BioTech company developing an oral device to deliver therapeutics that would otherwise require injection, has closed a €20 million funding round.
The round was backed by Verve Ventures and Megatrend Invest. HTGF, which led the company’s Seed syndicate in 2019, participated through its HTGF Opportunity growth fund. In July 2025, the company announced the first close of an €8.5 million financing round led by Verve Ventures.
“We first invested in Biograil in 2019 because we saw the potential of its approach to oral drug delivery. Our participation through the HTGF Opportunity reflects our continued conviction in that potential as the company prepares for clinical development,” said Anke Cassing, Principal at HTGF.
Founded in 2019, Biograil says it leverages its proprietary BIONDD technology to transform the large market for injectable pharmaceutical products into convenient oral capsules.
According to the company, the BIONDD device is contained in a standard-size, double-zero or single-zero capsule that is easy to swallow. The capsule dissolves in the stomach and releases a device with a spring-loaded grabbing mechanism. The device then safely attaches to the stomach wall and releases medication into the tissue for systemic distribution. 
The Biograil device uses a novel mechanism to facilitate the delivery of biologics into the stomach wall, utilising a proprietary platform technology manufactured by injection moulding. After the drug delivery, the bio-compostable device passes safely through the GI tract.
Biograil CEO Karsten Lindhardt said, “Excellent to see such strong support from existing internal investors and involve the HTGF Opportunity growth fund in the round. This, in combination with non-diluting funding from partnerships, will enable Biograil to continue to move our BIONDD® technology toward Phase 1 clinical studies.
“The BIONDD® technology can allow oral delivery of large market compounds for better convenience and medical benefit and, in addition, create development opportunities for new innovative combination products which may never have been feasible or attractive as conventional injectable or oral products”.
The company plans to use this capital to support the ongoing activities for the planned Phase 1 clinical testing of BIONDD® to achieve key milestones such as non-clinical GLP studies and establish manufacturing GMP process prior to a larger financing in 2027.
The Biograil team combines seasoned entrepreneurs with experience building successful BioTech companies and R&D executives behind the world’s first injection-moulded oral tablet approved by the FDA.
Its investor syndicate includes Megatrend Invest, Verve Ventures, High-Tech Gründerfonds, Eli Lilly and Co., Sanner Ventures, Evonik Venture Capital, Anobis GmbH and Roquette Ventures.

articles.title: Malicious cPGuard Updates Served in OpsShield Supply Chain Attack
articles.text:
Indian IT security company OpsShield on Monday fell victim to a cyberattack that resulted in malicious versions of cPGuard being served to its customers.
OpsShield specializes in server protection and web security software, and cPGuard is its most notable product, designed for Linux web hosting servers.
According to the company’s incident notice, the attackers used compromised credentials to access its update distribution infrastructure (CDN) and distribute a malicious script via cPGuard’s update channel.
cPGuard versions 5.88.12–5.88.19 contained the malicious code. The supply chain attack was discovered within 12 hours and the fake updates were distributed for roughly 70 minutes.
The attackers first targeted the company’s billing and licensing server. They registered a customer account and ordered a free cPGuard trial to study its communication with the licensing system, then started sending crafted requests to the portal.
After obtaining command execution on the billing and licensing server, the hackers started collecting data and then uploaded a fake cPGuard update using a stolen access key, the company explains in an updated report.
The update was executed as root on the servers that polled OpsShield’s update infrastructure during the compromise window. At the same time, the attackers copied three of the company’s cloud servers.
The malicious script in the updates was designed to collect data and upload it to OpsShield’s licensing server under a compromised account. According to the company, the hackers retrieved 32 collected files from the data uploaded by the script, each from a different customer server.
Additionally, the script deployed a hidden root shell and certain files in the temp folder of customers’ servers.
OpsShield estimates that 2,950 servers executed the fake cPGuard updates, and that the attackers copied approximately 7,900 client account records containing names, company, addresses, emails, and hashed passwords.
All password hashes, root SSH keys, and MySQL root passwords, as well as shell history on the infected customer servers, should be considered compromised and rotated.
“If cPGuard was not online during that window, your server did not receive the fake update. You should still reset your billing portal password,” OpsShield says.
The company says it evicted the attackers from all servers they may have touched, reset secrets on its account, removed the attacker’s SSH key and cloned assets from its cloud account, and replaced all SSH keys and passwords across its servers.
Additionally, it started reissuing all cPGuard license private/public keys because the attackers compromised them, reset all billing portal login sessions and rotated associated API keys, and is rebuilding its billing, licensing, and internal management servers.
OpsShield also released cPGuard updates (version 5.88.25 and later) that remove the hidden root shell and the additional files left behind by the script, and published indicators of compromise (IoCs).
“Attacks like this one are getting faster and cheaper to run. Our answer is to harden our own update and signing process first, and then to put what we learned here straight back into cPGuard for you,” the company notes.
