articles.title: Canada is creating more startups, but fewer are raising pre-seed capital: report | BetaKit
articles.text:
While Canada is on pace to produce more new technology startups in 2026 than in previous years, fewer of them have been raising capital at the earliest stages, according to a new report from Montréal-based venture capital (VC) firm Panache Ventures.
“Based on our data, there are more companies being created, but not as many getting funded, and that has always been the challenge for us as an ecosystem,” Panache managing partner and report co-author Prashant Matta told BetaKit in an interview.
“What’s interesting to us is that Canada isn’t only producing more companies—it’s producing better-prepared ones.”
Prashant Matta,
Panache Ventures
The report states that “lower pre-seed funding today means fewer growth-stage companies in the future.” As Matta points out, “This is pipeline development … If there are fewer companies graduating high school, there are going to be fewer companies graduating university.”
The VC firm’s latest annual Canadian tech startup formation report, which was penned by Matta and analyst Inshaal Qadir, gets its findings from a combination of proprietary and public data. Panache compiled the research as a measure of both the current health of the Canadian tech ecosystem and potential future demand for investment capital.
The report found that 1,703 new tech startups formed in 2025, more than 10 percent fewer companies than were launched in 2024. It also determined that the pace of business creation accelerated in early 2026 thanks to an especially strong first quarter that featured a 49 percent year-over-year spike, driven partly by rising activity across British Columbia, Alberta, and Québec.
Though the pace of tech companies being created decelerated a bit during the second quarter, 20 percent more net new firms (892 overall) were created in the first half of 2026 than during the same period in 2025, as more entrepreneurs opted to build startups in areas like AI infrastructure, deep tech, hardware, aerospace, and defence.
RELATED: Canada is gaining corporate VCs, but still has “a participation problem,” report finds
Matta expressed hope that this reflects founders seeing more opportunity in Canada today given macroeconomic shifts and the country’s renewed interest in defence and strategic tech.
While it is difficult to say for certain what has been driving this recent uptick in company creation, Matta’s hunch is that part of what’s so different this time around is that, thanks to AI, “it’s never been easier to build a new startup, especially at the app layer.”
Panache’s latest report also found that 44 percent of the founders who launched tech businesses in 2025 have prior experience at VC-backed startups (this was not a metric that Panache tracked in the report’s first edition).
“What’s interesting to us is that Canada isn’t only producing more companies, it’s producing better-prepared ones,” Matta said.
Back in 2023, when Panache began tracking Canadian tech startup formation in this way, approximately 13 percent (or one in eight) of the companies created secured pre-seed investment. That figure dropped to eight percent (or one in 12) in 2024 and held firm in 2025. Panache does not yet have enough confidence in its 2026 data to publish a ratio for the first six months of this year.
It’s unclear how much the rise in startup creation, and the coinciding drop in the share of these companies raising money, has been driven by AI that enables entrepreneurs to accomplish more with less capital.
RELATED: Canadian startup formation data from Panache Ventures points to future demand for capital
What is clear, Matta argued, is that “This is [an] opportunity for Panache and funds like Panache.” Panache, which has several new investments left to make out of the firm’s $100-million second fund, is currently raising its third, which is focused on pre-seed Canadian tech startups.
Panache did find that 60 percent of the startups launched in 2025 were building with AI in a meaningful way, which could itself be “a conservative minimum” given the report’s reliance on public signals. The “vast majority” of the startups Panache is meeting these days are also AI-native, Matta said.
The first six months of 2026 so far represent “a robust startup formation year,” Matta said. Time will tell whether the third and fourth quarters will bring more of the same. Once the full 2026 data is in, he said it will also be interesting to return to the question of what percentage of them have raised VC funding.
Feature image courtesy Panache Ventures.

articles.title: Mit dem Smartphone am Steuer erwischt? Experten fordern deutlich höheres Bußgeld
articles.text:
Smartphone am Steuer: Experten fordern deutlich höheres Bußgeld
Mit dem Handy am Ohr am Steuer des Autos telefonieren – das ist verboten und aus Expertensicht gefährlicher als das Fahren mit 0,8 Promille Alkohol im Blut. Deswegen macht sich der Deutsche Verkehrssicherheitsrat (DVR) für erheblich höhere Geldbußen stark. Zugleich unterstützt der Verband den Vorstoß von Verkehrsminister Steffen Bilger (CDU), sogenannte Monocams einzuführen, die automatisch erkennen können, ob Menschen am Steuer während der Fahrt ein Mobiltelefon in der Hand halten.
„Handy-Blitzer sind eine äußerst sinnvolle Investition in die Verkehrssicherheit“, sagte DVR-Präsident Manfred Wirsch den Zeitungen der Funke Mediengruppe. „Wer weiß, dass ein Verstoß jederzeit erkannt werden kann, wird eher darauf verzichten, das Smartphone während der Fahrt in die Hand zu nehmen.“
Als Beleg für den Nutzen der Handy-Blitzer nannte Wirsch Erfahrungen aus dem In- und Ausland. In Trier sei zum Beispiel die festgestellte Handynutzung am Steuer bei einem Testeinsatz um rund 70 Prozent zurückgegangen. Im australischen Bundesstaat New South Wales sei die Zahl der Verstöße seit 2019 um etwa 82 Prozent gesunken.
Elektronische Geräte häufig als Unfallursache erfasst
Wie gefährlich Ablenkung am Steuer ist, zeigen laut DVR Daten des Statistischen Bundesamtes. Die wiesen für 2025 Wirsch zufolge mehr als 1.100 Unfälle mit Personenschaden aus, bei denen die Nutzung elektronischer Geräte als Unfallursache erfasst wurde. „Dabei kamen 15 Menschen ums Leben, 199 wurden schwer und 1.257 leicht verletzt. Diese Zahlen beziehen sich allerdings auf elektronische Geräte insgesamt und nicht ausschließlich auf Smartphones.“
Vor diesem Hintergrund hält der Verkehrsexperte die bisherigen Geldbußen für zu niedrig. Wirsch verwies auf die 500 Euro Bußgeld bei einem Verstoß gegen die 0,5-Promille-Grenze: „Wir sprechen uns deshalb für eine deutliche Anhebung des Bußgeldes auf mindestens diesen Betrag aus.“ Einer in diesem Jahr veröffentlichten Studie zufolge „war das Kollisionsrisiko bei Ablenkung durch Smartphones, Touchscreens und andere digitale Anwendungen höher als unter einem simulierten Alkoholeinfluss von 0,8 Promille“, sagte Wirsch.
Derzeit 100 bis 200 Euro Geldbuße für erwischte Fahrer
Wer am Steuer beim Telefonieren mit dem Handy erwischt wird, muss laut ADAC mit einem Bußgeld von 100 Euro und einem Punkt in Flensburg rechnen. Bei einer Gefährdung oder dem Verursachen eines Unfalls steigt das Bußgeld auf 150 beziehungsweise 200 Euro an. Hinzu kommen zwei Punkte sowie ein einmonatiges Fahrverbot.
Der Deutsche Verkehrssicherheitsrat (DVR) ist ein gemeinnütziger Verein mit Sitz in Berlin. Als Dachverband vereint er über 200 Mitgliedsorganisationen aus Politik, Wirtschaft, Forschung und Zivilgesellschaft, die sich für mehr Verkehrssicherheit einsetzen.
Minister Bilger hatte der dpa gesagt: „Mehr als tausend Unfälle passieren jedes Jahr durch elektronische Geräte wie Handys am Steuer – Tendenz steigend. Das ist eindeutig zu viel.“ Innovative Technologien wie Handy-Blitzer würden helfen, konsequenter zu ahnden und die Verkehrssicherheit spürbar zu steigern.
Monocams fotografieren durch die Frontscheibe ins Auto hinein
Monocams sind hochauflösende, schräg nach unten gerichtete Kameras, die durch die Frontscheibe in das Auto hinein fotografieren. Das Monocam-System achtet auf Mobiltelefone im Bereich des Fahrenden und auf dessen entsprechende Handhaltung. Werden beide Kriterien erfüllt, löst die Kamera aus. Anschließend bewerten geschulte Polizisten die Bilder.
Telefonieren während der Fahrt ist laut ADAC nicht grundsätzlich verboten. Telefonate über eine Freisprechanlage, ein fest installiertes Fahrzeugsystem oder ein Bluetooth-Headset sind erlaubt. Verboten ist es aber, das Handy während der Fahrt in die Hand zu nehmen oder ans Ohr zu halten.

articles.title: Apple will check shared iCloud links for ‘harmful content’
articles.text:
Apple will start checking iCloud items that are accessible to anyone who has the link for “harmful content” starting with iOS 27.3 and other 27.3 updates, the company says.
Apple will check shared iCloud links for ‘harmful content’
If you make an item on iCloud available to anyone who has the link, Apple will be able to check it starting with iOS 27.3.
“When you share an item that can be accessed by Anyone with the Link in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, that content is made accessible to Apple to check for harmful content,” according to a support document reported on by 9to5Mac. Sharing something over iCloud with the “Anyone with the Link” permissions will also mean that it’s no longer end-to-end encrypted.
Apple’s support document does not define what “harmful content” is. But this new approach follows calls from protestors for Apple to crack down on child sexual abuse material stored in iCloud.
Apple says it “reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete” any harmful content that a user attempts to upload. Apple may also block or disable accounts, prevent a user from making a new account, or, “if necessary,” invoke law enforcement.
The company launched the first 27.3 developer betas yesterday, and said recently it plans to launch iOS 27.3 in December.

articles.title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
articles.text:
Sponsored
Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
Data lineage is the new security perimeter, providing the visibility needed for governance, accountability, and trust, without impeding AI adoption at scale.
In partnership withCyberhaven
A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.
This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.
Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.
This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

Artificial intelligence

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating.

Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny.
The US spent billions on border surveillance. Why can’t it catch people before they die?
Surveillance towers, increasingly powered by AI, promised faster responses to crossings. Our investigation of deaths near the towers found they are failing to deliver.

articles.title: STMicro Expands STM32 Roadmap for Cloud AI and Physical AI - EE Times
articles.text:
STMicroelectronics is expanding its STM32 microcontroller (MCU) roadmap with multicore devices, hardware accelerators, and AI-assisted development tools as it positions the platform for growing cloud AI and physical AI markets.
“There are two rapidly growing markets today, cloud AI and physical AI, and it is our duty at ST to make sure that the STM32 platform will be the king of the microcontroller market in cloud AI and physical AI,” said Remi El-Ouazzane, president, microcontrollers, digital ICs, and RF products group at STMicroelectronics, answering a query posed by EE Times at ST’s global press briefing.
The company has introduced a unified STM32 microcontroller platform spanning industrial, automotive, and robotics applications.
Maria Erez, executive VP of STMicroelectronics’ embedded processing subgroup, said the unified STM32 platform is designed to let customers reuse existing software, development expertise, and manufacturing investments across product generations and application domains.
The company also announced its STM32A automotive and high-safety MCU portfolio, a new STM32G5 mixed-signal MCU series, a high-performance STM32H7P with a neural processing unit (NPU), redesigned edge AI development tools, and STM32Cube for agentic AI.
El-Ouazzane said the semiconductor industry is experiencing convergence across automotive, industrial, and other domains in areas such as AI, security, safety, connectivity, sensing, and control, creating opportunities to reuse common technologies and expertise.
“Across many applications, the challenge for customers and developers is shifting from selecting a single device to finding ways to reuse software, tools, architectures, and engineering expertise across multiple products and evolving requirements,” El-Ouazzane said.
“In other words, the value is shifting from the individual MCU to the broader platform surrounding it.”
The company sees this convergence extending to systems that can perceive, make decisions, and act autonomously in the physical world, including industrial equipment, automotive systems, and robots. While these applications share requirements for connectivity, real-time control, safety, security, and software lifecycle management, their specific certification requirements may differ.
Arm partnership
As part of its longstanding partnership with Arm, STMicroelectronics said it will help define the future Cortex-M processor roadmap, aiming to set up a common foundation for embedded systems.
The partnership also gives ST early access to Arm cores, allowing it to optimize its platform for the processor roadmap.
Erez said STM32 has helped drive Cortex-M adoption. STMicroelectronics said more than 100 billion devices use Arm Cortex-M cores. STMicroelectronics is working with more than 100 ecosystem companies through Arm’s Total Design program for physical AI, announced in September.
Arm said the program brings ecosystem partners together to accelerate development in the market, with STMicroelectronics and Cadence as key partners.
“Now, we want the entire industry to adopt it,” a company spokesperson said during the Q&A session, referring to the Cortex-M roadmap.
“The next major frontier for computing is bringing intelligence into the machines that move, manufacture, and operate in the physical world,” said Drew Henry, executive VP, physical AI at Arm.
STM32A for automotive and high-safety systems
The STM32A family extends the STM32 platform into automotive and high-safety systems. The first three devices are sampling to customers, and STMicroelectronics plans broader availability in 2027.
The STM32A4 targets entry-level automotive local control nodes and safety systems. The STM32A5 addresses mid-range safety-critical applications in industrial automation, robotics, and energy systems, as well as automotive applications. The STM32A9 addresses safety-critical, multi-domain control where real-time control, low latency, Ethernet, and deterministic communication are essential.
“This is about continuity,” Erez said. “STM32A is not a separate story. It is an extension of the STM32 platform strategy, which we plan to continue and expand.”
Both STM32 and STM32A will be supported by the STM32Cube ecosystem. Process technologies and intellectual property (IP) such as Cortex-M cores, timers, clock sources, analog components, and power management can be reused across domains. Safety certification requirements still differ by market. Industrial and automotive products must meet different functional safety standards and qualification requirements, with automotive applications commonly assessed under ISO 26262 and its Automotive Safety Integrity Levels (ASILs).
The company said future STM32 products will be built on its 40-nm flash technology and 18-nm fully depleted silicon-on-insulator (FD-SOI) technology with embedded phase-change memory, supplemented by TSMC’s embedded non-volatile memory (eNVM) technologies.
Erez said nearly 2 million unique developers use the STM32 ecosystem, and the number of active users has grown by around 20% over the past three years.
The company said customers choosing its Stellar automotive MCUs or STM32A have different application requirements. ST also sees more automotive companies moving into humanoid robotics, citing commonalities in functional safety and architecture. The company expects this trend to continue in the coming quarters and years.
STM32G5 for digital power and motor control
The STM32G5 series of mixed-signal MCUs is in production now. It uses an Arm Cortex-M33 core running at 280 MHz. ST said the series delivers twice the compute performance of the STM32G4 series.
The company targets the series for data centers, robotics, photovoltaic installations, wind turbines, industrial drives, and commercial drones.
“This new generation of microcontrollers addresses the challenge to meet the growing energy needs of AI data centers efficiently, realize more sophisticated humanoid robots, and power more complex motor-control systems,” said Patrick Aidoune, general manager, general purpose and automotive microcontrollers division at STMicroelectronics.
ST said GPU clusters are driving rack power toward 1 MW, and the largest data centers could demand more than 2 GW of peak power by 2030. The company said the STM32G5 is the first MCU with the company’s enhanced 12-channel high-resolution timer. Equipment makers can use it to reconfigure power supply units dynamically as server workloads change. The timer also lets the MCU handle the higher switching frequencies of power supplies built with silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN).
The company also said that robotics company Ruiyan Intelligent is using the STM32G5 in its next-generation robotic hands.
“In humanoid robotics, dexterity depends on combining strength, precision, sensing, and real-time control in an extremely compact space,” said Paul Tian, CEO of Ruiyan Intelligent.
The company said the series includes a programmable logic array, PLAy, which lets developers implement custom hardware functions on chip. Security features include Arm TrustZone, an immutable root of trust for secure boot and firmware updates, and support for ST’s post-quantum cryptography (PQC) libraries. The device targets Platform Security Architecture (PSA) Level 3 certification.
STM32G5 devices offer 64 Kbytes to 512 Kbytes of on-chip flash, in packages from QFN32 to LQFP128. Prices start at $1.034 for orders of 10,000 pieces. ST plans to add dual-core products to the series in 2027.
Edge AI hardware and tools
The STM32H7P combines a Cortex-M7 core with ST’s proprietary NPU for AI processing. It will enter volume production in early 2027. Aidoune said one alpha customer working on solar inverters moved from managing arc-fault circuit breakers across four panels to 20 panels using a single MCU.
ST began rolling out new and redesigned edge AI tools at the end of October. These include Model Zoo for finding models, Model Factory for customizing and optimizing models, Dataset Factory for organizing datasets, and tools for basic model testing on ST boards. ST said it offers more than 400 pre-validated models and has supported more than 260,000 active projects with its AI tools over the past 12 months.
ST said deploying AI models on MCUs depends far more on development tools than on computing power.
STM32Cube for agentic AI gives AI agents access to STM32 knowledge, resources, and toolkits through a model context protocol (MCP) server. It provides validated reference code and STM32 code generation and review tools.
Aidoune said the tool complements STM32 Sidekick, ST’s AI-based technical support tool. “STM32 Sidekick helps answer developers’ technical questions, while STM32Cube for agentic AI integrates into the coding workflow itself,” he said.
El-Ouazzane said ST needs to strengthen its MCU portfolio with single-core and multicore devices, different security levels, and different types of accelerators, peripherals, and memory. “Today’s announcement of STM32Cube for agentic AI is a step in the right direction, but there is more we can do,” he said.
Ecosystem over compute
Responding to a question from EE Times China on whether the industry is heading toward a computing power race, ST said its ecosystem will be its biggest differentiator. The company expects multicore architectures to become a trend within the cost constraints of the microcontroller category.
The company defined physical AI as a subset of edge AI. Physical AI systems perceive, decide, and act in the physical world, with actual movement through components such as joints and actuators. It said this is where the convergence between automotive and industrial applications is strongest.
“The industry needs less fragmentation and a stronger focus on helping MCU technologies converge around a common foundation, while maximizing software reuse,” El-Ouazzane said.

MIPS, GlobalFoundries Bet on Physical AI

articles.title: NVIDIA CUDA 13.5 Brings NVIDIA Vera Rubin GA Support | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
As artificial intelligence and accelerated computing continue to push the boundaries of what’s possible, the latest NVIDIA CUDA release arrives to unlock unprecedented performance and scale.
NVIDIA CUDA 13.5 delivers general availability (GA) across major new platforms. NVIDIA Vera Rubin support moves from early developer access to general availability (GA), ready for enterprise production. Windows on Arm support, GA since CUDA 13.4, now extends to NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows.
CUDA 13.5 also introduces more customization of how GPU work is scheduled via locality domains and NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS). And CUDA 13.5 provides innovations across libraries, compilers, NVIDIA CUDA Tile, and developer tools.
This post will showcase the highlights of CUDA 13.5.
CUDA 13.5 enhancements
Some notable enhancements that come with CUDA 13.5 include:
Locality domain enhancements
CUDA 13.5 gives applications a choice between uniform streaming multiprocessor (SM) partitions across locality domains or partitions that include all available SMs. By default, localized green-context partitions use the same guaranteed SM count per domain, leaving supplemental SMs outside those partitions.
The new cudaDevSmResourceGroupLocalityDomainSupplementalSms flag, combined with cudaDevSmResourceGroupLocalityDomainId, includes these additional SMs within each selected domain. This enables applications to use all device SMs when partitioning across locality domains, although the resulting partitions may differ in size. 
Applications can use discovery mode in the cudaDevSmResourceSplit() API to obtain each partition’s SM count and distribute work accordingly. This allows you to choose between the uniformity and predictability of uniform SM size for each locality domain, or to choose the maximum number of SMs that each locality domain has, and utilize as much of the GPU hardware as possible. For more info see the CUDA Runtime API.
NVIDIA MPS
MPS v3 gives you more control over how workloads share a GPU, from scheduling individual servers to assigning resources to groups of clients.
Weighted timeslicing
Weighted timeslicing lets you give longer compute turns to servers hosting workloads that need them. Set a base timeslice, scale it per MPS server, and independently tune how aggressively the GPU switches between workloads.
SM partition load balancing
SM partition load balancing lets workloads use capacity beyond their base partition when resources are available. Enable borrowing with --max-chunks, and allow a partition to lend its SMs while it has no attached clients with --shareable=true. These settings are independent, so a partition can borrow, lend, or do both. MPS reclaims borrowed resources before reassigning them, while applications continue to see a stable base partition size.
Cgroup-based routing
Cgroup-based routing connects your workload launcher’s process groupings to MPS resource policies. Map a cgroup v2 subtree to an MPS namespace, and clients connecting through the daemon’s main socket are routed to that namespace automatically.
SM partition assignments
Per-namespace SM partition assignments let you choose a partition for each device once, then apply that selection to every client routed to the namespace. You no longer need to configure CUDA_MPS_SM_PARTITION separately for those clients. Namespace assignments take precedence, while devices without an assignment retain the environment-variable fallback.
Polling-based fallback for memory accounting
Polling-based memory accounting provides a fallback when cgroup threshold notifications are missing or unreliable. During eviction decisions, MPS can read current usage and limits directly instead of relying on cached notification state. To force polling, run nvidia-cuda-mps-control memacct set force_polling=true before memory accounting starts. This adds work per eviction decision but removes its dependence on notification delivery.
Batched 1d copies in CUDA graphs
CUDA 13.5 adds CUDA Graph support for batched 1D memory copies. Applications can now include existing cudaMemcpyBatchAsync calls in stream capture without changing the batched-copy call syntax, allowing multiple transfers to be captured and replayed as part of a reusable graph workflow. Applications can also add batched-copy nodes explicitly and update compatible copy addresses and sizes without changing the batch structure.
Windows driver modes on NVIDIA Rubin
Starting with the NVIDIA Rubin architecture, CUDA supports Windows Driver Display Model (WDDM) and Microsoft Compute Driver Model (MCDM), with MCDM providing the compute-only driver model. Tesla Compute Cluster (TCC) is not supported on Rubin and later GPUs. Applications and deployment tools that assume TCC mode should use the supported WDDM or MCDM configuration for their target system.
CUDA Tile updates
Multi-gpu communication in CUDA Tile
CUDA 13.5 adds support for multi-GPU communication directly within CUDA Tile kernels. Unicast pointers let a kernel access memory on another NVLink-connected GPU, while multicast pointers and dedicated multimem operations support reductions and stores across multiple GPUs on NVIDIA NVSwitch fabrics with NVIDIA NVLink SHARP support. Applications prepare the shared-memory mappings before launch, then combine communication with computation inside the kernel, enabling workloads such as fused matrix multiplication and cross-GPU reduction.
Tile to single instruction multi-thread (SIMT) interoperability (public preview)
CUDA 13.5 allows CUDA Tile kernels to call SIMT library device functions directly. Before this release, Tile and SIMT library code could only be combined across kernel boundaries, with data passing through global memory between them. With this preview, kernels written in cuTile Python or CUDA Tile C++ can call device functions from SIMT libraries in the middle of their own code, on data that is already in registers or shared memory. These libraries include NVIDIA NVSHMEM, NVIDIA CCCL Coop, NVIDIA Warp and NVIDIA MathDx, which covers NVIDIA cuFFTDx, NVIDIA cuBLASDx, NVIDIA cuSolverDx, and NVIDIA nvCOMPDx, and this interop support will be enabled by each of these libraries soon.
A tile library (.tilelib) packages interface and implementation information for SIMT library functions. The compiler partitions each tile across threads the way the library expects, communicates any shared memory and synchronization requirements, and produces a single kernel. To enable the preview in C++, compile with nvcc --tile-preview simt and pass the tilelib to the tile compiler. In cuTile Python, use cuda.tile_preview.foreign_call, provided by the cuda.tile_preview package.
In 13.5, the Tile-SIMT interop preview covers library functions only. Calling your own __device__ functions from tile code is planned for a future release. For more information, see the documentation.
NVIDIA CUDA Python
NVIDIA CUDA Python continues to expand Pythonic access to CUDA programming. The CUDA Python core library cuda.core 1.2 introduces batched memory copies, Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL), simpler runtime compilation, and more flexible CUDA Graph updates.
Batched memory copies
The new cuda.core.utils.copy_batch() submits multiple buffer copies through a single CUDA driver call. CopyOptions provides control over source access ordering, memory-location hints, and overlap behavior, giving applications more control over data movement.
The following example submits two independent copies using existing source and destination buffers:
from cuda.core.utils import copy_batch
# Each source and destination pair must have matching sizes.
# Copies within the batch must not alias.
copy_batch(
    stream,
    srcs=[src_a, src_b],
    dsts=[dst_a, dst_b],
)
stream.sync()
PDL from Python
LaunchConfig now exposes PDL through the programmatic_stream_serialization option. On GPUs with compute capability 9.0 or newer, cooperating kernels can overlap execution within the same CUDA stream, allowing a dependent kernel to begin independent work before its predecessor completes. This gives Python applications access to inter-kernel overlap while retaining explicit control over launch configuration. See the LaunchConfig documentation.
from cuda.core import LaunchConfig, launch
config = LaunchConfig(
    grid=num_blocks,
    block=256,
    programmatic_stream_serialization=True,
)
# The kernel must implement the PDL synchronization protocol.
launch(stream, config, dependent_kernel, *kernel_args)
More flexible CUDA Graph updates
Applications can update graph-definition nodes before future instantiations and modify executable graph nodes through graph[node] views without reinstantiating the graph. Supported updates include kernel parameters, memory copies, memory sets, child graphs, events, and host callbacks. These capabilities simplify reusing graphs as application parameters change.
from cuda.core import LaunchConfig
from cuda.core.graph import GraphDefinition
# Define a graph with one kernel node.
graph_def = GraphDefinition()
node = graph_def.launch(
    LaunchConfig(grid=1, block=256),
    kernel,
    output_a,
)
# Instantiate once and run with the original output buffer.
graph = graph_def.instantiate()
graph.launch(stream)
stream.sync()
# Update the executable node's arguments without reinstantiating.
graph[node].update(args=(output_b,))
# The same graph now launches the kernel with output_b.
graph.launch(stream)
stream.sync()
CCCL
CUDA Toolkit 13.5 brings CCCL 3.5, with public tuning APIs for CUB, reproducible floating-point scans, a new batch Top-K selection and reductions that consume problem sizes directly from GPU memory. These additions give developers more control over algorithm execution and simplify pipelines with data-dependent workloads.
Customize CUB performance with public tuning APIs
CCCL 3.5 introduces public tuning policies for CUB device-wide algorithms. Developers can customize parameters such as threads per block, items per thread, vectorization, and algorithm selection through cuda::execution::tune(...) in an execution environment.
The following example shows how a policy selector chooses tuning parameters for a GPU compute capability. This selector returns cub::ReducePolicy for device-wide reductions; a scan selector would return cub::ScanPolicy. Applications that do not supply custom policies continue to use CUB’s default tuning. For examples, see the CUB tuning documentation.
struct ReduceTuning
{
    __host__ __device__
    constexpr cub::ReducePolicy
    operator()(cuda::compute_capability cc) const
    {
        auto pass = cub::ReducePassPolicy{
            .threads_per_block = 256,
            // Use 20 items per thread for compute capability 10.0
            // and newer, and 16 for older GPUs.
            .items_per_thread =
                cc >= cuda::compute_capability{10, 0} ? 20 : 16,
            .vec_size = 4,
            .reduce_algorithm = cub::BLOCK_REDUCE_WARP_REDUCTIONS,
            .load_modifier = cub::LOAD_LDG
        };
        // Provide tuning for both multi-tile and single-tile reductions.
        return {.multi_tile = pass, .single_tile = pass};
    }
};
// Attach the selector to the execution environment using the public tuning API.
auto env = cuda::std::execution::env{
    cuda::stream_ref{stream},
    cuda::execution::tune(ReduceTuning{})
};
// Keep using the public device-wide API. CUB applies the custom policy
// supplied through the environment.
auto status = cub::DeviceReduce::Sum(d_input, d_output, num_items, env);
Batched Top-K selection
Top-K selection is an important operation in AI workloads, including token selection during text generation and selecting relevant tokens for sparse attention. The new cub::DeviceBatchedTopK selects the smallest or largest K items independently across many segments, supporting keys and key-value pairs, variable segment sizes, and a K value that can vary by segment. NVIDIA has developed this algorithm with AI workloads in mind. CUB’s batched Top-K is integrated into FlashInfer, a library of GPU kernels for LLM inference.
constexpr int segment_size = 4;
constexpr int k = 2;
auto segments_in = cuda::make_strided_iterator(
    cuda::make_counting_iterator(d_input), segment_size);
auto segments_out = cuda::make_strided_iterator(
    cuda::make_counting_iterator(d_output), k);
auto env = cuda::std::execution::env{
    ...
};
auto status = cub::DeviceBatchedTopK::MaxKeys(
    segments_in,
    segments_out,
    cuda::args::constant<segment_size>{},
    cuda::args::constant<k>{},
    num_segments,
    env);
Reproducible floating-point scans
cub::DeviceScan adds support for run-to-run reproducibility for floating-point summation. Now you can request a fixed reduction order through the execution environment, producing repeatable results on the same GPU with the same input and build configuration.
The following example requests reproducible results for an inclusive sum. See the cub::DeviceScan documentation for details.
auto env = cuda::std::execution::env{
    cuda::stream_ref{stream},
    cuda::execution::require(
        cuda::execution::determinism::run_to_run)
};
auto status = cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum(
    d_input, d_output, num_items, env);
Keep data-dependent reductions on the GPU
CUB reductions can now consume an element count stored in device-accessible memory using cuda::args::deferred. A preceding kernel or selection operation can produce that count, and the reduction can read it in stream order without transferring it to the host. This also enables captured reductions to process a different element count on each CUDA Graph replay without updating or recapturing the graph.
For example, after a selection operation writes its output count to d_count, a reduction can consume it directly:
auto env = cuda::std::execution::env{
    cuda::stream_ref{stream},
    cuda::execution::require(
        cuda::execution::determinism::run_to_run)
};
auto status = cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum(
    d_input, d_output, num_items, env);
See the cub::DeviceReduce documentation for details.
New developer tools
NVIDIA Nsight Perf SDK for AI—public preview
CUDA Toolkit 13.5 introduces the public preview of the NVIDIA Nsight Perf SDK for AI, bringing always-on profiling to long-running training and inference workloads. The SDK preserves selected GPU and CPU performance metrics and execution context from the original run, helping developers investigate intermittent performance issues that can be difficult to reproduce. Developers can explore the collected data in Perfetto. Learn more here.
Additional features
NVIDIA Nsight Compute 2026.4 introduces a dedicated timeline page in NVIDIA Nsight Compute, making it easier to explore GPU workload performance over time. The page brings time-resolved profiling data into a central view to help developers identify workload phases, transient stalls, and shifts in hardware utilization that aggregate metrics can hide. Developers can switch between timelines and access integrated function stats analysis without leaving the page, keeping related performance insights together. Direct links from the details page simplify navigation to the relevant timeline, while built-in guidance helps users get started when a report contains no timeline data.
CUDA Toolkit 13.5 adds support in CUDA-GDB for stopping execution on CUDA Driver log events, helping developers investigate errors when they occur. Configurable rules filter events by thread, severity, or message pattern, so developers can focus on relevant diagnostics. When a matching event stops execution, developers can inspect the host-side call stack to trace the triggering code and identify the root cause.
This release also supports GPU core dump generation while CUPTI tracing is enabled. Developers can capture GPU state when an exception occurs and inspect the dump later using a supported debugger, without having to reproduce the failure with tracing disabled.
A new NVIDIA Compute Sanitizer agent skill helps AI coding agents choose the right diagnostics and interpret CUDA memory, race-condition, and synchronization errors.
NVIDIA Nsight Cloud now supports OpenTelemetry trace integration and profiling configuration for NVIDIA Dynamo deployments through Nsight Operator, helping developers investigate AI workload performance at scale.
Math libraries
Core CUDA math libraries in CUDA 13.5 now have performance improvements on Vera Rubin. cuBLAS extends Ozaki-II scheme to FP64 symmetric rank-k updates. Other new features and notable performance improvements include:
NVIDIA cuBLAS
- Faster GEMMs on NVIDIA Vera Rubin: Updated heuristics and kernel tuning improve out-of-the-box NVFP4 and MXFP8 matmul performance on Vera Rubin, including mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLM training shapes. Training and inference workloads get higher throughput without per-shape autotuning.
- Ozaki-II for FP64 symmetric rank-k updates: The Ozaki-II scheme now supports {D,Z}SYR{K,2K,KX} and ZHER{K,2K,KX} on NVIDIA Ampere and newer GPUs. As a result, applications that exercise Cholesky factorizations and least-squares solvers built on cuSOLVER now get Tensor Core acceleration for these routines as well.
- Faster native FP64 symmetric updates on NVIDIA Blackwell: SYR2K, HER2K, SYRKX, and HERKX in double and double-complex precision are up to 1.5x faster on NVIDIA B200. Scientific codes that use native FP64 symmetric updates, such as eigensolvers and matrix factorizations, speed up with no code changes.
- Optimized BF16 kernels for unaligned shapes: BF16 matmuls whose dimensions aren’t multiples of eight now use the same optimized kernels as FP16 on NVIDIA Hopper and newer GPUs. Models with irregular layer sizes, including convolutions dispatched through NVIDIA cuDNN, no longer pay a penalty for choosing BF16 over FP16.
- Windows on Arm support for Blackwell GPUs: cuBLAS adds functional support for Blackwell GPUs, including GB300 workstations, on Windows on Arm. Developers on Arm-based Windows systems can run cuBLAS-accelerated applications without switching platforms.
NVIDIA cuSPARSE
- Faster FP32 and FP64 CSR SpMM with ALG3: Deliver 1.65x to 2.27x faster performance across data center GPUs, accelerating sparse matrix–dense matrix multiplication.
- New SpSV ALG2 algorithm: Deliver 2.7x faster solve performance than ALG1, measured by geometric mean, accelerating workloads that repeatedly solve sparse triangular systems.
- Faster SpSV analysis: Achieve a 2.79x geometric-mean speedup in the analysis phase, reducing setup time for sparse triangular solves.
- Lower SpSV memory usage: Reduce the memory footprint of sparse triangular solves, leaving more GPU memory available for application data.
- Expanded mixed-index support: Use 64-bit offsets with 32-bit indices across SpMV (CSR, SELL), SpMM (CSR), SpSV (SELL), and sparse-to-dense/dense-to-sparse conversions (CSR, CSC), enabling larger sparse matrices while keeping index memory usage lower than with fully 64-bit indexing.
- Mixed-precision CSR SpMV: Combine FP16 or BF16 matrix values with FP32 input/output vectors and FP32 computation in cusparseSpMV, reducing matrix storage requirements while retaining FP32 accumulation.
- New experimental cusparseSpMVGeneric API: Perform SpMV on symmetric matrices while storing only the upper or lower triangle, reducing storage requirements by avoiding duplicate off-diagonal entries.
- New experimental cusparseSpMatConvert API: Convert between CSR and CSC formats, making it easier to adapt sparse matrix layouts to different operations.
- Faster graph coloring with csrcolor: Achieve approximately 3x faster performance, measured by geometric mean, reducing time spent in sparse matrix coloring.
nvJPEG
- GPU Hybrid decode throughput: Decode throughput for NVJPEG_BACKEND_GPU_HYBRID backend improves by 10% to 600%, depending on the image size, and whether standard Huffman table is used.
- Automatic backend selection: NVJPEG_BACKEND_GPU_HYBRID is now also considered as part of automatic backend selection when using the nvjpegDecode API (previously only NVJPEG_BACKEND_HYBRID and NVJPEG_BACKEND_HARDWARE were considered)
Updated compilers
Precompile device code during packaging with nvprune
CUDA 13.5 introduces a --precompile option in nvprune, allowing developers to compile intermediate device code (PTX, TileIR) to native SASS/ELF during the prune step. 
This eliminates runtime JIT overhead for downstream consumers who deploy fat binaries to known target architectures (e.g. cloud providers, package distributors).
You should select targets that match your deployment environment and validate the resulting artifacts across the GPU architectures you intend to support.
Extending CompileIQ support
CUDA 13.5 extends advanced controls file (ACF) support to the PTX Compiler and NVVM libraries. This allows compilation workflows built on these libraries to apply CompileIQ-generated compiler controls.
More control over TMA addressing and faster cycle-based trigonometry
CUDA 13.5 expands PTX and device-intrinsic capabilities to help developers optimize data movement and mathematical operations.
Configure TMA out-of-bounds addressing inside kernels
Tiled computations frequently encounter tensor boundaries where part of a tile falls outside the tensor’s dimensions. Handling these ragged tiles efficiently is important for workloads such as MoE, matrix multiplication, and convolutions.
CUDA 13.5 extends the PTX tensormap.replace instruction so kernels can update a tensor map’s Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) out-of-bounds addressing mode directly. This gives developers control over addressing behavior when reusing tensor-map descriptors and can eliminate a performance-costly workaround for illegal-address failures in affected workloads.
Fast approximate single-precision trigonometric calculations with cycle-based inputs
CUDA 13.5 adds the __sin2pif, __cos2pif, and __sincos2pif device intrinsics for fast approximate single-precision trigonometric calculations with inputs expressed in cycles. 
This capability is useful for phase-based computations that can use fast approximate trigonometric results.
Corresponding PTX .2pi variants of the sin and cos instructions avoid an additional angle-conversion operation for workloads that already use cycle-based phase.
Read CUDA binary symbols more easily with cuobjdump
CUDA 13.5 improves ELF symbol-table output in cuobjdump, making it easier to understand the functions and variables contained in CUDA binaries.
| Column | Description | 
| Type | Identifies the symbol type, such as function or object | 
| Bind | Shows the symbol’s binding, such as local or global | 
| Vis | Shows symbol visibility | 
| Other | Identifies CUDA-specific attributes, such as kernel entry points and memory-space attributes | 
Previously, symbol information and CUDA-specific attributes appeared as raw hexadecimal fields that developers had to decode manually. The updated output presents descriptive values in four columns, following conventions familiar to users of readelf -s:
This makes it easier to distinguish kernel entry points from device functions and inspect attributes associated with global, constant, shared, and managed variables. When multiple CUDA attributes apply, the output lists their names together. Unrecognized attribute values remain visible as UNKNOWN(0xNN).
The enhancement applies to the existing --dump-elf and --dump-elf-symbols options. For example, developers can inspect a CUDA binary with:
cuobjdump --dump-elf-symbols application.cubin
No additional option is required to obtain the descriptive output. Existing information—including symbol names, values, sizes, and section indices—remains available.
If you use scripts to parse these symbol-table dumps, update the script parsers to accommodate the new columns and named attribute values.
Get started with CUDA Toolkit 13.5
CUDA Toolkit 13.5 provides GA support for NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPU architecture, updated GPU resource-management and communication capabilities, and enhancements across CUDA Python, CCCL, CUDA Tile, NVIDIA Nsight developer tools, and core math libraries.
Download CUDA Toolkit 13.5 and review the CUDA Toolkit 13.5 release notes for the complete list of features, supported platforms, and compatibility information.
Jackson Marusarz, Mahender Hari, Mridula Prakash, Daniel Rodriguez, and Sandeep Hiremath contributed to the work in this blog.

articles.title: Blog Review: Nov. 4
articles.text:
Chiplets for physical AI; rack-level considerations; verification complexity; sparse matrix workloads; AI data centers.
Cadence’s Mick Posner introduces a physical AI sub-project workstream to extend the OCP’s Foundation Chiplet System Architecture’s data center, cloud, and server-centric baseline with the specification requirements to satisfy real-time, safety-critical physical systems, while retaining everything FCSA already defines.
Synopsys’ Charlie Matar considers how design focus is shifting from the server to the rack, with silicon behavior shaping rack-level power and cooling requirements, while rack constraints influence decisions inside chips and packages.
Siemens’ Harry Foster warns that while verification complexity has been managed by dividing large problems into smaller pieces, new challenges are emerging as the number and diversity of interactions influencing correct SoC behavior grows.
Arm’s Zenon (Zhilong) Xiu examines how quarter-tile and structured sparsity outer product instructions make the SME2 programming model better suited to small, dense, quantized, and sparse matrix workloads in modern AI software.
Keysight’s Linas Dauksa digs into AI data center infrastructure, including key components, energy demands and power density challenges, the array of liquid cooling technologies available, and what differentiates hyperscale facilities.
SEMI’s Sungho Yoon considers factors related to a forecasted increase in wafer shipments, including rising process material sales and a high number of new and upcoming production lines.
Plus, check out the blogs featured in the latest Systems & Design newsletter:
Technology editor Brian Bailey poses the age-old question for anyone involved in the verification of semiconductor systems: in the age of AI, who verifies the verifier?
Axiomise’s Vidya Chandran Darbari and Ashish Darbari dig into what biological reasoning can teach us about verifying silicon systems.
Keysight’s Chris Mueth explains why applying the appropriate level of simulation and abstraction at each stage of the design process is needed for effective thermal analysis.
Siemens EDA’s Emma-Jane Crozier explores how self-verifying agents validate their decisions and why physics-based engines are the authority on correctness.
Arteris’ Leon Brown looks at which products may fall within the EU Cyber Resilience Act’s scope and what information may need to be provided to customers.
Movellus’ Aakash Jani and Siemens’ Henrique Mendes and Robert Wilcox separate false failures caused by voltage droop from real structural defects.
ChipAgents’ Zackary Glazewski demonstrates how to deal with difficult bugs while intelligently deciding what to investigate, what to rerun, and where to spend compute.
Vinci’s Hardik Kabaria examines why physics-based analysis becomes more consequential as chips, packages, boards, and systems are designed together.
Cadence’s Reela Samuel breaks down how to orchestrate multi-step engineering workflows to reduce repetitive effort and explore more design options.
Synopsys’ Anand Thiruvengadam outlines how autonomous engineering agents pursue an objective requiring hundreds or thousands of reasoning steps while maintaining context, evaluating results, and adapting along the way.

articles.title: Journify raises $12 million at fourfold valuation increase
articles.text:
Journify raises $12 million at fourfold valuation increase
- US-headquartered adtech startup Journify has raised $12 million in Series A funding round led by Al Mada Ventures and co-led by existing investor Silicon Badia. Shorooq and Bunat Ventures increased their investments, while Du Ventures and Oraseya Capital joined as new investors.
- Founded in 2022 by Taoufik El Jamali, Amine Chouki and Omar Al Shoubaki, Journify is headquartered in San Francisco, US, with regional offices in Dubai and Riyadh. Its advertising data infrastructure connects customer interactions and sales data across online and offline channels to improve advertising performance.
- The company serves more than 100 businesses, including Jarir Bookstore and Baytonia, and reported over fivefold revenue growth since Silicon Badia's initial investment. Its latest round was completed at four times its previous valuation.
- Journify will use the funding to expand into the US and European markets and strengthen its AI capabilities for monitoring, detecting, and resolving issues related to advertising data quality.
Press release:
Journify, the ad signal infrastructure company, today announced a $12 million Series A at four times its previous valuation. Al Mada Ventures led the round, co-led by returning investor Silicon Badia, with Shorooq and Bunat Ventures increasing their investment and Du Ventures and Oraseya Capital joining as new investors. The funding will take Journify into the US and Europe and expand the AI behind its platform.
Global ad spend will exceed $1 trillion in 2026, with algorithms expected to place three-quarters by 2028, according to dentsu. These systems learn from the customer outcomes brands send back. Browser restrictions, broken tracking, and disconnected offline sales leave them with an incomplete picture of who buys.
Journify makes sure ad platforms such as Google, Meta, TikTok, Snap and Amazon Ads see the purchases, sign-ups and store sales a brand's customers actually make. More than 100 businesses use Journify today, from fast-growing ecommerce brands to some of the region's largest retailers, representing hundreds of millions of dollars in annual ad spend.
Customers include Jarir Bookstore, one of Saudi Arabia's largest retailers, which increased its return on ad spend by 182%, and Saudi ecommerce brand Baytonia, which grew its return on ad spend by 80% while cutting cost per purchase by 44%.
"AI is transforming advertising, but the intelligence behind it is only as good as the signals it receives," said Taoufik El Jamali, Co-Founder and CEO of Journify. "Businesses know who buys, who comes back and what creates lasting customer value. Too little of that knowledge reaches the ad platforms driving their growth. Our vision is to close that gap, turning real customer outcomes into intelligence ad platforms can learn from. We're building toward a future where advertising AI understands what makes a customer valuable to each business, not just what makes them click."
"As AI takes on a greater role in marketing, we believe the connection between reliable customer data and the decisions built on it will become increasingly valuable," said Omar Laalej, Managing Director at Al Mada Ventures. "What interests us about Journify is its approach to building that connection from the data layer up: a privacy-first foundation that can evolve into intelligence and action. The founders' understanding of that opportunity gives us confidence in their ability to build a platform that marketers can increasingly rely on, both to understand their customers and to act on that understanding."
Hossam Shafick, Partner at Silicon Badia, Seed Lead and returning investor, added, "Since our initial investment, Journify has grown its valuation by more than 4x, and its revenues more than 5x, validating both the strength of its technology and the team's ability to execute at scale. That performance has deepened our conviction that Journify can become a global leader in ad signal infrastructure. We are proud to double down and co-lead this round as the company expands into the world's largest advertising markets."
Journify already uses AI to monitor every connection continuously, detect signal-quality issues and fix them. The new funding will grow those capabilities as Journify expands beyond the GCC. In the US alone, digital advertising revenue reached $294.6 billion in 2025, according to IAB and PwC.
"I'm excited to help Journify scale in the biggest ad market in the world," said Ryan Burke, a newly appointed member of Journify's board and three-time Chief Revenue Officer. "I've known Taoufik since our InVision days, and I've seen his product execution in action. Based on the success they're already seeing in the Middle East, it's not a question whether it works in the US, but how fast we can scale."

articles.title: Samsung’s official early Black Friday deals include up to AU$7,000 off TVs
articles.text:
Samsung’s official early Black Friday deals include up to AU$7,000 off TVs
Plus a range of savings on soundbars, gaming monitors and more
We’re still a month out from the official weekend of Black Friday sales in Australia, but that hasn’t stopped a number of Australian brands from dropping some respectable early deals.
Samsung is the latest to get in on the action, with a range of savings across mobiles, tablets, gaming monitors and home appliances. The standout deals, in my opinion, have to be the savings available on a range of TVs and soundbars.
For a limited time, there are discounts on Mini-LED and Micro RGB TVs, with the biggest saving being given to the brand's huge 115-inch MR95F. This monster of a screen is down from AU$41,999 to AU$34,777, a saving of AU$7,222. You can even get up to a further AU$1,100 knocked off when you trade in a TV.
Additionally, Samsung is offering a 20% saving on selected TV and soundbar bundles. For example, you can pick the 55-inch S95H OLED TV (AU$3,999) and pair it with the HW-Q800H soundbar (AU$1,999), for a total AU$4,078.40 — a saving of AU$1,019.60.
Obviously, as Samsung's flagship OLED, the S95H might not suit everyone, but fortunately, Samsung has a selection of other discounted TVs that are more accessible.
Samsung The Frame Pro | save up to AU$1,500
The latest update to the popular Frame TV series now benefits from Neo QLED mini-led technology, and it gets the wireless One Connect box too. The ushering in of Neo QLED dramatically improves picture quality, including brightness, contrast and black levels. This screen is available in 55, 65, 75 and 85-inch variants, with up to AU$1,500 knocked off depending on the price. Plus, you can save up to AU$725 extra when you trade in an old TV.
Samsung R85H Micro RGB TV | save up to AU$3,500
The R85H is the slightly lower-spec model in Samsung’s two-strong Micro RGB lineup (the other being the R95H). We haven’t had a chance to review it just yet, but Samsung regularly impresses us with its screens, so we have high hopes for this one. The biggest saving applies to the 100-inch model (now AU$9,499). Plus get up to AU$1,100 extra discount with trade in.
There are plenty more early Samsung Black Friday deals to get stuck into, and I’ve listed out the most appealing below:
Samsung is gunning for Sonos’ crown with the Music Studio 7. This 3.1.1-channel speaker can serve up "spatial sound" from a single unit, or you can pair two together for an authentic stereo presentation. They can be used with music or movies, complete with Hi-Res audio support, and the ability to be used as rear surrounds with a Q-series soundbar. Now better-than-half-price, you can concievably get a pair for less than the price of one — use code BFHOME to get the full discount.
The smaller member of the Music Studio family, the Studio 5 is a 2.1-channel affair that adopts a similarly minimalistic aesthetic. Given there’s no HDMI port, this model is best suited for music playback, but as with the 7, you can pair two together for stereo sound — use code BFHOME to save a further 5%.
This enormous 57-inch gaming monitor combines Dual UHD resolution, Mini-LED backlighting and a 240Hz refresh rate for incredibly immersive gaming. Use code BFHOME for the biggest discount.
I expect plenty more Samsung Black Friday deals to continue to pop up as we approach the official Black Friday and Cyber Monday weekend, so make sure to regularly check back to this page for all the latest highlights.

articles.title: SCX 26 : Naval Group ose le canon électromagnétique, arme que l’US Navy a abandonné après 500 millions de dollars
articles.text:
C’est un navire qui n’existe, pour l’instant, que sur papier, mais qui préfigure peut-être ce que sera la marine dans vingt ans. Pour l’édition 2026 du salon Euronaval à Paris, le géant de la défense Naval Group a présenté le concept SCX 26. Il s’agit d’un navire qui embarquerait des technologies futuristes, à côté de systèmes d’armes plus classiques.
Dans le détail, il s’agit d’un bateau long de 170 mètres, qui déplace 8 000 tonnes. Prévu pour un équipage de 150 marins (plus 100 places pour un état-major ou du personnel spécialisé), il est pensé pour parcourir plus de 8 000 milles nautiques (environ 14 800 kilomètres) et filer jusqu’à 30 nœuds (environ 55,5 km/h). Naval Group dit l’avoir conçu pour associer « puissance, évolutivité et résilience ».
Côté armement, Naval Group parle de plus de 100 silos VLS (Vertical Launching System, des cellules de lancement vertical pour missiles) de différentes classes, d’une artillerie secondaire téléopérée à 360°, de munitions téléopérées (des drones kamikazes, en clair) et même deux lanceurs modulaires polyvalents Rampart, système qui a été testé en mer récemment.
Mais Naval Group y ajoute aussi des armes encore expérimentales. On parle en particulier d’un « canon électromagnétique à capacité de salves rapides », à côté d’un laser de 100 kilowatts (kW), deux solutions que l’on croise surtout sur des prototypes et lors d’essais.
Pourquoi ajouter un canon électromagnétique à côté d’une centaine de silos à missiles ? Pour le prix du tir. Un canon électromagnétique (on parle aussi de railgun) fonctionne sans poudre. Il fait passer un courant électrique très intense dans deux rails parallèles, et le champ magnétique créé lance l’obus entre ces rails à plusieurs fois la vitesse du son.
Comme le projectile n’a ni explosif ni moteur, il coûte beaucoup moins cher qu’un missile. Cela correspond à ce que Naval Group dit viser : répondre aux menaces « multiples et saturantes », comme les essaims de drones, sans vider son stock de missiles. Accessoirement, comme il est inerte, ce projectile est aussi beaucoup plus sûr à stocker dans les soutes d’un navire.
Les précisions s’arrêtent là : l’industriel ne publie aucune caractéristique de l’arme, ni calibre ni portée. Le SCX 26 est surtout un exercice de prospective. Naval Group prévient d’ailleurs qu’il ne préfigure « pas nécessairement un programme à venir ». Le concept montre toutefois comment Naval Group imagine la guerre en mer de demain.
Une arme que la marine américaine a laissée tomber
Aujourd’hui, aucune marine n’utilise encore cette arme en dehors des essais. Les États-Unis ont fini par y renoncer, alors que la Navy américaine a longtemps cru au railgun. Elle a arrêté son programme en juillet 2021, après y avoir consacré environ 500 millions de dollars (environ 450 millions d’euros) en quinze ans, selon The Defense Post.
Plusieurs facteurs ont pesé dans la balance, selon la marine américaine : le budget pour développer ce programme, la difficulté à installer l’arme sur ses navires et les avancées de plusieurs autres systèmes, comme les lasers et les missiles hypersoniques. Surtout, le fonctionnement du canon lui-même posait problème.
Dès 2018, l’amiral John Richardson, alors chef des opérations navales américaines, expliquait devant le Congrès que le tube du canon était le maillon faible : ses matériaux devaient supporter à chaque tir une décharge électrique, une chaleur et une pression extrêmes. En clair, les rails s’usaient beaucoup trop vite.
Pas de quoi, donc, remplacer rapidement les missiles habituels et l’artillerie à l’ancienne.
Cela étant, d’autres continuent de s’y pencher. C’est le cas du Japon : sa marine a même tiré pour la première fois avec un canon électromagnétique sur un autre navire, lors d’essais en mer en 2025. La France travaille aussi sur le sujet : elle s’est associée en 2024 à l’Allemagne et au Japon pour développer ces canons.

articles.title: Il fait tourner iPadOS sur sa Nintendo Switch : une drôle de tablette avec des Joy-Con
articles.text:
Le développeur Bruno St John a montré le système de l’iPad en fonctionnement sur une Switch de première génération. L’écran d’accueil et les réglages sont accessibles, mais ce bricolage reste loin d’une tablette utilisable au quotidien.
Safari à l’écran, un Joy-Con de chaque côté : cette Nintendo Switch affiche une interface que ni Nintendo ni Apple n’avaient prévue pour elle. Le 1er novembre, Bruno St John a partagé une photo sur X, puis une vidéo du démarrage en réponse à un internaute qui demandait des preuves. Il s’agit d’une démonstration d’émulation, aux limites encore bien visibles.
Une Switch qui se présente comme un iPad Pro
La première photo montre Safari ouvert sur la console, avec sa barre latérale et l’adresse google.com. Dans la vidéo publiée ensuite, les messages de démarrage défilent pendant plusieurs minutes avant de laisser place à l’écran d’accueil, puis aux réglages.
La rubrique consacrée aux informations de l’appareil indique iPadOS 17.7.11 et identifie la machine comme un iPad Pro 12,9 pouces de deuxième génération. L’interface est adaptée aux dimensions de l’écran de la Switch, avec le dock et les icônes du système d’Apple.
Pour autant, iPadOS n’a pas été porté directement sur le matériel de Nintendo. Comme le rapporte OneJailbreak, le montage repose sur QEMU : cet outil permet d’émuler le matériel attendu par le système. La console, équipée d’une puce Nvidia Tegra X1, exécute ainsi un environnement qui se fait passer pour un iPad.
Ce fonctionnement suppose de pouvoir exécuter des logiciels non officiels sur la Switch. Il ne s’agit donc pas d’une installation proposée dans les menus habituels de la console. La configuration exacte utilisée par Bruno St John reste toutefois à préciser.
Un démarrage réussi, une tablette encore hypothétique
L’idée rappelle une précédente tentative que nous avions relayée en juin 2025. Un autre développeur, PatRyk, avait alors fait démarrer iOS sur une Switch à l’aide de QEMU. Le système demandait plus de vingt minutes de patience, plantait fréquemment et ne permettait pas d’ouvrir les applications.
La démonstration de Bruno St John va plus loin, puisque l’écran d’accueil, les réglages et Safari s’affichent. Une seule séquence ne suffit toutefois pas à établir la stabilité de l’ensemble.
Plusieurs questions restent en suspens : performances des autres applications, prise en charge de l’écran tactile ou possibilité d’utiliser les Joy-Con pour naviguer. OneJailbreak relève également que la Switch reste branchée pendant toute la vidéo. Celle-ci ne permet donc pas de juger son autonomie sur batterie.
Voir le système d’Apple sur une console Nintendo suffit à rendre ce détournement réjouissant. Pour recycler sa vieille Switch en tablette, il faudra encore davantage qu’un écran d’accueil et une fenêtre Safari.

articles.title: Indian startups with over $500M valuation grow to 51 despite low number of AI entities: Report
articles.text:
Indian startups with over $500M valuation grow to 51 despite low number of AI entities: Report
The combined value of these 51 entities is about Rs 3.3 lakh crore ($34.1 billion), with an average valuation of about Rs 6,400 crore, and they employ over 60,000 people.
Indian startups with a valuation of over $500 million have increased to 51 in 2026, from 47 in the year-ago period despite lower number of artificial intelligence (AI) companies, a report said on Tuesday.
The combined value of these 51 entities is about Rs 3.3 lakh crore ($34.1 billion), with an average valuation of about Rs 6,400 crore, and they employ over 60,000 people, as per the 2026 ASK Private Wealth Hurun India Gazelle Index report.
The entities have reported combined revenue of Rs 33,233 crore, growing 50% year-on-year, the report said.
Anas Rahman Junaid, founder and chief researcher, Hurun India, said the list includes three names engaged in AI, including Ema AI, Observe.AI and UnifyApps which is very low when compared with 54 in the US and 23 in China.
However, despite this, the number of Indian gazelles, or the companies with over $500 million, has grown to 51 this year, he added.
The lack of AI-themed companies is often cited as one of the biggest reasons for foreign investors withdrawing from the Indian public equity markets.
The report said seven startups crossed $1 billion to become unicorns in 2026, with Twin Health's valuation rising to $2 billion from $700 million. Financial services and healthcare account for six of the seven.
"It reflects an entrepreneurial base that is diversifying across sectors and geographies and building scalable businesses with the potential to compete globally," said Rajesh Saluja, Co-Founder, CEO & MD of ASK Private Wealth.
Further, the report said AI and CleanTech are the largest of the three frontier sectors, with three startups each.
AI group comprises Ema AI, Observe.AI and UnifyApps, and CleanTech comprises Carbon Clean Solutions, Lohum and Rayzon Solar.
A total of 34 startups have moved up to unicorn status on the CGU Index since inception. Two startups were listed on the public markets, Shadowfax in January 2026 and Turtlemint in June 2026, the report said.
FinTech is the largest sector with 13 startups, followed by SaaS and ecommerce with five each. Bengaluru is home to 17 startups in the list, ahead of NCR with 11 and Mumbai with eight.
The report said 10 startups maintain a headquarters outside India--seven in the US, two in Singapore, and one in the UK. India ranks third globally in startups--behind the US and China.
IIT Kharagpur is the most common undergraduate institution among startup founders with 13, followed by IIT Bombay and IIT Kanpur with six each, the report said.
Further, IIT Bombay is the most common postgraduate institution among startup founders with seven, followed by IIM Ahmedabad with five.
The report added that women founders are present across six startups, Prukalpa Sankar (Atlan), Shruti Aggarwal (StashFin), Sunita Sahney (Finova Capital), Amrita Sirohia (INDMoney), Pallavi Shrivastava (Progcap) and Nikita Prasad (GIVA).

articles.title: EEUU tuvo una idea hace 20 años para matar a los mosquitos. China la acaba de hacer realidad con una torreta láser automática para pulverizarlos
articles.text:
Hace casi dos décadas, un grupo de ingenieros estadounidenses tuvo una idea que parecía sacada de la ciencia ficción: construir un sistema capaz de identificar mosquitos en pleno vuelo y derribarlos con disparos láser. El proyecto llegó a funcionar, pero nunca se convirtió en un producto de consumo. Ahora, desde China han recuperado aquel concepto, le han añadido inteligencia artificial y están intentando llevarlo al mercado por unos 1.000 dólares.
El resultado parece un sistema de defensa antiaérea en miniatura.
La idea nació en Estados Unidos. En 2006, Nathan Myhrvold, antiguo director de tecnología de Microsoft y fundador de Intellectual Ventures, planteó a un grupo de ingenieros una pregunta insólita: ¿sería posible matar mosquitos con un láser? La propuesta surgió de conversaciones sobre cómo combatir la malaria, una enfermedad transmitida por mosquitos que seguía causando cientos de miles de muertes anuales.
Entre los especialistas involucrados estaba Lowell Wood, un físico que había trabajado en proyectos relacionados con la defensa estratégica estadounidense durante la Guerra Fría. Su respuesta fue diseñar una especie de barrera invisible que pudiera detectar insectos, distinguirlos de otros animales y dispararles automáticamente. La llamaron Photonic Fence, o valla fotónica, y en 2009 Intellectual Ventures ya había construido prototipos funcionales.
Una Estrella de la Muerte contra los mosquitos. En febrero de 2010, Myhrvold presentó públicamente la tecnología durante una conferencia TED en California. El sistema utilizaba sensores ópticos y cámaras para localizar mosquitos, seguir sus movimientos y dirigir un láser hacia ellos, con la posibilidad de distinguir insectos por características como su tamaño y el batido de sus alas. La demostración incluía una detección en directo mediante un láser inocuo y vídeos de insectos abatidos con disparos reales.
La comparación con la Estrella de la Muerte de Star Wars fue inevitable, y medios como TIME o Wired incluyeron el invento entre las innovaciones destacadas de aquel año. Sin embargo, convertir el prototipo en una solución asequible, segura y fácil de desplegar resultó mucho más complicado. La tecnología continuó desarrollándose, pero aquella prometedora arma contra la malaria nunca llegó a fabricarse de forma masiva para los consumidores.
China retoma el proyecto. Dieciséis años después de aquella demostración, la empresa Photon Matrix Lab, con sede en Changzhou, en la provincia china de Jiangsu, ha desarrollado su propio sistema de defensa contra mosquitos. Su dispositivo, llamado Laser Mosquito Air Defense System, tiene aproximadamente el tamaño de un ladrillo y combina sensores láser, cámaras e inteligencia artificial para localizar pequeños objetos voladores y neutralizarlos.
La compañía ofrece dos versiones: una con láser infrarrojo invisible, destinada principalmente a interiores, por 988 dólares, y otra con láser azul visible, orientada al uso exterior, por 1.088 dólares. Ambas prometen un rendimiento similar. La diferencia respecto al proyecto estadounidense no es haber descubierto que un láser puede derribar mosquitos, sino intentar integrar todos los componentes en un aparato compacto, fabricable y destinado al mercado doméstico.
Cien mil pulsos por segundo. El funcionamiento recuerda al de un pequeño sistema antiaéreo automatizado. El dispositivo utiliza tecnología lidar, habitual en vehículos autónomos, para emitir aproximadamente 100.000 pulsos láser de baja potencia por segundo y vigilar un plano bidimensional situado frente a la máquina. Cuando detecta un objeto volador diminuto, calcula su trayectoria y activa un láser de mayor potencia para interceptarlo. Cada disparo dura alrededor de una centésima de segundo y está diseñado para quemar las alas del mosquito, impidiéndole continuar volando.
Durante una demostración presenciada por The New York Times, el aparato derribó varios insectos consecutivamente, que cayeron al suelo con el cuerpo aparentemente intacto, pero sin capacidad para despegar. No murieron al instante necesariamente, de hecho, según el fundador de la empresa, Wang Chuan, algunos pueden sobrevivir durante horas o incluso días después de perder las alas.
El verdadero problema no son los mosquitos. Para conseguir una eficacia suficiente, Photon Matrix descartó los láseres de clase 3 y terminó utilizando uno de clase 4, la categoría de mayor peligrosidad. ¿Razones? Estos dispositivos pueden provocar lesiones oculares graves en una exposición extremadamente breve, por lo que la seguridad se ha convertido en el principal obstáculo comercial. La empresa asegura haber incorporado cámaras con inteligencia artificial para reconocer personas y mascotas, sistemas de detección de superficies reflectantes y sensores adicionales capaces de identificar movimientos incluso en completa oscuridad.
También exige superar un cuestionario de seguridad de 15 preguntas antes de permitir el registro de una huella dactilar para activar la máquina. Dicho esto, todas esas medidas dependen de que los sistemas funcionen correctamente, porque un disparo accidental o un reflejo inesperado podría tener consecuencias graves. Contaba el Times que la compañía está buscando las autorizaciones correspondientes en China, Europa y Estados Unidos, aunque todavía no ha demostrado públicamente que su producto sea seguro en todas las condiciones de uso doméstico.
De un experimento a negocio millonario. Porque la acogida comercial ha superado ampliamente las expectativas iniciales. Photon Matrix Lab lanzó una campaña en Indiegogo con el objetivo de recaudar 20.000 dólares y terminó superando los 2,8 millones, impulsada por vídeos que se viralizaron en las redes sociales. La empresa asegura haber recibido más de 5.000 pedidos, principalmente de Europa y Norteamérica, y anunció una capacidad inicial prevista de entre 3.000 y 5.000 unidades mensuales.
Con todo y, como explicaban en el Times, el salto del laboratorio a la fábrica está resultando algo más complicado. Wang Chuan reconoció que inicialmente pensaban desarrollar el producto en tres meses y terminaron necesitando tres años. La compañía esperaba comenzar la producción masiva en julio de 2026, después retrasó sus previsiones y, a finales de septiembre, admitió que todavía estaba realizando pruebas de preproducción. Dicho de otra forma, aunque anunció entregas iniciales para octubre, los pedidos y la recaudación no equivalen a miles de dispositivos ya entregados y funcionando en hogares.
La paradoja de una guerra diminuta. Si se quiere, la historia resume una transformación tecnológica que va mucho más allá de los mosquitos. Estados Unidos demostró hace casi dos décadas que era posible localizar insectos y abatirlos mediante disparos láser, pero no consiguió convertir aquella tecnología en un producto doméstico de fabricación masiva. China apunta a dar ese último paso aprovechando una cadena de suministro capaz de integrar sensores lidar, procesamiento local e inteligencia artificial en dispositivos relativamente compactos.
Eso no significa que haya inventado el concepto ni que haya ganado definitivamente la batalla, porque todavía quedan por demostrar la seguridad, la fiabilidad, las entregas comerciales y su eficacia fuera de las demostraciones controladas. Tampoco se trata de exterminar los mosquitos del planeta, sino de controlar su presencia en espacios concretos.
Entre una cosa y otra hay una imagen que resume el salto: una tecnología que nació pensando en combatir la malaria mediante barreras láser podría terminar instalada en jardines y terrazas, convertida en una torreta automática que dispara contra esos pequeños vampiros.

articles.title: 3,3 l/100 km : Toyota redonne une chance au thermique avec un moteur hybride d'un nouveau genre !
articles.text:
Toyota a beau vendre plus d’électriques que par le passé, l’hybride reste bel et bien son fonds de commerce. La marque japonaise continue donc d’investir massivement sur cette technologie avec un tout nouveau moteur qui ravira les automobilistes encore frileux de passer à l’électrique. Cette motorisation fera même d’une pierre deux coups en remplaçant le quatre-cylindres de 1.8 l et le trois-cylindres de 1.3 l. Autant dire qu’il ne faudra pas se louper !
La feuille de route a été claire : ce bloc inédit de 1.5 l a été conçu dès le départ pour fonctionner de concert avec un électromoteur. L’entente devrait donc être parfaite puisque Toyota annonce des frottements mécaniques réduits, une gestion thermique optimisée et des pertes électriques moindres. De quoi rendre cet ensemble 15 % moins gourmand que les mécaniques actuelles. Il sera proposé en version atmosphérique et turbocompressée.
Full-hybride, rechargeable et prolongateur d’autonomie : une polyvalence inédite
D’ailleurs, la partie électrique jouira également de plusieurs déclinaisons. Le système full-hybride qui a fait la réputation du constructeur japonais demeurera, tout comme l’hybride rechargeable, en majorité choisi par les entreprises. La nouveauté résidera sur la compatibilité avec une architecture à prolongateur d’autonomie, où le moteur thermique servira uniquement à produire de l’électricité afin d’augmenter le rayon d’action.
Dans les trois cas, les composants électriques seront plus légers et plus compacts grâce à des électromoteurs entièrement revus pour une meilleure efficience. Bénéfice inattendu de la chose, Toyota profitera de cette conception plus intelligente pour réduire la hauteur du capot par rapport aux modèles actuels. Moins de hauteur signifiant moins de prise au vent, l’aérodynamisme ne pourra qu’être amélioré.
3,3 l/100 km : la future Toyota Corolla prête à battre des records d’efficience
Un moteur unique génèrera en parallèle de confortables économies d’échelle. Ces dernières pourront ainsi être réinjectées dans le développement de projets futurs. Cela signifie donc que cette même motorisation sera déployée sur un nombre considérable de véhicules de la marque. Et carrément plus ? Il n’est en effet pas exclu que Lexus puisse aussi en profiter. Mais quelle sera la première voiture à bénéficier de cet ensemble très attendu ?
Tous les yeux sont tournés vers la future Toyota Corolla prévue pour 2028. La célèbre compacte intégrera dans son catalogue des motorisations hybrides, hybrides rechargeables et électriques. L’auto pourrait alors voir sa consommation mixte abaissée à 3,3 l/100 km en hybride autoréchargeable. De quoi permettre à l’une des voitures les plus populaires au monde de viser de nouveaux records d’efficience.
