articles.title: Sam Altman le dit tout haut : l’IA serait déjà plus intelligente que les meilleurs scientifiques
articles.text:
“Plus intelligente que nos meilleurs scientifiques” : le patron de ChatGPT assure que l'IA a franchi le cap
Sur la scène de l'Adipec, à Abou Dhabi, le patron d'OpenAI a tranché : en moins d'un an, l'intelligence artificielle aurait dépassé la plupart des plus brillants chercheurs. Son argument massue ? Un problème à un million de dollars que son entreprise dit avoir résolu, et que les mathématiciens regardent avec prudence.
Lundi 2 novembre, lors de la cérémonie d'ouverture de l'Adipec, grand rendez-vous mondial de l'énergie, Sam Altman, PDG d'OpenAI, a livré un diagnostic sans détour à Mina Al-Oraibi, rédactrice en chef du quotidien émirati The National. Selon lui, la bascule s'est produite depuis janvier.
	
L'IA n'était globalement pas aussi intelligente que nos meilleurs scientifiques, et elle l'est désormais globalement plus qu'eux.
Le dirigeant avait déjà tenu un discours voisin à propos de ses déclarations sur les capacités mathématiques de son IA.
Une IA qui grignote le travail de bureau
Altman, qui avait déjà annoncé que l'IA avait franchi un point de non-retour, a ajouté que ces systèmes savent désormais accomplir "a lot of parts" de nombreux métiers de cols blancs, sans préciser lesquels. Interrogé sur son principal défi, il a répondu d'un seul mot : l'énergie.
Il a livré un repère parlant. Il y a six ans, le plus gros consommateur interne d'OpenAI absorbait environ 100 000 tokens par mois, soit à peu près la moyenne mondiale par habitant aujourd'hui. Le premier consommateur actuel en engloutit près de 500 milliards, d'après le compte rendu de The National.
Le même jour, Abou Dhabi a annoncé quatre accords avec OpenAI, couvrant l'énergie, l'éducation, l'investissement et les services publics. L'un d'eux, conclu avec Adnoc et G42, confie les modèles les plus avancés de l'entreprise aux problèmes les plus complexes du secteur énergétique.
Navier-Stokes, la preuve brandie et ses zones d'ombre
Pour étayer sa thèse, Altman a invoqué un problème du prix du Millénaire, que The National rapporte sans le nommer et dont l'affirmation n'avait pas pu être vérifiée de façon indépendante à la publication. Il s'agit de Navier-Stokes, que OpenAI a dit avoir résolu le 8 septembre grâce à un modèle interne mobilisant environ 10 000 agents. Ces derniers ont échangé 2,7 millions de messages et produit près de 130 milliards de tokens, détaille l'entreprise, qui affirme ne pas vouloir toucher la récompense d'un million de dollars.
Le résultat divise. Scientific American rapporte que la preuve répond à la formulation officielle de l'institut Clay en exploitant une force extérieure, que la version recherchée par la plupart des experts exclut.
	
Le problème du Clay est réglé, mais le problème principal des équations de Navier-Stokes ne l'est pas.
Terence Tao avait lui aussi formulé des réserves sur cette prouesse mathématique.
La communauté, elle, reste secouée : 25 médaillés Fields se disent inquiets face aux progrès de l'IA.
Le 6 octobre, OpenAI a déposé sur GitHub 719 manuscrits rédigés par un modèle interne. Seuls 42 % des résultats principaux s'accompagnent d'une vérification formelle en Lean, reconnaît l'entreprise, et trois articles au moins ont déjà été retirés, d'après Fortune. Hugo Duminil-Copin, médaille Fields 2022, y a retrouvé seize de ses questions de prédilection. Selon Le Monde, il a confié à ses pairs "j'ai pleuré", lors d'un séminaire de la Société mathématique de France.
	
Le changement le plus radical en mathématiques depuis au moins quatre siècles.
Le contrôle humain, seule ligne non négociable
Altman a martelé qu'il ne devait y avoir "aucune place pour le débat" sur le fait que les humains restent aux commandes. L'IA ne doit pas faire l'objet d'un transfert de responsabilités. Elle doit rester un outil construit pour les gens et à leur service. Il estime que cette position distingue OpenAI des autres laboratoires, sans en citer aucun.
Reste à savoir si ce principe tient dans les faits, car les difficultés à maintenir un contrôle humain effectif sur les systèmes d'IA sont déjà bien documentées.

articles.title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts, even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review.
Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work.
Policy sets the boundary
Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions.
Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them.
How eligible actions are reviewed
Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation. It considers what the action does, where data goes, and who it affects. It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This helps it understand how recipients relate to the user, such as whether a recipient is in the user’s reporting chain. This lookup stays within your Quick account. Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service.
An action can match the request and still warrant human review. Examples include sending content outside the organization or to senior leaders in the user’s reporting chain, changing access, deleting records, or initiating payments. This list isn’t complete, and the classifier also weighs the surrounding context. Reviewing actions against the user’s request adds a check against indirect prompt injection, where instructions in retrieved content attempt to redirect the agent. Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions. Model review can still make mistakes, so actions that must always receive human approval, including those that move sensitive data, should require it through connector action permissions.
The classifier provides judgment. The permission service enforces authority. Each automatic approval is single-use, applies only to the exact action and parameters reviewed, and grants no ongoing permission. Quick labels automatic approvals in the conversation. Actions the classifier doesn’t approve return to the user, as do timeouts and other review failures, which never grant automatic approval. These enforcement boundaries limit what an approval authorizes. They don’t establish that the classifier’s judgment was correct.
When an action goes beyond the request
An account manager asks Quick to prepare a quarterly business review brief for AnyCompany using her team’s account notes and last quarter’s email. She then asks Quick to send it to two colleagues she names. Assuming the send is eligible for automated review, Smart Approvals evaluates the proposed action against her request and the available conversation context.
Now suppose an account note says the brief should also go to an all-sales distribution list of about 2,000 people. That would change the audience beyond the recipients she specified, so Smart Approvals is designed to return the proposed send to her for review, where she can decline it. An approval to send to the original recipients can’t be reused for the wider audience.
Audit evidence and investigation
The Quick permission service records permission updates associated with Smart Approvals in AWS CloudTrail in your account. Each event identifies the user, connector, action, and time, and marks the request as associated with Smart Approvals. That marker doesn’t establish that the permission service accepted the grant or that the action ran. Quick also records permission-check verdicts, including denials from connector action permissions, and changes to a user’s Smart Approvals setting.
Investigators can correlate these events by user and time with other Quick activity in CloudTrail and logs delivered through Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Chat logs capture the user’s request, system response, and conversation context. Agent metadata logs record changes to agents. Records from the destination system, such as a sent email or updated ticket, confirm whether the action completed. Together, these sources help reconstruct what happened without treating approval as proof of execution. CloudTrail Event history retains events for 90 days, so configure a trail for longer investigations. Because chat logs can contain sensitive content, restrict access and consider CloudWatch Logs data protection policies to mask sensitive data.
Where to start
Because Smart Approvals is on by default, begin by confirming that actions requiring human approval are configured through connector action permissions. Set up a CloudTrail trail and delivery of chat logs and agent metadata logs to CloudWatch Logs to support investigations. Chat logs capture only activity after delivery is configured, so earlier approvals will lack that conversation context. With approval requirements and logging in place, use Custom Permissions to limit Smart Approvals to a pilot team working on a defined workflow before extending it to other teams.
Before the pilot, define what success looks like: fewer prompts for routine actions, with consequential actions still returning to a person for review. During the pilot, review a sample of automatic approvals and test high-impact cases, such as sending content outside the organization or adding a recipient introduced by a document. Confirm that these cases come back to the user. Confirm that your team can trace each action from approval through execution. Expand to more teams and workflows only when the results meet those criteria, and reassess as actions and policies change.
The measure of effective oversight isn’t how often an agent asks for approval, but whether people retain control over consequential decisions. For security leaders, the case for expanding Smart Approvals should rest on evidence from the pilot. Fewer prompts are valuable when they preserve attention without weakening accountability.
For setup steps, see Smart Approvals in the governance section of the Amazon Quick User Guide.

articles.title: STATION F unveils 2026 Future 40 as its startups raise a record €2 billion | EU-Startups
articles.text:
The world’s biggest startup campus, STATION F, has revealed its top 40 companies for 2026, as well as announcing that STATION F companies have raised a record €2 billion in 2026 alone.
This is the 8th edition of the annual list, with 320 companies recognised to date. This year’s selected teams cover a variety of sectors, including AI and machine learning, DeepTech, infrastructure and developer tools, hardware and robotics, climate tech and more.
Founded by Xavier Niel in 2017 and based in Paris, the 50,000m2 campus supports over 1,000 startups a year, who take part in 40 different support programmes.
Every November since 2019, the STATION F Future 40 has named the most promising and best-performing startups on campus. The 2026 companies were chosen from over 1,000 startups at STATION F in 2026, which places them in the top 4% of all startups for this year.
Selection rests on strong metrics, traction and meaningful milestones, with no funding cap.
The list began in 2019 as a live pitch session on campus and moved online in 2020 so investors anywhere could take part. STATION F has also invested in select Future 40 teams since 2022 – including Pimento (recently acquired by Mistral) and Flowie (recently acquired by Sovos).
The 2026 Future 40 cohort is one of the better-funded cohorts and has raised €110 million to date. Arlequin AI (€28 million), CURA ($10 million), Cleavr (€8 million), Lemrock (€7 million) are amongst some of the funded teams.
From AICE’s underwater defence drones and Bleu Robotics’ humanoid robots to CURA’s cement decarbonisation technology and RainPath’s AI-powered cancer diagnostics, the cohort tackles challenges across defence, climate, healthcare and infrastructure. AI remains a dominant theme, with companies like Lemrock, NuMind and Arlequin AI developing applications spanning commerce, document processing and high-stakes decision-making.
Most of the companies are pre-Seed and Seed – 31 total, with and 2 at Series A. 5 companies are bootstrapped. Fourteen companies come from F/AI, and others joined through partner programmes run with CentraleSupélec, Microsoft, TotalEnergies, Entrepreneur First and HEC.
Across eight editions, Future 40 companies have raised a cumulative €1.2 billion. Past selections include Fintecture, Tomorro, Spore.bio, WhiteLab Genomics, Biolevate, Qevlar AI, Syntetica and more. Hugging Face and Mistral AI have both acquired Future 40 companies.
This momentum has been reflected in EU-Startups’ own coverage throughout 2026. We’ve reported on fresh funding for Cleavr (€1 million), Lemrock (€6 million), Qevlar AI (€25 million), Syntetica (26 million) and WhiteLab Genomics (€23 million), alongside Spore.Bio’s AI-driven research expansion and Multiverse Computing’s €500 million Series C – highlighting the breadth of innovation and investment emerging from the STATION F ecosystem.
In addition to the Future 40 selection, STATION F companies have raised a record €2 billion in 2026 alone – this surpasses the funding record set in 2025.
Since 2022, STATION F companies have raised more than €1 billion each year, with over €1.5 billion raised in 2025. Larger rounds from alumni such as Multiverse Computing (€500 million) and Alan (€480 million) helped set the new record.

articles.title: My therapist thinks I should chuck the Amazon Bee Frontier out a window
articles.text:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.
My therapist thinks I should chuck the Amazon Bee Frontier out a window
Filtering conversations and memories through AI is a reality-bending lesson in why intelligence can’t replace wisdom.
My therapist thinks I should chuck the Amazon Bee Frontier out a window
Filtering conversations and memories through AI is a reality-bending lesson in why intelligence can’t replace wisdom.
“How does that make you feel?”
I get asked this a lot in therapy. Plenty of life events, big and small, have triggered this question. Three weeks ago, it was the fact that I had to ask my therapist for her consent because I was wearing the Amazon Bee Frontier during our session.
That first week, I didn’t really have an answer. A lot had changed since I first tested Bee, an always-recording AI wearable, early last year. The elevator pitch is that it listens to all your conversations and uses AI to transcribe and summarize them. From there, it has a List feature that suggests to-dos, a Grow feature for identifying areas where you can improve, and various summaries that analyze the content, tone, and takeaways from your conversations. It’s even got a chatbot that can answer questions about yourself or what was said and when.
In the last 19 months, it’s gotten better at distinguishing my actual speech from TV dialogue. It can now pull in information from my calendar and photos app, and suggest things to buy on Amazon based on what I’ve said. At times, particularly for job-related tasks, it’s helped me remember talking points. But most of the time, it’s led to me questioning my reality.
My therapist usually lets me arrive at my own decisions, even if I often take the scenic route to the obvious conclusion. After 11 years, she’s intimately acquainted with the wackier parts of my job. But in my third week of talking about Bee, my therapist requested that I chuck this thing right out a window.
It’s a bit dark, but a big reason I’m in therapy is to build trust in my own memories. I grew up with a dad who might’ve been a spy and an immigrant family that never agreed on a single version of events. Growing up, I felt unmoored. Were things truly as I’d remembered them? Were my parents the unreliable narrators, or was I? Adding in their eventual dementia to the mix made discerning truth from fiction even harder.
In those moments, I had wished for a device like Bee. A reviewable record, so to speak, for moments where I wanted a sanity check. It’s funny in retrospect. Now that tech companies have started making this fantasy into a reality, what I feel is perpetually gaslit.
For example, it’s disorienting to see Bee’s transcripts and summaries of my conversations, often because the AI remembers and interprets them differently than I do. Like any AI, it’s not always precise about who said what. In the past three weeks, it’s concluded that I argue with a coworker’s spouse frequently (I’ve never met them), that I think a family member has undiagnosed bipolar disorder (No one ever said that!), and that I like to put my good pants on for important video calls. (That was a joke.) Sure, it’s a relief that Bee’s newly updated transcription prowess was able to discern that I personally was not working with detectives Rust Cohle and Marty Hart to find a serial killer named the Yellow King simply because I watched True Detective. But it still doesn’t know how to handle the fact that we call my two cats Petey and Pablo various nicknames. By Bee’s estimation, I have about six additional cats named Mr. Handsome, Mr. Stylish, District Attorney Hoss, Dabah Doo Bah, Potato Demon, and Tubby McTubberson Jones.
These mistakes are at least funny. It’s when the conversations are serious that I feel the strongest whiplash. That’s when the “improved” AI dislodges something in my brain.
In my second therapy session with Bee recording, I spent the majority of the time unpacking my feelings about You Can See Everything. It’s a reality-bending movie that questions the line between truth and fiction. As much as I enjoyed the film, witnessing compulsive liars for three hours was bound to take me back to unhappier moments in my life. I should’ve turned Bee off for this session. But the truth is, I just forgot. Because the design of these devices is, in many ways, built for you to forget they’re listening.
One of Bee’s capabilities is that it learns “facts” about you that you then swipe right to approve as true, or left to dismiss as false. After this session, it generated a “fact” about an instance of domestic violence I experienced as a child. This particular moment has come up multiple times in sessions over the years — revisiting it has been key to understanding and forgiving my parents, holding compassion for the circumstances that shaped them.
I did not expect how awful it felt to see a traumatic event summarized so starkly in plain English. I hated having to swipe right to say, “Yes, this is true.” I didn’t expect the accompanying summary to be titled “Reclaiming Reality from Manipulative Power.” Or for it to characterize the type of person I am (deeply unsettled), the timbre of the conversation (intense, reflective, emotionally raw), or how I felt during that session (grieving, angry, and clear-eyed about manipulation). I remember that session as cathartic. There were times when I laughed or joked around. The topic was serious, yes, but I wasn’t ranting, raving, or crying. I left that session feeling light — you’d never guess that from the summary. Looking at it weeks later, I’m now wondering who’s right: me, or the AI.
I also forgot to turn Bee off during my annual physical. I was late to the appointment, and when I changed into a gown for the exam, the damn thing was just sitting in a pile of my clothes. I only realized my mistake when it was time to leave.
On the one hand, it did memorialize that my doctor prescribed me Claritin for allergies and that the nurse and I talked about my dead dog Daisy. (It described me as wistful and grieving here, too, but I recall it as fond remembrance.) Ironically, it also memorialized my doctor’s feelings on AI transcription. My doctor’s AI transcription software requires patient consent and helps her with long conversations where she has to remember treatment notes. But it’s also garbage at distinguishing between two female speakers, and she spends a decent amount of time correcting it.
Depending on which Bee AI template I use, it can change the summary. With the default template, the AI’s conclusions about this particular meeting include tonal analysis and takeaways. If I filter to the medical visit template, suddenly everything is much more factual. It strips away the ruminations. It’s more useful and less uncomfortable to look back on. But I also can’t help but feel that the record of what was a fairly significant healthcare appointment differs from my memory. Who is right?
So, how does this all make me feel?
A little bit crazy and overwhelmed. Sometimes offended. Bee has a new-ish feature called Grow. Based on your conversation history, it compiles recommendations on how you can grow as a person. It also generates suggested to-dos.
To train Bee AI on my voice, during setup it asked me to describe my hobbies. I said I enjoy reading, calligraphy, cross-stitch, and running. I’ve recently gotten into fountain pens and ink swatching for journaling. You have to talk for about two minutes straight, so I ended up rambling about how I was unsure whether embroidery would be a natural progression from cross-stitch or an unnecessary side quest at this point in time.
The Grow insight based on this incredibly unserious, one-sided discussion? A conversation Bee itself prompted. I dabble in too many hobbies without serious commitment. A jack of all trades, master of none. I’ve shown no progression or tangible sign of “shareable output” and should spend the next three months picking one hobby. Because I allowed Bee to integrate with my reminders list, which has an old to-read list for books I want physical copies of, it confidently stated that despite calling myself a reader, I haven’t made much progress this year.
Bitch, I thought, I’ve finished 39 books in 2026 so far. I’ve been practicing calligraphy and journaling for 17 years. I finished 10 cross-stitch projects this year. Most importantly, hobbies aren’t something I do for “shareable output.” I happen to firmly believe that hobbies should be exempt from cockamamie Silicon Valley-brained KPIs.
Another Grow insight from some political discussion with my spouse about the midterms? “These frameworks help her contextualize current events but may also distance her from present-tense engagement; her tone in political discussion is more analytical than activist, more diagnostic than mobilized.” It then suggested that I “identify one concrete political action aligned with your values that requires less than 30 minutes and complete it this week.”
In my memory, this was because we watched an episode of The Daily Show and I said, jokingly, that I was tired of US political shenanigans. Never mind my actual lived experience canvassing and as a union organizer and representative.
These are just two examples. Imagine seeing some version of this every day for nearly a month. Summaries that are maybe 75 percent right, 15 percent taken out of context, and 10 percent out-of-pocket wrong. Things that are just presented to you as fact, regardless of whatever disclaimer that AI can make mistakes.
You can know the truth deep in your gut and still wonder what happens when your hypervigilance slips.
I said as much in my third therapy session wearing Bee. I asked my therapist to weigh in. What, I joked, did she feel watching me go through this experiment?
I’ve gone through the Bee transcript of that conversation. Ironically, it didn’t summarize her thoughts on how poorly designed this device is for anxious people. I had to dig into the raw transcript to find that. According to my therapist, a device like this likely supersedes a person’s ability to trust their own instincts about what they need to do. When you outsource that, AI can generate insights that aren’t emotionally attuned and, in turn, exacerbate many of the problems a person might be trying to solve. For me, it likely triggers rumination, spiraling, and perfectionism.
That’s the point where we joked that I should probably throw this thing out the window. We laughed that we’d both feel relieved when I’m not wearing this at my next session. I would say that was the most important takeaway.
Bee didn’t include that in my suggested to-do list. It did, however, say this: buy nail glue, complete with a link out to Amazon.

articles.title: Fibre cuts threaten Nigeria's digital economy, who pays?
articles.text:
When Nigeria’s president, Bola Tinubu, signed the Designation and Protection of Critical National Information Infrastructure (CNII) Order in June 2024, the Federal Government aimed to shield telecommunications assets from relentless vandalism and physical damage. By classifying fibre lines, base stations, and data centres as vital national security installations, the order sought to impose deterrent penalties and curb unauthorised tampering.
Yet two years on, chronic breaches continue to impose steep financial penalties on operators, diverting capital from network expansion to nonstop emergency repairs and destabilising internet reliability across the country.
In 2023, before the order, MTN Nigeria suffered more than 6,000 fibre cuts in a single year—averaging roughly 16-17 severed lines per day.
Fast-forward to 2025, past the presidential order: the numbers increased; between January and July, the telco recorded 5,478 fibre cuts. That pushed its daily average to over 26 snapped cables.
In plain terms, instead of scaring reckless diggers and vandals away and improving coordination between construction firms and other key stakeholders, the new rules led MTN Nigeria to fix about eight more broken cables per day than before the order was introduced.
The broader telecoms industry recorded 19,384 cuts between January and August 2025, further pushing the daily average to 80. In the first nine months of 2026 alone, Telecom networks suffered over 44,000 fibre cuts—averaging more than 160 cuts every single day, mostly from uncoordinated road construction, ditch digging, and theft. The primary culprits remain uncoordinated civil engineering projects, road expansions, and persistent vandalism.
These disruptions expose significant enforcement gaps, raising a central question of who ultimately pays when statutory protections fail to stop contractors and vandals from repeatedly severing the nation’s digital backbone
Building on Tinubu’s signing of the executive order, the legal framework establishes vital statutory mechanisms to defend the nation’s digital backbone.
Under the CNII Order, telecommunications assets—including submarine landing cables, terrestrial fibre-optic lines, switching centres, and data storage hubs—are formally designated as vital national security installations.
The framework empowers security agencies, led by the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) and the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), to monitor, inspect, and defend digital infrastructure against willful destruction, uncoordinated civil works, and cyber-physical intrusions.
Even so, its ultimate success hinges on swift and consistent prosecution.
Fibre cuts drain expansion capital
Constant network degradation forces telecommunications operators to absorb substantial operational costs, squeezing capital investment. In the first half of 2026, direct repairs across 5,934 fibre incidents cost operators over ₦2.2 billion ($1.64 million).
These emergency expenses undermine the ₦2.13 trillion ($1.58 billion) in capital expenditure committed by network and tower companies, diverting critical resources from new rollouts to restoring existing footprints.
This financial drain has a long track record; it is not new. According to the GSMA Nigeria Digital Economy Report, MTN Nigeria spent ₦11.1 billion ($8.26 million) repairing and relocating 2,502 kilometres of fibre across 2022 and 2023. That figure comprised ₦4.4 billion ($3.27 million) for 1,069 km in 2022 and ₦6.7 billion ($4.98 million) for 1,433 km in 2023—money that GSMA notes could have funded 870 kilometres of greenfield fibre in underserved communities.
Across the wider industry, losses in 2023 alone reached an estimated ₦27 billion ($20.08 million) in direct repairs and lost revenue.
The economic stakes are huge for a country where its ICT sector delivered over ₦6 trillion ($4.46 billion) in real output in Q2 2026, with telecoms contributing 9.72% (₦5.20 trillion / $3.87 billion) to total real GDP: every severed cable is no longer just a temporary network glitch, but an immediate drag on national GDP.
Connectivity gap worsens local challenges
Nigeria’s infrastructure struggles unfold against broader regional constraints. A recent GSMA report on African spectrum policy highlighted that African operators averaged 570 MHz of spectrum below 7 GHz in 2025—far below the global baseline of 750 MHz—while paying 24% more per unit of spectrum. GSMA cautions that every 10% increase in spectrum costs relative to revenue trims 5G coverage expansion by six percentage points.
Fast 5G networks require robust underground cabling to ensure that banking apps, POS machines, and online money transfers work instantly and without failure.
Underlying infrastructure carried massive financial volumes in early 2026: transactions on the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) surpassed ₦1.053 quadrillion ($783.2 billion) in Q1 alone, alongside millions of daily mobile money and point-of-sale payments. Governed by a 23-year-old regulatory model dating back to the 2G voice era, the sector is directly threatened by physical fibre cuts, which directly threaten overall financial stability.
Fibre backhaul links network base stations directly to core data centres. When cables are cut, the impact cascades into dropped voice calls, crippled data throughput, and widespread service outages.
For enterprises, cuts mean payment gateways collapsing, staff hours lost, and cloud downtime. For subscribers, disruptions translate into sluggish connections, failed payments, and paying higher rates for diminished service.
These disruptions compound consumer frustration following the NCC’s tariff revision, which permitted price hikes of up to 50% to offset soaring operational costs. When operators sink recurring revenue into avoidable repairs, network optimisation stalls, and users pay the price through degraded reliability.
Why has the CNII Order not solved the problem?
The NCC acknowledged the continuing challenge of stakeholder coordination in its August 2026 intervention: “Our interests are aligned; what has too often been missing is a dependable system of early coordination,” said the Executive Vice Chairman of the Nigerian Communications Commission, Aminu Maida.
But coordination can only work when manpower is adequate. The NSCDC’s limited manpower and operational resources expose the enforcement challenges facing one of Nigeria’s agencies tasked with protecting critical national infrastructure.
With roughly 63,000 personnel deployed across 774 local government areas to manage a broad range of national security duties, dedicated static protection for thousands of kilometres of buried fibre is logistically impossible. Even with its efforts on surveillance technology and systematic prosecution, legal protection on paper cannot secure infrastructure without adequate personnel.
The government must therefore measure the success of the CNII Order by tangible results: fewer cuts, faster remediation, and lower repair bills. Until enforcement deters would-be offenders, operators will keep burning through capital on repeated repairs instead of expanding coverage—leaving subscribers to foot the bill for an unprotected digital economy.

articles.title: Chrome 157 Rolls Out With 213 Security Fixes, Seven Rated Critical
articles.text:
Google has promoted Chrome 157 to the stable channel with patches for 213 vulnerabilities, including seven critical memory safety bugs.
At the top of the list is a buffer overflow issue in Dawn, the open source and cross-platform implementation of the WebGPU standard. It earned the reporting researcher a $10,000 reward.
The second is a memory corruption in the open source graphics engine abstraction layer ANGLE that was awarded a $1,000 bug bounty.
No rewards were listed for the remaining five critical flaws (four use-after-free defects and a buffer overflow). Google reported two of them, Anthropic’s Xinyang Ge reported two, and researcher Wenbin Liu reported the fifth.
Chrome 157 also fixes 77 high-severity vulnerabilities, including more than a dozen reported by external researchers. However, Google has disclosed only the bounties paid for two of them, namely $10,000 for an incorrect authorization, and $2,000 for an out-of-bounds read.
Per Google’s advisory, the company handed out $31,000 in rewards to the reporting researchers, but it has not determined the bug bounties to be paid for 39 of the flaws.
The most common types of vulnerabilities the fresh browser update resolves include incorrect/missing authorization (51), use-after-free (45), UI misrepresentation (19), type confusion (13), information leak (13), out-of-bounds read/write (11), improper input validation (9), and uninitialized resource (9).
Google makes no mention of any of these security defects being exploited in the wild, but users should update their browsers as soon as possible.
The latest Chrome iteration is now rolling out as versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and macOS, and as version 157.0.8103.38 for Linux.

articles.title: How TD is building the intelligent front door to modern banking for clients | BetaKit
articles.text:
For millions of Canadians, the front door to their bank is on their phone. At TD alone, 8.9 million active mobile clients open their banking app an average of 22 times a month to check their balance, transfer money, or pay a bill.
With the introduction of AI, more Canadians are now expecting a new level of predictive and personalized mobile experiences. TD is using the technology to take those experiences a step further and make them more human.
“We’re approaching this thoughtfully, because clients should feel supported as digital banking evolves.”
Instead of building experiences that make clients feel like they’re navigating menus, TD wants to build experiences that help clients anticipate what’s next and manage their finances with less effort. The technology may be evolving, but the client experiences are becoming simpler and faster instead of more complex.
TD is heading into this shift from a leading position. Its mobile app recently ranked first in customer satisfaction in the JD Power 2026 Canada Banking Mobile App Satisfaction Study, receiving the highest score for information, tools/capabilities, system performance, and design.
“We’re very proud of that recognition,” said Natasha Struminikovski, Vice-President of Digital Engagement at TD. “It reflects both the trust our clients place in our digital banking experience at TD, and the extreme level of focus we have in creating experiences that are fast, intuitive, personalized, and more proactive.”
The JD Power win gives the bank plenty to build on. TD is now looking at how best to use AI-powered features to make digital banking experiences feel more human and easier to navigate without compromising reliability, security, or trust.
In July, for example, TD introduced a new in-app payroll deposit switching experience for Canadian clients, a first among Canada’s financial institutions, helping clients switch payroll deposits quickly and securely in about a minute, with most employers. In collaboration with US-based FinTech company Atomic, TD has brought a once multi-step journey into a single, secure experience in the app.
“We need to make sure we are continuing to boost the level of service that our clients expect from us,” said Struminikovski. “With digital direct deposit, we’re transforming that experience through a secure, integrated solution that simplifies a critical step in establishing everyday banking relationships.”
Innovating without breaking what works
Finding the right balance isn’t easy. Startups tend to embrace a move-fast-and-break-things culture. But for banks, pushing forward looks different. Digital banking experiences must keep getting simpler and faster for clients, while remaining secure and accessible. At TD, the strategy includes exceeding client expectations now and in the future. The first step is to build the technical foundation, then introduce new experiences gradually.
Lawrence Wong, Vice-President of Enterprise Digital Servicing Technology at TD, said clients can try out different forms of interaction without feeling forced to adopt new habits. Clients paying a bill or completing some other tasks could follow the familiar screens on the app or ask the app’s AI assisted chat to help them.
“We’re approaching this thoughtfully, because clients should feel supported as digital banking evolves,” said Wong. “The goal is to give them more intuitive ways to bank while making sure the experience remains reliable, familiar, and easy to use.”
To help make that possible, Wong’s team has moved more of the organization’s digital capabilities to the cloud, and separated functions, such as bill payments and account transfers, so TD can manage them more independently. If bill-payment activity spikes, for example, TD can add capacity to that service without making the same change to other parts of the app. Engineers can also update the bill-payment experience with less risk of affecting other functions.
“Part of what we’ve done over the last five years is invest heavily in building a really solid architectural foundation,” Wong explained. “This gives us the confidence that we can move at a much faster pace and create change and innovation.”
That groundwork is going to support intent orchestration—that is, using AI to identify moments when a client may need guidance and sending them in the right direction.
It could be someone trying to add a utility company as a new bill payee, for example. They may pause because they’re unsure which account number to enter. Rather than leaving them to search for instructions, the app would recognize that they appear to be stuck, and offer to guide them through the remaining steps.
“This is an experience layer that we’re trying to embed into the app to deliver a seamless experience for clients,” said Wong. “Behind the scenes, the architecture is interpreting all these signals to try to figure out how best to help.”
Over time, that same technology could allow clients to state what they want to do instead of searching through menus for the right function. Wong expects those changes to evolve through optional assistants, prompts, and suggestions rather than an abrupt redesign.
Making banking easier, with human support when it matters
For Struminikovski, the first question to ask before making any changes is: does it solve a real client problem?
“We can’t just implement AI for AI’s sake,” she said. “What we’ve heard from our clients is that they’re looking for AI to make things easier for them by taking on some of the daily mental load they carry about banking tasks and planning. At TD, we’re keeping the human elements of trust and meaningful relationships at the centre of everything we do, while leveraging AI and data to offer the experiences and services clients need to thrive.”
To get a handle on where clients feel the most friction, TD continuously reviews client surveys and seeks out input from frontline colleagues. Designers then use focus groups and testing to verify both the problem and the proposed solution. That input shapes the entire process, from the initial idea through development, launch, and ongoing improvements to ensure that the Bank is constantly evolving and raising the bar to meet clients’ needs, said Struminikovski.
It also helps determine if AI is needed at all. Some routine tasks may lend themselves to automated assistance, while other situations call for a conversation with a person.
“If a client wants to talk to a human, they should be able to talk to a human,” she noted. “Our branch colleagues and phone agents are available to support clients during branch business hours and on EasyLine 24/7. Frontline colleagues are critical to our digital-first, human always approach, too: great technology backed by real support when it matters.”
Critically, not every client is expected to embrace AI at the same pace. Some will be ready to try new tools right away, while others may want more time or prefer to stick with what they know. Struminikovski said that TD’s digital strategy makes room for both.
“We need to make sure that if a client is interacting with us, regardless of what channel they’re in, they’re receiving consistency and modern digital convenience with the security, trust, advice, and support clients expect from a full-service bank. At TD, our focus is supporting clients not just in big moments, like buying a house, getting married, having a child, going off to university, or retiring, but also in small moments, like paying a bill, moving money between accounts, or finding a recent transaction. We want to ensure that we’re meeting them in every single moment of need, offering refreshingly simple experiences that help them thrive throughout their financial journeys.”

articles.title: Filme chinês feito com IA arrecada pouco, mas atrai investidores
articles.text:
A inteligência artificial (IA) ainda precisa provar que consegue conquistar o público nas salas de cinema. Pelo menos na China, a primeira grande tentativa de produzir um longa-metragem inteiramente com a tecnologia não teve o resultado esperado. Sanxingdui: Future Past arrecadou apenas 1,7 milhão de yuans (aproximadamente R$ 1,3 milhão) nas bilheterias, apesar de ter custado dezenas de milhões de yuans.
A produção foi lançada em Pequim (China) e chamou atenção por utilizar IA em praticamente toda a sua concepção visual. Os efeitos sonoros também tiveram participação da tecnologia, enquanto a edição ficou sob responsabilidade de profissionais humanos.
O desempenho comercial, porém, ficou muito abaixo das expectativas. O The Guardian relata que assistiu ao longa em uma sala de cinema praticamente vazia na capital chinesa.
A experiência também não impressionou particularmente a crítica. A história apresenta uma sociedade futurista que terceirizou todas as decisões para algoritmos e sistemas de IA, provocando uma catástrofe global. Para evitar o desastre, os personagens precisam descobrir um código secreto associado às esculturas de bronze de Sanxingdui, ligadas ao antigo reino de Shu.
A narrativa mistura astronautas, Egito Antigo e viagens por vórtices espaço-temporais. Os diálogos também evidenciam a participação de uma ferramenta interna de roteiro chamada Bowen, desenvolvida pela própria produtora.
Investidores ainda apostam no cinema feito com IA
- Apesar do fracasso de Sanxingdui: Future Past, profissionais da indústria cinematográfica chinesa acreditam que a produção representa apenas o começo de uma nova fase do setor;
- Segundo Yu Yaqin, crítica de cinema independente em Pequim, o principal problema do longa foi simplesmente não ser divertido. Ainda assim, ela acredita que filmes produzidos com IA continuarão recebendo investimentos no país;
- Uma profissional que trabalha com desenvolvimento de roteiros na capital chinesa afirmou que a maioria dos projetos que recebeu nos últimos meses envolvia produções com IA;
- O interesse dos investidores está relacionado principalmente à possibilidade de reduzir custos. Segundo ela, atividades que antes exigiam equipes de aproximadamente 100 pessoas poderiam ser realizadas por apenas cinco profissionais com o auxílio da tecnologia;
- Essa perspectiva também levanta preocupações sobre o futuro dos empregos no setor audiovisual.
Leia mais:
- Funcionários da OpenAI alertaram por anos sobre falhas de segurança nos sistemas da empresa
- Pioneiro da IA diz que mundo estaria melhor sem inteligência artificial
- Escolas que bloquearem IA poderão perder acesso à busca do Google
China já produz milhares de produções com IA
O fracasso do longa-metragem não significa que o público chinês rejeite completamente o conteúdo produzido por IA. O país já possui uma indústria expressiva de microdramas gerados por IA. São produções curtas, geralmente com episódios de um a três minutos, desenvolvidas para consumo em celulares.
De acordo com o The Guardian, dezenas de milhares desses conteúdos são enviados mensalmente para plataformas de streaming. Uma indústria que praticamente não existia há alguns anos já movimenta aproximadamente US$ 3 bilhões (cerca de R$ 16,5 bilhões).
Uma das explicações para o desempenho ruim de Sanxingdui: Future Past pode estar justamente na concorrência com esse formato. Enquanto o longa custava 50 yuans (cerca de R$ 37) por ingresso, conteúdos semelhantes podiam ser encontrados gratuitamente nos celulares.
Um blogueiro especializado em cinema resumiu a diferença: os microdramas feitos com IA oferecem uma maneira de passar o tempo, enquanto os filmes exibidos nos cinemas precisam proporcionar uma experiência que justifique o investimento do público.
Para a crítica Yu Yaqin, o público ainda parece mais disposto a pagar por produções que ofereçam uma experiência verdadeiramente diferenciada.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Neural Super Resolution
articles.text:
Insight into how neural graphics can improve image quality and performance while simplifying deployment on power- and bandwidth-constrained devices.
As AI becomes an increasingly important part of the graphics pipeline, Neural Super Resolution (NSR) offers a new approach to generating higher-quality images without the cost of rendering every pixel natively. This white paper explores how Imagination’s NSR technology uses neural reconstruction to upscale lower-resolution frames into higher-resolution outputs, combining current-frame data, temporal history and learned inference to deliver high visual quality with reduced bandwidth, power and memory demands. Unlike approaches that rely on separate AI accelerators, NSR runs directly within the GPU, enabling graphics, compute and AI workloads to work together in a unified execution environment.
Readers will learn the principles behind neural super resolution, the role of Converged Acceleration in modern GPU design, and how Imagination’s E-Series architecture integrates matrix acceleration and neural processing into the graphics pipeline. The paper also explains the importance of data locality, microtiling and Self-Compression in achieving efficient neural rendering, while examining the performance, bandwidth and energy benefits of GPU-native super resolution. For graphics architects, developers and SoC designers, it provides insight into how neural graphics can improve image quality and performance while simplifying deployment on power- and bandwidth-constrained devices.
Read more here.
Fig.1: Projected Doom Eternal performance and bandwidth improvements using NSR. Projected estimates for Doom Eternal compare native 4K rendering with 1080p rendering reconstructed to 4K using NSR on an EXD-64-2048 MC1 GPU modelled at 1 GHz. These figures should be treated as workload- and configuration-specific projections. Source: Imagination.

articles.title: ChatGPT will now make you animated GIFs
articles.text:
ChatGPT can now create GIFs using a prompt or a photo uploaded to the AI chatbot. The update, which is rolling out alongside OpenAI’s new Images 2.6 model, allows you to adjust the GIF’s animation speed, edit individual frames, and share it with others.
ChatGPT will now make you animated GIFs
You can use ChatGPT to edit a GIF’s animation speed and individual frames.
Before this change, ChatGPT couldn’t natively generate GIFs in a single step. An example shared by the company shows how ChatGPT can generate a GIF in response to the prompt, “can you make a gif of a cat dancing?” while also providing you with the option to change the playback speed and view it frame by frame.
Along with support for GIF-making, the Images 2.6 update also enables faster image generation in ChatGPT, OpenAI says. The company says users now generate over 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT and its API, a jump from the 3 billion per week it reported in September.
Images 2.6 is rolling out to all ChatGPT and Codex users across web, desktop, and mobile apps. OpenAI is also launching GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst in its API for faster and higher-quality image generation.

articles.title: Ataque a sistemas de refrigeração coloca bancos de sangue em risco na Europa
articles.text:
Hackers atacaram sistemas de refrigeração usados no armazenamento de plasma sanguíneo na França, entre 1º e 2 de novembro. A invasão alterou a programação de temperatura dos freezers, em mais um episódio de ataques contra equipamentos ligados a serviços essenciais.
O alvo foi a Coolworld, fornecedora do Estabelecimento Francês de Sangue (EFS). O caso ocorreu poucas semanas depois de ataques semelhantes a freezers de supermercados na Europa.
Ataque alterou temperatura de freezers de plasma
Segundo o site Cyberattaque, citado pelo Cyber Security News, os invasores programaram os equipamentos para elevar a temperatura de -30 °C para 110 °C. Não se sabe se os freezers chegaram efetivamente a esse nível.
O EFS é responsável pela coleta, preparação e distribuição de sangue e derivados na França, utilizados em cirurgias e outros procedimentos médicos. Entre os produtos potencialmente ameaçados estava o plasma congelado destinado a transfusões.
O Ministério da Saúde francês informou que o ataque não provocou consequências operacionais graves. As alterações de temperatura foram identificadas rapidamente e corrigidas. Ainda não foram divulgados o número de instalações atingidas, a duração da interrupção ou as temperaturas efetivamente alcançadas. Também não há confirmação de que algum estoque de sangue tenha precisado ser descartado.
De acordo com o Cyberattaque, os invasores não comprometeram diretamente as instalações médicas, mas os sistemas de manutenção de terceiros responsáveis pelo controle da temperatura dos freezers. Como essas empresas podem atender diferentes clientes, o comprometimento de uma única infraestrutura de manutenção pode expor vários sistemas de refrigeração, inclusive os utilizados em serviços essenciais.
Alertas europeus sobre vulnerabilidades na infraestrutura
O ataque ocorreu duas semanas depois de Vincent Strubel, diretor-geral da Agência Nacional de Segurança dos Sistemas de Informação da França (ANSSI), alertar, em outubro de 2026, que instalações de refrigeração, inclusive as utilizadas para armazenar recursos médicos, poderiam se tornar alvos de ataques.
No Reino Unido, Richard Horne, diretor-executivo do Centro Nacional de Segurança Cibernética (NCSC), também chamou a atenção para a fragilidade das estruturas tecnológicas e operacionais de organizações e cadeias de abastecimento.
Durante o lançamento do relatório State of the Cyber Nation, Horne apontou diferentes sistemas que podem ser explorados em ataques cibernéticos:
- Distribuição de eletricidade;
- Comportas de instalações de água e operações de barragens;
- Linhas de produção industrial;
- Sistemas de aquecimento;
- Controles de refrigeração.
O executivo descreveu o momento como uma encruzilhada para a segurança cibernética britânica e comparou as vulnerabilidades existentes a uma “Torre de Pisa digital”. Horne também advertiu que o Reino Unido enfrenta a possibilidade de um aumento sem precedentes no número de incidentes cibernéticos nos meses seguintes.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Glovo’s €461 million startup multiplier effect showcased at annual Startup Campus | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Glovo showcased its growing influence on Europe’s entrepreneurial ecosystem at its fourth annual Startup Campus, held at its Yellow Park headquarters in Barcelona. The three-day event brought together 19 startups and 33 founders and team members for mentoring, networking and pitching opportunities.
The event coincided with new research revealing that former Glovo employees have founded 35 startups with a combined estimated value of €461 million, highlighting the company’s success in fostering entrepreneurial mindsets and national innovation ecosystems.
Delivery Hero’s €7.5 Billion Founder Factory
The findings come from a report by Delivery Hero and startup data platform Dealroom.co, which identified 150 startups founded by alumni of Delivery Hero’s European brands, collectively valued at an estimated €7.5 billion.
According to the research, Delivery Hero ranks as Europe’s largest “founder factory” by number of startups created by former employees, ahead of companies including Klarna, Zalando and Spotify.
Glovo accounts for 35 of these businesses, demonstrating how experience gained at established technology companies can translate into new entrepreneurial ventures.
“When we started Glovo in Barcelona in 2015, we had to figure out the startup playbook the hard way,” said Glovo co-founder Sacha Michaud, emphasising the company’s commitment to sharing its experience with the next generation of founders.
Mentorship and investment opportunities for emerging startups
Startup Campus aims to accelerate early-stage businesses by providing access to industry expertise, strategic partnerships and potential investors.
Participants attended masterclasses, workshops and mentoring sessions led by technology experts, including Glovo co-founders Oscar Pierre and Sacha Michaud. The programme was supported by Endeavor Spain, ACCIÓ (Generalitat de Catalunya) and the Polish Development Fund (PFR).
The campus concluded with a pitching competition judged by representatives from Endeavor, ACCIÓ, BBVA Spark and Encomenda Smart Capital, giving founders an opportunity to present their solutions and receive strategic feedback.
Romanian startup .lumen wins pitch competition
Romanian assistive technology startup .lumen secured first place in the final pitching competition for its AI-powered navigation glasses designed to improve independent mobility for people with visual impairments.
Portuguese startup Granter finished second, while Spain’s Bleecker Technologies took third place.
“We’re incredibly honoured. We are building a technology which potentially can be of immense use for Glovo and its customers,” said .lumen CEO Cornel Amariei.
All three winning startups will continue receiving mentorship and strategic guidance from Sacha Michaud.
Since its launch in 2023, Glovo Startup Campus has hosted 53 startups, organised more than 20 local Power Up competitions and, according to the company, reached more than 1,000 people through its wider programme.
The latest edition reflects Glovo’s efforts to extend its influence beyond its core delivery business, connecting emerging founders with the experience, networks and resources needed to scale internationally.
From AI to food waste
This year’s Startup Campus brought together 19 startups working across AI, e-commerce, logistics, FinTech and sustainability.
Several focused on improving retail and delivery operations, including Prometei, based in Kazakhstan, which streamlines marketplace management, and Polish startup Berryboo, which optimises e-commerce pricing.
Spain-based Bleecker Technologies automates inventory tracking, while Ukraine’s Pickpad develops smart order pickup systems. Meanwhile, Slyce.io, from Germany, helps restaurant franchises optimise delivery performance, Moldova-based Renter provides e-bike subscriptions for couriers, and Kazakhstan’s NCSpeech connects delivery workers with paid AI-training tasks.
AI also featured prominently across the cohort. Kenya-based AI Champs gamifies AI education, while Jafar AI, from Morocco, develops virtual receptionists for clinics. Nigerian startup Curacel automates financial operations, and Portugal’s Granter simplifies grant applications.
Other participants included Spanish FinTech Wealthreader, which enables access to financial data, Morocco-based Tookeez, which consolidates loyalty rewards, and Ukrainian startups Getpin.ai and RankinAI, both helping businesses improve their visibility across digital search and AI platforms.
Other startups addressed social and environmental challenges, including Romanian winners .lumen, Kool & Save, from Morocco, and Tunisia-based Barakeat tackle food waste through discounted surplus meals, while Ukrainian food startup Mozaika brings a modern twist to traditional dumplings.
Editor’s note: This article was produced in collaboration with Glovo.

articles.title: Airtel Nigeria's open network to show nearby 4G, 5G sites
articles.text:
Airtel Nigeria, the country’s second-largest network operator, now lets subscribers see nearby 4G and 5G network sites, including those undergoing upgrades and planned installations, through a new feature on the My Airtel Africa app.
The feature, called Airtel Open Network, also allows customers to report poor network experiences directly to the telecom operator. Launched in Lagos on October 30, 2026, the platform displays network sites within a 500-metre radius of a subscriber’s location. It uses visual indicators to distinguish active sites, those being upgraded, and locations where new sites are planned.
Nigeria is the first of Airtel Africa’s 14 operating markets to introduce the feature. By combining network visibility with customer feedback, Airtel hopes to identify coverage gaps and direct engineering attention to areas where subscribers experience poor connectivity.
The move tackles a persistent problem in Nigeria’s telecoms market: network coverage does not always translate to reliable connectivity. Airtel hopes greater network visibility and direct customer feedback will help identify coverage gaps and improve service quality.
A Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) assessment reported by TechCabal found that 78% of major roads had mobile signals, but only about 42% offered stable, high-speed 4G or 5G connectivity. The report also identified more than 120 critical black spots where mobile signals were completely unavailable.
Speaking at the launch, Dinesh Balsingh, Airtel Nigeria’s CEO, said the platform was designed to make network information more accessible while giving customers a direct channel to communicate service problems.
Trust, he says, grows when customers can see what is happening and know that their concerns are being heard. “With Open Network, we are giving customers greater visibility into our network and a more direct way to tell us where their experience falls short,” Balsingh said.
Airtel said it would use feedback submitted through the platform alongside its infrastructure investments to guide network upgrades. This could help its engineering teams identify locations requiring improvements in coverage, capacity and reliability.
The initiative also gives subscribers a way to report localised problems that may not be apparent in broader network performance assessments.
In his remarks, NCC Executive Vice Chairman, Aminu Maida, said accessible network information could complement the regulator’s efforts to improve service quality.
“The Commission’s assessment of service quality will continue to be guided by evidence and the standards that apply across the industry,” Maida said.
Maida wants operators to continue improving their services beyond minimum regulatory requirements, particularly by addressing persistent connectivity challenges.
However, seeing a nearby mast does not guarantee reliable reception. Airtel acknowledged that indoor coverage, building structures, handset specifications, and network congestion can affect individual subscribers’ experience.
The NCC’s network quality assessment framework also considers factors such as dropped calls, network congestion, availability and data speeds, showing why the number of nearby sites alone cannot determine service quality.
Airtel said Open Network would not automatically resolve network problems but would make it easier for customers to understand available infrastructure and report service gaps. The company plans to roll out demonstrations and user guides across digital, retail, and traditional media channels in the coming weeks.

articles.title: God of War Laufey delayed until May
articles.text:
God of War Laufey’s release date is being delayed to May 20th, 2027, developer Santa Monica Studio announced today. It was set to launch on PlayStation 5 on February 16th.
God of War Laufey delayed until May
Santa Monica Studio’s next God of War game is now set for a May 20th release.
Here is Santa Monica Studio’s full message about the delay:
Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we’ve been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye’s journey through the Everywhen. We don’t take for granted the trust placed in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans.
With this in mind, we’ve made the decision to delay God of War Laufey’s release to May 20th, 2027. We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we’ll be back to share more updates soon!
Laufey stars Faye, the wife of usual God of War protagonist Kratos, and she is played again by Deborah Ann Woll. Based on a 23-minute gameplay reveal earlier this year, Laufey looks to play differently than the other recent God of War games, with more of a focus on acrobatic action.

articles.title: Why a Canadian startup staged a “protest” of its biggest competitor | BetaKit
articles.text:
When you’re competing against a Goliath, sometimes it’s best to take notes from the Davids that came before you.
“As a small Canadian startup, we have to come up with creative ways [to promote ourselves], because every company can just go ahead and spend a couple million dollars [on] billboard ads.”
Shivam Mahajan, Floqer
That’s why Halifax-founded, Toronto-based customer relationship management platform Floqer set up a protest outside of Clay’s Sculpt conference in San Francisco last month. Complete with signs, slogans, and memes, Floqer got in front of prospective customers by picketing its biggest competitor’s marquee event.
“As a small Canadian startup, we have to come up with creative ways [to promote ourselves], because every company can just go ahead and spend a couple million dollars [on] billboard ads,” Floqer CEO Shivam Mahajan told BetaKit in an interview last Thursday.
Clay, which itself is Canadian-founded, is fresh off a Series D round that valued it at $7 billion USD ($9.8 billion CAD). By contrast, Floqer announced a $2 million CAD pre-seed round earlier this year for its platform, which helps companies gather context on their customers in an “AI-ready format.” Mahajan considers Clay his startup’s only direct competitor.
Mahajan, alongside his colleague Aaron Joseph, explained that the protest was inspired by the guerrilla marketing tactics of Salesforce in the early 2000s and 2010s, when the now hundred-billion-dollar enterprise software giant was in a similar position to Floqer. Salesforce got its name out by hiring actors to pose as protesters outside a conference for its biggest rival, Siebel Systems. Salesforce used the protest tactic again in 2011 against Oracle.
Salesforce was competing against large legacy software companies that were not on the cloud, Mahajan explained. He said he took inspiration from the tactic because it was a way to get their message out without straining their resources.
Instead of actors, the Floqer team assembled its protestors from gig work platform RentAHuman, set them up with signs poking fun at Clay’s pricing model, and placed them at the conference’s exits. Most of the signs revolved around Clay users needing to spend credits to run actions on the platform, whether it was a slogan, a meme of Drake rejecting the practice, or of Will Poulter in We’re the Millers questioning, “wait, you guys don’t have to pay for action credits?” BetaKit has reached out to Clay to ask if the company has any comment on the stunt.
It was “very much lighthearted, and the whole team felt that,” Joseph said. “I think we felt that from the other side as well. It’s just lighthearted.”
Floqer already counts big-name companies like Perplexity and Wise as customers, and recently crossed $1.2 million USD in annual recurring revenue, Mahajan said. With less than $2,000 spent on the whole marketing stunt, he estimated the protest captured about $250,000 in leads for the company to pursue as the team witnessed their Slack blow up with new sign-up notifications.
“We’re standing there, we’re doing all this, and we’re all looking at our phones [seeing] sign up, sign up, sign up,” Joseph said. “Like, dude, this is awesome.”
Feature image courtesy Floqer.

articles.title: „Niemand wird seekrank“: Diese Startups bringen Tragflächenboote mit Hightech zurück
articles.text:
Elektrisch und mit Foil: Wie diese neuen Fähren Tragflächenboote zurückbringen
Leinen los – und Abflug! In wenigen Sekunden beschleunigt die Fähre auf der Linie 14X bei Stockholm auf 16 Knoten, knapp 30 Kilometer pro Stunde. Anfangs schlagen noch Wellen an den Bug, je nach Wetter kann es ein wenig rütteln, doch dann wird es plötzlich ruhig: Bei 16 Knoten hebt sich das Boot aus dem Wasser und fängt an zu schweben, saust mit einer Geschwindigkeit von maximal 25 Knoten (gut 46 km/h) seinem Ziel entgegen. Der Motor surrt leise, wie man es von E-Antrieben kennt. Es gibt keine Dieselfahne, kein Dröhnen, nicht mal Geschaukel: Eine ausgefeilte Elektronik hält das neuartige Gefährt in der Balance, während das Wasser in etwa einem Meter Abstand unter dem Bug hinwegflitzt.
Dieser Text erscheint in der Ausgabe 8/2026 von MIT Technology Review. Darin beschäftigen wir uns mit den Folgen des Klimawandels und wie wir uns an Hitze, Dürre und Überschwemmungen anpassen sollten. Das Heft erscheint am 06.11.2026 im Zeitschriftenhandel.
So erleben es Passagiere zwischen Sollenkroka und der Insel Möja täglich mehrmals, seit die Fähre P-12 des schwedischen Herstellers Candela im Juli ihren Betrieb im Schärengarten vor Stockholm aufgenommen hat. „Beim Start merkt man: Das Boot arbeitet hart, um aus dem Wasser zu kommen“, sagt Candela-Gründer Gustav Hasselskog. „Aber dann wird alles ganz ruhig. Niemand wird seekrank, selbst bei starkem Wellengang, und vielen Leuten zaubert das Erlebnis ein Lächeln ins Gesicht.“
Geht es nach Candela und einer Reihe von weiteren Startups, werden solche Fährfahrten bald nichts Ungewöhnliches mehr sein. Sie haben die „Foiling“-Technologie aus dem Segelsport auf kommerzielle Fähren übertragen, um die Schifffahrt klimafreundlicher zu machen und dabei auch noch deutlich die Kosten zu senken. „Studien zeigen, dass solche Boote mit Elektroantrieb den Energieverbrauch um 70 bis 80 Prozent reduzieren können“, sagt Arash Eslamdoost, Professor für Marinetechnik an der Chalmers-Universität in Göteborg. „Das lässt sich mit keiner anderen Technologie erreichen.“
