articles.title: Nintendo is losing a Switch cartridge supplier
articles.text:
Nintendo is about to lose a major memory supplier for its Switch cartridges. The supplier, Macronix, announced during a recent quarterly earnings call that it would be gradually phasing out ROM production and is instead focusing on NOR flash memory for data centers, Taipei Times reports.
Nintendo is losing a Switch cartridge supplier
Nintendo ROM supplier Macronix is leaving the business as demand for its data center memory booms.
Macronix’s ROM revenue fell 39 percent compared with last year in Q3 2026, but its revenue from NOR memory rose 158 percent, and its revenue from NAND memory surged 768 percent year over year. According to Taipei Times, Macronix chairman and CEO Miin Wu said during its Q3 2026 earnings call that “demand for NOR used in data centers is very robust. Customers are chasing us for more capacity, demanding that we deliver more NOR flash solutions for data centers.” The company also reportedly “expects chip price hikes to persist.”
Although Sony has announced a plan to stop production of physical game discs starting in January 2028, Nintendo remains committed to physical games, saying recently that it has “no plans” to ditch them. Physical games also remain a bigger portion of Nintendo’s sales than other gaming companies; Nintendo said in August that physical titles accounted for 38.5 percent of its games sales, which is higher than companies like Capcom.
Macronix’s exit from the ROM business comes nearly a year after Micron shut down Crucial, its consumer RAM and SSD brand, to turn its attention to meeting AI data center demand.

articles.title: Cyber-Spionage gestoppt: T-Mobile-Techniker kappt Hacker-Leitung mit der Schere
articles.text:
Kabel ab: Wie eine Schere zum effektivsten Security-Tool bei T-Mobile wurde
Wer an das Verhindern von Cyberattacken denkt, denkt wahrscheinlich oftmals an Software-Lösungen wie eine Firewall. Dass es aber auch ganz analog und pragmatisch geht, beweist eine Geschichte, von der Bloomberg berichtet. Im Herbst 2024 fand eine großangelegte Spionagekampagne mit dem Code-Namen „Salt Typhoon“ statt. Dabei wurden mehr als 200 Ziele in 80 Ländern angegriffen. Am gravierendsten waren davon die USA betroffen.
Wie Salt Typhoon neun US-Telekommunikationskonzerne infiltrierte
Schon vor der Entdeckung soll der Angriff eine Zeit lang unentdeckt gelaufen sein. Dabei haben die Angreifer:innen zunächst neun große US-Telekommunikationsunternehmen gehackt und sich Zugang zu deren Netzwerken und Routern verschafft. Dazu zählten Verizon und AT&T, aber auch T‑Mobile. Anhand von späteren Analysen wurde klar, dass die Angreifer:innen Metadaten von Anrufen und Nachrichten von Millionen Kund:innen abgreifen konnten.
Heute geht man davon aus, dass es sich um eine großangelegte Attacke des chinesischen Ministeriums für Staatssicherheit gehandelt hat, die Daten von US-Politiker:innen sammeln wollten. Dafür priorisierten sie die Region um Washington D.C. herum und sollen sogar Daten von Donald Trump und JD Vance ergattert haben. Verständlicherweise sorgte die Entdeckung schon damals dafür, dass die Telekommunikationsunternehmen mit Hochdruck daran arbeiteten, die Angreifer:innen wieder aus ihren Systemen auszusperren.
Jeff Simon, Chief Information Officer bei T-Mobile, sagte dazu: „Wir haben gejagt, gejagt und gejagt. Jeden Tag habe ich das Team persönlich gefragt, wo die Angreifer sind, ob wir sie gefunden haben. Haben wir überhaupt schon Kontakt zum Feind gehabt?“ Erste Hinweise auf die infizierten Systeme gab es durch einen ungewöhnlichen Router, der im Datenzentrum von T-Mobile in Kalifornien stand. Das Gerät kommunizierte mit einem anderen T-Mobile-Standort, obwohl es abgeschaltet war.
Ein Techniker hat das Gerät sofort abgesteckt und zur genaueren Untersuchung in die Hauptzentrale in Washington gebracht. Dort stellten die Techniker:innen aber fest, dass das Signal gar nicht vom abgeschalteten Router kam. Sie verfolgten das Signal zu einem anderen Telekommunikationsunternehmen in Chicago, dessen Name Simon nicht näher nennt. Die Angreifer:innen hatten den Router in Chicago so manipuliert, dass er im System wie ein T-Mobile-Gerät auftauchte und so mit anderen Geräten des Unternehmens kommunizieren konnte.
So verhinderte T-Mobile weitere Cyberangriffe
Als die Quelle gefunden war, haben sich die Techniker:innen in ein Auto gesetzt, sind zum Datenzentrum des anderen Unternehmens gefahren und haben dort das betroffene Gerät aufgespürt. Einer der Techniker nahm einfach eine Schere in die Hand und schnitt das Kabel des Routers durch. Simon meint, dass sie auch den Router ebenso erst hätten herunterfahren können. Aber dieser Weg war schneller: „Es gibt nichts, was das Durchschneiden eines Kabels ersetzt.“
Der Router wurde mitgenommen und in einer isolierten Testumgebung reaktiviert. Allerdings waren die Angreifer:innen dann nicht mehr zu finden. Laut Simon hatten sie lediglich Zugang zu äußeren Netzwerken, sind aber nie an Kundendaten herangekommen. Heute erinnert das abgeschnittene Kabel in einem Bilderrahmen an den Vorfall. Darüber steht: „Von Grund auf wachsam, sicher durch Handeln. Salt Typhoon 2024.“
Die schlimmsten Security-Patzer
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 20.08.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Hört sich wie eine erfundene US Propagandstory an. Warum wurde das LAN Kabel nicht einfach abgesteckt? Man steht vor dem Router und statt einfach das LAN Kabel herauszuziehen, macht man sich erst auf die Suche nach einer Schere. Das dauert vielfach länger

articles.title: Rotterdam’s Hardt Hyperloop secures multi-million-euro funding to bounce back from bankruptcy and expand into the Americas | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Hardt Hyperloop, a Rotterdam-based mobility systems developer, has secured a multi-million-euro investment, marking its return after one of its entities entered bankruptcy proceedings earlier this year.
The investment round was led by Green Rock, a US-based investment and project development firm focused on strategic infrastructure and technology. Several of Hardt’s existing investors and shareholders, including Perpetuum Ventures and Urban Impact Ventures, also participated in the round. The exact figure has not been disclosed.
“This investment marks a new chapter for Hardt Hyperloop after a challenging period, and enables us to continue with the development and deployment of our technologies. We are grateful for the continued support of our existing investors and pleased to welcome Green Rock. Our collaboration with Green Rock also opens up new hyperloop projects,” said Tim Houter, co-founder of Hardt Hyperloop.
Founded in 2017 by a group of students from Delft University of Technology, Hardt Hyperloop develops technology for fast, energy-efficient transport of passengers and freight. The company has spent years developing the core systems of the hyperloop, including magnetic levitation, propulsion, and high-speed lane switching.
It designs autonomous vehicles capable of reaching speeds of up to 700 kmph. Its product portfolio includes traction solutions such as hybrid electromagnet units, sensor systems for real-time air-gap control, silicon carbide-based magnet drivers, and laminated steel track sets. Alongside its product engineering, the company also offers services such as application engineering and route development.
The company had previously collaborated with Schiphol Airport on a hyperloop route plan, and its most significant demonstration came in the form of a 420-metre European Hyperloop Centre (EHC) in Veendam, the Netherlands, where its core technologies have been tested and demonstrated before an audience that included Prince Constantijn of the Netherlands, co-founder and Special Envoy of Techleap.
For Hardt Hyperloop, the road to this investment has not been easy. The company was declared bankrupt in early March 2026, with bankruptcy administrator Sjoerd Warringa confirming the news to RTL Z at the time. The company’s most recent annual statement had flagged that its survival was contingent on fresh capital and that it had funds only until January 2026.
With fresh capital now secured, Hardt Hyperloop plans to advance its technology, prepare for planned hyperloop projects across Europe, and develop new projects in additional markets. As part of the investment, it has also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with Green Rock to jointly develop hyperloop projects across North, Central, and South America.
“Hardt has spent ten years working on the hardest engineering problems in hyperloop, including safely switching vehicles between hyperloop lines at speed. We see real demand in the Americas for fast links between cities, and we want a technology partner that has built, tested and demonstrated the core technologies. Hardt is that partner,” said Cindy Huang, founder of Green Rock.
The lifeline for Hardt Hyperloop comes after the German government committed in its coalition agreement last year to build a national hyperloop reference line, with Federal Minister for Research, Technology, and Space Dorothee Bär announcing plans to make €100 million available for it.
For Hardt Hyperloop, this investment is not just a financial lifeline but a new strategic launchpad that not only allows it to build on its European plans but also expand on the other side of the Atlantic.

articles.title: Foto com milhares de satélites no céu é confundida com imagem de IA
articles.text:
Uma fotografia impressionante do céu noturno da Nova Zelândia ganhou enorme repercussão nas redes sociais. A imagem mostra centenas de rastros luminosos cruzando o horizonte e chamou tanta atenção que algumas pessoas chegaram a acusar o autor de ter utilizado inteligência artificial (IA) para criá-la.
O responsável pelo registro é Brendan Larsen, astrofotógrafo de 51 anos que fotografou o céu sobre o monte Taranaki, na Nova Zelândia. Apesar das suspeitas, a imagem é resultado de um trabalho fotográfico real, que exigiu planejamento, centenas de registros e muitas horas de edição.
Larsen capturou 578 fotografias durante aproximadamente duas horas. Cada registro teve exposição de oito segundos. Posteriormente, ele reuniu as imagens em uma composição que levou cerca de 40 horas para ser finalizada no Photoshop.
O resultado é uma fotografia que reúne aproximadamente 1,4 mil satélites e 14 mil rastros luminosos, evidenciando a quantidade de objetos artificiais que atravessam o céu noturno.
Leia mais:
- Astrônomos querem levar à ONU debate sobre excesso de satélites e poluição no céu noturno hoje
- Startup testa tecnologia que pode iluminar a Terra durante a noite
- Google testa IA em satélite e avança em projeto de data centers espaciais
Fotografia impressionante levanta debate sobre satélites
- A repercussão da imagem foi enorme. Larsen ganhou cerca de 15 mil seguidores e a publicação acumulou dezenas de milhões de visualizações;
- Entretanto, o fotógrafo não pretende apenas impressionar o público com a beleza do registro. A composição também chama atenção para um problema crescente: a presença cada vez maior de satélites na órbita terrestre e seus possíveis impactos na observação astronômica;
- A expansão das constelações de satélites tem provocado preocupações entre pesquisadores e entusiastas da astronomia. Além de interferir em observações científicas, esses equipamentos podem contribuir para a poluição luminosa do céu noturno;
- Nesse contexto, a fotografia de Larsen funciona como um retrato visual de uma transformação que acontece acima de nossas cabeças. O céu continua parecendo infinito, mas está cada vez mais ocupado por estruturas construídas pela humanidade.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: El Gobierno francés admite que varios bancos de sangre también han sido objetivo de ciberataques
articles.text: Bolsas de sangre almacenadas en un banco y destinadas a pacientes de hospital. Un ciberataque contra varios centros regionales del organismo público que gestiona las donaciones de sangre en Francia pusieron en riesgo la conservación de grandes reservas destinadas a transfusiones y ensayos clínicos. Los atacantes no entraron en los sistemas propios del organismo de conservación, sino en los de Coolworld, una empresa que suministra sus equipos de refrigeración. Así trataron de elevar a distancia los umbrales de temperatura y descongelación de las cámaras frías de tres centros donde se almacena plasma. Según las autoridades francesas, el objetivo era que esas cámaras pasaran de -30 °C a 110 °C. En ellas se conservan muestras y plasma congelado destinado a transfusiones. Seguir leyendo

articles.title: Use NVIDIA NeMo to Turn Agent Failures into Tests and Harness Fixes | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Turn production evidence into prioritized issues and custom evaluations that help you improve prompts, tools, models, memory, skills, and harness code.
When you build an agent for your domain, generic benchmark scores may not explain its failures. An agent might choose the wrong tool, follow the wrong workflow branch, miss relevant context, use an unnecessarily expensive model, or complete a task without meeting a domain-specific requirement.
Improving an agent requires more than model tuning. Prompts, tools, routing, memory, skills, control flow, and other code all shape production reliability. Traces help you investigate failures, while evaluations help you measure whether a change improves agent behavior.
This tutorial walks you through one complete optimization cycle: use NVIDIA NeMo Compass to identify a failure in recorded traces, create an evaluation with NVIDIA NeMo Eval Author, update the agent’s instructions, and compare results on development and held-out tasks. Follow along with the NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprint for agent optimization.
The blueprint uses Hermes Agent in an NVIDIA OpenShell sandbox, with recorded traces from a fictional company.
The agent harness is the optimization surface
One wrong tool call can derail an entire task. The cause may be an unclear tool description, a routing rule, or missing context in the agent harness. A trace helps identify where the run went wrong. 
Our example agent is a Hermes enterprise assistant for a fictional company, connected through Model Context Protocol (MCP) to the company’s chat, email, files, and tickets. We asked it to “draft a message with project updates.” It drafted the message but also called the send_message tool without user confirmation. Addressing this error requires examining both the harness instructions and tool execution.
Prerequisites
Use a Linux machine running Docker natively. The recommended configuration is Ubuntu 24.04 with 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of RAM. You also need:
- OpenShell 0.1.2 and Harbor 0.22.0
- An NVIDIA API key from build.nvidia.com
- A coding agent that NeMo Eval Author supports, such as Codex or Claude Code
Follow the full step-by-step tutorial on GitHub or get started with an NVIDIA Brev launchable.
NeMo Compass: Find what to fix first
The NemoClaw blueprint for agent optimization uses three libraries: NeMo Compass, NeMo Eval Author, and NVIDIA NeMo Relay.
NeMo Compass analyzes stored agent traces and evaluation evidence to find recurring problems, identify evaluation gaps, and prioritize improvements. Rather than requiring you to inspect each run, NeMo Compass reduces a large trace corpus to a structured backlog of issues, supporting examples, and recommended areas for improvement or experimentation.
Each Hermes run in the example is recorded as one JSON trace per line. We pointed NeMo Compass at the 42 traces in the repository, along with ETHOS.md, a short file that defines the assistant’s expected behavior.
compass --config configs/trace-analyst.yaml \
--trace.filesystem.path traces/world-v3/production/insights.jsonl
NeMo Compass returns findings based on multiple signals:
- Signs of unusual behavior
- How the agent uses tools
- Divergence from the agent’s intended behavior
NeMo Compass also provides trace IDs that link each signal to the relevant agent runs.
These trace IDs support the overall finding. In these runs, the agent sent messages without user confirmation. NeMo Compass identified this error by comparing the agent’s actions with the rules in ETHOS.md.
In our internal benchmarks, running the full set of NeMo Compass signals against a dataset of thousands of traces identified anomalies that a coding agent assigned a similar task missed.
Build evaluations around real agent work with NeMo Eval Author
After finding an issue with NeMo Compass, create a test that reproduces the problem. NeMo Eval Author provides coding agent skills and workflows to help you create these tests. NeMo Eval Author supports two agent evaluation formats: Harbor evaluations and NVIDIA NeMo Gym evaluations.
Install NeMo Eval Author’s skills in your coding agent and instruct it to use them. Provide the NeMo Compass findings, raw traces, the agent’s ETHOS.md file, and access to your agent repository as context. The evaluations should measure agent behavior relevant to your agent’s requirements. Review and tune the generated evaluations to make sure they reflect those requirements.
In our example, the coding agent created four Harbor evaluations with tasks similar to “draft a response.” NeMo Eval Author also creates verifiers that determine whether an agent meets specific criteria. In this example, the verifier checks whether the agent called the send_message tool without human confirmation and marks that run as a failure.
NeMo Eval Author can help you create custom evaluations before production data exists, using agent requirements from ETHOS.md and code details such as tool definitions and existing workflows. As real traces and known failures become available, use NeMo Eval Author to expand your evaluation suite, so it continues to reflect how your agent is used.
Change one part of the harness
After identifying an issue and writing tests for it, update the harness. In our example, we changed the Hermes agent’s SOUL.md (a Hermes concept similar to a system prompt):
Requests to write, draft, compose, prepare, or suggest a message authorize preparation only. Provide the draft for review and stop before sending it. A token returned by a preparation tool is a technical capability to execute an action. It does not establish the user's consent to that action.
Harness changes can range from simple fixes like this to more complex middleware implementations, plugin extensions, and other agent harness patterns. Provide the coding agent with the NeMo Compass outputs, your agent’s ETHOS.md file, and your agent implementation. This context grounds the coding agent’s proposal. Earlier posts cover harness optimizations with LangChain Deep Agents and Nous Research Hermes.
Measure before and after
After updating the agent, we reran the evaluation tasks created by NeMo Eval Author. Two tasks, labeled “Held out,” were withheld from the coding agents proposing harness changes. These held-out tasks help assess whether the changes generalize beyond the development tasks.
| Evaluation set | Baseline passes/runs | Updated-agent passes/runs | Tool calls, before/after | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Development, 2 tasks x 3 runs | 3/6 | 6/6 | 10 to 6 | 
| Held out, 2 tasks x 3 runs | 4/6 | 6/6 | 28 to 15 | 
In our example, we started with a small set of evaluation tasks focused narrowly on the NeMo Compass findings. For your production agent, build an evaluation suite that covers a broad range of behaviors. In our experience, production suites often contain hundreds to a few thousand examples. Accept changes only when they improve both the test cases and the held-out set. If results are inconclusive, or a change fixes one problem but introduces a regression, run NeMo Compass on the new traces from the proposed agent. The coding agent can use these new insights to refine the change. As you iterate on this process, ensure that the held-out cases remain hidden from the coding agent to avoid overfitting.
Run the loop again
After a successful harness change, repeat the analysis to identify the next issue. We ran NeMo Compass on the updated agent’s scored traces, and it no longer reported the sending-without-confirmation finding. It identified another issue: for some queries, the agent found the answer but failed to ground its response in the retrieved evidence. That finding is the focus of the next round of testing and fixes.
Apply the optimization loop to an engineering agent
The same trace-to-evaluation loop can be applied to agents that perform more complex technical tasks. In an engineering workflow, evaluations need to measure engineering outcomes as well as the efficiency of the agent’s tool use.
A car door design example illustrates how NVIDIA NeMo tools can support this process. The example uses LEO, the engineering Virtual Companion from Dassault Systèmes, to propose design changes and test them through simulation with the goal of creating a stronger, safer car door.
NeMo Compass analyzes the agent’s traces to identify areas for improvement. A coding agent uses the findings to make targeted prompt and configuration changes, and evaluations measure the updated agent’s performance in the engineering environment. Additional scenarios check whether those changes introduce regressions.
In this example, NeMo Compass identified a recurring issue in which the agent placed QueryModel arguments outside the expected options field. It returned an empty error message, leaving the agent unable to recover. The issue appeared across multiple traces. Based on this finding, the coding agent added a validation step that catches misplaced arguments and names in tool calls. Compared with the baseline, malformed tool calls fell from 142 to zero. Accuracy was unchanged, and no regressions were observed in the remaining scenarios.
During the initial pass, the optimization loop ran overnight without human intervention. In approximately 12 hours, the reported results showed a 28% relative improvement in the door design workflow’s overall evaluation score and 35% fewer tool calls per run across six tested scenarios, with no regressions reported in the other scenarios.
The example connects the NeMo workflow to two measures of agent performance: task quality and execution efficiency. It follows the process described in this tutorial—use traces to identify what to change, then use custom evaluations to assess the targeted improvement and check for regressions before adopting the change.
Try the NemoClaw blueprint for agent optimization
Start with the NemoClaw blueprint for agent optimization, the workplace assistant example from this post, or the CAD guide.
Run the example agent and establish a baseline score. Then complete one optimization cycle: find an issue with NeMo Compass, build a test for it with NeMo Eval Author, and try one change to the harness. After that, point the same loop at your own agent.

articles.title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited.
Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. As enterprise data grows across multiple platforms, pipelines, and business domains, maintaining consistent data quality has become increasingly difficult. Manual data quality rule creation, fragmented governance, and evolving business definitions make it challenging to scale data quality across the enterprise.
This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, large language model (LLM) powered Data Quality Agent within its NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python code under centralized, human-in-the-loop governance. Together, these capabilities help organizations improve data quality at enterprise scale while reducing the effort required to build and maintain data quality programs.
About Indegene
Indegene Limited (BSE: 544172, NSE: INDGN) is the strategic operating partner to the life sciences industry, orchestrating commercial, medical, R&D, and safety operations across the product lifecycle. Trusted by the world’s top 20 biopharma companies, Indegene helps run complex, highly regulated workflows at global scale. Indegene combines deep life sciences expertise with AI-embedded platforms and governed operating models to improve speed, consistency, and compliance across mission-critical operations. By integrating technology into how work is executed and scaled, Indegene helps life sciences organizations deliver measurable outcomes in regulated environments.
Why conventional data quality programs break down
Most organizations have established data quality processes but keeping them effective is becoming increasingly difficult as enterprise data ecosystems evolve.
One of the biggest challenges is the divide between technical and business rule ownership. Data engineers typically define technical rules that confirm whether data is structurally correct. For example, verifying that an HCP ID (Healthcare Professional ID) isn’t null, follows the required format, is unique, and maps to a valid reference record. Business teams define rules that determine whether the data makes sense in its operational context. For example, confirming that product market share totals 100 percent within a territory or that an HCP’s prescription activity aligns with their specialty and eligibility criteria. Because technical rules are often maintained in code while business rules reside in glossaries, SOPs, and subject-matter expertise, keeping them aligned and consistently governed across datasets and platforms becomes difficult.
Traditional validation techniques also have inherent limitations. Checks for null values, data types, uniqueness, or referential integrity remain essential, but they can’t capture business-specific context. Validating product hierarchies, customer segmentation, territory alignment, or commercial business rules requires domain knowledge that static validation logic can’t easily represent.
Creating and maintaining data quality rules is equally demanding. Every new dataset requires data profiling, rule definition, SQL development, validation, and ongoing maintenance. These rules are often spread across SQL scripts, pipeline code, spreadsheets, data catalogs, and tool-specific configurations. As schemas, business definitions, or validation thresholds change, the effort required to update and govern these rules grows significantly.
Additionally, the operational impact is significant. Onboarding new datasets becomes slower because many activities are repeated manually. Maintaining quality rules across hundreds of datasets consumes valuable engineering effort. Business users lose confidence when validation rules are difficult to understand, trace, or relate to business context.
As a result, data quality often becomes a periodic governance activity rather than a continuous, scalable capability.
Rethinking data quality with generative AI
Traditional data quality tools often operate as standalone capabilities, disconnected from the broader enterprise data ecosystem. As organizations scale AI and analytics, data quality needs to be embedded within the data platform itself, where governance, metadata, lineage, and analytics work together.
Indegene addresses this through the NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP), a modern, AI-driven data platform built specifically for life sciences. NEXT UDP brings together fragmented commercial, medical, clinical, and enterprise data into a single, governed environment so organizations can manage the complete data lifecycle from ingestion to analytics. NEXT UDP provides several standalone AI agents, such as the Data Ingestion agent, Data Quality agent, Orchestration agent, Data Catalog agent, and SQL Bot Generator agent. You can use them standalone within your data pipelines or customize them further for agent-to-agent communication.
By integrating data ingestion, transformation, data quality, governance, metadata management, and analytics within a unified platform, NEXT UDP helps organizations:
- Consolidate fragmented enterprise data into a trusted source of truth.
- Standardize data quality and governance across business domains.
- Improve metadata visibility, lineage, and traceability.
- Reduce manual effort across data engineering workflows.
- Deliver trusted, AI-ready data for enterprise analytics and decision-making.
Indegene’s life sciences clients needed an agent that could run reliably in production and meet strict governance requirements, while giving the team flexibility in how they build it. Within NEXT UDP, Generative AI powers an intelligent Data Quality Agent that augments existing data quality processes. The agent boosts data engineer and data steward productivity by accelerating rule creation, simplifying validation, and helping maintain consistent governance at enterprise scale.
Indegene built the Data Quality Agent on a set of AWS services, with Amazon Bedrock, Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore at its core. Amazon Bedrock, provides a choice of foundation models (FMs), built on a foundation of security, privacy, and responsible AI controls. For life sciences organizations, this matters because their data often includes sensitive healthcare professional and patient information. Strands Agents streamlines building and updating the agent, and its evaluation tools help Indegene test rule accuracy, which is critical in regulated life sciences environments. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The solution also inherits existing AWS security and audit controls, so Indegene can focus on data quality logic instead of agent infrastructure.
What makes the Data Quality Agent unique? Two knowledge bases that power context-aware data quality
Any data quality tool can check for null values, duplicates, or invalid data types. Services such as AWS Glue Data Quality, a capability of AWS Glue, already recommend rules like these from data statistics, and they remain a strong foundation. The harder problem is determining whether the data makes sense for its business purpose. To address this, the Data Quality Agent uses two complementary knowledge bases that combine curated domain knowledge with experience gained from governed usage.
The first is an Internal Enterprise knowledge base: It combines internal business glossaries, data dictionaries, SOPs, regulatory guidance, approved data quality rules, validated scripts, profiling results, historical anomalies, and subject matter expert (SME) feedback. Content is ingested, vectorized, and retrieved through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to generate data quality rules grounded in enterprise standards and proven outcomes.
The second is an External Reference knowledge base: It’s built and periodically updated using approved standardized data quality frameworks, web search, and controlled web-scraping. When a dataset is selected, the agent analyzes table and column metadata and retrieves relevant data quality standards, reference values, and validation best practices from trusted sources. For example, for an NPI (National Provider Identifier) column, it can identify applicable quality standards, recommend format (the required 10-digit numeric format) and perform reference-validation checks.
How it works
The Data Quality Agent takes users from data profiling to rule creation and governance in a single workflow:
- Select source: Connect to a supported source such as Amazon Redshift or Snowflake.
- Select database and schema: Browse the available tables, with the rule count and active rule status for each.
- Profile data: The solution computes quality metrics and column patterns for the table, which users review.
- Detect anomalies: The solution flags anomalies against historical baselines, and users review the total, critical, and warning issues and the affected records.
- Manage rules: Review a table’s existing rules or start creating new ones.
- Choose rule mode: Pick Column Level, Table Level, or Custom Query.
- Generate rule suggestions: The agent uses metadata, profiling results, anomalies, existing rules, and knowledge base context to recommend technical and business rules, each with a severity.
- Review, refine and apply: Users edit or approve each recommendation.
- Generate and validate code: The agent produces SQL and Python for approved rules, and a validation step checks them.
- Store in the central rule repository: Approved rules become available for execution, monitoring, and audit.
Solution architecture of the generative AI-powered Data Quality Agent on AWS
The following diagram shows the end-to-end architecture of the Data Quality Agent on the NEXT UDP platform, from the data steward request to rule execution.
Data stewards and data quality analysts call the solution from the Indegene application. The following table provides a walkthrough of the solution pipeline and lists the AWS services used for each layer. It also captures other options the solution supports, so you can adapt it to your data volumes, existing tools, and operational preferences.
| Layer | AWS / platform services | Also supported | Role | 
| API and access | AWS WAF, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Cognito | – | Data stewards and data quality analysts call the solution through Amazon API Gateway. AWS WAF filters requests before they reach the API, and Amazon Cognito authenticates users with OAuth 2.0 and validates the JWT on each request. | 
| Data source layer | Amazon Redshift | Snowflake connector, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), JDBC/ODBC sources | Provides structured and semi-structured data for data quality profiling and rule execution. | 
| Metadata catalog layer | AWS Glue Data Catalog | AWS Glue crawlers for automatic schema discovery | Captures databases, schemas, tables, columns, data types, and rule coverage. | 
| Profiling and anomaly detection layer | AWS Lambda (Python), with results stored in Amazon DynamoDB | AWS Glue jobs, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift SQL | Column statistics, such as null rates, distinct counts, data type conformance, patterns, value ranges and table-level signals are computed by a Python-based profiling process on AWS Lambda, The same Lambda performs anomaly detection using statistical comparison against historical baselines to flag unexpected shifts, such as a null-rate spike or a cardinality change. | 
| Knowledge/RAG layer | Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL (pgvector) and S3 for storing knowledge documents exposed as tools through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector store, Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3 | Retrieves from the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases (external reference standards and internal enterprise knowledge). AgentCore Gateway connects the agent to its knowledge bases as tools. | 
| LLM intelligence layer | Strands Agents on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, AgentCore memory | Other foundation models available in Amazon Bedrock | Generates data quality rules and uses the assembled context and few-shot prompting to recommend both technical checks (completeness, format, uniqueness) and pharma-specific business rules. Amazon Bedrock provides a choice of FMs to generate rules. AgentCore runtime provides a managed, session-isolated environment, AgentCore memory retains reviewer feedback to improve future recommendations. | 
| Orchestration and human review layer | AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), Amazon EventBridge | – | Coordinates profiling, LLM calls, rule generation, rule execution, status updates, and human review. | 
| Rule metadata repository | Amazon DynamoDB | Amazon Aurora / Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) | Stores rule ID, name, type, column, status, author, created date, severity, and version details. | 
| Code generation, validation and storage | Amazon Bedrock – Claude Sonnet 4.5 and AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with approved scripts store in Amazon S3 | – | Generates Python / SQL code and checks before storage | 
| Execution layer | AWS Lambda | AWS Glue jobs, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift SQL | Runs data quality checks and writes violation counts and detailed anomalies. | 
| Monitoring and dashboard layer | Amazon CloudWatch, AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or application UI | Amazon Quick, Amazon OpenSearch Dashboards | Data quality dashboard displays the rules applied and their status, along with total anomalies, critical anomalies, checks run, and issue details. | 
| Security and governance | AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM), AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), AWS Secrets Manager, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints | – | Authentication, encryption, secrets, audit, and threat detection | 
How the Data Quality Agent builds context
Before recommending any validation rule, the Data Quality Agent assembles context from six distinct sources, each answering a different question about the data:
| Context Source | What it provides | Question it answers | 
| Table/Column Metadata (Catalog) | Schema, data types from the Data Catalog | What is this data? | 
| Data Profile | Column-level statistics computed from the actual data, such as null rates, distinct counts, value ranges, frequent values and detected patterns | What does the data look like right now? | 
| Anomaly Detection Results | Unexpected changes flagged by comparing the latest profile with historical baselines, such as a sudden rise in nulls, a change in distinct values, or out-of-range values | What has changed or looks wrong? | 
| Existing Active Data Quality Rules | Rules already applied at the table or column level, retrieved from the rule repository | What rules already exist, so we don’t duplicate or conflict? | 
| External Reference Knowledge Base | Universal, publicly established data quality standards and validation best practices (for example, format and structural rules for identifiers like the National Provider Identifier) | What are the industry standards for this field? | 
| Internal Enterprise Knowledge Base | Organization-specific data quality rule patterns, prior reviewer feedback, and curated business/technical rule libraries | How does this organization define quality? | 
Together, these sources let the agent reason like an experienced data steward. Grounding every recommendation in what the data is, what the standards require, how the enterprise defines quality, and what has already been implemented.
What the solution does
The Data Quality Agent generates several categories of checks and keeps data stewards in control of the results.
Anomaly checks generation
The solution generates anomaly checks that catch values which are technically valid but don’t match how a pharmaceutical market behaves. These include negative switch percentages, market shares that don’t add up to 100 percent within a market, inconsistent drug rankings (for example, a drug ranked first with a lower share than the drug ranked second), rating values outside the defined scale, and panel sizes that are too small or don’t match the number of respondents.
Context-aware rule generation with RAG
The Data Quality Agent generates rule recommendations in three modes:
| Rule Type | Description | 
| Column Level | Generates data quality rules for a specific, individual column selected by the user. The agent reads that column’s metadata and profiling signals to suggest checks such as data type validation, null and mandatory-field checks, length and range validation, pattern/format validation, and uniqueness. | 
| Table Level | Generates data quality rules for the table as a whole, driven by the table’s metadata and relationships across its columns. This covers record consistency, duplicate detection, cross-column validation, referential integrity checks, and table-wide business consistency. | 
| Custom Query | Generates SQL-based rules from natural language input. The user describes the business validation in plain English and the agent produces the corresponding SQL, which can then be refined conversationally or edited directly to support complex validations that fall outside standard column and table checks. | 
The Create New Quality Rule interface provides dedicated Column Level, Table Level, and Custom Query modes.
The platform supports both technical validation and business-specific quality checks.
For technical rules, the agent generates checks that confirm the data is structurally sound. These include null checks for mandatory fields, data type validation, range validation for numeric and date values, pattern validation for formatted fields such as identifiers and codes, duplicate detection, and referential integrity checks between related tables.
For business rules, the agent generates life sciences checks that confirm the data is consistent with how the business operates. These include account affiliation consistency (for example, a healthcare provider linked to the correct organization), segmentation logic, eligibility criteria, and market share and product share validation (for example, shares within a territory not exceeding 100%).
Real use-case example
Consider an HCP Product Performance table with the columns HCP_ID, Specialty, Territory_ID, Product_ID, Prescription_Volume, Market_Share_Pct, Switch_Pct, Rating_Scale, and Reporting_Month. Using the table profile and the two Knowledge Bases, this is how the Data Quality Agent generates and performs the following checks:
- Anomaly checks performed. 
         
  - Negative switch percentage.
  - Market share total mismatch.
  - Sudden increase or decrease in prescription volume.
  - Inconsistent product rankings.
  - Invalid rating-scale values.
- Technical rules generated. 
         
  - HCP_ID must not be null or duplicated.
  - Prescription_Volume must be numeric and non-negative.
  - Market_Share_Pct and Switch_Pct must be between 0 and 100.
  - Reporting_Month must follow the required date format.
  - Territory_ID and Product_ID must match their reference tables.
- Business rules generated. 
         
  - Market share across all products must total 100 percent for each territory and reporting month.
  - The HCP’s product eligibility must align with their specialty.
  - Only eligible HCPs can be included in the target segment.
AI-assisted severity recommendation
The solution recommends severity based on dataset context, rule type, and business impact. Severity categories help distinguish between:
- Critical issues, such as invalid commercial metrics, incorrect identifiers, or business rule violations.
- Basic validations, including schema conformance, null checks, and length validation.
- Complex validations involving advanced SQL logic, multi-column rules, or domain-specific business checks.
- Information: Validation conducted for awareness and transparency purposes only. No action is required unless concerns are identified.
SQL/Python code generation and ETL integration
After a rule is approved, the LLM generates the equivalent SQL, Python, and PySpark code. Before it’s stored, the code is validated automatically with syntax checks, a check against the target schema, and a test run on sample data where the language supports it. This means existing extract, transform, and load (ETL) and orchestration tools can run them as part of the current data pipelines.
AI-assisted validation
Using an LLM as a Validation Agent to review data quality (DQ) rules/scripts generated by another LLM for reducing hallucinations and improving governance. Further, Amazon Bedrock provides security, privacy, and responsible AI controls. Prompts and outputs aren’t used to train the models or shared with model providers. Amazon Bedrock is HIPAA eligible and in scope for compliance programs such as SOC, ISO and GDPR, which helps Indegene meet the requirements of its life sciences clients. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails adds configurable safeguards on model inputs and outputs. It detects and masks personally identifiable information (PII), blocks harmful content and prompt injection attacks, and uses contextual grounding checks to flag responses that aren’t supported by the retrieved knowledge.
Human oversight remains central
The Data Quality Agent is designed to augment existing data quality processes. Each generated rule receives a confidence score. Only high-confidence, low-risk rules are approved automatically, while critical and business rules always go to an SME for review. Every decision is recorded in the rule repository, so rule management stays governed, traceable, and aligned with enterprise standards.
Delivering operational impact and business value
In production, across Indegene’s deployments of NEXT UDP for life sciences clients, the Data Quality Agent has reduced the effort to define and implement data quality rules from about 30 hours to about 4 hours per dataset. That’s roughly 85 percent less effort, or about 7x higher productivity. Onboarding a new table now takes 2–4 hours instead of 2–5 working days. Data engineers and data stewards now spend their time reviewing and approving rules rather than writing them from scratch.
Key outcomes include:
- Less manual effort through AI-generated rules, SQL, and Python.
- Faster onboarding of new tables, schemas, and business domains.
- More consistent rules, grounded in approved standards, enterprise knowledge, and existing rules.
- Better collaboration between business and technical teams through the review, refine, and approve workflow.
- Earlier detection of data quality issues through automated profiling and anomaly detection.
Table 1: Performance and Scale
| Metric | Impact* | 
| Enterprise profiling | 25–50 schemas; 500–2,000 tables; 10,000–50,000 columns | 
| Table profiling | 45–90 sec (~1M rows); 2–5 min (~10M rows) | 
| AI rule generation | 20–45 sec per table | 
| SQL generation | 3–8 sec per rule; 20–60 sec for 10–15 rules | 
| Rule execution | 20–30 sec (standard); 1–3 min (complex SQL) | 
| Central rule repository | 1,000–10,000 rules | 
| DQ checks per execution | 100–500 per domain. Scalable to 1,000+ | 
*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments
Table 2: Rule quality and validation
| Metric | Impact* | What does it mean | 
| Rule suggestion accuracy | 80–90% | Suggestions that are technically valid and apply correctly to the column or table | 
| Rule acceptance rate | 60–75% | Suggestions approved without any changes | 
| Rule refinement rate / Human Override Rate | 20–35% | Suggestions approved after the reviewer edited logic or thresholds | 
| SQL validity | 90–97% (schema-grounded); 80–90% (custom SQL) | Generated SQL that passes validation on the first attempt | 
| Severity recommendation accuracy | 75–85% | Recommended severity matching the reviewer’s final severity | 
| Business relevance (SME rating) | 4.0–4.5 / 5 | SME rating of how useful the recommended rules are to the business | 
| Hallucination rate | <5–8% | Suggestions that reference non-existent columns or incorrect business logic | 
*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments
Table 3: Operational efficiency
| Metric | Impact* | 
| Manual SQL rule authoring | 60–80% reduction in end-to-end effort, including review and refinement | 
| New table onboarding | 2–5 working days → 2–4 hours | 
| Rule reuse | 40–60% of new rules adapted from existing approved rules | 
| LLM cost optimization | Up to 90% lower input-token cost on cached context with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching | 
| Compute optimization | ~45–51% reduction with metadata-first profiling | 
*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments
Table 4: Manual compared to agent-assisted data quality
| Activity | Traditional DQ Approach | Generative AI-powered DQ approach | Impact* | 
| Rule Discovery | Manual review of schemas, profiling reports, sample data, and documentation. Existing tools can generate basic profiling checks but often miss domain-specific business logic | Agent uses metadata, profiling results, table context, existing rule patterns, and optional business descriptions to recommend technical and life sciences-specific data quality rules | 80-85% faster | 
| Technical Rule Generation | Manual creation of null, data type, range, uniqueness, and integrity rules | Automated rule generation with human review | 80-85% faster | 
| Business Rule Definition | Validation is often based on technical metadata with limited understanding of product, segment, customer, or eligibility logic. Business context depends heavily on SME discussions and manual translation into validation logic | Uses RAG to retrieve business glossaries, data dictionaries, existing rules, and historical anomaly patterns to generate context-aware recommendations. | 70-75% faster | 
| Rules authoring and SQL/Python Development | Engineers manually define validation rules and perform coding, debugging, and testing for each dataset or business requirement. | Auto-generated rules at the Column Level, Table Level, and Custom Query levels, and generate SQL/Python for the selected DQ checks. Users can review, refine, and apply the recommendations. | 80-85% faster to first working code | 
| Rule Validation | Rules are validated manually, involving multiple iterations of executing the queries and refining | Agent scores, refines, and optimizes rules automatically | 80-85% faster | 
| Rule Reuse | Manual copy, modify, and reuse | Approved rules and feedback added to the agent’s knowledge | 50% faster onboarding for new datasets in an existing domain | 
| Anomaly Detection | Manual analysis of profiling outputs and records | Automated anomaly detection with business-context explanations | 80-85% faster | 
| Severity classification | Rule severity and business impact are determined manually, which can lead to inconsistent prioritization. | Recommends severity based on rule type, dataset context, and business impact. | Consistent, context-based severity | 
| Governance & Traceability | Rules are often distributed across tools, scripts, spreadsheets, or catalogs, making governance and traceability difficult. Approval and review workflows vary across teams. | Central, versioned rule repository with ownership | 85% reduction in maintenance effort | 
| Human Effort | SMEs and engineers drive every step | SMEs focus on review and approval. The agent handles discovery and generation | Higher productivity & scalability, ~7x productivity | 
*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments
Looking ahead
As enterprise data ecosystems continue to grow, maintaining consistent and scalable data quality becomes increasingly difficult using manual rule creation and fragmented governance processes. Generative AI provides an opportunity to augment these workflows by accelerating rule generation, incorporating business context, and supporting governed decision-making.
The generative AI-powered Data Quality Agent within the NEXT Unified Data Platform demonstrates how large language models, RAG, and centralized rule governance can work together to simplify data quality management while keeping humans in control of review and approval. Future enhancements will continue to build on this foundation, including:
- AI-assisted remediation recommendations to help users resolve failed data quality checks.
- Root cause analysis to identify recurring anomaly patterns and support faster investigation of repeated data quality issues.
As these capabilities evolve, the focus remains the same: helping organizations improve data quality through AI-assisted automation while maintaining governance, transparency, and business oversight.
To learn more, refer to the following resources:
- Indegene in the life sciences space
- Generative AI in Healthcare & Life Sciences
- AWS Skill Builder course: Building Generative AI Applications Using Amazon Bedrock
- GitHub repo: Sample Healthcare and Life Sciences Agents on AWS

articles.title: Awfis Q2 profit jumps 93% to Rs 31 Cr, revenue rises to Rs 464 Cr
articles.text:
Awfis Q2 profit jumps 93% to Rs 31 Cr, revenue rises to Rs 464 Cr
During April-September period of FY27, the company's net profit rose to Rs 54.76 crore from Rs 25.95 crore in the year-ago period.
Realty firm Awfis Space Solutions Ltd has reported a 93% increase in its consolidated profit to Rs 30.8 crore for the quarter ended September on higher income amid strong demand for managed workspaces.
Its net profit stood at Rs 15.97 crore in the year-ago period.
Total income increased to Rs 464.29 crore in the second quarter of this fiscal from Rs 392.97 crore in the year-ago period, according to a regulatory filing on Tuesday.
During April-September period of FY27, the company's net profit rose to Rs 54.76 crore from Rs 25.95 crore in the year-ago period.
Total income also grew to Rs 913.16 crore in the first six months of this fiscal from Rs 746.01 crore in the corresponding period of the preceding year.
Awfis has a presence in 18 cities with more than 250 coworking centres.
Amit Ramani, the company's CMD, noted that the company has reported another quarter of steady performance, supported by continued office demand from large enterprises & GCCs (Global Capability Centres)
The company continues to focus on premiumisation and operational efficiency, he said.
During the September quarter, Ramani said the company has added 6 new centres, taking the total supply to 254 centres with about 1,74,000 seats across 18 cities.
The overall portfolio occupancy stood at 76.2%, he said.

articles.title: La "zona cero" de la demografía en Europa: entre Ourense y Zamora la fertilidad está por debajo de 1 hijo por mujer
articles.text:
¿Se está quedando España sin hijos? En ‘Hijos de los hombres’, la obra maestra de Alfonso Cuarón, la humanidad lleva 18 años sin un solo nacimiento y la historia transcurre en 2027. Faltan dos meses para ese vaticinio, y siguen naciendo niños, pero un mapa de Eurostat que ha circulado estos días en redes explica por qué encaja dicha comparación: en 2024 16 regiones españolas bajaron de un hijo por mujer. ¿Causas? Decenas, pero la principal preocupación no es biológica.
Qué dicen los datos. La tasa de fertilidad de la UE fue de 1,34 hijos por mujer en 2024, la más baja desde 2001, y España cerró con 1,10, solo por encima de Malta. Dentro de España, las cuatro islas canarias tienen los valores más bajos de la UE, con La Palma en 0,76.
Si dejamos esto a un lado, Eurostat cita entre las siguientes a Ourense y Pontevedra, junto a regiones de Grecia e Italia. Los datos del INE para 2024 lo confirman: Ourense 0,88, Pontevedra 0,93, Asturias 0,95, León 0,95 y Zamora 0,96. Lugo, con 1,03, queda algo por encima. A Coruña rondaba el 1,01 en 2023. En Ourense nacen 4,15 niños por cada mil habitantes, frente a los 6,49 de la media nacional.
Qué significa un 0,88. El nivel de reemplazo está en torno a 2,10, sin hablar de inmigración. Ourense, con 0,88, está en menos de la mitad. Si esa cifra se mantuviera sin migración, cada generación de mujeres sería menos de la mitad que la anterior. El propio INE avisa de que los indicadores de poblaciones pequeñas son más inestables y este dato es un histórico, no una constante, pero apunta a una dirección.
Nada nuevo. Galicia lleva sin alcanzar el nivel de reemplazo desde 1979. Un estudio de la REIS ya la situaba en 1970 en 2,26 hijos por mujer, frente a los 2,86 de la media española. En 2002 el Instituto Galego de Estatística documentaba en Galicia 0,93 hijos por mujer, y 0,80 a Lugo y Ourense. Después llegó el boom y la inmigración, y España llegó a rozar los 1,5 en 2008. Ya lo contamos en 2019: en el primer semestre de aquel año Galicia registró 7.600 nacimientos y más de 16.000 muertes, el doble.
Maternidad tardía. Eurostat apunta como causas la mayor formación de las gestantes, donde se opta por carreras profesionales antes de tener hijos. El empleo precario y el coste de la vivienda y de criar son determinantes. Frente a los 31,9 de la UE, en 2024, la mediana de edad de las madres era de 34,7 años en A Coruña y León y de 34,5 en Pontevedra.
Ellas deciden. La fecundidad es la suma de innumerables decisiones privadas, y las encuestas apuntan a que muchas mujeres acaban teniendo menos hijos de los que querrían: según la Encuesta de Fecundidad del INE, casi tres de cada cuatro desearían tener al menos dos y, a partir de los 35, los motivos más citados para quedarse cortas son laborales, económicos o de conciliación.
Y presionar nunca es la vía. Polonia aprobó en 2020 un veto casi absoluto al aborto y en 2024 su fecundidad bajó a 1,099, un mínimo histórico, sin que pueda atribuirse solo a la ley, porque la caída viene de antes. El propio Gobierno que impulsó las ayudas “500+” admitió en 2020 que no habían elevado la fecundidad a largo plazo. En 2022, el 52 % de los polacos y el 67 % de las polacas creía que la ley hacía a la gente menos dispuesta a tener hijos. En EE.UU., un estudio de JAMA halló 22.181 nacimientos más de los esperados en los primeros 14 estados que restringieron el aborto, aunque a la vez subió la mortalidad infantil.
El efecto generación. Las nacidas en los noventa, cuando la fecundidad estaba en mínimos, son las que ahora tienen edad de ser madres, y son menos. A esto se suma que la inmigración, la cual sostiene las cifras, llega sobre todo a otros lugares: las madres nacidas en el extranjero aportaron el 33,3 % de los nacimientos en 2024. En Galicia, las extranjeras tenían 1,24 hijos por mujer y las españolas 0,96 en 2023.
Pequeño repunte. En 2025 hubo 321.164 nacimientos, un 1,0 % más, primer aumento tras años de caídas. Pero las muertes superaron a los nacimientos en 122.167 personas y el crecimiento natural fue negativo en todas las comunidades. En el primer semestre de 2026 se registraron 156.887 nacimientos, un 1,07 % más, con Galicia perdiendo nacimientos y Asturias ganándolos. El INE publicará en unos días los datos definitivos de 2025.
Progenie perdida. ‘Hijos de los hombres’ imaginaba cero nacimientos, un escenario de no retorno, pero con un 0,88 en Ourense, todavía estamos muy lejos de algo así. Entre 2014 y 2024, dos regiones del noroeste de España estuvieron entre las que tuvieron pérdidas naturales de población superiores al 10 por mil, según Eurostat.
La baja es contributiva; el cuidado, no. En España, desde julio de 2025, cada progenitor dispone de diecinueve semanas de permiso por nacimiento al 100 % de la base reguladora. El desamparo asoma después: la excedencia por cuidado de hijos, de hasta tres años, no devenga sueldo y nadie ingresa cuotas a nombre del trabajador mientras dura, aunque el tiempo se computa como cotizado.
El sistema lo remienda con 112 días de cotización ficticia por parto y hasta 270 por hijo y con un complemento de 36,90 euros mensuales por hijo, hasta un máximo de cuatro: parches modestos ante una brecha que persiste, pues la pensión media de jubilación de las mujeres es un 29,3 % inferior. Por comparar, Alemania equipara el cuidado a tiempo trabajado: cada hijo aporta hasta tres años de cotización obligatoria, con las cuotas a cargo del Estado, lo que hoy se traduce en hasta 127,56 euros más de pensión al mes por hijo. Tengamos estos datos en cuenta antes de buscar responsables.
