articles.title: North Korea Launches Missiles Toward the Sea as Pyongyang Protests Against US Claims on Binance Hack
articles.text:
North Korea launched multiple missiles toward the sea on Wednesday, South Korea’s military said, hours after Pyongyang said it saw no need to resume diplomacy with Washington in protest of accusations that North Korean hackers were behind the recent cryptocurrency heist at Binance.
Observers say North Korea was likely pressuring the U.S. to drop what it calls its hostility against the North and offer concessions if it wants to restore ties between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launches of several missiles fired toward North Korea’s eastern waters. It said South Korean and U.S. authorities were analyzing details of the launches. It said South Korea maintains readiness to repel any potential provocations by North Korea.
Earlier Wednesday, Kim’s sister, senior official Kim Yo Jong, again disputed an FBI announcement that North Korean hackers were responsible for the hack at Binance, calling it “an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward” Pyongyang.
“It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons,” she said. “The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.”
In a Tuesday statement, she described the FBI announcement as “a trite provocation.”
Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The FBI later said the theft was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year.
In recent months, North Korea has accelerated its weapons tests in a likely bid to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un. The news of the latest launches came amid vote counting in the U.S. midterm elections.
Also Wednesday, North Korea’s state KCNA news agency released a photo showing parts of a warship under construction that would likely be its biggest naval vessel. KCNA said Kim Jong Un expressed satisfaction this week during a visit to the Nampho Shipyard over the warship that it said “is incomparably huge” relative to its 5,000-ton destroyers. Kim previously said North Korea planned to build a 10,000-ton strategic guided missile cruiser.
Tensions between the two Koreas have also deepened since mine blasts at their border in September wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the border and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.
North Korea later threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.

articles.title: Anker’s new window-mounted camera monitors the outside of your home from within it
articles.text:
Anker announced a new indoor security camera that’s designed to watch your yard, driveway, or front porch through a window, instead of monitoring what’s inside your home. The new Anker Eufy Window Camera E10 takes a similar approach to the Wyze Window Cam that launched nearly a year ago. It installs right against a window using an including mounting sticker to reduce glare and reflections, but the camera doesn’t require any weatherproofing since it’s not enduring the elements outdoors.
Anker’s new window-mounted camera monitors the outside of your home from within it
The Eufy Window Cam E10 sticks directly to the inside of a window so installation takes less than a minute.
The Eufy Window Camera E10 is available now for $79.99 through Anker’s online store and Amazon, making it more than twice as expensive as the $34.98 Wyze Window Cam. But the E10 comes with a few useful upgrades. Wyze’s camera is limited to 1080p, while the E10 has a much higher maximum resolution of 2.5K, capturing more detailed 15fps videos at 2,688 x 1,520.
The E10 also offers a slightly wider and taller field of view than Wyze’s camera at 105 degrees horizontal and 57 degrees vertical. But to accommodate a wider range of installations such as an upstairs window the angle of the E10’s camera can be manually adjusted up and down by 25 degrees using a wheel on the back to ensure the areas you want monitored are properly in frame.
Other features of the E10 include color night vision, AI-powered motion detection and alerts that can differentiate between humans, animals, and vehicles, and a microphone that’s limited to louder noises given the camera’s location. Footage can be recorded locally to a microSD card up to 256GB in size, or pushed to the cloud with an optional subscription. And while Anker claims installation can take less than a minute, you will have to deal with potentially routing and hiding a power cord since the E10 lacks a rechargeable battery.

articles.title: Test de The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, et c'est toujours 10 sur 10
articles.text:
Lorsque Nintendo a officialisé ce que certains créateurs de contenu en manque de buzz ont pris bien trop de plaisir à faire fuiter, l’industrie du jeu vidéo a quelque peu tremblé. Après tant d’années à fantasmer sur une version modernisée de celui que beaucoup considéraient toujours comme le plus grand chef-d’œuvre de tous les temps, le retour de The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time sous forme d’un remake exclusif à la Nintendo Switch 2 est devenu une improbable réalité. Mais à l’heure des possibilités infinies d’une IA que personne ne maîtrise vraiment, cette firme si traditionnaliste était-elle capable d’offrir aux joueurs une expérience à la hauteur de ce que des années de projets de fans sous Unreal Engine nous ont fait espérer ? N’ayons pas peur des mots : Nintendo a fait opérer sa magie une fois de plus, dans des proportions que nous n’imaginions pas, et dont nous n’osions même pas rêver.
Points forts
- Un game design d’ensemble qui n’a finalement pas vraiment vieilli
- Les cinématiques et réorchestrations musicales sont formidables
- Ce sentiment unique de revivre un des plus grands chef-d’œuvre de tous les temps avec des moyens modernes
Points faibles
- Pas de mode difficile ni de Master Quest à débloquer
- Le choix de bouton pour courir n’est pas ergonomique du tout
- Vous voyez à quel point on en vient à inventer des défauts ?
Un remake foncièrement indispensable
Est-il vraiment nécessaire de vous faire l’affront de réexpliquer ce qu’est vraiment The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time et pourquoi son remake fait tant sens ? Bien sûr que oui : si Nintendo propose de redécouvrir son tour de force historique de 1998, ce n’est pas uniquement par simple appât du gain. La licence Zelda a certes fêté ses 40 ans cette année, et le chef-d’œuvre de la Nintendo 64 en est le troisième volet le plus vendu derrière les deux mastodontes de la Nintendo Switch, mais le remettre au goût du jour fait plus que sens, notamment à l’approche de la sortie en salles du premier film live-action autour de son univers, dans un peu moins de six mois.
Même s’il a connu une première révision salvatrice en 2011 pour accompagner la sortie de la Nintendo 3DS et célébrer le quart de siècle de la franchise, Ocarina of Time est une œuvre vieillissante et difficile à apprécier pour les novices sur des supports officiels, surtout pour celles et ceux qui ont découvert la licence avec Breath of the Wild ou Tears of the Kingdom, et leur approche d’ensemble résolument plus moderne.
En effet, on rappellera que la boucle de gameplay de ce qui fut le premier opus Zelda en trois dimensions souffre presque d’une trop grande absence de prise de risques, tant il reprenait à sa sauce la structure du légendaire A Link to the Past, paru en 1991 sur Super Nintendo. Grossièrement, Link se réveille et se sent confier bien malgré lui la destinée du royaume d’Hyrule, réunit trois artefacts légendaires en complétant autant de donjons labyrinthiques dont il terrasse les gardiens, avant de comprendre que sa véritable aventure commence en retirant de son socle une épée légendaire.
À partir de là débute une exploration plus complète d’un monde qui s’ouvre de plus en plus au gré des objets acquis (entre autres) dans les donjons, l’objectif étant de se mesurer au fléau menaçant Hyrule (l’abominable Ganon) au terme d’un ultime combat épique, délivrant au passage la princesse Zelda. Une structure efficace, au rythme brillant et aux mécanismes de progression ingénieux, qui plus est magnifiés par la science du level design du jeune Eiji Aonuma, concepteur à l’époque des donjons et devenu depuis producteur de la saga. Oui, sauf que cette formule, il n’en veut plus aujourd’hui pour les futurs Zelda, et il nous a bien fait comprendre à de multiples reprises qu’elle appartenait au passé…
En outre, si le « game changer » dirigé par Shigeru Miyamoto et Eiji Aonuma en 1998 jouira éternellement d’un statut indiscutable à ce sujet, tant il a révolutionné le jeu vidéo d’action-aventure en trois dimensions, seuls les plus grands nostalgiques prennent encore du plaisir à y rejouer en version originale. N’ayons pas peur des mots : comme quasiment tous les grands jeux de son époque, où cette 3D naissante était encore mal maîtrisée et où stabiliser un framerate à 30 images par seconde relevait de l’authentique exploit, la version originale d’Ocarina of Time est horrible à jouer en 2026. Lorsque son vrai-faux rival de l’époque, Final Fantasy Ⅶ (1997) se vit offrir un remake ultra ambitieux à destination de la PlayStation 4 en 2020, nous avions été très nombreux à rêver de voir Nintendo faire enfin preuve d’ambition. Il était temps d’exploiter sa console du moment pour offrir à son joyau maison mieux qu’un simple lifting HD d’une version 3DS acceptable, mais elle aussi déjà d’un autre âge. Le problème ? Nintendo étant Nintendo, il ne le ferait sans doute pas. Probablement même jamais.
Des ambitions à la hauteur de l’œuvre
Seulement voilà : contre toute attente, Nintendo l’a fait, et il a fallu attendre la puissance d’une machine comme la Switch 2 pour sublimer Ocarina of Time à sa juste valeur, et concrétiser des espoirs que personne n’osait avoir. Parce que oui, vous l’avez très probablement vite compris en voyant les différentes bandes-annonces et les innombrables visuels diffusés par l’éditeur depuis l’officialisation : l’éditeur japonais a mis les petits plats dans les grands pour sublimer le joyau de sa couronne. Là où tant de ses classiques n’ont eu droit qu’à un joli lissage et à une amélioration de la résolution et des performances, Ocarina of Time n’est pas un jeu comme les autres, et ça, son créateur en est heureusement pleinement conscient. L’expérience nous avait laissé croire que les développeurs n’en avaient rien à faire, et nous nous sommes trompés à leur sujet, une fois de plus.
Ainsi, nous faisons véritablement face à la première production 100 % interne de Nintendo donnant l’impression que le constructeur est enfin entré dans une nouvelle génération de machines. Le remake d’Ocarina of Time est assurément un jeu que la première Switch n’aurait jamais été fichue de faire tourner convenablement, ou alors peut-être en 30 images par seconde, et sans cette finesse graphique à laquelle la firme kyotoïte ne nous avait pas habitués. Cela pourrait presque sonner comme une insulte aux yeux des puristes, mais celles et ceux qui rêvaient de voir un traitement visuel « à la PlayStation » combiné à la science innée du gameplay de Nintendo seront aux anges : Ocarina of Time est le jeu vidéo le plus impressionnant visuellement que le constructeur japonais ait jamais conçu. Nous n’allons pas (trop) nous étendre en longueurs sur ce point : le remake d’Ocarina of Time est incroyablement beau et soigné, dans des proportions que nous ne soupçonnions aucunement chez son créateur.
Le souci du détail d’ensemble, les animations de Link (et des ennemis) et les effets de lumière sont proprement ahurissants, qu’il s’agisse de décors extérieurs ou intérieurs, à tel point que ce qui était terrifiant sur Ninteno 64 l’est toujours autant 28 ans plus tard. Le rendu d’ensemble était si saisissant que l’on avait redouté initialement la première utilisation enfin efficace de l’Unreal Engine 5 sur une console qui semble mal à l’aise avec, ou a minima celle d’un DLSS embarqué dans sa nouvelle génération de machine hybride. Rien de tout cela : Nintendo a choisi de polir le plus beau de ses diamants sur un moteur maison, et a opté pour le FSR d’AMD pour gérer l’upscale et l’anti-aliasing.
Il en résulte un jeu sublime, presque trop réaliste pour les fans les plus hardcore qui ne veulent pas voir Nintendo « faire du PlayStation », à tel point que la finesse de réalisation des bâtiments, notamment dans le Temple de la Forêt, rappelle un peu le niveau de finition incroyablement immersif que permet le RE Engine de Capcom sur les derniers Resident Evil. Osons donc le dire : sur le plan purement graphique, ce remake est indiscutablement le plus beau jeu vidéo de l’histoire de Nintendo. Et on n’a pas encore parlé des cinématiques.
Une performance à l’épreuve du temps
Toutefois, comme Ocarina of Time est basé sur un game design d’ensemble très ancré dans des standards de 1998, il y avait toutes les raisons du monde de craindre que même en opérant un lifting graphique désarmant de beauté (et foncièrement inhabituel connaissant les habitudes de Nintendo), son aspect un peu désuet gâche vite le feeling manette en mains. C’est ici que réside en vérité l’exploit le plus retentissant de ce remake, et qui le fait passer d’un travail de retouche visuel phénoménal (que tout le monde n’aimera peut-être pas mais qu’il faut saluer) à une prouesse de modernisation hors normes. Nous en étions quasiment convaincus mais il fallait y jouer pour le comprendre : si Nintendo ose enfin un véritable remake ambitieux, c’est qu’il sait ce qu’il fait, et nous devons lui faire confiance.
N’y allons pas par quatre chemins : désireux de profiter pour la troisième fois (après les versions N64 et 3DS) de tout ce dont est capable de proposer son univers si enchanteur, nous avons passé une trentaine d’heures à nous émouvoir de ce dont nous ne saurions pas permis de rêver, à savoir que Ocarina of Time est toujours un jeu vidéo incroyable à parcourir près de trente ans après, tant l’intelligence de son game design est stratosphérique. Il y a ainsi fort à parier qu’en plus de celles et ceux qui le redécouvriront avec passion, nombreux seront les nouveaux joueurs qui ne le trouveront aucunement daté et, oui nous osons l’affirmer, déploreront l’absence de titres usant de ce type de structure dans le catalogue contemporain de Nintendo (et, plus largement de l’ensemble de l’industrie). C’est d’ailleurs très probablement l’un de ses objectifs premiers : rassembler plusieurs générations de joueuses et de joueurs autour d’un titre dont cela est finalement, d’une certaine manière, le cœur du propos.
Il a en effet fallu quelques minutes aux commandes de Link évoluant au sein de la forêt Kokiri, en quête de l’épée et du bouclier l’autorisant à rencontrer l’Arbre Mojo, pour comprendre que Nintendo était intégralement en charge de la réalisation de ce remake en interne. Chaque séquence de gameplay jouit d’un niveau de précision redoutable, porté par les améliorations de confort évidentes d’un jeu de 2026 (bouton de saut, gestion manuelle de la caméra à 360°, mapping des touches modernes… sauf peut-être pour courir) qui donnent l’impression d’évoluer dans l’univers magique du classique de 1998 avec la fluidité de gameplay d’un Breath of the Wild, voire d’un Super Mario Odyssey (les 60 images par seconde, littéralement jamais prises à défaut, offrant une fluidité d’action particulièrement plaisante).
On en rêvait, Nintendo l’a fait : Ocarina of Time est divin à jouer, davantage que dans nos plus beaux fantasmes d’adolescent ou d’enfant, et surtout meilleur que n’importe quel projet de fan semblant limite trop beau par rapport aux ambitions habituellement affichées par la marque. On aimerait se perdre en explications pour vous le faire comprendre mais honnêtement, on ne saura que trop vous recommander d’y succomber à votre tour pour réaliser le plaisir intense que procure cette nouvelle expérience.
Oui, c’est le même jeu, et alors ?
Cependant, et c’est peut-être cela qui lui sera le plus reproché en fin de compte (mais pas par nous) : ce remake est Ocarina of Time et n’a aucune intention d’en offrir beaucoup plus ni de chambouler quoi que ce soit. Le jeu a bien été recréé à l’échelle 1:1 l’essentiel du temps, rajoutant quand même quelques coffres qui n’existaient pas en 1998, décalant certains murs, agrandissant des espaces précis, ou rallongeant un petit peu certaines séquences pour leur donner un peu plus de profondeur. Du coup, c’est le même jeu ou presque : seuls les plus grands puristes verront les différences. Si vous connaissez l’œuvre originale par cœur, rien ne vous surprendra si ce n’est la qualité époustouflante de sa réalisation, et surtout de sa mise en scène dans les cinématiques. Le jeu est par ailleurs intégralement doublé en français (et oui, des références habituelles sont au rendez-vous), et la VF est particulièrement soignée. Mention spéciale à Navi qui n’est plus aussi envahissante, mais constitue enfin une compagnie appréciable.
Quant à la bande son… ne nous lancez pas dessus, sinon on est parti pour trois paragraphes de plus. Sachez juste que, comme en 1998 là encore, chaque composition est phénoménale, allant de la réorchestration fidèle et efficace à la tentative audacieuse et maîtrisée d’offrir une touche ambiante et évolutive (notamment à travers les thèmes nocturnes assez formidables) à des classiques que l’on pensait intouchables. Un constat qui résume assez bien l’expérience de ce remake artistiquement audacieux, d’une maîtrise d’ensemble sans faille, et auquel rien ne manque si ce n’est peut-être l’ajout d’un mode difficile (le jeu reste très simple) ou d’une Master Quest à débloquer. Une absence modérément déplorable néanmoins, tant son ajout faisait davantage sens à l’époque. Et honnêtement, si c’est le prix à payer pour que Nintendo offre le même privilège à Majora’s Mask dans le futur, qu’il en soit ainsi. On en viendrait presque à signer pour également voir Super Mario 64 recréé de la sorte.
En fin de compte, le fait que Ocarina of Time n’ait quasiment pas changé, et que Nintendo se soit « contenté » de le conformiser à l’exigence du cahier des charges d’un jeu vidéo de 2026, n’est jamais un problème. On en vient même à trouver l’Amphithéâtre des monstres (nouvelle zone exclusive où l’on peut affronter à nouveau tous les ennemis et boss déjà abattus), seule véritable nouveauté en termes de contenu, anecdotique sans être de trop.
L’équilibrage d’ensemble de l’expérience de ce chef-d’œuvre, qui sait moderniser sa maniabilité sans jamais trahir ses fondamentaux, donne l’impression d’un vrai nouveau jeu terriblement satisfaisant, envoûtant et émouvant. Surtout, ce remake constitue l’un des plus beaux exploits de l’histoire d’une entité réputée pour sa frilosité et son incapacité à capitaliser avec aisance sur la montagne d’or qu’elle a constituée en cumulant les best-sellers et merveilles de cet acabit. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time était un des plus grands jeux vidéo de tous les temps ; sa version 2026 est assurément un des plus grands remakes de jeux vidéo de tous les temps.
Le verdict
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
Voir la fiche
On a aimé
- Un game design d’ensemble qui n’a finalement pas vraiment vieilli
- Les cinématiques et réorchestrations musicales sont formidables
- Ce sentiment unique de revivre un des plus grands chef-d’œuvre de tous les temps avec des moyens modernes
On a moins aimé
- Pas de mode difficile ni de Master Quest à débloquer
- Le choix de bouton pour courir n’est pas ergonomique du tout
- Vous voyez à quel point on en vient à inventer des défauts ?

articles.title: La récente Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 s'allège déjà de 140 € grâce au Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
C’est cet été, lors de son traditionnel Galaxy Unpacked, que Samsung a levé le voile sur sa nouvelle gamme de montres connectées. Outre la Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, le géant sud-coréen a présenté sa Galaxy Watch 9, une tocante qui s’inscrit certes dans la continuité de la Galaxy Watch 8, mais qui profite tout de même de plusieurs améliorations. Si elle vous intéresse, sachez qu’en ce pré-Black Friday, il est possible de trouver la version 40 mm affichée à moins de 270 euros.
Ce qu’il faut savoir sur la Samsung Galaxy Watch 9
- Un design toujours aussi confortable
- Un écran lumineux
- Un excellent suivi cardio et GPS
Lancée à 409 euros, la Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 (40 mm, Bluetooth) est aujourd’hui disponible en promotion à 269 euros chez PC Componentes.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant la Samsung Galaxy Watch 9. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Une montre confortable avec une excellente dalle
En matière de design, Samsung n’a visiblement pas voulu bouleverser une recette qui fonctionne. Pour sa nouvelle Galaxy Watch 9, la marque a donc repris le boîtier « carrondi » en aluminium de sa Galaxy Watch 8. Les deux montres connectées affichent le même format, mais la Galaxy Watch 9 est un poil plus lourde que sa prédécesseure, une augmentation qui s’explique sans doute par l’intégration d’une nouvelle batterie. Dans l’ensemble, la Galaxy Watch 9 reste très confortable et se fait même oublier au quotidien, grâce à sa finesse de 8,6 mm. Et elle reste solidement fixée au poignet lors des entraînements.
La Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 est aussi une montre très robuste, avec son écran protégé par un verre saphir et ses certifications IP68, 5 ATM et MIL-STD810H. En d’autres termes, elle ne craint pas l’eau de la douche et peut être portée durant les séances de natation. Mais attention, elle n’a pas été conçue pour la plongée sous-marine. Côté écran, Samsung n’a pas changé sa formule et a misé une nouvelle fois sur une dalle Amoled de 1,34 pouce et de 438 x 438 pixels (327 pixels par pouce) pour cette version de 40 mm. Et tout comme la Galaxy Watch 8, cette Galaxy Watch 9 atteint les 3 000 cd/m² en pic de luminosité.
La Galaxy Watch 9 reprend le même OS et la même interface logicielle que la Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, donc Wear OS 7 et One UI 9 Watch. Retenez que pour configurer la montre et l’appairer à votre smartphone, vous devrez télécharger Galaxy Wearable et Samsung Health. À l’image de la Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, la tocante embarque une puce Snapdragon Wear Elite, et non Exynos. En bref, la montre séduit par la fluidité de son interface, par la richesse de son catalogue d’applications et par ses contrôles gestuels. L’assistant Gemini peut de son côté être invoqué d’un simple lever de poignet.
Des mesures précises au quotidien
Comme toute bonne montre connectée, la Galaxy Watch 9 embarque différents capteurs : un accéléromètre, un baromètre, un capteur d’analyse d’impédance bioélectrique, un électrocardiogramme, un gyroscope, une boussole, un capteur de température, un tensiomètre, un cardiofréquencemètre, un oxymètre de pouls et une puce compatible avec plusieurs constellations GNSS : GPS, Glonass, Beidou, Galileo et QZSS. On profite en outre d’une connectivité GPS double-fréquence, qui assure une meilleure précision.
La montre propose en outre un excellent suivi de la fréquence cardiaque. On aurait toutefois aimé pouvoir connecter nativement un capteur cardio externe. Notez aussi que pour profiter de l’électrocardiogramme et du tensiomètre, vous devrez obligatoirement posséder un smartphone Samsung. Par ailleurs, la montre bénéficie, comme la Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, des nouveaux indicateurs de vitalité, de charge cardio, d’indice fitness ou de score de cœur. La détection avancée de l’apnée du sommeil, encore indisponible en Europe, pourrait également arriver dans un futur proche. Côté sport, notez que la Galaxy Watch 9 est privée de cartographie, ce qui est franchement dommage.
Enfin, lors de notre test, la montre a peiné à dépasser les 39 heures dans sa version de 44 mm. Attendez-vous donc à devoir recharger la Galaxy Watch 9 tous les jours. Et la charge magnétique est vraiment lente avec près de 2h30 pour un plein complet.
Pour en savoir encore plus, n’hésitez pas à lire notre test complet de la Samsung Galaxy Watch 9.

articles.title: Leipzig-based JawBuddy raises €818k to help people reduce jaw pain, bruxism, and TMJ-related tension | EU-Startups
articles.text:
JawBuddy, a Leipzig-based HealthTech startup that helps people reduce jaw pain, bruxism, and TMJ-related tension, has raised €818k in a pre-Seed round led by healthcare platform HALBZEIT.
The round was also backed by Dr. Siegfried Marquardt, a specialist in aesthetic and functional dentistry and implantology, and oral and maxillofacial surgeon Dr. Guido Sigron. Mittelständische Beteiligungsgesellschaft Sachsen (MBG) and business angels Christophe Barriolade, Aldrich Huang, Jens Kosche, and Marc Scheidegger also participated. The total funding also includes the Business Angel Bonus from Sächsische Aufbaubank.
“I suffered from jaw pain myself for years and saw how little you can do between two dental appointments. That is exactly the gap we close. With this funding, we are now starting the clinical trial and taking the next step towards reimbursement,” said Leon Rauch, co-founder and CEO of JawBuddy.
Founded in 2025 by Leon Rauch, Moritz Scherer and Benjamín Cádiz de Gracia and based at SpinLab in Leipzig, JawBuddy is a clinically backed digital health startup that helps people reduce jaw pain, bruxism, and TMJ-related tension through guided physiotherapist-designed routines.
The company states that it guides patients through a personalised self-therapy programme at home and measures progress via the smartphone camera. The app also supports people with bruxism, the unconscious grinding or clenching of teeth.
It claims to combine medical expertise, personalised insights, and simple daily exercises to help users understand the root causes of their jaw pain and achieve long-lasting relief.
The company highlighted that all exercises are evidence-based, created by Scherer, a physiotherapist and M.Sc. and PhD candidate in Health Technologies, and Dr. Christian Wolf, a practising oral and maxillofacial surgeon at Kantonsspital Aarau. The content combines clinical expertise with the latest research in jaw disorders.
JawBuddy says it uses clients’ assessments, daily feedback, and symptoms to continuously adapt their exercise plan. The more the app is used, the better it understands what works for the users. It also generates exportable medical reports that users can share with their dentist, doctor, or physiotherapist to support treatment.
The app is registered as a Class I medical device under the EU MDR and complements dental care. The German startup reported that clinical pilot projects are running at five sites, including University Hospital RWTH Aachen.
“We invest where a large, underserved market, a clear clinical need and a reimbursable model come together. JawBuddy brings all of that, and it tackles a problem every dental practice knows: patients with jaw problems who keep coming back,” said Luisa Wasilewski, Pool Captain at HALBZEIT.
JawBuddy is also negotiating a care contract with a major statutory health insurer, due to start in early 2027. A multicentre randomised controlled trial (RCT) with 130 patients also starts in December 2026. The company plans to use this capital to fund its own efficacy study and reimbursement by health insurers.

articles.title: AMD Q3 2026 Earnings Data Center Growth Drives Record Quarter
articles.text:
AMD posted a massive Q3 2026. Revenue hit $13.377 billion, up 45% year over year and 16% sequentially. Data Center revenue reached $8.546 billion, up 97% year over year. Embedded Revenue was up big, and client revenue fared better than Intel in many respects.
AMD Has Record Quarter Driven By Data Center
Here is AMD’s Q3 2026 summary slide. This is an enormous quarter. Embedded revenue was up 29% year over year, and yet that almost feels like a footnote.
AMD delivered GAAP operating income of $2.832 billion on revenue of $13.377 billion, with net income of $2.428 billion and diluted earnings per share of $1.46. On a non-GAAP basis, which excludes stock-based compensation, amortization of acquisition-related intangibles and other items, operating income was $3.923 billion, net income was $3.471 billion and EPS came in at $2.09.
Even the quarterly numbers were up a lot, with 16% growth on the GAAP side.
AMD’s Data Center Is Big Time
The Data Center segment generated $8.546 billion in revenue, up 97% year over year and 27% sequentially. AMD attributes this Data Center surge to strong EPYC demand and the launch of Instinct MI450 GPUs. The company says major clients, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, are running workloads on Helios rack-scale solutions powered by these chips.
The comparison to Intel’s data center results from last week saw its quarterly revenue of $7.3 billion, up 78% year-over-year. AMD’s Data Center segment at $8.546 billion grew faster at 97%. Both companies are clearly seeing surging demand for AI infrastructure and server processors, but AMD seems to be accelerating.
Venice is coming, and we expect AMD to have clear x86 performance leadership, as Intel’s PCIe Gen6 Diamond Rapids platform, we expect, will be later in 2027. On technical merits, we expect AMD to be in a great place, and it seems like AMD is better managing its supply to get chips out.
AMD Client and Gaming Segment
The combined Client and Gaming segment saw revenue down 8% year-over-year, at $3.722 billion. Client notched up a bit, while gaming went down. Memory and NAND prices are keeping a lid on this market.
Of note, AMD said its Ryzen AI Halo Platform with the Ryzen AI Max Pro 400 series is not available, so that means Gorgon Halo? We will have our first Gorgon Halo review soon, as that machine is running benchmarks now. Somewhat notable on the slide is that AMD has three AI-related products highlighted, while Intel’s three summary bullets on its CCPG segment were focused on shortages, demand for future products, and a generic AI PC nod. AMD, with the Strix Halo platform, at least has something it can use to run reasonably large models locally, and you have to wonder if that is a driver here.
AMD’s Embedded Grows
The Embedded segment delivered $1.109 billion in revenue, up 29% year-over-year. AMD says growth came from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications and industrial end markets.
Just as a frame of reference, Xilinx’s annual revenue was something like $3.1-3.2B when AMD completed its acquisition of Xilinx. In most markets, if you grow 29% year over year and see a huge margin increase, it is time to throw a party. This seems to simply offset client’s (gaming) weakness.
AMD Q4 Guidance Points To Acceleration
AMD expects fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of approximately $17 billion plus or minus 3%. At the midpoint, that represents year-over-year growth of about 66% and sequential growth of roughly 27%.
If this quarter seems big, then next quarter seems like it will be significantly bigger.
Final Words
AMD has its Helios rack-scale infrastructure rolling out, and Venice. Ryan recently went into the Venice architecture. If AMD was ahead in many metrics with its Turin generation, then adding more cores, updated cores, and higher memory bandwidth should be a recipe for clear x86 socket leadership, at least until Intel is able to field Diamond Rapids. It will be interesting to see how much of a price premium AMD can extract for a generational advantage and first-mover status. Socket refresh generations are less exciting than the Turin-to-Venice transition, which is a major platform update (DDR5 channel count and PCIe Gen6). That also means PCIe Gen6 development, like PCIe Gen4, will likely happen more often on AMD than on Intel. Gluing chips together seems to be working out reasonably well.

articles.title: Plus rien de ce que vous voyez en direct ne sera sûr : Microsoft veut breveter une IA qui change les mots dans la bouche des gens
articles.text:
Même les vidéos en direct pourront mentir : Microsoft va breveter une IA qui réécrit les paroles et les lèvres en temps réel
Vous regardez une conférence, une remise de prix ou un match en direct. L'orateur parle, ses lèvres bougent, sa voix sonne juste. Rien ne vous permet de savoir que certaines phrases ont été retouchées, voire réécrites, une fraction de seconde avant d'arriver sur votre écran. Microsoft vient de décrire cette machine noir sur blanc, dans un document officiel.
Microsoft Technology Licensing, la filiale qui gère la propriété intellectuelle du groupe, a déposé une demande de brevet au titre aussi technique que vertigineux : une "amélioration par intelligence artificielle, en quasi temps réel, de vidéos ou de présentations en réalité augmentée d'événements en direct".
Repéré par le service de veille Patentlyze, le document décrit des agents IA capables d'écouter un discours pendant qu'il est prononcé, de repérer certains mots, de les supprimer ou de les remplacer. L'IA retouche ensuite le visage et la bouche de l'orateur pour que l'image colle au nouveau son. Microsoft n'a pas commenté.
Une IA qui réécrit les discours selon le profil du spectateur
Le système s'appuie sur des paramètres définis à l'avance et sur le profil de chaque spectateur. Il retouche l'audio et la vidéo juste avant et juste après chaque mot modifié, pour gommer toute coupure visible. Les mots de remplacement pourraient même provenir d'une recherche sur Internet, selon l'analyse publiée par Futurism. Google a déjà montré jusqu'où va la retouche : en mai, une démonstration de Gemini Omni modifiait une vidéo réelle sans que personne ne voie la différence. Microsoft ajoute le direct.
Le brevet vise large : conférences, présentations, cérémonies de remise de prix, jeux télévisés, émissions culinaires et retransmissions sportives. Il évoque des usages séduisants, comme une traduction instantanée qui ferait parler l'orateur dans la langue du spectateur, avec les lèvres synchronisées. Le procédé existe déjà en différé : Prime Video mise sur l'IA pour caler la bouche des acteurs sur leur doublage. Le brevet prévoit aussi la suppression des "euh", des bégaiements et des expressions régionales. La liste des mots à effacer va beaucoup plus loin.
	
Mots marmonnés, mal prononcés, mal employés, lapsus, mots offensants, insensibles ou inappropriés.
Chaque spectateur pourrait ainsi recevoir sa propre version d'un même direct, expurgée de ce qu'il ne souhaite pas entendre.
La brique technique existe déjà dans les laboratoires du groupe. En avril 2024, Microsoft Research Asia a présenté VASA-1, un modèle capable d'animer un visage réaliste à partir d'une seule photo et d'un enregistrement de voix. Les lèvres suivent le son au millimètre, la tête bouge naturellement, et le tout tourne en temps réel, jusqu'à 40 images par seconde selon la publication de ses chercheurs. Microsoft avait alors renoncé à le rendre public.
Deepfake en direct : la parade prévue par Microsoft et la loi européenne
Microsoft semble avoir mesuré le risque. Le document prévoit que la vidéo et le son originaux puissent être enregistrés et conservés comme "vérité de référence", pour retrouver ce qui a réellement été dit. Il ne précise pas qui pourrait consulter cet enregistrement, ni comment.
Une demande de brevet reste une intention : les géants de la tech en déposent des milliers chaque année, et beaucoup ne deviennent jamais des produits. En Europe, un tel outil se heurterait de toute façon au règlement européen sur l'intelligence artificielle. Depuis le 2 août 2026, son article 50 oblige ceux qui diffusent un hypertrucage, une vidéo dont les paroles ou le visage ont été manipulés par l'IA, à le signaler au public.
Côté détection, les outils restent partiels. Google permet de vérifier si une vidéo sort de ses propres modèles grâce à son filigrane SynthID, sans rien pouvoir dire des contenus produits ailleurs. Quant aux réflexes qui permettent de repérer un deepfake, ils supposent d'avoir le temps d'observer la vidéo. Face à une retouche invisible glissée au milieu d'un direct, le spectateur n'a ni ce temps, ni l'original sous les yeux.
Suivez toute l'actualité des Numériques sur Google Actualités et sur la chaîne WhatsApp des Numériques

articles.title: Meta Shares Top Muse Bug Bounty Findings as Payouts Reach $1.2 Million
articles.text:
Meta has paid roughly $1.2 million in bug bounties for its Muse AI agent, including $300,000 for a pre-launch flaw that exposed data on internal test systems.
Muse is a personal AI agent that acts on a user’s behalf across their email, calendar, messaging and other accounts. Each user’s agent gets its own virtual machine.
The bug bounty program ran privately from April and went public at the agent’s September 8 launch, Meta’s David Singleton said in a blog post. Of the more than 630 reports received, 64 were valid.
The $300,000 reward was handed out four months before launch, while Muse was at an early internal testing stage. The researcher demonstrated access to conversations and tokens on pre-release VMs used by Meta staff to test the product.
“An authentication check treated a header added by a local HTTPS proxy as proof that a request came from a trusted source. During a system migration, the environment gained a second proxy layer. That meant requests from outside could carry the trusted header too,” Singleton explained.
Meta took the service offline, fixed the bug and stopped treating the local machine as trusted.
A $90,000 bounty was paid for a report involving a malicious web page that, when Muse was asked to summarize it, mimicked status messages from the agent’s browsing tool. “It got the agent to execute some actions which should have been caught,” Singleton noted.
Meta has since added detection signals and changed how Muse treats tool output that looks suspicious. It says that, in testing, its classifiers now catch the attack and 100 variants.
Another $90,000 went to a report showing that specific formatting could slip one-time passcodes past Muse’s email redaction filters. Meta described it as one piece of an end-to-end attack.
A $50,000 reward went to an Android app flaw that let a malicious app pass a link to a privileged web view. “The link handler recognized a shared-page path without validating its host and loaded it,” Singleton wrote, allowing an attacker’s page to grab the web view’s credentials.
A $1,000 bounty covered a Mac app flaw that let an attacker with access to the computer hijack the auto-update feature to execute code with the app’s permissions.
Meta pays up to $300,000 per valid report, which it claims is several times more than the top rewards advertised by other leading AI developers. Prompt injection attacks affecting a single user can earn up to $130,000, while a fleetwide compromise can earn as much as $250,000.
Related: Google Introduces $250,000 Root-in-Cloud Bug Bounty Reward
Related: Google Partially Reverses Chrome Bug Bounty Cuts
Related: Microsoft Bug Bounty Program: $20 Million Paid to 500 Researchers

articles.title: EloElo Group raises $80M in Series C led by Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal
articles.text:
EloElo Group raises $80M in Series C led by Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal
EloElo Group will use the funds to launch original content across local languages, expand into international markets and develop AI platforms.
EloElo Group, a consumer AI and entertainment company that operates micro-drama platform Story TV, has raised $80 million in a Series C round of funding led by Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal.
This funding round also saw participation from MIT Investment Co. and existing investors Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures, Griffin Gaming Partners and others.
The funding was done at a valuation of $500 million, which is almost a 5X jump from its previous fundraise in April 2025, sources indicated. The new round brings EloElo Group’s total capital raised to $130 million to date.
Bengaluru-headquartered EloElo Group was founded in 2020 by former Flipkart executive Saurabh Pandey and it will use this latest fund raise to fund original content across local languages, launch its micro dramas internationally, and continue investments in Dolphin AI, its proprietary agentic platform.
In an interaction with YourStory, EloElo Group Founder & CEO Saurabh Pandey said, “This funding will expand on our vision and usher in a new era of sorts of mobile entertainment. This entertainment in the form of storytelling has never been solved for the mobile phone.”
Story TV has over 5,000 micro dramas in six languages, a new drama launched every three hours and 95 minutes of time spent per user every day. The group also runs Master (micro learning), Dolphin AI (its agentic AI creative suite) and Voxy AI (an AI companion agent).
Across its apps, EloElo Group has over 40 million monthly active users.
“Story TV shows us what India wants to watch, and Dolphin AI gives us the economics to make it, which is how we have scaled with solid unit economics. Consumer AI will change how content is created, distributed and consumed, and we intend to lead that shift from India,” Pandey remarked.
According to the founder, EloElo Group's key strength has been its ownership across all three layers of mobile entertainment: creating content, distributing content and imbibing AI into the whole process.
This fundraise also gives EloElo Group the ability to go deeper into various languages through a combination of live action shows, hybrid shows with AI, and pure AI shows. These will be original content.
On the investment, Manoj Thakur, Founder and Managing Partner of Hornbill Capital said, “EloElo Group combines strong creative capabilities with the ability to scale content through technology, which is something we deeply believe in. The team’s execution, financial discipline, and AI capabilities position it well for its next phase of growth.”
Micro dramas are among the fastest-growing formats in global entertainment. According to Omdia, the industry will generate $14 billion globally by the end of 2026. In India, Redseer estimates that 40 million people paid for a microdrama at least once in FY26, and Lumikai’s State of India Interactive Media Report projects the market will reach $4.5 billion by 2030.

articles.title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity.
When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer.
Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories.
In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it.
The problem: Too many systems, too much friction
U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud.
Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration.
The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars.
- Reach: agents that coordinate across backend systems in real time.
- Depth: chain-of-thought reasoning for multi-step root cause analysis.
- Community: a secure multi-tenant framework with role-based access control and built-in guardrails, available to every division.
The journey: From knowledge base to agentic platform
AiDaH started with a principle: think big, start small. U Mobile began conceptualization in late 2025 with two pilot agents and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability. A Q1 2026 pilot brought the internal IT helpdesk online with 4 agents and 20 operational scenarios. Through 2026 the platform hardened and expanded, adding three-tier routing and reaching 6 agents by mid-year. AiDaH went live to 50 L2 call center and branch users in Q3 2026 with 8 agents, and now covers more than 150 documented operational scenarios.
What agentic means in practice
The difference between traditional AI assistance and agentic AI is best illustrated through a real example.
With a traditional AI assistant, a support agent handling “mobile data not working overseas” gets help drafting a response and some suggested troubleshooting steps, but still manually checks roaming status, verifies eligibility, raises tickets, and sends the final reply.
With AiDaH, the system independently checks the subscriber’s roaming configuration, verifies international data eligibility, and identifies the specific point of failure. It then assembles a remediation plan: which services to reset, what configuration to push, and whether a network ticket is warranted. The support agent reviews and confirms, and the actions execute. The investigation that used to consume the agent’s time now happens before they read the first line. The human decision point is preserved where it matters: at the moment something changes on a live subscriber account.
In one production case, a subscriber reported being unable to purchase an add-on. AiDaH traced the failure to an error code, “Subscriber has pending order.” It also revealed that the customer had attempted the same purchase more than 30 times across multiple channels over three days, every attempt blocked by the same underlying pending order. AiDaH surfaced the root cause and the remediation steps in a single response. Previously that would have required manual investigation across several systems.
Architecture: Six layers, one interface
AiDaH runs on a layered architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, deployed in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region. Staff interact through Microsoft Teams, a deliberate choice to meet most users where they already work, with no new application to learn and no portal switching.
The following diagram shows how the layers fit together.
As shown in Figure 1, the platform is organized into six layers.
Layer 1: Staff interface
Staff reach AiDaH through Microsoft Teams and a web portal served by Amazon CloudFront and protected by AWS WAF, with an AWS Lambda backend and a REST API for programmatic triggers.
Layer 2: Orchestration
The routing brain on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Every request passes a pre-flight security check covering role-based access control, identity validation, and guardrails, then enters a cost-optimized routing tier. Roughly 70 percent of requests resolve through deterministic keyword matching with no model invocation, 20 percent are classified by a lightweight model, and only 10 percent require the full orchestrator. The cheapest path that can confidently handle the request is the one that runs.
Layer 3: Specialist agents
Eight experts spanning customer relationship management, customer problem management, number portability, order and SIM operations, infrastructure monitoring, big data analytics, cloud cost management, and finance operations. They communicate over the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, which lets them delegate subtasks and complete cross-system workflows no single agent could handle alone.
Layer 4: Gateways and backend APIs
AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes U Mobile’s backends to agents through a unified Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Behind each gateway sit AWS Lambda functions and MCP servers that translate agent intent into calls against a specific system.
Layer 5: Data and knowledge
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed RAG capability, grounds agent responses in governed content, using an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store. Content spans a shared enterprise knowledge base and a separate finance corpus. AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, maintains conversational context across turns, and Amazon DynamoDB holds the six-tier role-based access control model and session metadata.
Layer 6: Operational systems
U Mobile’s on-premises and cloud operational systems are reached over AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Site-to-Site VPN, an IPsec-encrypted tunnel with no public internet exposure.
How a request flows through the layers
Tracing a single request makes the interaction between the layers concrete. Consider a support agent who types a port-in status question into the AiDaH channel in Microsoft Teams.
- Interface: The Teams message reaches an AWS Lambda function, which forwards the request and the caller’s federated identity to the orchestrator.
- Pre-flight check: The orchestrator resolves the caller against the six-tier role-based access control model held in Amazon DynamoDB, validates the token issued by AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to the incoming prompt. A request that fails any of these checks stops here.
- Routing: The orchestrator selects the cheapest tier that can handle the request. A recognized phrase such as “port-in status” matches deterministically and skips model invocation entirely. An ambiguous phrasing goes to the lightweight classifier. A novel or multi-part question goes to the full orchestrator.
- Agent instantiation: The selected specialist agent runs as a session in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore memory rehydrates the conversation so the agent inherits the subscriber number and any prior findings from earlier turns, instead of asking the user to repeat them.
- Tool discovery and invocation: The agent queries AgentCore Gateway for the tools it is entitled to use. Each gateway publishes its backend as MCP tools with typed inputs and outputs, so the agent picks a tool by name and schema rather than by hand-coded integration logic. Amazon Cognito brokers the OAuth authorization for the call.
- Backend call: The gateway’s Lambda function or MCP server translates the tool call into a request against the target system, traversing AWS Transit Gateway and the Site-to-Site VPN tunnel to reach the on-premises number portability platform. Sensitive fields are masked on the way back, before the response reaches the model.
- Reasoning and collaboration: If the answer spans domains, the agent delegates over the Agent2Agent protocol. A port-in query that turns out to be a billing block, for example, hands off to the business support systems agent, and the results are merged into one narrative.
- Response and audit: The agent grounds its explanation against Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, then returns the finding and proposed remediation to Teams for human confirmation. AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, writes the full trace of prompts, tool calls, token counts, and latencies to Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS CloudTrail records the corresponding API activity.
Onboarding a new operational domain adds a gateway and its MCP tool definitions at step 5. Steps 1–4, and steps 7 and 8, are unchanged. The stable core is what keeps the marginal cost of each new domain low.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities in production
The following table maps each AgentCore capability to the job it does in AiDaH.
| Capability | Role in AiDaH | 
| Runtime | Hosts AiDaH and its sub-agents as managed containers that scale automatically, with no servers to provision | 
| Memory | Maintains conversational context such as subscriber number, order IDs, and prior findings across turns | 
| Identity | Issues short-lived access tokens so only authorized users can invoke agents | 
| Gateway | Connects agents to U Mobile backends through a unified, secure MCP interface | 
| Observability | Streams every prompt, tool call, token count, and latency measurement to Amazon CloudWatch | 
Securing the foundation
Deploying an agentic AI platform that reaches subscriber data, billing systems and network infrastructure demands more than application-level security. It requires a secure cloud foundation. U Mobile took a two-pronged approach: validating and enhancing the underlying AWS Landing Zone, and building on the security capabilities in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
Landing Zone security – Before scaling AiDaH to production, U Mobile engaged AWS to run a Well-Architected Security Review of the Landing Zone hosting the platform. The review validated the environment against AWS security best practices. Infrastructure protection came first, through AWS Control Tower guardrails and AWS Organizations service control policies. The review then examined centralized identity federation and network security controls for ingress and egress. Consolidated security findings in AWS Security Hub and encryption standards across every architecture tier completed the assessment. The outcome was twofold: confidence that every AiDaH component operates on an independently validated foundation, and a prioritized roadmap for continuous improvement.
Application-layer security – Every agent action traces to a specific authenticated user. Staff federate through Microsoft Entra ID, and AgentCore Identity issues the short-lived token that authorizes agent invocation. Amazon Cognito brokers OAuth authorization at the gateway. An agent can therefore reach only the systems its invoking user is entitled to see. A six-tier role-based access control model enforces permissions per agent, per tool, and per data source. Sensitive subscriber data is masked at the gateway before it reaches the model, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforcing content policies.
Every prompt, tool invocation and response is streamed to Amazon CloudWatch Logs through AgentCore Observability, and AWS CloudTrail records the underlying API activity. That audit trail matters: AiDaH is now written into U Mobile’s L2 support standard operating procedures and is subject to operational audit. All compute runs in private VPC subnets, on-premises connectivity is exclusively over encrypted VPN, and AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) manages encryption keys for data at rest and in transit.
Over 150 documented operational scenarios
The scenarios AiDaH covers currently span six domains. The following table summarizes the coverage in each.
| Domain | Coverage | 
| Customer management | Account details, billing history, payment status, active plans and contracts, SIM information, service status | 
| Order operations and logistics | Order and delivery status, pending orders, resource allocation, tracing workflows, delivery tracking, shipment history | 
| Customer problem management | Root-cause diagnosis for failed add-on purchases, plan changes and top-up failures. Number portability port-in and port-out checks. Service disruption diagnosis across SMS, calls and data | 
| IT infrastructure operations | Server and device status monitoring, IP and hostname lookups, network device inventory | 
| Business intelligence and analytics | Subscriber trend analysis, device take-up trends, revenue trending, anomaly detection, individual subscriber analytics. The analytics agent converts plain-language questions into SQL queries, so no technical skills are required | 
| Knowledge retrieval | Enterprise-wide retrieval with context-aware, grounded responses and citations back to source evidence | 
Measuring progress: An AI competency model
To track progress and establish a shared vocabulary across the organization, the team adopted an eight-level AI competency model, from basic digital access to autonomous self-healing operations. It draws on industry thinking, including the TM Forum Autonomous Networks maturity levels, adapted to U Mobile’s operational context. The following table lists the eight levels.
| Level | Name | Description | 
| 1 | Digital access | Self-service portals, online tools and dashboards | 
| 2 | Scripted automation | Rules-based workflow triggers and auto-routing | 
| 3 | Basic AI assistance | Simple chatbots, FAQ look-ups, intent classification | 
| 4 | Contextual intelligence | Context-aware suggestions, basic natural language understanding with memory | 
| 5 | Proactive AI | Predictive alerts, anomaly detection, recommendation engines | 
| 6 | Autonomous task execution | AI completes defined tasks end to end with guardrails | 
| 7 | Collaborative multi-agent | Specialist agents collaborate, use tools, retrieve governed knowledge | 
| 8 | Self-healing and adaptive | Autonomous systems that detect, diagnose, remediate, and learn continuously | 
AiDaH reached Level 7 within nine months of the first pilot: specialist agents collaborate, use tools, retrieve governed knowledge, and support operational decision-making across domains. Level 8, where problems are detected, diagnosed, and resolved without human involvement, is the current target.
Driving adoption: From tool to teammate
Deploying AiDaH was one challenge. Getting people to trust and use it was another.
ISD recognized early that adoption isn’t a technology problem but a behavior change challenge. Staff were accustomed to established workflows, trusted tools, and familiar escalation paths. Introducing AiDaH meant asking them to change deeply embedded habits. It also meant trusting an AI to retrieve information, diagnose problems, and propose next steps on their behalf.
The team leaned on directed prompting. Rather than expecting open-ended exploration, ISD provided structured prompt templates for common scenarios. Those templates turned “ask AiDaH anything” into “here is exactly how to ask for a billing check or a port-in status.” That reduced hesitation and produced immediate, tangible results. When responses proved fast, accurate, and actionable, word spread. An internal survey rated the platform 4.6 out of 5 for ease of use, and daily use is now routine among frontline teams.
The clearest signal came when AiDaH was formally incorporated into U Mobile’s L2 support standard operating procedures. Moving from optional tool to auditable SOP is what marked the shift from experimentation to operations.
ISD’s approach was never about buying a finished solution. It was about owning the journey: building internal AI capability, encouraging responsible experimentation, and embedding practical AI fluency into the daily operating rhythm. Beyond AiDaH itself, ISD maintains a dedicated internal AI channel where teams share use cases, techniques, and early experiments. The goal isn’t to concentrate AI expertise in one team but to distribute it, so every division can use AI confidently within governed guardrails. Progress was not linear. The path involved setbacks and recalibrations, and each one made the platform and the team stronger.
Results
According to U Mobile’s internal measurements, monthly trouble ticket volumes declined across three major categories between January and September 2026:
- Provisioning and network tickets fell 84.5 percent.
- General inquiries dropped 81.6 percent.
- Billing and charging reduced by 48.7 percent.
How the team built it: Spec-driven development with Kiro
U Mobile accelerated AiDaH’s development using Kiro, the AWS agentic IDE built around spec-driven development. In Kiro, a new capability begins as a spec rather than a prompt: requirements, design, and task breakdown are written down and reviewed first, and code generation works against that agreed artifact. For AiDaH, this mattered most at the agent and tool boundary. Each new operational domain means a new gateway, a set of MCP tool definitions, and the role-based access control entries that decide who might call them. Writing those down first made each new domain a repeatable unit of work rather than a fresh design exercise.
The supporting toolchain is conventional. The team used Kiro IDE for local development, with agent hooks and MCP integrations, alongside Kiro CLI for pipeline automation. Source control runs on GitLab, with AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild driving continuous integration, container images published to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), and SonarQube providing continuous code quality scanning. Specifications drove the code generation. The discipline let a small team grow from a two-use-case proof of concept to over 150 documented use cases on a 12-week sprint cadence.
Key architectural decisions
Several choices shaped how AiDaH scaled from proof of concept to production platform. Four stand out, each one reducing the cost of adding the next operational domain or keeping the platform governable as it grew.
AgentCore as managed infrastructure – Rather than building a custom agent framework, the team used the built-in scaling, identity, memory, and observability capabilities in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AWS manages the underlying provisioning, scaling, and patching, which removed an entire layer of infrastructure engineering.
MCP for universal tool connectivity – Standardizing on the Model Context Protocol means AiDaH can onboard new backend systems without rebuilding agent logic. Each new operational domain needs a new gateway, not a new integration architecture.
A2A for specialist collaboration – The Agent2Agent protocol lets domain specialists delegate subtasks to each other. A query spanning customer records, interface logs and billing data routes naturally across the relevant agents.
Secure foundation first – Running the Well-Architected Security Review on the Landing Zone before scaling to production means security controls are inherited by every new agent and gateway, rather than bolted on afterwards.
What’s next
U Mobile’s roadmap focuses on expanding both breadth and depth: onboarding additional operational domains and backend integrations, while evolving the platform’s capabilities from single-system queries toward multi-system correlated diagnosis. The longer-term goal, Level 8 on the competency model, is to move from informing support agents to autonomously resolving issues.
Security governance matures in parallel. The team is aligning practices with NIST SP 800-53, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the CSA AI Trust Framework, and MITRE ATLAS. Compliance with Malaysia’s Personal Data Protection Act and Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission regulations continues alongside it.
Conclusion
AiDaH shows what changes when AI stops assisting and starts acting. In under a year, U Mobile went from a two-agent proof of concept to eight specialist agents serving over 150 documented operational scenarios. According to U Mobile’s internal measurements, trouble tickets fell by up to 84.5 percent in key categories, and U Mobile has now written the platform into its formal L2 support procedures.
We walked through the six layers, followed a request from Teams to an on-premises system and back, and described the Well-Architected Security Review that preceded the production scale up. The technical foundation mattered, but so did the less glamorous work. That meant validating the Landing Zone before scaling, writing structured prompts so staff knew how to start, and treating adoption as a behavior change problem rather than a deployment milestone. Teams facing similar system fragmentation might find the same pattern useful. Start with a managed agent runtime, add a standard tool protocol at the integration boundary, and run a security review before the scale up rather than after it.
The direction remains clear: expand securely, automate responsibly, and move steadily toward autonomous, self-healing operations, one deliberate and governed step at a time.
To learn more, visit Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. To explore spec-driven development, see Kiro.

articles.title: See the agents, set the terms: new visibility and control for personal agents
articles.text:
See the agents, set the terms: new visibility and control for personal agents
Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site.
Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business.
See how agents access your site
Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time.
In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use.
For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. Every login and sign-up event now shows whether a personal agent made the request, and which one. Fraud teams can filter accounts by AI assistant events or number of AI assistants.
Additionally, each user's account overview shows the agents acting for that account. A fraud analyst investigating an unusual login can tell whether it came from an agent the customer has relied on for weeks, or from an agent that appeared for the first time today and needs a closer look. If it looks like an attacker is using an agent on an account, fraud analysts can mitigate that account directly, with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID, without blocking the agent for everyone else who relies on it.
Together, these views give you a clearer basis for deciding which personal agents to welcome, limit, or block.
Set access policies that reflect your preferences
We introduced AI bot policies this summer so site owners could make separate access control choices for AI bots used for Search, Training, and Agent behaviors. Now we’re expanding the existing Agents policy to include granular control options for supported personal agents. To reflect this broader scope, we’re renaming the setting AI Crawler and Agent access policies.
In Security Settings, you can set an overall Agents policy, then choose a different policy for each supported personal agent: Allow (do not block), Block on pages with ads, or Block. For example, you can set the overall Agents policy to Block on pages with ads, then choose Allow (do not block) for a supported personal agent you want to welcome. Your existing Search and Training policies stay as they are.
You can also make these choices when you add a new zone to Cloudflare. During onboarding, we ask whether you monetize pages with ads and then tailor the recommended policies to your answer. You can always revisit your access controls later in Security Settings.
The right policy depends on your site. One publisher may allow a supported personal agent throughout its site so readers can find its articles, while another may block that same agent on pages where ads support the content. Both publishers are choosing the access control that works for their business.
Agent identity is only part of the story
The analytics and policies we’re launching today give site owners visibility into personal agent activity and control over their access. Our next goal is to help site owners preserve the context of their relationships with users when personal agents act as intermediaries. A site may recognize the agent making a request but lack information it would otherwise have about the user: whether they are an existing customer, what they authorized the agent to do, whether they have a subscription, or which protections should apply.
Reaching that goal will require privacy-aware ways to (1) carry user context through an agent, (2) help sites assess reputation, and (3) establish clear accountability when something goes wrong. We’ll be sharing more as we work with agent operators and others across the ecosystem, so site owners can choose whether to grant agents greater access while continuing to build relationships with their users.
Make the choice for your site
That person asking a personal agent to compare products, find support, or complete a purchase is still a customer trying to reach your business. Review how personal agents are accessing your site, then visit Security Settings → AI Crawler and Agent access policies to set the terms that work for your site.

articles.title: Escolas que bloquearem IA poderão perder acesso à busca do Google
articles.text:
Alunos que utilizam as ferramentas educacionais do Google poderão perder acesso ao mecanismo de busca se suas escolas não aceitarem recursos de inteligência artificial (IA) integrados às pesquisas. Anunciada na terça-feira (3), a nova política provocou críticas de educadores, políticos e especialistas.
As instituições poderão controlar os serviços individualmente, mas terão de aceitar algum recurso de IA na busca para continuar oferecendo o Google Search. A implementação está prevista para o início de 2027.
Escolas terão controle sobre ferramentas, mas com uma condição
A decisão ocorre após meses de resistência ao Gemini nas salas de aula. Até agosto, o Google só permitia habilitar o chatbot para estudantes com 18 anos ou mais. Naquele mês, anunciou sua disponibilização para alunos mais novos em redes que autorizassem ferramentas de IA.
Agora, os administradores poderão escolher quais serviços estarão disponíveis, incluindo Gemini, Gemini Notebook e Google Search. Todos ficarão desativados por padrão até que as instituições autorizem seu uso.
As escolas poderão manter o Gemini desativado, mas precisarão aceitar algum recurso de IA incorporado às pesquisas para liberar o buscador. Chris Phillips, vice-presidente e gerente-geral de educação do Google, explicou ao The New York Times que os serviços estão profundamente conectados. Sem essa autorização, os estudantes receberão uma mensagem de indisponibilidade.
A empresa também prepara o Guided Learning, recurso que deverá orientar os estudantes na resolução de problemas, em vez de apresentar respostas prontas. Em matemática, por exemplo, poderá incentivar o aluno a revisar regras de divisão de expoentes antes de chegar ao resultado.
Decisão provoca críticas de políticos e educadores
Lina Khan, ex-presidente da Comissão Federal de Comércio dos Estados Unidos (FTC), acusou o Google de usar sua posição dominante nas buscas para pressionar as escolas.
“O Google está usando seu monopólio nas buscas para coagir as escolas a adotarem inteligência artificial. Isso evidencia o perigo de permitir que uma empresa monopolista, sem regulamentação, controle um serviço essencial”, escreveu.
O senador Bernie Sanders classificou a iniciativa como extorsão. Richard Blumenthal afirmou que a empresa estaria mais preocupada em impor o Gemini às escolas do que em ajudar os estudantes. O prefeito de Nova York, Zohran Mamdani, também questionou o poder de uma companhia sobre as políticas de ensino.
As redes públicas de Nova York e Los Angeles estabeleceram proibições temporárias ao uso de IA generativa nas escolas de ensino fundamental, enquanto avaliam a segurança dessas tecnologias e desenvolvem regras. Educadores temem que os resumos gerados por IA desestimulem a pesquisa independente e facilitem a cola e o acesso a respostas prontas, em vez de estimular o pensamento crítico.
Especialistas apontam riscos e Brasil discute limites da IA na educação
Josh Golin, diretor-executivo da Fairplay, organização de defesa dos direitos das crianças, disse que a pressão pode produzir o efeito contrário ao pretendido. Para ele, a presença dos produtos do Google nas escolas está ligada à construção de fidelidade à marca desde a infância. Golin defendeu que as instituições desativem as ferramentas de IA da empresa, considerem abandonar outros produtos do Google e adotem buscadores com maior proteção à privacidade.
No Brasil, o Conselho Nacional de Educação (CNE) também discute limites para o uso dessas tecnologias. O órgão apresentou propostas para regulamentar a IA no ensino e apontou riscos relacionados à perda de habilidades cognitivas, a vieses algorítmicos e ao aprofundamento das desigualdades educacionais.
A mudança levanta questões sobre a autonomia das instituições para definir suas regras e a dependência de plataformas controladas por grandes empresas.
Em resposta às críticas, o Google afirmou na rede social X que ouviu os educadores. Disse que deixar os recursos de IA desativados por padrão atende aos pedidos por maior controle e que continuará trabalhando com as escolas para oferecer mais opções e aprimorar a busca para a aprendizagem.
Segundo a empresa, 150 milhões de estudantes e professores em todo o mundo utilizam o Google Classroom. Muitos alunos também dependem de Chromebooks fornecidos pelas próprias instituições.
Entramos em contato com o Google para entender se a regra também valerá para as escolas brasileiras e quando isso pode ocorrer. Assim que a empresa se posicionar, a matéria será atualizada.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).
